|url-status=live }}</ref>\n\nOrr used to spend winters in Florida and summer in Cape Cod.<ref name=\":1\" /> However, he and his wife bought a house in the Balsam Mountain Preserve located in [[North Carolina]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dojc |first=Mike |title=Bobby Orr On Balsam Life, The Goal And That Second Scoop Of Ice Cream |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/mikedojc/2025/07/07/bobby-orr-on-balsam-life-the-goal-and-that-second-scoop-of-ice-cream/ |access-date=December 24, 2025 |website=Forbes |language=en}}</ref>\n\n==Accomplishments and legacy ==\n[[File:Bobby Orr Community Centre.jpg|thumb|The Bobby Orr Community Center in [[Parry Sound, Ontario]]]]\nOrr is one of the most successful and decorated athletes in history of the NHL. Hockey journalists Mike Moore wrote on Orr in 2011 stating \"When Bobby Orr was at his peak, he was the best hockey player in the world. No other human was close. It was unbelievable how much better he was than anyone else in the pack behind. The NHL wasn’t good enough for Orr. Too bad there was no higher league.\"<ref>{{Cite news |last=Archives |first=THW |date=November 8, 2025 |title=Bobby Orr's Landmark Season - The Hockey Writers Bruins History Latest News, Analysis & More |url=http://thehockeywriters.com/bobby-orrs-landmark-season/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251124110007/http://thehockeywriters.com/bobby-orrs-landmark-season/ |archive-date=November 24, 2025 |access-date=January 4, 2026 |work=The Hockey Writers |language=en-US}}</ref>\n\nHis accomplishments include two [[Stanley Cup]] Championships with the Boston Bruins. He won the Hart Memorial Trophy as the league's [[Most valuable player|Most Valuable Player]] three straight years from 1970 to 1972.<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 12, 2025 |title=NHL Hart Memorial Trophy Winners {{!}} NHL.com |url=https://www.nhl.com/news/nhl-hart-memorial-trophy-winners-complete-list-287743272 |access-date=January 4, 2026 |website=www.nhl.com |language=en}}</ref> Orr is the only defenceman in league history to win the [[Art Ross Trophy]] as league leader in scoring capturing the trophy in both 1970 and 1975.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Art Ross Trophy {{!}} NHL Records |url=https://records.nhl.com/awards/trophies/art-ross-trophy |access-date=January 4, 2026 |website=records.nhl.com}}</ref> He is also the only player ever to win the [[James Norris Memorial Trophy|Norris Trophy]], Art Ross Trophy, Hart Trophy, and [[Conn Smythe Trophy]] in one season in [[1969–70 NHL season|1970]].{{Sfn |Dryden |2000 |p=72}} He then became the first two-time winner of the Conn Smythe in 1972.<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 18, 2025 |title=NHL Conn Smythe Trophy Winners {{!}} NHL.com |url=https://www.nhl.com/news/nhl-conn-smythe-trophy-winners-complete-list-287709808 |access-date=January 4, 2026 |website=www.nhl.com |language=en}}</ref> During his rookie year in [[1966–67 NHL season|1967]] he won the [[Calder Memorial Trophy]] as the league's top rookie.<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 10, 2025 |title=NHL Calder Memorial Trophy Winners {{!}} NHL.com |url=https://www.nhl.com/news/nhl-calder-memorial-trophy-winners-complete-list-287749198 |access-date=January 4, 2026 |website=www.nhl.com |language=en}}</ref> He is the only defenceman to win the [[Ted Lindsay Award|Lester B. Pearson Award]], and was selected to the [[NHL first All-Star team]] eight straight years from 1968 to 1975.\n\nOrr is often considered the greatest defenceman in NHL history, and won the [[James Norris Memorial Trophy|Norris Trophy]] as the league's best defenceman a record eight straight years from 1968 to 1975.<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 11, 2025 |title=NHL James Norris Memorial Trophy Winners {{!}} NHL.com |url=https://www.nhl.com/news/nhl-james-norris-memorial-trophy-winners-complete-list-287778852 |access-date=January 4, 2026 |website=www.nhl.com |language=en}}</ref> In a 2020 poll held by the NHL Orr was unanimously selected as the greatest defenceman of all time, senior writer for NHL.com Dan Rosen wrote \"Orr revolutionized the position with his skating, speed, puck-handling and offensive ability. The Bruins defenseman turned defense into offense with a rapid acceleration better than arguably anyone in NHL history.\"<ref>{{Cite web |date=April 23, 2020 |title=Super 16: Orr, Karlsson among best defensemen of expansion era {{!}} NHL.com |url=https://www.nhl.com/news/nhl-best-defensemen-of-expansion-era-316688968 |access-date=January 4, 2026 |website=www.nhl.com |language=en}}</ref> He was voted the second greatest hockey player of all time by an expert committee in 1997 by ''[[The Hockey News]]'', he was only behind [[Wayne Gretzky]] and ahead of [[Gordie Howe]] as well as being named the top defenceman of all time. Gretzky said he would have voted for Orr or his hero, Gordie Howe.<ref name=\":7\" /> In a separate poll held by ''The Hockey News'' in 2010 he was named the top defenceman of all time.<ref name=\":8\" /> In 2017, Orr was named by the NHL as one of the \"[[100 Greatest NHL Players]]\" in history.<ref name=\":0\" /> In 2023, ''[[The Athletic]]'' put Orr at #3 on their list of the 100 greatest hockey players of all time.<ref name=\":11\">{{Cite news |last=Staff |first=The Athletic NHL |date=December 23, 2025 |title=NHL99: A project ranking the greatest players in modern NHL history |url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/3550299/2023/02/08/nhl99-ranking-the-greatest-players-in-modern-nhl-history/ |access-date=January 4, 2026 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>\n\nFor his achievements Orr was named \"Sportsman of the Year\" by ''[[Sports Illustrated]]'' in 1970.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sports Illustrated every Sports person of the year |url=https://www.si.com/sports-illustrated/sports-illustrated-sportsperson-year-covers}}</ref> That same year he also received the [[Lou Marsh Trophy]] as Canada's top athlete of the year.<ref>{{Cite web |date=May 18, 2022 |title=Lou Marsh Memorial Trophy Winner - Canada's Top Athletes |url=https://www.loumarsh.ca/ |access-date=January 4, 2026 |language=en-CA}}</ref> He was voted the greatest athlete in Boston history in the ''[[Boston Globe]]'' newspaper's poll of New Englanders in 1975, beating out baseball and basketball stars such as [[Ted Williams]], [[Bill Russell (basketball)|Bill Russell]], [[Carl Yastrzemski]], and [[Bob Cousy]].<ref name=\":12\" /> Additionally he was named Bostons greatest athlete by [[Bleacher Report]] and in a [[NESN]] poll in 2010.<ref name=\":13\" /><ref name=\":14\" /> In 2022, as part of their SN Rushmore project, ''[[The Sporting News]]'' named Orr on their \"Boston Mount Rushmore of Sports\", along [[Boston Celtics]] basketball player [[Bill Russell]], [[Boston Red Sox]] baseball player [[Ted Williams]], and [[New England Patriots]] football player [[Tom Brady]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=July 25, 2022 |title=Boston's Mount Rushmore of Sports: Tom Brady, Bill Russell, Ted Williams, Bobby Orr voted best of the best {{!}} Sporting News |url=https://www.sportingnews.com/us/nfl/news/bostons-mount-rushmore-sports-tom-brady-bill-russell-ted-williams-bobby-orr/eghhfjzkq6zf1oyj2tcdqahz |access-date=March 21, 2026 |website=www.sportingnews.com |language=en-us}}</ref> Orr was ranked 31st in [[SportsCentury|SportsCentury: 50 Greatest Athletes of the 20th Century]].<ref name=\":15\" />\n\nThroughout his career Orr set many scoring milestones for defenceman. Before he entered the league in 1966, no defenceman had scored 20 goals in more than two decades. Orr was able to accomplish this feat in seven straight seasons.<ref name=\":16\">{{Cite web |title=ESPN Classic - Orr brought more offense to defense |url=https://www.espn.com/classic/biography/s/orr_bobby.html |access-date=January 4, 2026 |website=www.espn.com}}</ref> Being the first one to score 30 goals in a season ([[1969–70 NHL season|1969-70]]) and 40 goals ([[1974–75 NHL season|1974–75]]) in a season. During the [[1970–71 NHL season|1970-71]] season, Orr became the first player to record 100 assists in a season,{{Sfn |Dryden |2000 |p=73}} he led the NHL in assists 5 times throughout his career.<ref name=\":17\">{{Cite web |date=January 1, 2017 |title=Bobby Orr: 100 Greatest NHL Players {{!}} NHL.com |url=https://www.nhl.com/news/bobby-orr-100-greatest-nhl-hockey-players-285636896 |access-date=January 4, 2026 |website=www.nhl.com |language=en}}</ref> Orr was the first NHL player to have consecutive 100+ point seasons, in 1969–70 and 1970–71,<ref name=\":9\" /> and was the first defenceman to score 900 career points.<ref name=\":10\" /> The town of [[Dedham, Massachusetts]], held a [[History of Dedham, Massachusetts, 1900–1999#Bobby Orr Day|Bobby Orr Day]] on March 23, 1970.<ref>{{cite news | url = https://bostonglobe.newspapers.com/image/435202953/?match=1&clipping_id=194200146 | title = Orr addresses Dedham students | newspaper = The Boston Evening Globe | page = 28 | date = March 23, 1970 | accessdate = March 25, 2026 }}</ref>\n\nHe is often credited for altering the role of a defenceman being the first to have a sensational scoring ability.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Haggerty |first=Joe |date=October 19, 2016 |title=B's still marvel at 'legend of the game' Bobby Orr 50 years later |url=https://www.nbcsportsboston.com/nhl/boston-bruins/bs-still-marvel-at-legend-of-the-game-bobby-orr-50-years-later/349942/ |access-date=January 4, 2026 |website=NBC Sports Boston |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Campbell |first=Ken |date=October 19, 2016 |title=Bobby Orr changed the hockey world 50 years ago today |url=https://thehockeynews.com/news/news/bobby-orr-changed-the-hockey-world-50-years-ago-today |access-date=January 4, 2026 |website=The Hockey News |language=en}}</ref> His former coach [[Don Cherry]] stated \"He changed how defense should be played. He broke the mold because before that defensemen were big, slow guys. They just cleared the guys out and got the puck up. Bobby changed the whole face of the game and how it's played.\"<ref name=\":17\" /> ''Sports Illustrated's'' writer E.M. Swift wrote \"He changed the sport by redefining the parameters of his position, \"A defenseman, as interpreted by Orr, became both a defender and an aggressor, both a protector and a producer. Orr was more than an opportunist: He created opportunities.\"<ref name=\":16\" />\n\nFrank Deford also of ''Sports Illustrated'' added \"As far as his place in history, \"It's not necessary to get into who may be better, Orr, the defenseman, or Wayne Gretzky, the center, except to note that Orr did something that Gretzky had no opportunity to do, and that was change the very nature of the game.\"<ref name=\":16\" />\n\n=== Honors ===\n[[File:Olympic flag carried into BC Place at 2010 Winter Olympics opening ceremony (cropped).jpg|left|thumb|Orr (centre, back), one of eight Canadians to carry the Olympic flag during the 2010 Vancouver Olympics opening ceremonies]]\nIn 1970, Orr received the Golden Plate Award of the [[Academy of Achievement|American Academy of Achievement]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Golden Plate Awardees of the American Academy of Achievement|website=www.achievement.org|publisher=[[American Academy of Achievement]]|url=https://achievement.org/our-history/golden-plate-awards/#sports|access-date=August 28, 2020|archive-date=December 15, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161215023909/https://achievement.org/our-history/golden-plate-awards/#sports|url-status=live}}</ref> In 1979, Orr was invested as an officer of the [[Order of Canada]].<ref>{{cite news |work=Ottawa Citizen |title=Order of Canada Presented to 62 |date=October 25, 1979 |page=8 |author=Canadian Press}}</ref> The official citation on why he received the honor reads, “For his unique achievements as a professional hockey player of international renown and for his interest in young athletes, to whom he devotes much of his spare time.”<ref>{{Cite web|title=Mr. Robert G. Orr|url=https://www.gg.ca/en/honours/recipients/146-13658|website=The Governor General of Canada|access-date=November 29, 2025|language=en}}</ref> Two buildings in his hometown of Parry Sound are named after Orr. The first is the Bobby Orr Hall of Fame, where his Order of Canada medal is on display along with other exhibits, on Orr's childhood, charity work while also including multiple pieces of his memorabilia from his career.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Exhibits < Bobby Orr Hall of Fame|url=https://bobbyorrhalloffame.com/exhibits/|website=Bobby Orr Hall of Fame|access-date=November 29, 2025|language=en-CA}}</ref> The second is the Bobby Orr Community Centre, a multi-purpose entertainment facility.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://bobbyorrhalloffame.com/ |title=Bobby Orr Hall of Fame website |access-date=July 13, 2009 |archive-date=November 2, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111102101809/http://www.bobbyorrhalloffame.com/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Orr was inducted into [[Canada's Sports Hall of Fame]] as an individual in 1982, and as a member of Canada's Summit Series in 2005.<ref name=\":3\">{{Cite web |title=Hall of Famers {{!}} Canada's Sports Hall of Fame {{!}} Home: Mobile |url=https://halloffamers.sportshall.ca/mobile.html#bobby_orr |access-date=August 4, 2025 |website=halloffamers.sportshall.ca}}</ref> In 1982, Orr received an honorary Doctor of Humane Letters degree from [[Siena University (New York)|Siena University]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Honorary Degree Recipients |url=https://www.siena.edu/alumni-and-giving/alumni-engagement/awards-recognitions/honorary-degree-recipients/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250809234530/https://www.siena.edu/alumni-and-giving/alumni-engagement/awards-recognitions/honorary-degree-recipients/ |archive-date=August 9, 2025 |access-date=December 26, 2025 |website=Siena College}}</ref> In 1984, Orr was the commencement speaker for [[Northeastern University]] and received an honorary Doctor of Humanities degree.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Honorary degree recipient Bobby Orr with President Ryder |url=https://repository.library.northeastern.edu/files/neu:182290 |access-date=December 26, 2025 |website=Northeastern University Library}}</ref> In 1995, Orr was inducted into the [[Ontario Sports Hall of Fame]].<ref name=\":4\">{{cite web |title=Bobby Orr |url=http://oshof.ca/index.php/honoured-members/item/103-bobby-orr |website=oshof.ca |publisher=[[Ontario Sports Hall of Fame]] |access-date=September 23, 2014 |archive-date=December 29, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141229012136/http://www.oshof.ca/index.php/honoured-members/item/103-bobby-orr |url-status=dead }}</ref> He has also been honoured with a star on [[Canada's Walk of Fame]] in Toronto.<ref name=\"oct92008\" /> In 2004, an elementary school in South Oshawa named after Orr opened.<ref>{{cite web|title=Bobby Orr Public School|url=http://www.ddsb.ca/Schools/OurSchools/Pages/Bobby-Orr-P-S.aspx|access-date=April 5, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150416231416/http://www.ddsb.ca/Schools/OurSchools/Pages/Bobby-Orr-P-S.aspx|archive-date=April 16, 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref>\n\nOn November 27, 2008, the Oshawa Generals retired Orr's number 2 jersey; the Generals had not issued the number since Orr transferred to the NHL in 1966. Orr thanked all who helped him in the four years he played in Oshawa: \"I did a lot of growing up in Oshawa from ages 14 to 18 and I'll be forever grateful for those people who helped me in that time of my life.\"<ref>{{cite news |work=The Globe and Mail |date=November 28, 2008 |title=Generals Retire Orr's no. 2 |page=S02}}</ref> In 2004, Orr was ranked the 19th [[The Greatest Canadian|greatest Canadian]] in a poll by CBC which received more than 1.2 million votes.<ref>{{cite book|last=Wall|first=Karen L.|title=Game Plan: A Social History of Sports in Alberta|publisher=University of Alberta Press|year=2012|isbn=978-0888645944|page=276 pp}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Sornberger|first=Joe|title=Dreams and Due Diligence: Till & McCulloch's Stem Cell Discovery and Legacy|publisher=University of Toronto Press|year=2011|isbn=978-1442644854|page=? pp}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=MacGregor|first=Roy|title=Canadians: A Portrait Of A Country And Its People|publisher=Penguin Canada|year=2008|isbn=978-0143053088|page=? pp}}</ref>\n\nOrr was one of eight Olympic flag bearers at the [[2010 Winter Olympics opening ceremony]].<ref>{{cite news|work=[[Toronto Star]]|date=February 14, 2010|title=Marsh winners carry the flame|page=S6}}</ref> The [[Bobby Orr Trophy]] named in Orr's honor, is awarded annually to the champion of the Eastern conference playoffs in the [[Ontario Hockey League]]. The defunct [[Central Hockey League (1963–84)|CHL]] also awarded their own annual [[Bobby Orr Trophy (CHL)|Bobby Orr trophy]] that was given to the league's best defenceman.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bobby Orr Trophy award winners at hockeydb.com |url=https://www.hockeydb.com/ihdb/awards/awarddetail.php?award_id=25 |access-date=August 28, 2025 |website=www.hockeydb.com}}</ref> In 2012, he received the [[Queen Elizabeth II Diamond Jubilee Medal]].<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/entertainment/diamond-jubilee-gala-toasts-exceptional-canadians-1.1226414| title=Diamond Jubilee Gala toasts exceptional Canadians| date=June 18, 2012| publisher=CBC| access-date=June 19, 2012| archive-date=June 19, 2012| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120619053044/http://www.cbc.ca/news/arts/story/2012/06/18/jubilee-gala-toronto.html| url-status=live}}</ref> In 2014, Orr was one of 5 NHL defencemen to be honored on Canada's official set of Original Six era postage stamps.<ref>{{Cite web |title=New Bobby Orr Canadian Stamp Unveiled |url=http://www.bostonbruinsalumni.com/1/post/2014/10/new-bobby-orr-canadian-stamp-unveiled.html |access-date=August 28, 2025 |website=BOSTON BRUINS ALUMNI |language=en}}</ref> In 2024, Orr returned to [[TD Garden]] to take part in the Bruins Centennial celebrations as he was named to the [[List of Boston Bruins award winners|Boston Bruins All-Centennial Team]].<ref name=\":2\" />\n\n=== Statue ===\n[[File:Harryweberorr.jpeg|thumb|250x250px|Orr's statue outside of the [[TD Garden]]]]\nA bronze statue of Orr stands next to Boston's [[TD Garden]], the Bruins' home arena. It was unveiled on May 10, 2010, the 40th anniversary of the Bruins' first Stanley Cup victory with Orr, and depicts him immediately after scoring the winning goal. The unveiling ceremony was attended by Orr and several of his former teammates. Orr said of the statue at the ceremony, \"This specific moment and time we celebrate with this statue is something we can all now nostalgically remember with fondness, together, each time we enter Boston Garden. To all of you, thank you very much from the bottom of my heart. I'm honoured. Guys, thank you.\"<ref>{{cite web |date=May 11, 2010 |title=Statue of Bruins legend Orr unveiled |url=https://www.espn.com/boston/nhl/news/story?id=5178338 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151107074926/http://sports.espn.go.com/boston/nhl/news/story?id=5178338 |archive-date=November 7, 2015 |access-date=October 26, 2010 |publisher=ESPN}}</ref>\n\n==Career achievements==\nDespite playing only twelve seasons and 657 games (of which only his first nine seasons, totalling 621 games, were full seasons), and only playing 47 games after his 27th birthday, Orr accomplished many records and achievements, a number of which still stand today, and are listed below.\n\nAs of the end of the {{NHL Year|2018}} season:\n* First and only defenceman to score nine hat tricks.\n* Only defenceman to win the [[Ted Lindsay Award|Lester B. Pearson Award]].\n* Only player ever to win the Norris Trophy, Art Ross Trophy, Hart Trophy, and Conn Smythe Trophy in one season ([[1969–70 NHL season|1969–70]]){{Sfn |Dryden |2000 |p=72}}\n* Only defenceman to win the Art Ross Trophy as league leader in scoring ([[1969–70 NHL season|1969–70]], [[1974–75 NHL season|1974–75]])\n* First defenceman to score 30 goals ([[1969–70 NHL season|1969–70]]){{Sfn |Dryden |2000 |p=72}} and 40 goals ([[1974–75 NHL season|1974–75]]) in a season.\n* First player to record 100 assists in a season ([[1970–71 NHL season|1970–71]]){{Sfn |Dryden |2000 |p=73}}\n* Highest single season [[Plus-minus (ice hockey)|plus-minus]] rating, +124 in [[1970–71 NHL season|1970–71]].\n**Second all-time in career plus-minus rating (+597; retired as the overall leader)\n**Never finished a full season less than +30 since +/- became a statistic (beginning with the {{NHL Year|1968}} season)<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/leaders/plus_minus_career.html |publisher=Hockey-reference.com |access-date=December 10, 2010 |title=NHL & WHA Career Leaders and Records for Plus/Minus |archive-date=May 19, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110519110106/http://www.hockey-reference.com/leaders/plus_minus_career.html |url-status=live }}</ref>\n* Fourth in league history in career point-per-game average, all-time, (1.393) (highest among defencemen, minimum 500 career points).{{Sfn|Dinger|2010|p=173}}\n* Sixty-sixth overall in league history in career assists and tied for 109th in career points.{{Sfn|Dinger|2010|pp=180,182}}\n\n===Awards===\n* OHA first All-Star team – 1964, 1965, 1966{{Sfn|Brunt|2006|p=101}}\n* [[J. Ross Robertson Cup]] champion (1966)\n* Awarded the [[Calder Memorial Trophy]] (rookie of the year) in [[1966–67 NHL season|1967]], the youngest ever to win the award, and the youngest ever to win a major NHL award up to that time.<ref>{{cite news |work=Rome News-Tribune |date=June 6, 1980 |title=Gretzky claims two awards |page=6}}</ref>\n* Named to the [[NHL All-Star team|NHL second All-Star team]] in [[1966–67 NHL season|1967]] (his only full season when he did not make the First Team, as a rookie){{Sfn|Dinger|2010|p=227}}\n* Won the [[Elizabeth C. His blond hair, skating speed, end-to-end rushes, and ability to shoot the puck at very high velocity all earned him the nickname \"'''the Golden Jet'''\". His talents were such that an opposing player was often assigned just to shadow him.\n\nDuring his 23-year playing career, from 1957 to 1980, he played in both the [[National Hockey League]] (NHL) and [[World Hockey Association]] (WHA) with the [[Chicago Black Hawks]], [[Winnipeg Jets (1972–1996)|Winnipeg Jets]], and [[Hartford Whalers]]. He won the [[Hart Memorial Trophy]] as the NHL's most valuable player twice and the [[Art Ross Trophy]] as the NHL's leading point scorer three times, while helping the Black Hawks win the [[Stanley Cup]] in 1961. He also led the WHA's Winnipeg Jets to [[Avco Cup]] championships in 1976 and 1978. He led the NHL in goals seven times, the second most of any player in history, and led the WHA in goals one additional time while being the WHA's [[Gordie Howe Trophy|most valuable player]] two times; his 77 goals scored in the [[1974–75 WHA season]] was the [[List of WHA players with 50-goal seasons|most in league history]].\n\nHe was elected to the [[Hockey Hall of Fame]] in 1983, the [[Ontario Sports Hall of Fame]] in 1997, and received the [[Wayne Gretzky International Award]] in 2003.<ref>{{cite web |title=Bobby Hull |url=http://oshof.ca/index.php/honoured-members/item/78-bobby-hull |publisher=Ontario Sports Hall of Fame |access-date=September 24, 2014 |archive-date=June 28, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180628015719/https://oshof.ca/index.php/honoured-members/item/78-bobby-hull |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://beta.theglobeandmail.com/sports/bobby-hull-wins-gretzky-award/article25288290/?ref=https://www.theglobeandmail.com&service=mobile|title=Bobby Hull wins Gretzky award|date=July 31, 2003|newspaper=The Globe and Mail|access-date=March 19, 2018}}</ref> In 2017 Hull was named one of the '[[100 Greatest NHL Players]]' in history.<ref>{{cite web|title=100 Greatest NHL Players|url=https://www.nhl.com/history/nhl-centennial/nhl-100-greatest-players|publisher=National Hockey League|access-date=January 27, 2017|date=January 27, 2017}}</ref>\n\n==Early life==\nHull was born in [[Point Anne, Ontario]], on January 3, 1939.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.upi.com/Top_News/2019/01/03/UPI-Almanac-for-Thursday-Jan-3-2019/1811546209344/|title= UPI Almanac for Thursday, Jan. 3, 2019|work=[[United Press International]]|date=January 3, 2019|access-date=September 3, 2019|archive-date=January 3, 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20190103223323/https://www.upi.com/Top_News/2019/01/03/UPI-Almanac-for-Thursday-Jan-3-2019/1811546209344/|url-status=live|quote=hockey Hall of Fame member Bobby Hull in 1939 (age 81)}}</ref> He was the son of Lena Cook and Robert Edward Hull, a cement company foreman.<ref>{{cite book|last=Rayner|first=William|editor=Nicole Chaplin|title=Canada on the Doorstep: 1939|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=s91HjbxUaGYC&q=%22Robert+Edward+Hull,+a+cement-company+foreman,+and+Lena+Cook+Hull%22&pg=PA36|year=2011|publisher=Dundurn Press|location=Canada|language=en|isbn=978-1-55488-993-8|page=36}}</ref> He played his minor hockey in nearby [[Belleville, Ontario|Belleville]], and then Junior B hockey for the Woodstock Warriors in the fall of 1954. Hull led the Warriors to the 1955 [[Sutherland Cup]] as Ontario champions. Later, he played for the [[Galt Black Hawks]] and the [[St. Catharines Teepees]] in the [[Ontario Hockey Association]], before joining the [[Chicago Black Hawks]] in [[1957–58 NHL season|1957]] at the age of 18.\n\n==Playing career==\n\n===NHL career===\n[[File:Hastings County Archives HC01957A (38140064474).jpg|thumb|upright|Hull with the Black Hawks in 1968]]\nHull had a solid debut year, finishing second in voting for the [[Calder Memorial Trophy]]. Hull originally wore numbers 16 and 7 as a Black Hawk but later switched to his famous number 9, a tribute to his childhood idol [[Gordie Howe]]. By his third season (1959–60), he led the league in goal- and point-scoring (the [[Art Ross Trophy]]), a double feat which he also achieved in 1961–62 and 1965–66. He led Chicago to the [[1961 Stanley Cup Final|Stanley Cup in 1961]]—their third overall and first in 23 years. He finished second in point-scoring three further times.\n\nOn March 12, 1966, Hull became the first NHL player to score more than 50 goals in a season, surpassing [[Maurice Richard]]'s, [[Bernie Geoffrion]]'s, and his own mark of 50 goals. His 51st goal, scored on [[Cesare Maniago]] of the [[New York Rangers]], earned him a seven-minute standing ovation from the [[Chicago Stadium]] faithful.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/classic/s/moment010312hull.html|website=ESPN Classic|date= November 19, 2003|title=Bobby Hull first to top 50-goal mark|first=Larry|last=Schwartz}}</ref> Hull eventually scored 54 goals that season, the highest single-season total of the [[Original Six]] era. That same year, Hull set the record for the most points in a season with 97, one more than the previous record set by [[Dickie Moore (ice hockey)|Dickie Moore]] seven years earlier.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/stathead/tiny/UjUMk|website=Stathead|access-date=June 10, 2026|title=For single seasons, from 1942-43 to 1966-67, playing skater, in the regular season, sorted by descending Goals.}}</ref> His point total was tied the next year by teammate [[Stan Mikita]] in the final season with six teams in NHL history; in the {{nhly|1968}} season, [[Phil Esposito]] broke the points record. Hull led the league in goal-scoring seven times during the 1960s.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nhl.com/news/bobby-hull-100-greatest-nhl-hockey-players-283864624|website=NHL.com|access-date=June 10, 2026|title=Bobby Hull: 100 Greatest NHL Players|first=Bob|last=Verdi}}</ref> In the {{nhly|1967}} season, he joined the 400 goal club on January 7.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1968/01/08/archives/hull-scores-pair-as-hawks-win-42-raises-goal-output-to-401-in.html|website=New York Times|date=January 8, 1968|title=HULL SCORES PAIR AS HAWKS WIN, 4-2; Raises Goal Output to 401 in Triumph Over Bruins|agency=UPI|access-date=June 10, 2026}}</ref>\n\nIn the [[1968–69 NHL season|1968–69]] season, despite Hull breaking his own goals in a season record by four goals (netting 58) and setting a career NHL high of 107 points (second in the league that year), the Hawks missed the playoffs for the first time since his rookie season. By his final [[1971–72 NHL season|NHL season]], he had scored 50 goals or more a remarkable five times. This was only one time less than all other players in NHL history combined up until that point in time.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/stathead/tiny/vQTPu|website=Stathead|title=For single seasons, up to 1971-72, playing skater, in the regular season, requiring Goals >= 50, sorted by descending Goals}}</ref>\n\nIn his first fifteen seasons, he was voted the First-Team All-Star left winger ten times and the Second-Team All-Star left winger twice. His slapshot was once clocked at 118.3&nbsp;mph (190.5&nbsp;km/h) and he could skate 29.7&nbsp;mph (47.8&nbsp;km/h).<ref name='Hawk on the Wing'>{{cite magazine | title=Hawk on the Wing | date=March 1, 1968 | url =https://content.time.com/time/subscriber/article/0,33009,941234,00.html | magazine =[[Time (magazine)|Time]] | access-date = January 25, 2021}}</ref> During his drive to be the first to eclipse the 50 goal mark, Hull's [[wrist shot]] was said to be harder than his [[slapshot]].<ref>{{cite magazine|author=William Leggett |url=https://www.si.com/vault/1965/01/25/606983/go-bobby-goto-beat-the-magic-50 |title=In the boldest attack yet on hockey's seemingly impassable barrier, Bobby Hull has sent his lightning-fast slap and wrist shots into the net 36 times to put him and Chicago on the road to a championship |magazine=[[Sports Illustrated]] |date=January 25, 1965 |access-date=April 17, 2024 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20161114004138/https://www.si.com/vault/1965/01/25/606983/go-bobby-goto-beat-the-magic-50 |archivedate=November 14, 2016}}</ref>\n\n====\"Bobby Hull Rule\"====\nHull and teammate [[Stan Mikita]] were two of the first players to curve the blades of their hockey sticks, with their greatly warped sticks widely referred to as \"banana blades\".<ref name=YahooAugust2010>{{cite news|last=Wyshynski|first=Greg|title=The 10 best player-inspired NHL rules changes|url=https://ca.sports.yahoo.com/blogs/nhl-puck-daddy/10-best-player-inspired-nhl-rules-changes--nhl.html|work=Yahoo! Sports|date=August 19, 2010}}</ref> The curved blade made the puck's trajectory unpredictable and was quickly adopted across the sport. Hull is the player typically linked most to a rule that curbed this practice because of the potential danger to goalies, few of whom wore masks in that era.<ref name=YahooAugust2010/> The rule originally limited the blade curvature to between {{cvt|0.5|in|mm}} and {{cvt|0.75|in|mm}}; in 1970, it was set at {{cvt|0.5|in|mm}}.<ref name=YahooAugust2010/> NHL Rule 10.1 currently limits the curvature to {{cvt|0.75|in|mm}}.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nhl.com/nhl/en/v3/ext/rules/2018-2019-NHL-rulebook.pdf|title=Official rules 2018–2019|publisher=National Hockey League}}</ref>\n\n===WHA career===\n{{see also|1974–75 WHA season#77 goals in 78 games}}\n[[File:BobbyHullJets.png|thumb|Hull with the Jets in 1975.]]\nLong unhappy with his poor salary despite being one of hockey's preeminent superstars, Hull responded to overtures from the upstart [[World Hockey Association]]'s [[Winnipeg Jets (1972–1996)|Winnipeg Jets]] in [[1972–73 WHA season|1972]] by jesting that he would jump to them for a million dollars, a sum then considered absurd. Gathering the other league owners together to contribute to the unprecedented amount on the grounds that inking such a major star gave instant credibility to the new rival league that was competing directly against the entrenched NHL, Jets owner [[Ben Hatskin]] agreed to the sum, and signed Hull as a [[player-coach]] for a contract worth $1.75&nbsp;million over 10 years plus a $1&nbsp;million signing bonus, on June 27, 1972.<ref name=\"wapo_obit\">{{cite news |last1=Sumner |first1=Ben |title=Bobby Hull, hockey's 'Golden Jet' of the ice, dies at 84 |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/obituaries/2023/01/30/bobby-hull-hockey-dead/ |access-date=November 16, 2024 |work=Washington Post |date=January 30, 2023}}</ref> Although his debut with Winnipeg was held up in litigation by the NHL, Hull instantly became the WHA's greatest star, winning the [[Gordie Howe Trophy]] as league MVP in that very first season despite being bugged by bone chips in his elbow that still saw him score 51 goals.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://newspaperarchive.com/other-clipping-may-15-1973-5731757/?utm_source=newspaperarchive&utm_medium=copy_link&utm_campaign=share_link&utm_content=newspaper_clipping/|via=Newspaper Archive|title=Operating Table For Dunc, Danny|first= Reyn |last=Davis|date=May 15, 1973|work=Winnipeg Free Press}}</ref> He then won the MVP award again in the 1974–75 season. With Swedish linemates [[Anders Hedberg]] and [[Ulf Nilsson (ice hockey)|Ulf Nilsson]] he formed one of the most formidable forward lines of the 1970s (known as \"The Hot Line\"), leading the Jets to two [[Avco World Trophy|AVCO Cup]]s during his time with the club. His best performance was during the [[1974–75 WHA season|1974–75 season]], when he [[List of WHA players with 50-goal seasons|scored 77 goals]] to set a new professional mark, while adding 65 assists for a total of 142 points, five behind the league leader, one of two times he finished second in the point-scoring race in the WHA; he set a then record for goals in a professional season at home in Winnipeg on April 6, 1975, in his 78th and last game played that season; he did so off [[Russ Gillow]] of the [[San Diego Mariners]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://newspaperarchive.com/other-clipping-apr-08-1975-5731756/?utm_source=newspaperarchive&utm_medium=copy_link&utm_campaign=share_link&utm_content=newspaper_clipping/|via=Newspaper Archive|title=Hull sets scoring record|work=Billings Gazette|agency=Associated Press|date=April 8, 1975}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.coloradohistoricnewspapers.org/?a=d&d=RMD19750407-01.2.170&e=-------en-20--1--img-txIN%7CtxCO%7CtxTA--------0------|access-date=June 11, 2026|title=The Rocky Mountain News (Daily) April 7, 1975 - Colorado Historical News Collection Archives|website=Colorado Historical News Collection}}</ref>\n\nIn October 1975, Hull sat out a game as a form of protest against hockey violence, stating, “Setting an example for kids should be hockey's main theme. Bodychecking and aggressiveness is part of hockey. So is the odd fight because of the tempo. But not the stuff that's going on. The intimidation. The stick‐swinging, flailing it like an ax. The high stick. The spear. That's not hockey. Intimidation isn't hockey.”<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1975/10/30/archives/dave-anderson-why-bobby-hull-made-hockey-blush.html|first=Dave|last=Anderson|date=October 30, 1975|work=The New York Times|title=Why Bobby Hull Made Hockey Blush}}</ref> In the five WHA seasons in which he played more than half the schedule, he was voted a [[WHA All-Star Team|First-Team]] All-Star thrice and a Second-Team All-Star twice, while tallying 50 goals and 100 points four times each. The Jets won the [[1978 WHA playoffs]] with Hull delivering eight goals in the postseason run. In the game four victory over the New England Whalers, Hull scored in the third period to make it 4–2 in the eventual 5–3 victory that meant Hull delivered the series-clinching goal. As it turned out, this was his last postseason goal in his career. Hull scored 43 goals in the WHA playoffs, the most in WHA postseason history.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/leaders/goals_career_p.html|title=NHL & WHA Career Playoff Leaders and Records for Goals|website=Hockey Reference|date=July 22, 2025}}</ref>\n\nBecause he joined the rival league, Hull was not allowed to represent [[Canada men's national ice hockey team|Team Canada]] in the [[1972 Summit Series]], which pitted Canada's top NHL players against the [[Soviet Union national ice hockey team|USSR's national team]]. Two years later, a [[1974 Summit Series|second Summit Series]] was held in which Hull and other top WHA stars (including [[Gordie Howe]], who had been retired from the NHL at the time of the initial Summit Series) competed against the Soviet national team. The WHA lost the series four games to one (three ending in a tie), despite Hull's seven goals. He was a key member of the Canadian squad that won the [[1976 Canada Cup]], though, scoring five goals and three assists in seven games. On March 11, 1978 in Quebec, Hull scored his 1,000th combined goal (including regular season and playoffs of both the NHL and WHA) against the [[Quebec Nordiques]], making him only the second player with 1,000 goals in hockey history next to [[Gordie Howe]].<ref>{{cite web|via=Newspaper Archive|date=March 13, 1978|website=Winnipeg Free Press|title=Long has hand in Hull history|url=https://newspaperarchive.com/other-clipping-mar-13-1978-5731745/?utm_source=newspaperarchive&utm_medium=copy_link&utm_campaign=share_link&utm_content=newspaper_clipping/|access-date=June 5, 2026}}</ref> He initially announced his retirement in the fall of 1978.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1978/11/06/archives/exit-hull-on-skates.html|website=The New York Times|title=Exit Hull, On Skates|access-date=June 10, 2026}}</ref>\n\n===Later career and retirements===\nSlowed by injuries and age, Hull played only a few games in the WHA's final season of [[1978–79 WHA season|1978–79]], retiring on November 2, 1978. However, after the 1979 merger of the two leagues (including the Jets) and reportedly in financial straits, Hull came out of retirement to play once more for the NHL Jets. He played in eighteen games before being traded to the [[Hartford Whalers]] for future considerations on February 27, 1980, bringing the two-time [[Gordie Howe Trophy]] winner together with the 51-year-old Howe himself (who, after Hull's initial contest with the Whalers, told the press, \"The kid looks good in his first game.\"). Hull played effectively in nine games (two goals and five assists) as the Whalers reached the postseason. In the Preliminary Round against the [[Montreal Canadiens]], Hull did not record a statistic as the Whalers were swept with an overtime loss at the [[Hartford Civic Center]] on April 11. As it turned out, this was Hull's last game as a professional player, as he retired soon after to care for his partner, who had been injured in an automobile accident.<ref name=NYT>{{cite news|last=Clarity|first=James|title=Hull Shows Spirit in Ranger Tryout|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1981/09/10/sports/hull-shows-spirit-in-ranger-tryout.html|date=September 10, 1981|work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref>\n\nIn September 1981, Hull attempted one final comeback with the [[New York Rangers]] at age 42, at the suggestion of Rangers coach [[Herb Brooks]], who wanted to try reuniting Hull with his former Jets teammates, Hedberg and Nilsson.<ref name=\"comeback\">{{cite web |last1=Clarity |first1=James F. |title=Hull Fails to Make Rangers |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1981/10/09/sports/hull-fails-to-make-rangers.html |work=The New York Times |access-date=January 27, 2019 |date=October 9, 1981}}</ref> The comeback attempt lasted five exhibition games, during which Hull had one goal and one assist, before he and the Rangers both decided it was best to end the comeback.<ref name=\"comeback\" /> It was the second time in Hull's career that he had played exhibition games with the Rangers; in 1959, after missing the playoffs the previous spring, the Rangers and the [[Boston Bruins]] had been sent on an exhibition tour of Europe, and then-emerging star Hull and [[Eddie Shack]] were added to the Rangers' roster for the tour. Hull and Shack co-led the Rangers in scoring, each netting 14 goals over the 23-game tour.<ref name=\"Rangers 1\">{{cite book|last=Kreiser|first=John|title=The New York Rangers : Broadway's longest-running hit|year=1996|publisher=Sagamore Pub.|location=Champaign, IL|isbn=1571670416|page=139|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sSlinBzTL0QC&q=%22bobby+hull%22%22rangers%22%22tour%22%22europ%20e%22&pg=PA139|author2=Smith, Lou Friedman |author3=foreword by Neil }}</ref>\n\nHull ended his career having played in 1,063 NHL games, accumulating 610 goals, 560 assists, 1,170 points, 640 penalty minutes, three [[Art Ross Trophy|Art Ross Trophies]], two [[Hart Memorial Trophy|Hart Memorial Trophies]] (he finished second or third in the voting an additional six times), a [[Lady Byng Memorial Trophy]], and a [[Stanley Cup]] Championship, adding 62 goals and 67 assists for 129 points in 119 playoff games. He played in 411 WHA games, scoring 303 goals, 335 assists, and 638 points, adding 43 goals and 37 assists in 60 playoff games. His North American major league professional total of 1,018 goals (NHL and WHA including playoffs) is the third most of all-time after [[Wayne Gretzky]] (1,072) and Gordie Howe (1,071), although the NHL does not recognize scoring statistics from the WHA in players' career totals.\n\n==Post-playing career==\nIn 1978, he was made an Officer of the [[Order of Canada]]. Besides his Hall of Fame induction, Hull's no. 9 jersey has been retired by the Black Hawks, the Jets, and their successor team, the [[Arizona Coyotes]]. When Bobby's son [[Brett Hull]] joined the Coyotes, they unretired the number for Brett to wear during his brief stint there to honour his father. [[Evander Kane]], who wore number 9 for the [[Atlanta Thrashers]] when they became the current [[Winnipeg Jets]] franchise, sought and received Hull's permission to wear the number.\n\nIn 2003, he was named the figurehead commissioner of a new [[World Hockey Association (proposed)|World Hockey Association]], intended to operate during the [[2004–05 NHL lockout]]; it never entered play, and the organization subsequently ran several ephemeral low-minor league and unsanctioned Tier II junior leagues. Hull served as an ambassador for the Blackhawks through part of the 2021–22 season until the organization announced, \"When it comes to Bobby, specifically, we jointly agreed earlier this season that he will retire from any official team role.\"<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cbc.ca/sports/hockey/nhl/bobby-hull-no-longer-serving-as-chicago-team-ambassador-1.6359410|title=NHL legend Bobby Hull no longer team ambassador for Chicago|agency=Associated Press|date=February 21, 2022|publisher=Canadian Broadcasting Corporation|accessdate=January 30, 2023}}</ref>\n\n==Personal life and death==\n[[File:Bobby Hull.jpg|thumb|upright|Hull in 2006]]\n\nHull's younger brother [[Dennis Hull|Dennis]] (nicknamed \"the Silver Jet\") starred alongside him with the Chicago Black Hawks for eight seasons, scoring over 300 goals in his own right. When Bobby was excluded from the [[1972 Summit Series]] because he had signed to play in the WHA, Dennis initially planned to boycott the event as well as a show of support for his brother, but Bobby persuaded him to stay on Team Canada.{{citation needed|date=September 2022}}\n\nHull's marriage to Joanne McKay ended in divorce in 1980 after several abusive incidents.<ref name=\"ESPNClassic\" />\n\nIn 1986, he was arrested and charged with assault and battery after allegedly hitting his third wife, Deborah, after an argument.<ref name=\"LATimes\">{{cite web |date=December 11, 1986 |title=LA Times - Bobby Hull Charged With Assault on Wife |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1986-12-11-sp-2174-story.html |access-date=January 30, 2023 |website=[[Los Angeles Times]]}}</ref> She eventually dropped the charges.<ref name=\"ESPNClassic\">{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/classic/biography/s/Hull_Bobby.html |title=ESPN Classic – Hull helped WHA into hockey family |publisher=ESPN |access-date=November 21, 2011}}</ref>\n\n<!---YOU MUST USE A RELIABLE SOURCE IF ADDING THE NAMES OF ANY SUPPOSED RELATIONSHIPS PER [[WP:PROVEIT]]--->\nHull was romantically involved with a woman named Claudia Allen. In 1980, Hull retired from the Hartford Whalers to take care of Allen, who was injured in a severe automobile accident.<ref name=NYT /> The couple never married.\n\nIn 1998, Hull allegedly made pro-[[Nazism|Nazi]] comments to ''[[The Moscow Times]]''. He was quoted as saying, \"[[Hitler]], for example, had some good ideas. He just went a little bit too far.\"<ref name=\"moscow\">{{cite web |title=Bobby Hull to Moscow Paper: Hitler Had Some Good Ideas |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/news/ct-xpm-1998-08-26-9808270083-story.html |website=[[Chicago Tribune]] |access-date=November 26, 2018 |date=August 26, 1998}}</ref> Hull later denied having complimented Hitler and said journalists had raised the subject.<ref name=\"denies\">{{cite web |title=Hull Denies Remarks on Hitler, Blacks |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1998-aug-27-sp-17129-story.html |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |access-date=November 26, 2018 |date=August 27, 1998}}</ref> The incident was parodied on the Canadian [[news satire]] show ''[[This Hour Has 22 Minutes]]'', with [[Rick Mercer]] reading a spot saying Hull had been misquoted, and had actually said, \"''[[Darryl Sittler|Sittler]]'' had some good ideas.\"\n\n===Children===\n[[Brett Hull]] (the \"Golden Brett\"), was also a hockey star, finishing his NHL career with 741 goals (currently the fifth-highest goal total in NHL history). Bobby and Brett are the only [[List of professional sports families|father-and-son tandem]] to achieve the marks of more than 50 goals in an NHL season and more than 600 NHL goals. They are also the only father-and-son duo to win the [[Hart Memorial Trophy]] (Bobby twice and Brett once) and [[Lady Byng Trophy]], and to lead the league in goal scoring (Bobby seven times and Brett three times). While playing for the [[Phoenix Coyotes]] in 2005, Brett donned his father's retired No. 9 for the last five games of his career.\n\n[[Bart Hull]] was a standout [[running back]] for the [[Boise State University]]' [[Boise State Broncos football|Broncos football]] team and played with the [[Ottawa Rough Riders]] and [[Saskatchewan Roughriders]] in the [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL) as well as one season of professional [[Indoor American football|indoor football]] prior to recurring injuries. Post football, he briefly played professional hockey with the [[Idaho Steelheads]].\n\nBobby Jr. and Blake both played junior and senior hockey. Bobby Jr. played hockey at the University of British Columbia but graduated from University of Manitoba before getting into the garment industry in 1985.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1994-07-05-sp-12176-story.html|title=Coming Into His Own Light : Bobby Hull Jr. Finds His Niche in Roller Hockey|first=Michael|last=Itagaki|date=July 5, 1994|website=The Los Angeles Times}}</ref> Bobby Jr. won the [[Memorial Cup]] with the 1980 [[Cornwall Royals]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://chl.ca/memorial-cup-championship-rosters/|website=CHL.ca|title=Memorial Cup Championship Rosters|access-date=June 10, 2026}}</ref> Blake decided instead to attend [[Wilfred Laurier University]] and pursued a golf career rather than college hockey.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aspentimes.com/sports/blake-hull-son-of-bobby-named-new-coach-for-aspen-leafs-u20-hockey-team/|title=Blake Hull, son of Bobby, named new coach for Aspen Leafs U20 hockey team|access-date=June 10, 2026|first=Austin|last=Colbert|website=The Aspen Times|date=May 19, 2017}}</ref> He played for the [[Allan Cup]]-winning Brantford Mott's Clamatos of the [[OHA Senior A Hockey League]] (AAA Men's Amateur) in 1985.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.brantfordareasportshall.ca/Members/Honouree-Teams/Hockey/1985-Motts-Clamatos-Sr-A-Allan-Cup-Champions|access-date=June 10, 2026|title=1985 Motts Clamatos Senior A Allan Cup Champions|website=Brantford Area Sports Hall of Recognition}}</ref>\n\nHull's daughter, Michelle, became a lawyer.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://pictongazette.ca/post/editorial-hull-was-as-bright-as-stadium-lights-and-as-dark-as-moonless-nights|website=Picton Gazette|title=EDITORIAL: Hull was as bright as stadium lights and as dark as moonless nights|access-date=June 10, 2026}}</ref> She works with battered women as a result of witnessing her father's treatment of her mother, Joanne McKay.<ref name=\"wapo_obit\"/>\n\n===Bobby Hull Community Rink===\n[[File:Bobby-hull-community-ice-arena.jpg|thumb|upright|Statue of Hull at the Bobby Hull Ice Rink (Cicero, Illinois)]]\n[[File:Bobby-hull-community-ice-arena-1.jpg|thumb|upright|Bobby Hull Ice Rink (Cicero, Illinois)]]\n\nThe Town of [[Cicero, Illinois]] created a public outdoor rink in his name. The rink hosts skating lessons, public skate, public Stick & Puck, High School Hockey games, and more.\n\n===Death===\nOn January 30, 2023, Hull died at his home in [[Wheaton, Illinois]], at the age of 84.<ref>{{cite web |title=Bobby Hull dies at 84, legendary Blackhawks goal-scorer, Cup champion |url=https://www.nhl.com/news/bobby-hull-dead-at-age-84-340587082 |publisher=National Hockey League |access-date=January 30, 2023 |date=January 30, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dailyherald.com/sports/20230130/former-blackhawks-great-bobby-hull-dies-at-84|title=Former Blackhawks great Bobby Hull dies at 84|date=January 30, 2023|website=Daily Herald}}</ref><ref name=\"wapo_obit\"/> His son Brett released a statement following his father's death via the Twitter account of the [[St. Louis Blues]].<ref>{{cite tweet |user=StLouisBlues |number=1620163012131983363 |date=January 30, 2023 |title=A message from Brett Hull. |access-date=January 31, 2023}}</ref>\n\nIn February 2025, Hull's family released a statement saying that researchers had determined that Hull had stage 2 [[chronic traumatic encephalopathy]] (CTE) at the time of his death.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-02-19 |title=Hockey great Hull had CTE, researchers confirm |url=https://www.espn.com/nhl/story/_/id/43918445/hall-famer-bobby-hull-had-cte-researchers-find |access-date=2025-02-19 |website=ESPN.com |language=en}}</ref>\n\n==Awards and achievements==\n* [[Art Ross Trophy]] winner ([[1959–60 NHL season|1960]], [[1961–62 NHL season|1962]], and [[1965–66 NHL season|1966]])\n* [[National Hockey League|NHL]] First All-Star Team left wing (1960, 1962, [[1963–64 NHL season|1964]], [[1964–65 NHL season|1965]], 1966, [[1966–67 NHL season|1967]], [[1967–68 NHL season|1968]], [[1968–69 NHL season|1969]], [[1969–70 NHL season|1970]], and [[1971–72 NHL season|1972]])\n* [[Stanley Cup]] champion ([[1960–61 NHL season|1961]])\n* [[National Hockey League|NHL]] Second All-Star Team left wing ([[1962–63 NHL season|1963]] and [[1970–71 NHL season|1971]])\n* [[Hart Memorial Trophy]] winner (1965 and 1966)\n* [[Lady Byng Memorial Trophy]] winner (1965)\n* [[Lester Patrick Trophy]] winner (1969)\n* 7x NHL goalscoring leader (1960, 1962, 1964, 1966, 1967, 1968, 1969).\n* Became third hockey player to appear on the [[List of covers of Time magazine (1960s)|cover of ''Time'' magazine]]<ref>{{cite magazine| url=http://www.time.com/time/covers/0,16641,19680301,00.html |
