Marie, Ontario]]\n[[Category:St. Catharines Teepees players]]\n[[Category:St. Louis Braves players]]\n[[Category:St. Louis Braves (EPHL) players]]\n[[Category:Stanley Cup champions]]\n[[Category:Tampa Bay Lightning announcers]]\n[[Category:Tampa Bay Lightning executives]]\n[[Category:Canadian expatriate ice hockey players in the United States]]\n[[Category:20th-century Canadian sportsmen]]"}}}]},{"pageid":333309,"ns":0,"title":"Martin Brodeur","revisions":[{"slots":{"main":{"contentmodel":"wikitext","contentformat":"text/x-wiki","content":"{{short description|Canadian-American ice hockey player (born 1972)}}\n{{Featured article}}\n{{pp-pc}}\n{{Use mdy dates|date=May 2025}}\n{{Infobox ice hockey biography\n| name = Martin Brodeur\n| hall_of_fame = 2018\n| image = {{CSS image crop |Image=Martin Brodeur during game at Prudential Center vs Ottawa 11-25-09 3.jpeg |bSize=480 |cWidth=230 |cHeight=325 |oTop=35 |oLeft=35 |Location=center}}\n| image_size =\n| caption = Brodeur with the [[New Jersey Devils]] in November 2009\n| birth_date = {{birth date and age|1972|5|6}}\n| birth_place = [[Montreal]], Quebec, Canada\n| height_ft = 6\n| height_in = 2\n| weight_lb = 220\n| position = [[Goaltender]]\n| catches = Left\n| played_for = [[New Jersey Devils]]<br>[[St. Louis Blues]]\n| ntl_team = CAN\n| draft = 20th overall\n| draft_year = 1990\n| draft_team = [[New Jersey Devils]]\n| career_start = 1991\n| career_end = 2015\n}}\n'''Martin Pierre Brodeur''' ({{IPA|fr|maʁtɛ̃ bʁɔdœʁ}}; born May 6, 1972) is a Canadian-American<ref name=\"citizen\" /> professional [[ice hockey]] executive and former player. He played 22 seasons as a [[goaltender]] in the [[National Hockey League]] (NHL), 21 of them for the [[New Jersey Devils]], with whom he won three [[Stanley Cup]] championships and five [[Eastern Conference (NHL)|Eastern Conference]] championships in 17 postseason campaigns. He also won two [[Olympic medal|Olympic gold medal]]s with [[Canada men's national ice hockey team|Canada]], his first as the starting goaltender for the team in [[Ice hockey at the 2002 Winter Olympics|2002]], and his second as the backup goaltender in [[Ice hockey at the 2010 Winter Olympics|2010]], as well as several other medals with Canada in other international competitions. Brodeur is widely regarded as one of the greatest goaltenders of all time. In 2017, he was named by the league as one of the \"[[100 Greatest NHL Players]]\",<ref>{{cite web|title=100 Greatest NHL Players|url=https://www.nhl.com/history/nhl-centennial/nhl-100-greatest-players| website = NHL.com|access-date=January 27, 2017|date=January 27, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|last=NHL|title=Martin Brodeur owns many key career goalie records|date=March 22, 2017|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fz-ygz38_AU&index=41&list=PL1NbHSfosBuHEp2Bphcgz16OKz0kjnCH6| archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211114/fz-ygz38_AU| archive-date=November 14, 2021 | url-status=live|access-date=April 25, 2017}}{{cbignore}}</ref> and the following year, he was elected to the [[Hockey Hall of Fame]].<ref>{{cite web |title=HHOF - Player Details - Martin Brodeur |url=https://www.hhof.com/HonouredMembers/MemberDetails.html?type=Player&mem=P201801 |website=hhof.com |access-date=March 2, 2022}}</ref>\n\nBrodeur holds numerous NHL and franchise records among goaltenders; he ranks as the league's all-time regular season leader in [[List of NHL goaltenders with 300 wins|wins]] (691), losses (397), [[Shutout#Ice hockey|shutouts]] (125), and games played (1,266).<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=414407 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090322035304/http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=414407 | url-status = dead | archive-date = March 22, 2009 | title = Is Brodeur setting the bar beyond reach? | publisher = NHL.com | first = Dan | last = Rosen | date = March 18, 2009 | access-date = March 19, 2009}}</ref> He won at least 30 games in twelve straight seasons between [[1995–96 NHL season|1995–96]] and [[2007–08 NHL season|2007–08]] and is the only goaltender in NHL history with eight 40-win seasons.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nhl.com/gamecenter/cbj-vs-njd/2010/03/23/2009021081|title=Brodeur reaches 40 wins again as Devils rip Jackets|publisher=NHL.com|author=Morreale, Mike G.|date=March 23, 2010|access-date=March 24, 2010}}</ref> He is a four-time [[Vezina Trophy]] winner, a five-time [[William M. Jennings Trophy]] winner, a ten-time [[NHL All-Star Game|NHL All-Star]], and a [[Calder Memorial Trophy]] winner. He is one of 18 [[List of goalscoring NHL goaltenders|NHL goaltenders to score a goal]] in the regular season and the second to do so in the playoffs; his three goals are the most of any NHL goaltender. He only had three seasons where he posted more losses than wins.<ref name=\"nhl.com\">{{cite web | url = https://www.nhl.com/player/martin-brodeur-8455710 | title = Martin Brodeur, Devils – Notes | publisher = NHL.com | access-date = March 19, 2009}}</ref><ref name=\"MainBio\">{{cite web|url=http://www.hockeygoalies.org/bio/brodeurm.html|title=Martin Brodeur Biography|publisher=hockeygoalies.org|access-date=December 31, 2006}}</ref>\n\nBrodeur used a [[Butterfly style#Profly and hybrid|hybrid style]] of goaltending by [[stand-up style|standing up]] more than typical [[butterfly style]] goaltenders, though he adapted to more modern techniques at the latter stage of his career.<ref>{{cite news |author=Saed Hindash |newspaper=The Star-Ledger |url=http://www.nj.com/devils/index.ssf/2012/02/devils_goalie_martin_brodeur_t_3.html |title=Devils' goalie Martin Brodeur tweaks leg pads and has won 4 of his last 5 starts |access-date=November 24, 2012}}</ref><ref name=\"cox\">{{cite news | url = https://www.espn.com/nhl/columns/story?columnist=cox_damien&id=3990924 | title = Brodeur the best? There's no debate | work = [[ESPN.com]] | first = Damien | last = Cox | date = March 18, 2009 | access-date = March 18, 2009}}</ref><ref name=\"unmasked\">{{cite web|last=Woodley|first=Kevin|title=Unmasked: Old-school style helped Brodeur stand out|publisher=National Hockey League|date=January 29, 2015|url=https://www.nhl.com/news/unmasked-old-school-style-helped-brodeur-stand-out/c-750819|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161018214230/https://www.nhl.com/news/unmasked-old-school-style-helped-brodeur-stand-out/c-750819|url-status=dead|archive-date=October 18, 2016|access-date=October 14, 2016}}</ref> He was known for his puck handling, his positional play, and his reflexes, especially with his glove hand.<ref name=\"cox\" /> Brodeur's prowess at puck handling was so well known that it led in part to the NHL changing its rules to restrict where goaltenders were allowed to handle the puck outside of the goal crease, adding what is known as \"[[Ice hockey rink#Goaltender trapezoid (\"Martin Brodeur\" Rule)|the Brodeur rule]]\" after the [[2004–05 NHL lockout]].<ref name=\"Diamos2007\" /> He announced his retirement in the middle of the [[2014–15 NHL season|2014–15 season]] after a brief stint with the [[St. Louis Blues]], having played in just seven games with the team.{{r|PlayoffStats}} He is the current executive vice president of business development for the Devils.\n\n==Early life==\nBrodeur was born on May 6, 1972, in Montreal.<ref>{{cite book|last=Zeisler|first=Laurel|title=Historical Dictionary of Ice Hockey|publisher=Scarecrow Press|year=2012|pages=48–49|isbn=9780810878631}}</ref> He is one of five children of [[Denis Brodeur|Denis]] and Mireille Brodeur.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Brodeur|first1=Martin|last2=Cox|first2=Damien|title=Brodeur: Beyond the Crease|publisher=John Wiley & Sons Canada|year=2007|pages=[https://archive.org/details/brodeurbeyondcre0000brod/page/139 139–140, 143]|isbn=978-0-470-15377-2|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/brodeurbeyondcre0000brod/page/139}}</ref> Denis played in the [[Ice hockey at the 1956 Winter Olympics|1956 Winter Olympics]] for [[Canada men's national ice hockey team|Canada]] and won a bronze medal.<ref name=\"Olympics\">{{cite news |last=Allen |first=Kevin |url=https://www.usatoday.com/sports/olympics/torino/2006-01-29-brodeur_x.htm |title=Brodeur following in father's mask |date=January 29, 2006 |access-date=December 1, 2006 |newspaper=USA Today |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060911191341/http://www.usatoday.com/sports/olympics/torino/2006-01-29-brodeur_x.htm |archive-date=September 11, 2006}}</ref><ref name=\"HHOFjournal\">{{cite web|url=http://www.hhof.com/HTML/exSCJ_33.shtml|title=Stanley Cup Journal|access-date=December 1, 2006|date=August 22, 2003|work=HHOF.com|publisher=[[Hockey Hall of Fame]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110604124252/http://www.hhof.com/HTML/exSCJ_33.shtml|archive-date=June 4, 2011}}</ref> After his playing career, Denis was a longtime photographer for the [[Montreal Canadiens]]. For more than 20 years, he attended all Montreal games and practices, and when Martin was old enough, he came along. Brodeur idolized Canadiens goaltender [[Patrick Roy]], as well as Flyers goaltender [[Ron Hextall]].<ref>{{cite journal|url = http://business.highbeam.com/62653/article-1G1-75434961/q|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180505134759/https://business.highbeam.com/62653/article-1G1-75434961/q|url-status = usurped|archive-date = May 5, 2018|title = Q&A – hockey players Patrick Roy and Martin Brodeur – Brief Article – Interview|last = Wigge|first = Larry|date = June 4, 2001|journal = The Sporting Times|access-date = June 30, 2015|url-access = subscription|via = [[HighBeam Research]]}}</ref>\n\nBrodeur started playing hockey as a forward. His goaltending career began when his coach asked him if he wanted to play as a backup at the position in a youth tournament. Brodeur explained:<ref name=\"GoalieDecision\">{{cite web|url=http://www.martinbrodeur.net/index.php?lng=en&vyber=fakty |title=Martin Brodeur – Facts about ...|work=MartinBrodeur.net |publisher=[[Wayback Machine]] |access-date=April 6, 2007 |year=2007 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070217114025/http://www.martinbrodeur.net/index.php?lng=en&vyber=fakty |archive-date=February 17, 2007}}</ref>\n\n{{blockquote|The next season my coach came up to me and said, 'Do you want to be a goalie or forward this year?' It was the biggest decision of my life, and I was seven years old. I don't know why I decided, but I thought it would be fun to play goal.}}\n\nWhen he was 12 years old, Brodeur briefly intended to stop playing hockey, after he had been removed from his team's lineup for not showing up at a game. Following a conversation with his brother Claude, though, he decided to continue playing.<ref name=\"always\"/> When receiving goaltending instructions in his teens, Brodeur was taught a variety of different styles, ranging from [[Butterfly style|butterfly]] to stand-up, and paid attention to the technique of others playing the position. He attended a camp run by retired Soviet goaltender [[Vladislav Tretiak]], who encouraged the use of multiple methods; Brodeur believes that the concept made him \"a student of the game.\"<ref>Brodeur and Cox, pp. 56–58.</ref> In the 1989–90 season, he made it to the [[Quebec Major Junior Hockey League|Quebec Major Junior League]]. While playing with the [[Saint-Hyacinthe Laser]], Brodeur made the QMJHL All-Rookie team in 1989–90 and the QMJHL Second All-Star Team in [[1991–92 QMJHL season|1991–92]].<ref name=\"HHOF\">{{cite web|title=NHL Player Search: Martin Pierre Brodeur|publisher=Hockey Hall of Fame|url=http://www.hhof.com/LegendsOfHockey/jsp/SearchPlayer.jsp?player=18223|access-date=September 28, 2016|archive-date=August 7, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160807125543/http://www.hhof.com/LegendsOfHockey/jsp/SearchPlayer.jsp?player=18223|url-status=dead}}</ref> Brodeur was drafted by the [[New Jersey Devils]] in the first round (20th overall) in the [[1990 NHL entry draft]].<ref name=\"HHOF\"/>\n\n==NHL career==\n\n===New Jersey Devils===\n\n====1991–1995====\nIn the [[1991–92 NHL season]], Brodeur spent most of his time with Saint-Hyacinthe in the QMJHL, but was called up to the NHL on an emergency basis for four games when New Jersey goaltenders [[Chris Terreri]] and [[Craig Billington]] became injured. Brodeur won his NHL debut against the [[Boston Bruins]], 4–2,<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=413372&navid=DL | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20121021170626/http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=413372&navid=DL | url-status = dead | archive-date = October 21, 2012 | title = Brodeur was a scorer before he was a goalie | publisher = [[NHL.com]] | first = Dan | last = Rosen | date = March 12, 2009 | access-date = March 17, 2009}}</ref> and played in one playoff game that season. Brodeur spent the following season with the [[Utica Devils]] of the [[American Hockey League]] (AHL). However, in the [[1993–94 NHL season|1993–94 season]], Brodeur returned to the NHL permanently and gained recognition when he won the [[Calder Memorial Trophy|Calder Trophy]], an annual award for the best rookie in the NHL. He led the Devils to the second-best record in the league and the [[1994 Stanley Cup Playoffs#Eastern Conference Final|Eastern Conference finals]] in the playoffs, where they lost to the [[New York Rangers]] in seven games.<ref name=\"1994 Playoffs\">{{cite web|url=http://nbpfaus.net/~pfau/nhl/1994.html|title=1994 National Hockey League Playoffs|publisher=nbpfaus.net|access-date=February 9, 2007|year=2001}}</ref> He finished second in [[goals against average]] (GAA) (2.40) and fourth in [[save percentage]] (.915) in 47 games played during the regular season,<ref name=\"hr\">{{cite web|title=Martin Brodeur |publisher=Hockey-Reference |url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/players/b/brodema01.html |access-date=September 30, 2016 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140618151917/http://www.hockey-reference.com/players/b/brodema01.html |archive-date=June 18, 2014}}</ref> helping him eventually land the starting job over Terreri.<ref>{{cite magazine|last=Elliott|first=Josh|title=Top Five Unsung Backup Goalies To Martin Brodeur|magazine=The Hockey News|date=February 1, 2015|url=https://thehockeynews.com/news/news/top-five-unsung-backup-goalies-to-martin-brodeur|access-date=September 30, 2016}}</ref>\n\n[[File:The N.J. Devils win the 1995 Stanley Cup.jpeg|thumb|left|Brodeur is mobbed by teammates upon the Devils winning the [[1995 Stanley Cup Final]]]]\nIn the [[1994–95 NHL season]], which was shortened to 48 games due to an [[1994–95 NHL lockout|extended lockout]], the Devils finished tied for ninth overall, fifth in their conference.<ref name=\"oral2\">{{cite web|last=Pickens|first=Pat|title=1994–95 champion Devils: An oral history, Pt. 2|publisher=Sportsnet|date=September 16, 2014|url=http://www.sportsnet.ca/hockey/nhl/1994-95-champion-devils-an-oral-history-pt-2/|access-date=September 30, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=1994–95 NHL Summary|publisher=Hockey-Reference|url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/leagues/NHL_1995.html|access-date=September 30, 2016}}</ref> With the leadership of Brodeur, they defeated the Boston Bruins in the first round, shutting them out in three of their four wins.<ref name=\"oral2\"/> In the second round against the [[Pittsburgh Penguins]], Brodeur gave up nine goals and helped the Devils defeat the Penguins in five games. In the third round, the Devils defeated the [[Philadelphia Flyers]] in six games,<ref>{{cite web|last=Pickens|first=Pat|title=1994–95 champion Devils: An oral history, Pt. 3|publisher=Sportsnet|date=September 17, 2014|url=http://www.sportsnet.ca/hockey/nhl/1994-95-champion-devils-an-oral-history-pt-3/|access-date=September 30, 2016}}</ref> giving them their first [[1995 Stanley Cup Final|Stanley Cup Final]] appearance in franchise history,<ref>{{cite news|title=New Jersey Devils playoff history|work=Yahoo! Sports|date=April 28, 2009|url=https://sports.yahoo.com/nhl/news?slug=newjerseypost|access-date=September 30, 2016|archive-date=October 7, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161007152752/https://sports.yahoo.com/nhl/news?slug=newjerseypost|url-status=dead}}</ref> against the heavily-favoured [[Detroit Red Wings]]. The strong play of Brodeur and the Devils' \"[[Neutral zone trap|trap]]\" method of defence made the series lopsided in favour of New Jersey, who swept the Red Wings in four games, while holding them to just seven goals in those games.<ref>{{cite web|last=Pickens|first=Pat|title=1994–95 champion Devils: An oral history, Pt. 4|publisher=Sportsnet|date=September 18, 2014|url=http://www.sportsnet.ca/hockey/nhl/1994-95-champion-devils-an-oral-history-pt-4/|access-date=September 30, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Pickens|first=Pat|title=1994–95 champion Devils: An oral history, Pt. 5|publisher=Sportsnet|date=September 19, 2014|url=http://www.sportsnet.ca/hockey/nhl/1994-95-champion-devils-an-oral-history-pt-5/|access-date=September 30, 2016}}</ref> Brodeur won a Stanley Cup in his second full season in the NHL.<ref>{{cite web|last=LeBrun|first=Pierre|title=Penguins goalie Matt Murray has played more like a Hall of Famer than a rookie|publisher=ESPN|date=June 9, 2016|url=https://www.espn.com/nhl/story/_/id/16050169/nhl-2016-stanley-cup-playoffs-pittsburgh-penguins-rookie-goalie-matt-murray-channeling-ken-Dryden|access-date=September 30, 2016}}</ref> After the victory, he was quoted as saying:<ref name=\"MainBio\"/>\n\n{{blockquote|In the last game against Detroit, the time from ten minutes left to one minute left was probably the longest nine minutes of my life. But from one to zero was probably the greatest time I've ever had. I didn't want the clock to run out. It was such a great feeling: people crying in the stands, people jumping up and down, people cheering. Guys couldn't even sit up on the bench. It was probably the best minute of my life.}}\n\n====1995–1999====\nAfter a year of success, the Devils were in the middle of the pack for most of the [[1995–96 NHL season|1995–96 season]] and barely missed the playoffs. Brodeur played in 74 of his team's 82 games, setting a single-season record for most minutes played by a goaltender, while having the second-most shutouts (6) in the league. He was named the starter in the [[1996 NHL All-Star Game|All-Star Game]] for the [[Eastern Conference (NHL)|Eastern Conference]] and stopped all 12 shots he faced.<ref name=\"MainBio\"/> He finished fourth in voting for the [[Vezina Trophy]],<ref>{{cite web|title=1995–96 NHL Awards Voting|publisher=Hockey-Reference|url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/awards/voting-1996.html|access-date=October 3, 2016}}</ref> which is awarded to the league's top goaltender.<ref>{{cite web|title=Vezina Trophy winners|publisher=ESPN|date=June 24, 2015|url=https://www.espn.com/nhl/news/story?page=nhlvezina|access-date=October 3, 2016}}</ref> Brodeur also played for [[Canada men's national ice hockey team|Canada]] during the [[1996 World Cup of Hockey]], where Canada lost to the United States in the gold medal games.<ref>{{cite web|last=Burnside|first=Scott|title=Five greatest teams in World Cup/Canada Cup history|publisher=ESPN|date=September 15, 2015|url=https://www.espn.com/nhl/story/_/id/13632109/2016-world-cup-hockey-five-greatest-teams-world-cup-canada-cup-history|access-date=October 3, 2016}}</ref>\n\nIn the [[1996–97 NHL season|1996–97 season]], the Devils finished third in the NHL. Brodeur was runner-up for the Vezina Trophy, was named to the [[1997 NHL All-Star Game|All-Star Game]], and had the lowest goals against average by a goaltender in almost 30 years, earning him the [[Jennings Trophy]]. He also had 10 shutouts and a .927 save percentage. On April 17, 1997, in the first game of a first-round playoff matchup against the Montreal Canadiens, Brodeur fired the puck the length of the ice and into the Canadiens' empty net to ensure a 5–2 victory. It was the second time in NHL history that a [[List of goalscoring NHL goaltenders|goaltender had scored]] in the playoffs, and the fifth time overall.<ref name=\"GoalScored\">{{cite web|url=http://www.martinbrodeur.net/index.php?lng=en&vyber=fakty |title=Martin Brodeur – Facts |publisher=MartinBrodeur.net |access-date=December 31, 2006 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070217114025/http://www.martinbrodeur.net/index.php?lng=en&vyber=fakty |archive-date=February 17, 2007}}</ref> The Devils went on to win that series, but lost in the second round to the rival New York Rangers.<ref>{{cite web|title=1997 NHL Stanley Cup Playoffs Summary|publisher=Hockey-Reference|url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/playoffs/NHL_1997.html|access-date=October 3, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Ng|first=Rob|title=With outdoor game at Yankee Stadium, Devils–Rangers rivalry enters new chapter|work=New York Daily News|date=January 26, 2014|url=http://www.nydailynews.com/sports/hockey/rangers/rangers-devils-rivalry-article-1.1591883|access-date=October 3, 2016}}</ref>\n\nThe following year, Brodeur had 43 wins and 10 shutouts in the regular season. The Devils finished first in the Eastern Conference,<ref name=\"1stplace1998\">{{cite web|url=http://www.hockeydb.com/ihdb/stats/leagues/seasons/nhl19271998.html|title=1997–98 NHL Standings|publisher=hockeydb.com|access-date=March 3, 2007|year=1998}}</ref> but lost in the first round of the playoffs to the eighth-seeded [[Ottawa Senators]].<ref name=\"98playoffs\">{{cite web|url=http://www.hockeydb.com/ihdb/stats/playoffdisplay.php3?league=NHL1927&season=1998&leaguenm=NHL|title=1997–98 NHL Playoff Results|publisher=hockeydb.com|access-date=March 3, 2007|year=1998}}</ref> Once again, Brodeur made the [[1998 NHL All-Star Game|All-Star Game]], finished as a runner-up for the Vezina Trophy, and won the Jennings Trophy.<ref name=\"98Jennings\">{{cite web|url=http://www.hockeynut.com/9899/awards98.html|title=1998 NHL Awards|publisher=hockeynut.com|access-date=March 3, 2007|year=1998}}</ref>\n\nIn the [[1998–99 NHL season|1998–99 season]], the Devils finished first in the Eastern Conference for the third straight year, with Brodeur winning 39 games. He was among the contenders for the Vezina Trophy and started in the [[1999 NHL All-Star Game|All-Star Game]], making his fourth appearance. However, the Devils lost in the first round to the Penguins. It was Brodeur's worst playoff performance statistically, as he allowed 20 goals in seven games with an .856 save percentage.<ref name=\"PlayoffStats\">{{cite web|url=https://www.nhl.com/player/martin-brodeur-8455710|title=Martin Brodeur – Career statistics|publisher=NHL.com|access-date=March 3, 2007|year=2007}}</ref>\n\n====1999–2004====\nDuring the [[1999–2000 NHL season|1999–2000 season]], on February 15, 2000, Brodeur was credited with his second career goal, as Brodeur was the last Devils player on the ice to touch the puck before [[Daymond Langkow]] of the Flyers accidentally put the puck into his own empty net during a delayed penalty call against the Devils.<ref name=\"2ndGoal\">{{cite web|author=Bostrom, Don.|url=https://www.mcall.com/2007/02/11/devils-brodeur-is-closing-in-on-becoming-nhls-new-zero-hero/|title=Devils' Brodeur is closing in on becoming NHL's new zero hero|publisher=mcall.com|date=February 11, 2007|access-date=October 14, 2016}}</ref> Brodeur had previously stopped an attempted Flyers shot.<ref>{{cite news|last=Hofmann|first=Rich|title=A Game-winner Never Brodeur's Goal|work=Philadelphia Daily News|date=February 16, 2000|url=http://articles.philly.com/2000-02-16/sports/25576341_1_puck-devils-goaltender-martin-brodeur-flyers-daymond-langkow|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161009101724/http://articles.philly.com/2000-02-16/sports/25576341_1_puck-devils-goaltender-martin-brodeur-flyers-daymond-langkow|url-status=dead|archive-date=October 9, 2016|access-date=October 5, 2016}}</ref>\n\nThat season, Brodeur won 43 games for the second time in his career, and the Devils finished with the fourth spot in the Eastern Conference after losing the division to the Flyers by two points.<ref name=\"9900standings\">{{cite web|url=http://hockeydb.com/ihdb/stats/leagues/seasons/nhl19272000.html|title=1999-00 NHL Standings|publisher=hockeydb.com|access-date=March 20, 2007|year=2000}}</ref> Brodeur helped the Devils sweep the [[Florida Panthers]] in the first round, giving up six goals in four games. In the next round against the [[Toronto Maple Leafs]] he recorded two shutouts, including one in game six of the series as the Devils won 4–2, setting up a showdown with [[Devils–Flyers rivalry|rival Philadelphia Flyers]] in the Eastern Conference finals. The Flyers took a 3–1 series lead and could close out the series at [[First Union Center]] in Philadelphia, but Brodeur gave up only one goal in each of the remaining three games of the series, propelling the Devils to a comeback series victory in seven games. They went on to play the [[Dallas Stars]] in the [[2000 Stanley Cup Final|Stanley Cup Final]], who had a higher seed but one fewer regular season points, giving the Devils home-ice advantage in the series. After taking game one with a seven-goal rally against Dallas, Brodeur led the Devils the rest of the way as he gave up six goals in the next five games, giving the team their second Stanley Cup championship in six years.<ref name=\"9900playoffs\">{{cite web|url=http://hockeydb.com/ihdb/stats/playoffdisplay.php3?league=NHL1927&season=2000&leaguenm=NHL|title=1999-00 NHL Playoffs|publisher=hockeydb.com|date=June 10, 2000|access-date=March 20, 2007}}</ref>\n\nThe next year, Brodeur topped the 40-win mark for the third time in his career, despite having an average GAA and save-percentage throughout the season. He played in the All-Star Game for the sixth consecutive season, and helped the Devils earn the top seed in the Eastern Conference. In the first round Brodeur recorded two shutouts against the [[Carolina Hurricanes]] and the Devils took the series in six games. After struggling to beat seventh-seeded Toronto in seven games, the Devils defeated the sixth-seeded Penguins in the Eastern Conference finals, where Brodeur added two more shutouts, both on the road. In their second straight [[2001 Stanley Cup Final|Stanley Cup Final]] appearance, the Devils played a back-and-forth series against the top seeded [[Colorado Avalanche]], who were led by star goaltender [[Patrick Roy]],<ref name=\"2001finals1\">{{cite news|url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/hockey/nhl/recaps/2001/06/07/njd_col|title=Game 6 recap|publisher=CNN SI|date=June 8, 2001|access-date=March 20, 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20031217225859/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/hockey/nhl/recaps/2001/06/07/njd_col/|archive-date=December 17, 2003|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=\"2001finals2\">{{cite news|agency=Associated Press|url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/hockey/nhl/2001/playoffs/news/2001/06/10/devils_folo_ap|title=Devils fall one game short in repeat quest|publisher=CNN SI|date=June 10, 2001|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010627084151/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/hockey/nhl/2001/playoffs/news/2001/06/10/devils_folo_ap/|archive-date=June 27, 2001|url-status=dead|access-date=March 20, 2007}}</ref> and lost in seven games.<ref>{{cite web|title=Raising the Cup presents: Game 7 2001 Stanley Cup Final|publisher=National Hockey League|date=August 12, 2011|url=https://www.nhl.com/news/raising-the-cup-presents-game-7-2001-stanley-cup-final/c-569837|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170819190721/https://www.nhl.com/news/raising-the-cup-presents-game-7-2001-stanley-cup-final/c-569837|url-status=dead|archive-date=August 19, 2017|access-date=October 5, 2016}}</ref>\n\n[[File:Brodeur2003.jpg|thumb|right|Brodeur during pre-game warmups in March 2003]]\nIn the [[2001–02 NHL season|2001–02 season]], Brodeur finished among the league leaders in wins and GAA.<ref name=\"hr\"/> Brodeur continued to lead the league in victories and remained a Vezina and MVP candidate. However, the Devils lost in the first round to the Hurricanes. The next season, in [[2002–03 NHL season|2002–03]], Brodeur won the Vezina Trophy for the first time.<ref name=\"Vezina\">{{cite web|url=http://www.legendsofhockey.net/LegendsOfHockey/jsp/SilverwareTrophyWinner.jsp?tro=VZT&year=2002-03|title=Vezina Trophy Winner: Brodeur, Martin|publisher=Hockey Hall of Fame|access-date=August 19, 2012}}</ref> He also won the Jennings Trophy again, was a [[Hart Memorial Trophy]] finalist for the league's Most Valuable Player, and was named a First Team All-Star and started in the All-Star Game. With one of the most impressive playoff performances of his career, Brodeur guided the Devils to their third Stanley Cup victory after seven-game series wins against the top-seeded Ottawa Senators and the seventh-seeded [[Mighty Ducks of Anaheim]]. He posted 3 shutouts against Anaheim and had a playoff total of 7 overall,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://scores.espn.go.com/nhl/recap?gameId=230609011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121009172206/http://scores.espn.go.com/nhl/recap?gameId=230609011|url-status=dead|archive-date=October 9, 2012|title=NHL Scoreboard – June 9, 2003: Anaheim Ducks at New Jersey Devils (recap)|publisher=ESPN Internet Ventures|access-date=April 17, 2007|date=June 9, 2003}}</ref> breaking the NHL record of 6 that had been set by [[Dominik Hašek]] the previous year.<ref>{{cite news|agency=Associated Press|url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/hockey/2003/playoffs/news/2003/06/10/devils_btn|title=2003 NHL playoffs – Statitudes|publisher=CNN SI|year=2003|access-date=April 12, 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20031229115104/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/hockey/2003/playoffs/news/2003/06/10/devils_btn/|archive-date=December 29, 2003|url-status=dead}}</ref> Despite this, the [[Conn Smythe Trophy]] for playoff MVP was awarded to Anaheim goaltender [[Jean-Sébastien Giguère]], who became the fifth player not on the championship team to be named playoff MVP since [[Ron Hextall]] of Philadelphia in 1987.<ref name=\"ConnSmythe\">{{cite web|url=http://www.nhl.com/ice/page.htm?id=24964|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100110120537/http://www.nhl.com/ice/page.htm?id=24964|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 10, 2010|title=Conn Smythe Trophy|publisher=NHL.com|access-date=October 14, 2016}}</ref> Some hockey writers speculated a New Jersey player did not win because there were multiple candidates, resulting in a [[split vote]] among the sportswriters who selected the winner.<ref name=\"PreSmythe03\">{{cite news|url=https://www.cbc.ca/sports/hockey/who-will-win-the-conn-smythe-1.399798|title=Who will win the Conn Smythe?|publisher=CBC Sports|access-date=November 28, 2006|date=June 6, 2003}}</ref><ref name=\"GiguereSmythe\">{{cite news|url=https://www.usatoday.com/sports/hockey/cup/2003-06-09-giguere-smythe_x.htm|title=Trophy, stats no consolation for Giguere|newspaper=[[USA Today]]|date=June 9, 2003|access-date=November 28, 2006 | first1=Rod | last1=Beaton}}</ref>\n\nIn the [[2003–04 NHL season|2003–04 season]], Brodeur won his second consecutive Vezina Trophy and Jennings Trophy. He was a first Team All-Star,<ref name=\"hr\"/> a starter in the NHL All-Star Game,<ref>{{cite news|last=Beaton|first=Rod|title=Messier sets All-Star game assist record in East's 6–4 win|work=USA Today|date=February 8, 2004|url=http://usatoday30.usatoday.com/sports/hockey/allstar/2004-02-08-all-star-game_x.htm|access-date=October 5, 2016}}</ref> and a finalist for the Hart Trophy again.<ref>{{cite web|title=2003–04 NHL Awards Voting|publisher=Hockey-Reference|url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/awards/voting-2004.html|access-date=October 5, 2016}}</ref> The Devils lost the [[Atlantic Division (NHL)|Atlantic Division]] title by 1 point to the Philadelphia Flyers, who thus obtained the third seed and home ice advantage against the sixth-seeded Devils in the first round of the playoffs. This would be too much for Brodeur and the Devils to overcome, as the Flyers went on to defeat them in five games.<ref>{{cite web|title=2003–04 NHL Summary|publisher=Hockey-Reference|url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/leagues/NHL_2004.html|access-date=October 5, 2016}}</ref>\n\n====The Brodeur Rule====\n[[File:NHL Hockey Rink.svg|thumb|upright=.65|The goaltender trapezoids behind each goal, added by the NHL before the 2005–06 season, were widely viewed as singling out Brodeur for his puck-handling skills.]]\nAfter the 2004–05 lockout and before the start of the 2005–06 season, the league instituted a new rule preventing goaltenders from playing the puck behind the [[goal line (ice hockey)|goal line]], except within a [[trapezoid]]-shaped zone located behind the net. The trapezoid began at the goal line with angled lines six feet from each [[goal post]] and widened to 28 feet at the [[boards (ice hockey)|end boards]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nhlofficials.com/images/Rules001-084.pdf|title=National Hockey League Official Rules 2005–06|publisher=National Hockey League|year=2005|page=64|access-date=October 14, 2016|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070313204543/http://www.nhlofficials.com/images/Rules001-084.pdf|archive-date=March 13, 2007}}</ref> This meant that if Brodeur or any other goaltenders played the puck behind the goal line and not in the trapezoid, a two-minute minor penalty for delay of game would be assessed. Former Flyers general manager Bobby Clarke was one of the leaders in getting the trapezoid implemented. This was viewed by many as singling out Brodeur, who was one of the best at getting behind the net to handle the puck, and has come to be known as the \"Brodeur Rule\".<ref name=\"Diamos2007\">{{cite news |author=Diamos |first=Jason |date=September 16, 2005 |title=New Rule Will Take a Weapon Away from Brodeur |url=https://select.nytimes.com/gst/abstract.html?res=F10616F835550C758DDDA00894DD404482 |access-date=March 2, 2007 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last= |date=September 12, 2014 |title=NHL Rule Changes for 2014-15 |url=https://scoutingtherefs.com/2014/09/4571/nhl-rule-changes-2014-15/ |access-date=December 26, 2024 |website=Scouting The Refs}}</ref>\n\nAt the 2009 NHL General Managers' Meeting, it was discussed whether the rule should be eliminated as a solution to the increasing number of injuries on defenceman who were being hit hard by forechecking forwards. The forecheckers were no longer impeded by defencemen holding them up because of the crackdown on interference, which created situations where defencemen were being hit at high speeds. Brodeur believed that revoking the trapezoid could result in more scoring and more exciting games. He explained, \"If you give the liberty to the goalies to play the puck, they'll mess up more than they're successful.\" He also expressed his concern for defencemen, \"It's a no-brainer if they want to start to eliminate these huge hits for the defencemen ... Whenever my defencemen or somebody was getting a big hit, I felt guilty that I let that guy get hit like that. Now, I've got to sit and watch all the time ... You've got to try to find something because so many guys are getting hurt.\" At the time of his statement, Devils defencemen [[Paul Martin (ice hockey)|Paul Martin]], [[Johnny Oduya]] and [[Bryce Salvador]] were all out with injuries.<ref name=\"Brodeur hopes NHL banishes trapezoid\">{{cite web|last=Gulitti|first=Tom|url=http://blogs.northjersey.com/blogs/fireice/comments/brodeur_hopes_nhl_banishes_trapezoid/|title=Brodeur hopes NHL banishes trapezoid|publisher=Fire&Ice|access-date=November 10, 2009|date=November 10, 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091113050802/http://blogs.northjersey.com/blogs/fireice/comments/brodeur_hopes_nhl_banishes_trapezoid|archive-date=November 13, 2009|url-status=dead}}</ref>\n\nUltimately the suggestion was rejected and the rule stayed in place. Former Maple Leafs' general manager [[Brian Burke (ice hockey)|Brian Burke]] said, \"We had originally approved a rule where the goaltenders couldn't handle the puck behind the net at all. The game was turning into a tennis match. You'd dump it in and the goalie would throw it out and now with the soft chip into the corner it turns into a puck battle and a forecheck opportunity, which is what we wanted.\"<ref name=\"NHL decides to keep trapezoid\">{{cite web|url=http://blogs.northjersey.com/blogs/fireice/nhl_decides_to_keep_trapezoid/|title=NHL decides to keep trapezoid|publisher=Fire&Ice|access-date=November 10, 2009|year=2009|archive-date=July 14, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110714195405/http://blogs.northjersey.com/blogs/fireice/nhl_decides_to_keep_trapezoid/|url-status=dead}}</ref>\n\nThe rule was later adopted into the KHL rulebook for the [[2019–20 KHL season]], and the IIHF rulebook in 2021.<ref>{{cite web |title=Rule changes for the 2019/20 season |url=https://en.khl.ru/news/2019/07/25/454577.html |access-date=May 2, 2023 |website=en.khl.ru}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=IIHF - New Rule Book for global game |url=https://www.iihf.com/en/events/2021/wm/news/26308/new_rule_book_for_global_game |access-date=May 2, 2023 |website=IIHF International Ice Hockey Federation}}</ref>\n\n====2005–2009====\nAfter the [[2004–05 NHL lockout]] canceled the [[2004–05 NHL season|2004–05 season]], Brodeur signed a contract extension with the Devils on January 27, 2006, that would pay him $31.2&nbsp;million over six years. In the [[2005–06 NHL season|2005–06 season]] he posted 43 wins, adding onto his NHL records of what were now five 40-win seasons and ten consecutive 30-win seasons.<ref name=\"30and10\">{{cite web|author=[[Associated Press]]|url=https://www.tsn.ca/nhl/teams/news_story/?ID=157193&hubname=nhl-devils|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070310131328/http://www.tsn.ca/nhl/teams/news_story/?ID=157193&hubname=nhl-devils|archive-date=March 10, 2007|title=Brodeur sets goaltending mark in Devils win|date=March 4, 2006|access-date=December 6, 2006|publisher=TSN}}</ref> After struggling early in the season, his improved play later on made him a finalist for the Vezina Trophy for the third straight year,<ref name=\"Vezina0506\">{{cite web|url=http://panthers.nhl.com/club/news.htm?id=440530|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131031212014/http://panthers.nhl.com/club/news.htm?id=440530|url-status=dead|archive-date=October 31, 2013|title=NHL Announces 2005–06 Trophy Finalists|publisher=Florida Panthers|date=May 4, 2006|access-date=May 17, 2013}}</ref> and helped lead the Devils to a surprising comeback in the last two months of the season that resulted in them winning the Atlantic Division in the final game of the year.<ref name=\"Atlantic2006\">{{cite web|url=http://www.msgnetwork.com/content_news.jsp?articleID=v0000msgn20060419T023023461&newsgroup=ap.sportsml.columnist.article&sports=ice-hockey&team=Devils&league=nhl|title=Devils complete comeback to capture Atlantic Division title|publisher=MSG Network|access-date=March 5, 2007|year=2006|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070928105410/http://www.msgnetwork.com/content_news.jsp?articleID=v0000msgn20060419T023023461&newsgroup=ap.sportsml.columnist.article&sports=ice-hockey&team=Devils&league=nhl|archive-date=September 28, 2007|url-status=dead}}</ref> In the first round of the playoffs, he won a postseason series against the Rangers for the first time in his career, leading the Devils to a four-game sweep.<ref>{{cite magazine|last=DeLessio|first=Joe|title=Rangers vs. Devils: A Postseason History|magazine=New York|date=May 14, 2012|url=http://nymag.com/daily/sports/2012/05/rangers-vs-devils-a-postseason-history.html|access-date=October 17, 2016}}</ref> But a 4–1 series loss to the Carolina Hurricanes eliminated the Devils in the next round.<ref>{{cite web|title=2006 NHL Stanley Cup Playoffs Summary|publisher=Hockey-Reference|url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/playoffs/NHL_2006.html|access-date=October 17, 2016}}</ref>\n\n[[File:MartinBrodeur.jpg|thumb|upright=0.75|Brodeur in December 2007]]\nIn the [[2006–07 NHL season|2006–07 season]], Brodeur made his ninth NHL All-Star Game appearance in [[Dallas, Texas]], won his third Vezina Trophy and rose on several NHL records lists. On December 8, 2006, he posted a 2–0 victory over the Philadelphia Flyers for his 462nd career win, moving him into second place on the all-time list ahead of [[Ed Belfour]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nhl.com/gamecenter/phi-vs-njd/2006/12/08/2006020421|title=Devils 2, Flyers 0|publisher=New Jersey Devils. Associated Press|year=2006|access-date=October 5, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130528001459/http://devils.nhl.com/club/recap.htm?id=2006020421|archive-date=May 28, 2013|url-status=live}}</ref> Just a few weeks later, on December 26, Brodeur beat the Pittsburgh Penguins 3–0 to record his 85th career shutout, moving him past Glenn Hall for third place on that all-time list and first place among all active goaltenders.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://sports.yahoo.com/nhl/recap;_ylt=AtFCxMTuQK_xMxtSoR30ZsZ7vLYF?gid=2006122611&prov=ap|title=Penguins Devils Recap – Tuesday December 26, 2006|publisher=Yahoo Sports!|year=2006|access-date=December 26, 2006}}</ref> On February 1, 2007, Brodeur beat the Philadelphia Flyers 6–5 in overtime to take the all-time lead in overtime (non-shootout) wins with 45, passing Roy.<ref>{{cite book|last=Weekes|first=Don|title=Crease-Crashing Hockey Trivia|publisher=Greystone Books|year=2007|page=49|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7gxQrPbdsCEC&pg=PA49|isbn=9781926685113}}</ref> The Devils' first 38 wins of the season were all with Brodeur in net, leading him to set an NHL record for most consecutive wins for a team.<ref name=\"38consecutive\">{{cite web|url=http://sports.espn.go.com/nhl/recap?gameId=270225023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110604042159/http://sports.espn.go.com/nhl/recap?gameId=270225023|url-status=dead|archive-date=June 4, 2011|title=Devils goalie Clemmensen gets first win in 11 months|publisher=ESPN|access-date=April 12, 2007|year=2007}}</ref>\n\nOn April 3, 2007, Brodeur tied the NHL record for most wins in a single season with 47, set by [[Bernie Parent]] in [[1973–74 NHL season|1973–74]], in a 2–1 shootout victory against the Ottawa Senators.<ref name=\"Standings0226\">{{cite news|url=https://sports.yahoo.com/nhl/standings;_ylt=Ah6GJ3htsMPCh5StqCrl7Ih7vLYF|title=2006–07 NHL Standings|work=Yahoo! Sports|access-date=April 4, 2007|year=2007}}</ref> Two days later, he broke the record with his 48th win in a 3–2 victory over the Philadelphia Flyers, which helped the Devils clinch the Atlantic Division title.<ref>{{cite news|last=Gelston|first=Dan|title=Brodeur Breaks NHL Mark With 48th Win|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|agency=Associated Press|date=April 5, 2007|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2007/04/05/AR2007040502193.html|access-date=October 17, 2016}}</ref>\n\nIn the Eastern Conference quarterfinals against the [[Tampa Bay Lightning]], Brodeur started out shaky and the Devils fell behind two games to one.<ref name=\"oust\">{{cite news|last=Goodall|first=Fred|title=Martin Brodeur, Devils oust Lightning|work=USA Today|agency=Associated Press|date=April 23, 2007|url=http://usatoday30.usatoday.com/sports/hockey/2007-04-23-807091474_x.htm|access-date=October 17, 2016}}</ref> He rebounded, however, to finish the series, and helped the team advance in six games, while passing [[Grant Fuhr]] for second place in all-time playoff victories.<ref name=\"oust\"/> In the second round against the Ottawa Senators, the Devils were defeated in five games as the Senators scored 15 goals during the series.<ref>{{cite web|title=2007 NHL Stanley Cup Playoffs Summary|publisher=Hockey-Reference|url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/playoffs/NHL_2007.html|access-date=October 17, 2016}}</ref>\n\nIn the [[2007–08 NHL season|2007–08 season]], Brodeur became the second goaltender in NHL history to reach 500 wins with a victory against the Flyers on November 17, 2007.<ref>{{cite web |title=Brodeur closes down Flyers to collect 500th victory |url=https://www.espn.com/nhl/recap/_/gameId/271117015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211213201118/https://www.espn.com/nhl/recap/_/gameId/271117015 |url-status=dead |archive-date=December 13, 2021 |website=ESPN |access-date=December 12, 2021 |date=November 17, 2007}}</ref> The only other goaltenders to achieve the feat are Roy<ref>{{cite news|title=Devils' Brodeur joins Roy as member of 500-win club|work=USA Today|agency=Associated Press|date=November 19, 2007|url=http://usatoday30.usatoday.com/sports/hockey/nhl/2007-11-17-devils-flyers-brodeur-500_N.htm|access-date=October 17, 2016}}</ref> and [[Marc-André Fleury]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.espn.com/nhl/story/_/id/32833948/marc-andre-fleury-earns-500th-win-chicago-blackhawks-win-montreal-canadiens|title=Marc-Andre Fleury earns 500th win in Chicago Blackhawks' win over Montreal Canadiens|work=ESPN|date=December 10, 2021|access-date=December 10, 2021}}</ref> Brodeur was also named the starting goaltender for the Eastern Conference in the [[2008 NHL All-Star Game]] in [[Atlanta]]. However, he was unable to participate because of a family obligation.<ref>{{cite web|last=Gulitti|first=Tom|title=Brodeur pulls out of all-star game|publisher=Fire&Ice|date=January 22, 2008|url=http://fireandice.northjersey.com/fire-ice-1.174987/brodeur-pulls-out-of-all-star-game-1.99470|access-date=October 17, 2016}}</ref>\n\n[[File:Averyrule.jpg|right|thumb|Sean Avery attempts to distract Brodeur during game three of the first round of the 2008 Stanley Cup Playoffs.]]\nAfter losing a bitter series against the rival Rangers in the opening round of the 2008 NHL playoffs, Brodeur refused to shake [[Sean Avery]]'s hand. During game three of the series, in an unusual move, Avery turned to face Brodeur during a 5-on-3 [[Power play (sporting term)|power play]], and began waving his hands and stick in front of Brodeur's face in an effort to distract him. The day after this game the NHL announced that it had revised its [[unsportsmanlike conduct]] rule, now known as [[Sean Avery#The Avery Rule|The Sean Avery Rule]], effectively outlawing such antics.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=377787|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130614064305/http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=377787|url-status=dead|archive-date=June 14, 2013|title=NHL reacts quickly to Avery's antics, amends unsportsmanlike conduct rule|publisher=NHL.com. Associated Press|date=April 14, 2008|access-date=August 10, 2012}}</ref>\n\nBrodeur started wearing a new painted mask design for the [[2008–09 NHL season]] with a stylized \"MB30\" on the front, replacing the \"J\" that had been on his mask for nearly his entire NHL career.<ref>{{cite web|last=Marin|first=Eric|title=Brodeur debuts new mask at practice|publisher=National Hockey League|date=October 8, 2008|url=https://www.nhl.com/devils/news/brodeur-debuts-new-mask-at-practice/c-458441|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190919043953/https://www.nhl.com/devils/news/brodeur-debuts-new-mask-at-practice/c-458441|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 19, 2019|access-date=October 17, 2016}}</ref> During a game on November 1, 2008, Brodeur suffered a \"bruised elbow\" which would later be diagnosed as a torn distal [[biceps]] tendon, the first major injury in his career. Following surgery on November 6, he would miss 16 weeks of the season before playing his next game on February 26, 2009. Upon returning from the injury, Brodeur registered a 4–0 shutout against the Colorado Avalanche for his 99th career shutout.<ref>{{cite web|agency=Associated Press|url=https://www.nhl.com/gamecenter/col-vs-njd/2009/02/26/2008020909|title=Marty's back, as good as ever|publisher=[[NHL.com]]|date=February 26, 2009|access-date=February 26, 2009}}</ref> Three days later, he recorded his 100th career shutout against the Philadelphia Flyers, three short of [[Terry Sawchuk]]'s NHL record.<ref>{{cite news|title=Brodeur records 100th shutout as Devils widen gap on Flyers|work=USA Today|agency=Associated Press|date=March 2, 2009|url=http://usatoday30.usatoday.com/sports/hockey/nhl/2009-03-01-devils-flyers_N.htm|access-date=October 17, 2016}}</ref>\n\n====2009–2014====\nBeginning in 2009, Brodeur broke a number of career records for goaltenders. He missed 50 games in the 2008–09 season, but a winning streak upon his return pushed him near the NHL's all-time win record.<ref name=\"winningest\">{{cite news|title=Martin Brodeur becomes all-time winningest NHL goalie|work=USA Today|date=March 17, 2009|url=http://usatoday30.usatoday.com/sports/hockey/nhl/2009-03-17-martin-brodeur-wins-record-devils-blackhawks_N.htm|access-date=October 7, 2009}}</ref> On March 14, 2009, the Devils defeated the Canadiens 3–1 to give him the 551st win of his career, tying him with Roy for the NHL record.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=413927 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090316042346/http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=413927 | url-status = dead | archive-date = March 16, 2009 | title = Roy glad to be there for Brodeur's big night | publisher = NHL.com | first = Dan | last = Rosen | date = March 15, 2009 | access-date = March 19, 2009}}</ref> Three days later, Brodeur surpassed Roy with a 3–2 win over the [[Chicago Blackhawks]] in New Jersey.<ref name=\"winningest\"/>\n\nBrodeur topped another of Roy's previous marks on November 27, as he set the record for the most minutes played in the NHL, which had been 60,235.<ref>{{cite news|title=Brodeur sets minutes mark as Devils beat Bruins|work=New York Daily News|agency=Associated Press|date=November 27, 2009|url=http://www.nydailynews.com/sports/hockey/new-jersey-devils-beat-boston-bruins-goalie-martin-brodeur-nhl-all-time-minutes-leader-article-1.417597|access-date=October 7, 2016}}</ref> His 1,030th career appearance, which happened on December 18, broke Roy's record of 1,029.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nhl.com/ice/m_news.htm?id=510467|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161009170252/http://www.nhl.com/ice/m_news.htm?id=510467|url-status=dead|archive-date=October 9, 2016|title=Devils goalie Brodeur plays in 1,030th game, breaks Patrick Roy's NHL record |access-date=October 7, 2016|agency=Canadian Press |date=December 18, 2009 |publisher=[[NHL.com]]}}</ref> He also set the mark for the most regular season shutouts with a 4–0 win against the Penguins on December 21, breaking Sawchuk's record of 103.<ref>{{cite web|title=Martin Brodeur Sets NHL Shutout Record, Devils Win 4-0|work=NESN.com|date=December 21, 2009|url=https://nesn.com/2009/12/martin-brodeur-sets-nhl-shutout-record-devils-win-40/|access-date=February 7, 2026|archive-url=https://archive.today/20260207090856/https://nesn.com/2009/12/martin-brodeur-sets-nhl-shutout-record-devils-win-40/|archive-date=February 7, 2026}}</ref> On December 30, 2009, Brodeur and the Devils shut out the Penguins, 2–0. It was his 105th career shutout, giving him the all-time professional record, surpassing [[George Hainsworth]]'s total of 104 combined in the NHL (94) and [[Western Canada Hockey League]] (10).<ref>{{cite news|last=Stephenson|first=Colin|title=Martin Brodeur's 32 saves lead NJ Devils to a 2–0 victory over the Pittsburgh Penguins|work=The Star-Ledger|date=December 31, 2009|url=http://www.nj.com/devils/index.ssf/2009/12/martin_brodeur_makes_32_saves.html|access-date=October 24, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine|last=Zweig|first=Eric|title=Brodeur Still Needs One More Shutout To Become The 'Major League' King|magazine=The Hockey News|date=December 23, 2009|url=https://thehockeynews.com/news/news/brodeur-still-needs-one-more-shutout-to-become-the-amajor-leaguea-king|access-date=October 24, 2016}}</ref> On April 6, 2010, Brodeur reached his 600th career win by defeating the Thrashers 3–0. This was also his 110th career shutout.<ref>{{cite news|title=Martin Brodeur grabs 600th career win, New Jersey Devils blank Thrashers, 3–0|work=New York Daily News|agency=Associated Press|date=April 6, 2010|url=http://www.nydailynews.com/sports/hockey/martin-brodeur-grabs-600th-career-win-new-jersey-devils-blank-thrashers-3-0-article-1.168577|access-date=October 24, 2016}}</ref>\n\n[[File:Martin Brodeur vs Islanders in Nov 2011.jpg|thumb|left|Brodeur tending goal in November 2011]]\nIn the [[2009–10 NHL season]], Brodeur led the NHL in wins (45), shutouts (9), games played (77) and minutes played (4,499). He also won his fifth Jennings Trophy and had the third-best GAA in the league, leading his team to back-to-back division wins that included a 6–0 regular season sweep of the defending Stanley Cup champion Penguins. However, the Devils lost in the first round of the playoffs, losing to the seventh-seeded Flyers in five games.\n\nBrodeur had a 5–18–1 stretch to begin the [[2010–11 NHL season|2010–11 season]],<ref>{{cite web|last=Mazzeo|first=Mike|title=Martin Brodeur thinking return|publisher=ESPN|date=May 29, 2012|url=https://www.espn.com/espnw/news-commentary/story/_/id/7981230/2012-stanley-cup-finals-martin-brodeur-leaning-returning-season|access-date=October 12, 2016}}</ref> as New Jersey slumped to the bottom of the NHL.<ref>{{cite news|title=Devils' Martin Brodeur has sprained right knee|work=USA Today|agency=Associated Press|date=February 8, 2011|url=http://usatoday30.usatoday.com/sports/hockey/nhl/devils/2011-02-08-martin-brodeur-sprained-knee_N.htm|access-date=October 12, 2016}}</ref> Although the Devils improved in the second half of the season, they did not reach the [[2011 Stanley Cup playoffs|playoffs]];<ref name=\"back\">{{cite web|last=Morreale|first=Mike|title=DeBoer's task: Get Devils back into playoffs|publisher=New Jersey Devils|date=August 31, 2011|url=https://www.nhl.com/devils/news/deboers-task-get-devils-back-into-playoffs/c-587531|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161030075422/https://www.nhl.com/devils/news/deboers-task-get-devils-back-into-playoffs/c-587531|url-status=dead|archive-date=October 30, 2016|access-date=October 12, 2016}}</ref> Brodeur recorded 23 wins and a 2.45 GAA,<ref name=\"hr\"/> but had his lowest save percentage (.903) in 16 seasons.<ref name=\"back\"/>\n\nThe Devils returned to the [[2012 Stanley Cup playoffs|playoffs]] in the [[2011–12 NHL season]], as Brodeur recorded his 14th 30-win season. In game one of the conference quarterfinals against the Panthers, Brodeur became the second goaltender to record 100 playoff wins in a 3–2 Devils victory. In game four with a 4–0 victory, Brodeur broke the NHL career playoff shutout record with his 24th, surpassing Roy, who had 23.<ref>{{cite news|title=NHL: Martin Brodeur's record-setting 24th playoff shutout helps New Jersey Devils tie series with Florida Panthers|work=San Jose Mercury News|agency=Associated Press|date=April 19, 2012|url=http://www.mercurynews.com/2012/04/19/nhl-martin-brodeurs-record-setting-24th-playoff-shutout-helps-new-jersey-devils-tie-series-with-florida-panthers/|access-date=October 7, 2016}}</ref> The Devils advanced by winning game seven in double overtime, after Brodeur had made 43 saves to keep his team in the contest.<ref name=\"last\">{{cite web|last=Rosen|first=Dan|title=Brodeur enjoyed last hurrah in 2012 Final|publisher=National Hockey League|date=February 8, 2016|url=https://www.nhl.com/news/martin-brodeur-2012-stanley-cup-final-278449674|access-date=October 19, 2016}}</ref>\n\nFollowing a second round series win over the Flyers, Brodeur and the Devils defeated the Rangers in six games in the Eastern Conference finals.<ref name=\"last\"/> New Jersey won the sixth game 3–2 on an overtime goal by [[Adam Henrique]], leading to Brodeur's fifth [[2012 Stanley Cup Final|Stanley Cup Final]] appearance.<ref>{{cite magazine|last=Proteau|first=Adam|title=Brodeur Shows Lundqvist How To Win In Playoffs|magazine=The Hockey News|date=May 25, 2012|url=https://thehockeynews.com/news/news/brodeur-shows-lundqvist-how-to-win-in-playoffs|access-date=October 19, 2016}}</ref> The Devils lost in the series to the [[Los Angeles Kings]] in six games. Brodeur was 14–10 in the postseason with a save percentage of .917, after winning 16 playoff games in the previous eight years.<ref name=\"last\"/>\n\n[[File:Martin Brodeur - New Jersey Devils.jpg|thumb|upright|Brodeur before a game in April 2014]]\nDuring the off-season of 2012, Brodeur hired agent [[Pat Brisson]], leading many analysts to believe he would test free-agency or retire. However, on July 2, 2012, Brodeur agreed to a two-year, $9&nbsp;million deal to remain with the Devils, alongside backup goaltender [[Johan Hedberg]].<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=636924 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120704195627/http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=636924 | url-status = dead | archive-date = July 4, 2012 | title = Brodeur and Hedberg staying with Devils | publisher = NHL.com | first = Dan | last = Rosen | date = July 2, 2012 | access-date = July 3, 2012}}</ref> On March 21, 2013, in his first game back from a month-long absence due to a pinched nerve injury in his upper back, Brodeur was credited with a power play goal against the Carolina Hurricanes,<ref name=\"scores\">{{cite web|title=Devils goalie Martin Brodeur scores 3rd career goal in win|publisher=ESPN|agency=Associated Press|date=March 21, 2013|url=https://www.espn.com/nhl/recap?gameId=400442920|access-date=October 24, 2016}}</ref> making him the only NHL goaltender to record three career goals,<ref>{{cite web|last=McIndoe|first=Sean|title=Great Moments in Goalie Goal-Scoring History|publisher=Grantland|date=October 23, 2013|url=http://grantland.com/the-triangle/great-moments-in-goalie-goal-scoring-history/|access-date=October 24, 2016}}</ref> and the first goaltender to score on the power play since [[Evgeni Nabokov]] in 2002.<ref name=\"scores\"/> Brodeur had a 13–9–7 record in his 29 appearances in 2012–13, with a 2.22 GAA.<ref name=\"hr\"/>\n\nThe following season, he shared the Devils' starting goaltender position with [[Cory Schneider]], whose 45 games played were six more than Brodeur's total.<ref name=\"exits\">{{cite web|last=Rosen|first=Dan|title=Devils' Brodeur exits to cheers, unsure of future|publisher=National Hockey League|date=April 13, 2014|url=https://www.nhl.com/news/devils-brodeur-exits-to-cheers-unsure-of-future/c-714485|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161104010012/https://www.nhl.com/news/devils-brodeur-exits-to-cheers-unsure-of-future/c-714485|url-status=dead|archive-date=November 4, 2016|access-date=November 2, 2016}}</ref> Brodeur's statistical performance declined, as his GAA increased to 2.51, more than half a goal higher than Schneider. In 39 games played, Brodeur had a .901 save percentage, lower than the league average.<ref name=\"test\"/> Among his 19 wins in 2013–14 was a victory in the season finale against Boston, his 688th for New Jersey.<ref name=\"exits\"/> On June 6, 2014, Brodeur told ESPN he would test the free agency market for the 2014–15 season,<ref name=\"test\">{{cite web|last=Peters|first=Chris|title=Martin Brodeur says he'll test free agency this offseason|work=CBS Sports|date=June 6, 2014|url=http://www.cbssports.com/nhl/news/martin-brodeur-says-hell-test-free-agency-this-offseason/|access-date=October 24, 2016}}</ref> and his 21-year tenure with the Devils ended.<ref>{{cite web|title=Retired Martin Brodeur: 'My Hockey Career Is All About The Devils'|publisher=WCBS-TV|agency=Associated Press|date=January 29, 2015|url=http://newyork.cbslocal.com/2015/01/29/retired-martin-brodeur-my-hockey-career-is-all-about-the-devils/|access-date=October 24, 2016}}</ref>\n\n===St. Louis Blues===\nOn November 26, 2014, Brodeur signed a tryout contract with the [[St. Louis Blues]] after their starting netminder, [[Brian Elliott]], was injured.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=740984&navid=DL%7CNHL%7Chome | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150119183935/http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=740984&navid=DL%7CNHL%7Chome | url-status=dead | archive-date=January 19, 2015 | title=Blues' Elliott week-to-week; Brodeur in as tryout | date=November 26, 2014 | access-date=November 26, 2014 | author=Louie Korac |publisher=NHL.com}}</ref> A week later, on December 2, Brodeur signed a one-year, $700,000 deal with the Blues.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=741941&navid=DL%7CNHL%7Chome | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150119183404/http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=741941&navid=DL%7CNHL%7Chome | url-status=dead | archive-date=January 19, 2015 | title=Brodeur signs one-year contract with Blues | date=December 2, 2014 | access-date=December 2, 2014 | author=Louie Korac |publisher=NHL.com}}</ref>\n\nOn January 27, 2015, it was reported that Brodeur had decided to retire from the NHL.<ref name=\"always\">{{cite news|last=Allen|first=Kevin|title=Martin Brodeur retiring with Blues, will always be Devil|work=USA Today|date=January 27, 2015|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/nhl/2015/01/27/martin-brodeur-retire-st-louis-blues-new-jersey-devils/22413675/|access-date=October 31, 2016}}</ref> The decision followed Elliott's return to the Blues, as Brodeur had been demoted to the team's number-three goaltender behind Elliott and [[Jake Allen (ice hockey)|Jake Allen]]. Brodeur announced the news at a press conference two days later.<ref name=\"retires\"/> He retired having started just five games with the Blues, going 3–3–0 in seven appearances.<ref name=\"hr\"/> His final NHL win was a 3–0 shutout against the Avalanche on December 29, 2014.<ref name=\"retires\"/>\n\n==Post-playing career==\nUpon announcing his retirement, Brodeur was hired by the Blues as a special assistant to general manager Doug Armstrong.<ref name=\"retires\">{{cite news|title=Martin Brodeur retires, joins Blues management|work=Toronto Star|agency=Canadian Press|date=January 29, 2015|url=https://www.thestar.com/sports/hockey/2015/01/29/martin-brodeur-retires-joins-blues-management.html|access-date=October 21, 2016}}</ref> On May 22, 2015, Armstrong announced that Brodeur and the Blues had agreed to a three-year contract naming Brodeur as an assistant general manager of the team.<ref>{{cite web|url = https://www.espn.com/nhl/story/_/id/12922448/martin-brodeur-named-assistant-general-manager-st-louis-blues|title = Blues name Martin Brodeur assistant GM|date = May 22, 2015|access-date = May 22, 2015| website = ESPN|last = Strang|first = Katie}}</ref> On February 8, 2016, the New Jersey Devils unveiled a bronze statue of Brodeur which is displayed outside the [[Prudential Center]]. The statue was formally dedicated on October 22, 2016, in a ceremony before the game against the [[Minnesota Wild]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Martin Brodeur statue unveiled: Devils great gets emotional seeing himself in bronze|url=http://www.nj.com/devils/index.ssf/2016/02/marty_brodeur_statue_unveiled_devils_gets_emotiona.html|publisher=NJ.com|date=February 8, 2016|access-date=May 31, 2016}}</ref> On February 9, 2016, Brodeur's number 30 jersey was retired by the Devils.<ref>{{cite web|last=Mazzeo|first=Mike|url=https://www.espn.com/nhl/story/_/id/14750379/new-jersey-devils-retire-martin-brodeur-no-30-jersey|title=Martin Brodeur: Fan response to jersey retirement 'as good as it gets'|publisher=ESPN|date=February 10, 2016|access-date=May 31, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Ryan|first1=Chris|title=Devils to dedicate Martin Brodeur statue on Oct. 22|url=http://www.nj.com/devils/index.ssf/2016/08/devils_to_dedicate_martin_brodeur_statue_on_oct_22.html| website = NJ.com|date=August 29, 2016|access-date=October 20, 2016}}</ref>\n\nOn July 25, 2017, Brodeur was appointed as management team member for [[Canada men's national ice hockey team|Canada's men's team]] for the [[Ice hockey at the 2018 Winter Olympics|2018 Winter Olympics]] in [[Pyeongchang]], South Korea.<ref name=\"cbc072017\">{{cite news|last1=Harrison|first1=Doug|title=Willie Desjardins fronts Canadian Olympic hockey coaching staff|url=http://www.cbc.ca/sports/olympics/winter/watch-hockey-canada-olympic-announcement-1.4220399|access-date=July 25, 2017|publisher=CBC Sports|date=July 25, 2017}}</ref> On August 29, 2018, Brodeur joined the Devils as executive vice president of business development.<ref>{{cite web |title=Devils name Martin Brodeur Executive VP of Business Development |url=https://www.nhl.com/devils/news/devils-name-martin-brodeur-executive-vp-of-business-development-299886572 |website=NHL.com |access-date=August 30, 2018 |date=August 29, 2018}}</ref> On January 12, 2020, Brodeur became an advisor on hockey operations after general manager [[Ray Shero]] was fired.<ref>{{cite web |title=Statement from Josh Harris, Devils Managing Partner & Chairman |url=https://www.nhl.com/devils/news/statement-from-josh-harris-devils-managing-partner-chairman-313848508 |website=NHL.com |access-date=January 13, 2020 |date=January 12, 2020}}</ref>\n\n==International play==\n{{MedalTableTop|Martin Brodeur Switzerland vs. Canada (4371447238) (cropped1).jpg|220px|Brodeur playing for the [[Canada men's national ice hockey team|Canadian national team]] in the [[Ice hockey at the 2010 Winter Olympics|2010 Winter Olympics]]|name=no}}\n{{MedalSport|Men's [[ice hockey]]}}\n{{MedalCountry|{{ih|CAN}}}}\n{{MedalCompetition|[[Ice hockey at the Olympic Games|Winter Olympics]]}}\n{{MedalGold|[[Ice hockey at the 2002 Winter Olympics|2002 Salt Lake City]]|}}\n{{MedalGold|[[Ice hockey at the 2010 Winter Olympics|2010 Vancouver]]|}}\n{{MedalCompetition|[[Ice Hockey World Championships|World Championships]]}}\n{{MedalSilver|[[1996 Men's World Ice Hockey Championships|1996 Austria]]|}}\n{{MedalSilver|[[2005 Men's World Ice Hockey Championships|2005 Austria]]|}}\n{{MedalBottom}}\nBrodeur was selected as [[Canada men's national ice hockey team|Canada]]'s back-up goaltender to Roy for the [[Ice hockey at the 1998 Winter Olympics|1998 Winter Olympics]] in [[Nagano (city)|Nagano]], Japan, but did not get to play. Canada failed to win a medal after losing the bronze-medal match to [[Finland men's national ice hockey team|Finland]], a game in which many people thought Brodeur should have played.<ref name=\"NoBronze\">{{cite news |agency=[[Canadian Press]] |url=https://www.tsn.ca/story/print/?id=133888|title=Backup battle heats up at Canada camp |publisher=TSN.ca |date=August 18, 2005 |access-date=February 27, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110604035017/http://www.tsn.ca/story/print/?id=133888 |archive-date=June 4, 2011 |url-status=dead}}</ref>\n\nIn the [[Ice hockey at the 2002 Winter Olympics|2002 Winter Olympics]] at [[Salt Lake City]], U.S., Brodeur was initially named the backup behind [[Curtis Joseph]]. But following Joseph's losing the tournament opener against [[Sweden men's national ice hockey team|Sweden]], Brodeur was named the starting goaltender the rest of the way, and won gold for Canada.<ref name=\"change\">{{cite web|last=LeBrun|first=Pierre|title=It's time Canada made a change in net|publisher=ESPN|date=February 22, 2010|url=https://www.espn.com/olympics/winter/2010/icehockey/columns/story?id=4935120&columnist=lebrun_pierre|access-date=November 14, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Rosen|first=Dan|title=Olympic gold medal put Broduer 'on a pedestal'|publisher=National Hockey League|date=February 6, 2016|url=https://www.nhl.com/devils/news/olympic-gold-medal-put-brodeur-on-a-pedestal/c-867519|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161115133938/https://www.nhl.com/devils/news/olympic-gold-medal-put-brodeur-on-a-pedestal/c-867519|url-status=dead|archive-date=November 15, 2016|access-date=November 14, 2016}}</ref> He went undefeated in the tournament, stopping 31 of 33 shots in the gold-medal victory over the [[United States men's national ice hockey team|United States]].<ref name=\"sr\">{{cite Sports-Reference|title=Martin Brodeur|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/athletes/br/martin-brodeur-1.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200418000227/https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/athletes/br/martin-brodeur-1.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 18, 2020|access-date=November 14, 2016}}</ref>\n\nBrodeur then led Canada to the [[2004 World Cup of Hockey]] championship, allowing five goals in five games. He led all goaltenders in GAA and save percentage while going undefeated.<ref name=\"better\">{{cite web|last=Hradek|first=E. J.|title=Brodeur better than lucky|publisher=ESPN|date=September 14, 2004|url=https://www.espn.com/nhl/worldcup04/columns/story?id=1881826&columnist=hradek_ej|access-date=November 14, 2016}}</ref> He had another impressive performance for the team at the world hockey championships in the following year. After this, ''The Sports Forecaster 2005–06'' said the following:<ref name=\"MainBio\"/>\n\n{{blockquote|Brodeur is arguably the top goaltender in the world. Fresh off a World Cup win in 2004 and another strong performance at the 2005 IIHF World hockey championships. He's the game's best puck-handling goaltender, though the NHL's new rules changes may somewhat alter that effectiveness.}}\n\nBrodeur was selected as Canada's starter in the [[Ice hockey at the 2006 Winter Olympics|2006 Winter Olympics]] in [[Turin]], Italy.<ref>Brodeur and Cox, p. 116.</ref> He started in 4 games, but Canada failed to win a medal after losing to [[Russia men's national ice hockey team|Russia]] in the quarterfinals.<ref name=\"sr\"/>\n\nHe was one of the three goaltenders for Canada in the [[Ice hockey at the 2010 Winter Olympics|2010 Winter Olympics]] in [[Vancouver]], Canada.<ref name=\"change\"/> He registered a shootout win against [[Switzerland men's national ice hockey team|Switzerland]] and a loss to the United States. After the loss to the US, he was benched for the remainder of the 2010 Games in favour of [[Roberto Luongo]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Olympic Men's Hockey: 2010 Vancouver Summary|publisher=Hockey Hall of Fame|url=https://www.hhof.com/htmlTimeCapsule/oly2010.shtml|access-date=November 14, 2016|archive-date=November 15, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161115135336/https://www.hhof.com/htmlTimeCapsule/oly2010.shtml|url-status=dead}}</ref>\n{{clear}}\n\n==Personal life==\nBrodeur married Melanie Dubois (a native of [[Saint-Liboire, Quebec]]) in August 1995. They have four children:<ref name=\"HHOFjournal\"/> Anthony, born in 1995; twin sons, William and [[Jeremy Brodeur|Jeremy]], born in 1996; and Anabelle Antoinette, 2002. Melanie filed for divorce during the 2003 playoffs amid reports that Brodeur was having an affair with Genevieve Nault, the wife of Melanie's brother.<ref name=\"divorce\">{{cite news |url=http://sports.espn.go.com/nhl/playoffs2003/story?id=1557270|title=Brodeur's wife files for divorce|work=ESPN.com|date=May 21, 2003|access-date=April 12, 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060519202430/http://sports.espn.go.com/nhl/playoffs2003/story?id=1557270|archive-date=May 19, 2006|url-status=dead}}</ref> The incident was referred to by opposing fans during the playoffs.<ref name=\"heckling\">{{cite news |url=http://archive.sportingnews.com/nhl/articles/20030510/472987.html|title=Canada's capital primed for East finals|publisher=sportingnews.com|year=2003|access-date=April 15, 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081014113451/http://archive.sportingnews.com/nhl/articles/20030510/472987.html|archive-date=October 14, 2008|url-status=dead}}</ref> The reports proved to be true, as he and Genevieve married in June 2008.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://sports.yahoo.com/nhl/blog/puck_daddy/post/Romantic-or-insane-Marty-Brodeur-gets-married-a?urn=nhl,91034|title=Romantic or insane: Marty Brodeur gets married again|date=June 30, 2008|access-date=June 30, 2008|author=Puck Daddy|work=Yahoo! Sports|archive-date=October 22, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121022172018/http://sports.yahoo.com/nhl/blog/puck_daddy/post/Romantic-or-insane-Marty-Brodeur-gets-married-a?urn=nhl,91034|url-status=dead}}</ref> Their first child together, Maxime Philippe Brodeur, was born in November 2009.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://blogs.northjersey.com/blogs/fireice/comments/brodeur_a_happy_father_--_again/|title=Brodeur a happy father—again; Eckford and Corrente switch spots|last=Gulitti|first=Tom|date=November 24, 2009|work=The Bergen Record|access-date=November 24, 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091128095610/http://blogs.northjersey.com/blogs/fireice/comments/brodeur_a_happy_father_--_again|archive-date=November 28, 2009|url-status=dead}}</ref>\n\nBrodeur is regarded as an engaging [[raconteur]] in his spare time.<ref name=\"HHOFjournal\"/> He has hosted a [[street hockey]] tournament in his hometown of [[Saint-Leonard, Quebec]], for each of the Devils' [[Stanley Cup]] championships, where he played as a [[forward (hockey)|forward]]. His oldest brother, Denis Jr., is a photographer like their late father, [[Denis Brodeur]], and his other older brother, Claude, was a minor league baseball pitcher in the [[Montreal Expos]]' organization. He has two sisters, Line and Sylvie.<ref name=\"HHOFjournal\"/>\n\nIn 2005, Brodeur began co-authoring his autobiography, ''Brodeur: Beyond the Crease'', with long-time ''[[Toronto Star]]'' columnist and [[ESPN]] contributor [[Damien Cox]], which was released in October 2006. Some of the things Brodeur talks about in the book are player salaries and contracts, NHL marketing, [[Lou Lamoriello]], and the Devils' new arena in Newark, the [[Prudential Center]]. Brodeur also includes his views on the \"new NHL\" after the lockout, and how it affected his career.<ref name=\"biography\">{{cite book|title=Brodeur: Beyond the Crease (Hardcover)|year=2006|isbn=0470838515|last1=Brodeur |first1=Martin |last2=Cox |first2=Damien |publisher=Wiley}}</ref>\n\nBrodeur co-owns a business called La Pizzeria Etc. with former teammate [[Sheldon Souray]]. The idea came about after Souray was traded to play in [[Montreal]], the city in which the business now operates.<ref name=\"Pizzeria\">{{cite web|url=http://www.martinbrodeur30.com/about_1757_en/|title=About Martin – La Pizzeria Etc.|access-date=February 26, 2009|publisher=MartinBrodeur30.com|year=2009|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090304024031/http://www.martinbrodeur30.com/about_1757_en/|archive-date=March 4, 2009}}</ref>\n\nBrodeur resides in New Jersey,<ref>{{cite web|last=Ross |first=Sherry |url=http://www.nydailynews.com/archives/sports/devil-angels-puck-stops-brodeur-clan-article-1.830799 |title=The Devil's Little Angels Puck Stops Here For Brodeur Clan |newspaper=New York Daily News |date=January 3, 1999 |access-date=October 21, 2016}}</ref> and became a naturalized [[United States]] citizen on December 1, 2009, but per IIHF rules would only be able to compete for Canada.<ref name=\"citizen\">{{cite news |url=https://www.nhl.com/news/brodeur-now-u-s-citizen-but-remains-loyal-to-canada/c-508358 |title=Brodeur now U.S. citizen, but remains loyal to Canada|author=Dan Rosen|publisher=NHL.com|date=December 2, 2009|access-date=October 20, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160313214040/https://www.nhl.com/news/brodeur-now-u-s-citizen-but-remains-loyal-to-canada/c-508358|archive-date=March 13, 2016}}</ref>\n\nOn June 30, 2013, the Devils traded for the 208th pick in the [[2013 NHL entry draft]] and Brodeur was asked to make the announcement to select his son, Anthony. In August 2015, Anthony signed with the [[Penticton Vees (junior A)|Penticton Vees]] of the [[British Columbia Hockey League]].<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.pentictonwesternnews.com/sports/320303881.html |title=Martin Brodeur's son Anthony joins Penticton Vees &#124; Penticton Western News |newspaper=pentictonwesternnews.com |date=August 5, 2015 |access-date=November 13, 2015 |archive-date=November 17, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151117014713/http://www.pentictonwesternnews.com/sports/320303881.html |url-status=dead}}</ref>\n\nFans picked Brodeur to appear on the cover of the video game ''[[NHL 14]]'', choosing him in a series of votes that included 60 players. He was the first goaltender to have his image on the cover since [[John Vanbiesbrouck]] on ''[[NHL 97]]''.<ref>{{cite web|title=Devils' Brodeur earns EA NHL 14 cover honor|publisher=National Hockey League|date=June 29, 2013|url=https://www.nhl.com/news/devils-brodeur-earns-ea-nhl-14-cover-honor/c-675547|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161220081037/https://www.nhl.com/news/devils-brodeur-earns-ea-nhl-14-cover-honor/c-675547|url-status=dead|archive-date=December 20, 2016|access-date=December 8, 2016}}</ref>\n\n==Career statistics==\n\n===Regular season and playoffs===\n<small>'''Bold''' indicates led league<br>'''''Bold italics''''' indicate NHL record</small>\n{| border=\"0\" cellpadding=\"1\" cellspacing=\"0\" style=\"width:75%; text-align:center;\"\n|- bgcolor=\"#e0e0e0\"\n! colspan=\"3\" bgcolor=\"#ffffff\"|\n! rowspan=\"99\" bgcolor=\"#ffffff\"|\n! colspan=\"10\" bgcolor=\"#e0e0e0\"|[[Regular season]]\n! rowspan=\"99\" bgcolor=\"#ffffff\"|\n! colspan=\"8\" bgcolor=\"#e0e0e0\"|[[Playoffs]]\n|- bgcolor=\"#e0e0e0\"\n!
