countrymen's deaths and that the league was culpable for the [[Casualties of the Russo-Ukrainian War|war's casualties]] by letting him play.<ref name=\"Hasek says he received death threats\">{{cite news|last=Coote|first=Darryl|url=https://www.upi.com/Top_News/World-News/2025/04/23/Hasek-life-threatened-Medvedev/7441745459617/|title=NHL legend Dominik Hasek says he received death threats from predicted he would commit suicide once Ovechkin got the record.<ref name=\"Hasek says he received death threats\" /> Interpreting his words as death threats, Hašek reported Medvedev to the [[International Ice Hockey Federation]] and [[International Olympic Committee]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/nhl/2025/04/23/dominik-hasek-czech-russian-threats-dmitry-medvedev/83238388007/|title=Dominik Hasek receives threats from former Russian president, Czech Press]]|website=[[ESPN.com]]|publisher=[[ESPN]]|date=23 April 2025|access-date=14 August 2025}}</ref><ref name=\"Hasek says he received death threats\" /> Hašek also called out Ovechkin and Fetisov when they appeared in a [[2026 Russian legislative election]] campaign video for the Putin-backed [[United Russia]] party,<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/sports/ovechkin-was-asked-appear-ad-putin-backed-united-russia-capitals-say-2026-09-15/|title=Ovechkin was asked to appear in ad for Putin-backed United Russia, Capitals say|website=[[Reuters]]|date=15 September 2026|access-date=18 September 2026}}</ref> and compared the former's support of Putin to [[Germany national football team|German national football team]] captain [[Fritz Szepan]] campaigning for [[Adolf Hitler]] during the [[Nazi Germany|Nazi period]].<ref>{{cite news|last1=Kolga|first1=Marcus|last2=Hašek|first2=Dominik|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/opinion/article-ovechkin-putin-russia-politics-nhl/|title=Alexander Ovechkin used his fame to back Putin. Otherwise, the game would be an endorsement of Russia's crimes.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://sport7.dnes24.sk/202658/dominik-hasek-by-rad-isiel-na-zapas-hviezd-nhl-a-khl-jeho-podmienka-zahrna-prezidenta-putina|title=Dominik Hašek by rád išiel na zápas hviezd NHL a KHL: Jeho podmienka zahŕňa prezidenta Putina|website=Sport7.sk|date=13 August 2025|access-date=14 August 2025|language=sk}}</ref>\n\n===Inline hockey game incident===\nDuring an inline hockey game on 18 May 2003, Hašek was accused of assaulting another player. He was playing as a defender for Bonfire Střída when he crosschecked [[Martin Šíla]]. The prosecutor in the case, Lenka Strnadová, ruled two months later that there was no evidence that Hašek intended bodily harm and recommended the case be treated as a misdemeanor, punishable only by fine (US$95 maximum), rather than a felony where jail time would have been possible.<ref>{{cite magazine|title=Some blood, no foul |url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/hockey/news/2003/08/08/hasek_czech_ap/ |magazine=Sports Illustrated |date=8 August 2003 |access-date=21 April 2007 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080424004021/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/hockey/news/2003/08/08/hasek_czech_ap/ |archive-date=24 April 2008}}</ref> Hašek's lawyer Pavel Jelínek announced in a statement that media reports about the incident were exaggerated, with Šíla not having sustained any documented injuries. In October 2003, the country's top prosecutor overruled Strnadová, saying her ruling was unlawful because the case had not been properly investigated. The Pardubice prosecutor's office then investigated the case again, and reached the same decision as Strnadová.<ref>{{cite web|last=Willoughby |first=Ian |title=Hasek to get off with fine for in-line hockey attack |url=http://www.radio.cz/en/news/52012#7 |publisher=Radio Prague |date=23 March 2004 |access-date=31 August 2006 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060109053552/http://www.radio.cz/en/news/52012 |archive-date=9 January 2006}}</ref>\n\n==Legacy==\n\n===Milestones===\nHašek earned his 300th National Hockey League win on 15 October 2005, in a 5–1 home victory with the Ottawa Senators over the Boston Bruins. He stopped 34 of 35 shots and was holding a shutout until Bruins forward [[Pat Leahy (ice hockey)|Pat Leahy]] jammed a loose puck under him three minutes into the third period. He became the twenty-second goaltender to reach the milestone.<ref name=\"MainBio\" />\n\n===Records===\nIn nine seasons with the Buffalo Sabres, Hašek acquired over 25 franchise records, including most all-time games played, wins, shutouts and lowest goals against average.<ref name=\"HockeydCentral\" /> He also holds the Sabres' record for most shutouts in a single season with 13 in 1997–98, and lowest goals against average in a single season with a total of 1.87 in 1998–99.<ref>{{cite web|title=Buffalo Sabres Season Leaders|publisher=Hockey-Reference|url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/teams/BUF/leaders_season.html|access-date=25 August 2017}}</ref> During the Detroit Red Wings' championship run in 2002, Hašek set franchise records for most games played, minutes played, wins and shutouts in a playoff year.<ref name=\"records\">{{cite web|last=Fox|first=Luke|title=Hasek's deep list of career awards and records|publisher=Sportsnet|date=15 November 2014|url=http://www.sportsnet.ca/hockey/nhl/dominik-hasek-list-of-career-achievements-hockey-hall-of-fame-2014-goaltender-awards-records/|access-date=4 September 2017}}</ref> He holds several notable NHL records:\n\n<div style=\"float:left; margin-right:1.5em;\">\n;<u>General</u>\n;All-time\n* 1st place – Highest career save percent (.922)<ref>{{cite web|title=NHL & WHA Career Leaders and Records for Save Percentage|publisher=Hockey-Reference|url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/leaders/save_pct_career.html|access-date=14 September 2017}}</ref>\n* 6th place – Most shutouts (81)<ref name=\"records\" />\n* 7th place – Lowest goals against average (2.20)<ref>{{cite web|title=NHL & WHA Career Leaders and Records for Goals Against Average|publisher=Hockey-Reference|url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/leaders/goals_against_avg_career.html|access-date=5 October 2017}}</ref>\n* 11th place – Most wins (389)<ref name=\"records\" />\n</div><div style=\"float:left; margin-right:1.5em;\">\n;<u>Regular season</u>\n* First European goaltender to lead the NHL in GAA (1993–94)<ref name=\"records\" />\n* First goaltender since 1974 to have a GAA below 2.00 (1993–94)<ref name=\"records\" />\n* Most shutouts in one month (six in 1997–98)<ref name=\"records\" />\n</div><div style=\"float:left;\">\n;<u>Playoffs</u>\n;All-time\n* 2nd place – Most shutouts in one season (6)<ref name=\"records\" />\n* 3rd place – Most shutouts (15)<ref name=\"records\" />\n* 10th place – Most wins (61)<ref name=\"records\" />\n</div>{{Clear}}\n\nOne of the most impressive single-game performances by any player in NHL history came on 27 April 1994. Hašek made 70 saves in a four-overtime shutout. The opposing goaltender was Martin Brodeur, then a rookie, who made 49 saves before being beaten by [[Dave Hannan]], and the Sabres beat New Jersey 1–0, helping them to tie the series 3–3 in the first round of the Stanley Cup playoffs. Hašek's 70 saves set a record, which still stands, for the most saves in a game without allowing a goal.<ref>{{Citation|last=NHL|title=Memories: Hasek turns away 70 shots by the Devils|date=27 April 2017|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nqRyEUj9Ync| archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211114/nqRyEUj9Ync| archive-date=14 November 2021 | url-status=live|access-date=28 April 2017}}{{cbignore}}</ref>\n\n===Influence===\nIn a 2023 interview, [[Petr Čech]] described Hašek as one of his major sporting idols.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://m.belfasttelegraph.co.uk/sport/ice-hockey/petr-cech-belfast-is-a-very-special-place-for-me-and-im-delighted-to-achieve-my-professional-dream-with-giants/a1790454886.html | title=Petr Cech: Belfast is a very special place for me and I'm delighted to achieve my professional dream with Giants | newspaper=Belfasttelegraph.co.uk | date=24 November 2023}}</ref>\n\n==Career statistics==\n\n===Regular season and playoffs===\n'''Bold''' indicates led league<br />'''''Bold italics''''' indicate NHL record\n{| border=\"0\" cellpadding=\"1\" cellspacing=\"0\" style=\"width:75%; text-align:center;\"\n|- bgcolor=\"#e0e0e0\"\n! colspan=\"3\" bgcolor=\"#ffffff\"|\n! rowspan=\"99\" bgcolor=\"#ffffff\"|\n! colspan=\"10\" bgcolor=\"#e0e0e0\"|[[Regular season]]\n! rowspan=\"99\" bgcolor=\"#ffffff\"|\n! colspan=\"8\" bgcolor=\"#e0e0e0\"|[[Playoffs]]\n|- bgcolor=\"#e0e0e0\"\n! Jennings Trophy winners]]\n[[Category:University of Hradec Králové alumni]]"}}}]},{"pageid":431953,"ns":0,"title":"Doug Harvey (ice hockey)","revisions":[{"slots":{"main":{"contentmodel":"wikitext","contentformat":"text/x-wiki","content":"{{short description|Canadian ice hockey player and coach (1924–1989)}}\n{{For|the baseball umpire|Doug Harvey (umpire)}}\n{{Infobox ice hockey player\n| name         = Doug Harvey\n| image        = DougHarvey.png\n| caption      = Harvey with the [[Montreal Canadiens]] {{c.|1940s}}\n| position     = [[Defenceman|Defence]]\n| shoots       = Left\n| height_ft    = 5\n| height_in    = 11\n| weight_lb    = 190\n| played_for   = [[Montreal Canadiens]] <br>[[New York Rangers]] <br>[[St. Louis Blues]] <br>[[Detroit Red Wings]]\n| birth_date   = {{birth date|1924|12|19}}\n| birth_place  = [[Montreal]], Quebec, Canada\n| death_date   = {{death date and age|1989|12|26|1924|12|19}}\n| death_place  = Montreal, Quebec, Canada\n| career_start = 1945\n| career_end   = 1969\n| hall_of_fame = 1973\n| module       =\n{{Infobox military person\n| embed            = yes\n| honorific-prefix = \n| allegiance       = Canada\n| rank             = [[Chief Petty Officer]]\n| battles          = [[World War II]]\n| service_years    = 1942–1945\n| branch           = [[Royal Canadian Navy]]\n| units            = \n}}\n}}\n'''Douglas Norman Harvey''' (December 19, 1924 – December 26, 1989) was a Canadian professional [[ice hockey|hockey]] [[defenceman (ice hockey)|defenceman]]. Widely regarded as one of the greatest defenders in [[National Hockey League]] (NHL) history, Harvey was elected to the [[Hockey Hall of Fame]] in 1973 and was named one of the [[100 Greatest NHL Players]] in history in 2017. Individually he won the [[James Norris Memorial Trophy]] as the best defenceman seven times, and was named to the end of season [[NHL All-Star team]] as a First All-Star 10 times. He played from 1947 until 1964, and from 1966 until 1969. Best known for playing with the [[Montreal Canadiens]], Harvey also played for the [[New York Rangers]], [[Detroit Red Wings]], and [[St. Louis Blues]], as well as several teams in the minor leagues. He also served as the [[player-coach]] of the Rangers for one season, and served a similar role for the minor-league [[Kansas City Blues (ice hockey)|Kansas City Blues]]. He was also a [[head coach|coach]].\n\nBorn and raised in Montreal, Harvey played [[Junior ice hockey|junior hockey]] for local teams. He joined the [[Royal Canadian Navy]] during the [[World War II|Second World War]], and while he spent the bulk of his time with the naval hockey team, he did see active service defending merchant shipping. A standout athlete, Harvey also played [[Canadian football]] and [[baseball]] at this time, though he gave up on both sports to concentrate on hockey. Signed by the Canadiens he made the team in 1947, though initially he was criticized for his style of play. After a few years, Harvey began to demonstrate his abilities and became regarded as one of the top defenders in the NHL. Regarded as a team leader he was voted [[Captain (ice hockey)|captain]] of the team in 1960, though he clashed with Canadiens management due to personal differences, which, combined with his age, led to him being traded to New York in 1961.\n\nHarvey spent two years with the Rangers before the team felt he was no longer effective and assigned him to their minor-league affiliate, then released him in 1963. Harvey would spend the next five years in the minor leagues, briefly playing for Detroit, before he joined the Blues during the 1968 playoffs. He spent one final year in the NHL with the Blues before retiring in 1969. Following his playing career, Harvey served in coaching and scouting roles for a few years, but a serious [[alcoholism|alcohol problem]] developed during the latter stages of his career kept him from serving in any capacity for long. He reconciled with the Canadiens a few years before his death, having his [[retired number|#2 sweater retired]], and served as a part-time scout for the team. With the Canadiens, Harvey won the [[Stanley Cup]] six times and played in the [[Stanley Cup Final]] five more times.\n\n==Early life==\nHarvey was born in Montreal on December 19, 1924, the second child of Alfred and Martha Harvey.<ref name=\"Brown 66\">{{harvnb|Brown|2002|p=66}}</ref> Alfred was born in [[Hammersmith]], [[United Kingdom]] in 1896 and had moved to Canada with his parents in 1905, while Martha was born in [[Pennsylvania]] to Welsh immigrants.<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|pp=66–67}}</ref> The family lived in [[Notre-Dame-de-Grâce]] (NDG), an English-speaking working-class neighbourhood of Montreal, where Alfred worked in the warehouse of N.C. Polson.<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|p=68}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Jenish|2008|p=127}}</ref> Doug was the second child, following Alfred Jr. (Alf) and preceding Howard and Mary.<ref name=\"Brown 66\"/>\n\nAs a child Harvey was physically active, playing in many sports, and was also known as a troublemaker, often getting into fights with neighbouring children.<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|p=70}}</ref> Outside of sports he delivered newspapers, with one of his customers being future Canadiens' teammate [[Bill Durnan]].<ref name=\"Leonetti 55\">{{harvnb|Leonetti|2003|p=55}}</ref> He first showed his athletic ability in [[Canadian football]], and when he entered [[West Hill High School]] in 1939 he joined the team there, playing both on offence and defence.<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|p=72}}</ref> He also played for the West Hill hockey team, and he first began to demonstrate his skills as a hockey player there.<ref name=\"Brown 73\">{{harvnb|Brown|2002|p=73}}</ref> Harvey had played hockey from a young age, but only joined an organised league when he was 13, asked to join a team by his brother Alf.<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|p=69}}</ref> Initially he played [[goaltender]], owing to his small stature, but soon moved to [[centre (ice hockey)|centre]]. Only later would he switch to [[defenceman|defence]].<ref name=\"One on One\">{{harvnb|Shea|2008}}</ref>\n\nThe [[World War II|Second World War]] was ongoing while Harvey was completing high school, and in 1942, one month before his 18th birthday, he enlisted in the [[Royal Canadian Navy]], following the advice of Alf, who had already done so.<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|p=78}}</ref> Recognized as a skilled hockey player, Harvey was initially assigned to the Navy's hockey team, which was used to boost public morale. However, Harvey wanted to serve actively in the war, so requested a transfer to active service, though this was not addressed until 1944.<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|pp=78–81}}</ref> In the spring of 1944, Doug Harvey was assigned to a [[defensively equipped merchant ship]]; this was again a suggestion of Alf, as it meant a less rigorous lifestyle on board a naval vessel. Harvey would spend the next year regularly crossing the Atlantic while helping protect supplies being shipped to Europe and Africa. Throughout this time Harvey's ships were never fired upon, and he would later look back fondly on his service. It was also during this period that biographer William Brown believes Harvey began to develop an alcohol addiction; neither of his parents drank, which was in stark contrast to the naval service, though Brown concedes it only became a serious problem for Harvey later in life.<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|pp=86–88}}</ref>\n\n==Amateur career==\n===Minor league hockey===\nHarvey played minor league hockey in [[Oxford Park, Montreal|Oxford Park]], NDG, then began his professional career with the Montreal Royals of the [[Quebec Senior Hockey League]] where he played from 1945 to 1947, helping them win the [[Allan Cup]]. He then played one season with the [[Buffalo Bisons (AHL)|Buffalo Bisons]] of the [[American Hockey League]]. He made the jump to the [[Montreal Canadiens]] of the NHL in the [[1947–48 NHL season]] and remained with the team until [[1960–61 NHL season|1961]].\n\n===Football and baseball===\nIn the early 1940s, Harvey also played [[Canadian football|rugby football]] (later known as Canadian football). He started to play competitively while at West Hill, and though he could play both offence and defence equally well, he was most known as a defensive [[Halfback (Canadian football)|halfback]].<ref name=\"Brown 24\">{{harvnb|Brown|2002|p=24}}</ref> He continued on with the sport when he joined the navy, playing for their Montreal-based team, [[St. Hyacinthe–Donnacona Navy]]. In 1942 Harvey was named the most valuable player of the [[Quebec Rugby Football Union]].<ref>{{harvnb|Feige|2011|pp=89–90}}</ref> The Donnacona Navy won the [[32nd Grey Cup|1944 Grey Cup]] as Canadian champions, though Harvey had been sent into active service and did not play in the game.<ref name=\"One on One\"/> After the war he briefly played for the newly formed [[Montreal Hornets]], but a mid-season injury forced him out.<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|p=90}}</ref> Though skilled at football, Harvey gave up the sport as it was only [[semi-professional sports|semi-professional]] in Canada at that time, while hockey was fully professional.<ref name=\"Brown 24\"/>\n\nHarvey also played baseball at a competitive level, spending summers on teams from 1947 to 1950, mainly playing as a [[third baseman]].<ref name=\"McKenna 165\">{{harvnb|McKenna|2007|p=165}}</ref> In 1947 he was invited to join the [[Ottawa Nationals (baseball)|Ottawa Nationals]], a team run by [[Tommy Gorman]] (who had recently left his position as [[general manager]] of the [[Montreal Canadiens]] hockey team) and competed in the [[Minor League Baseball|Class C]] [[Border League (baseball)|Border League]].<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|p=28}}</ref> A skilled ball player, in 1949 Harvey led the Border League in [[Run (baseball)|runs]], [[runs batted in]], and [[batting average (baseball)|batting average]].<ref name=\"McKenna 165\"/> He was also offered a contract by [[Major League Baseball]]'s [[Boston Braves]], but he turned down the offer as it would only see him play in Class B (another level in the minor leagues).<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|p=57}}</ref>\n\n==Professional career==\n===Montreal Canadiens===\nBeginning in the [[1951–52 NHL season]] under coach [[Dick Irvin]], Harvey was named to the [[NHL All-Star team|All-Star team]] 11 consecutive times. He won the [[James Norris Memorial Trophy]] in [[1954–55 NHL season|1955]], as the league's best defenceman, for the first of seven times. In an era when the defenceman's role did not include scoring points, Harvey used his skating speed and passing ability to become a factor in making the Canadiens a high-scoring team.\n\nHe won the [[Stanley Cup]] six times, all with Montreal. During the [[1954 Stanley Cup Final|1954 Finals]], however, he scored a Cup-losing own-goal when he tried to block a shot by [[Tony Leswick]] of the [[Detroit Red Wings]] with his glove but instead tipped it past goalie [[Gerry McNeil]].<ref>{{harvnb|Jenish|1992|p=173}}</ref> McNeil, who struggled with the pressure of being an NHL goalie, quit hockey the following year.<ref>{{harvnb|Leonetti|2003|p=64}}</ref>\n\nBetween 1955 and 1962, Harvey won the James Norris Memorial Trophy as the NHL's top defenceman every year except [[1958–59 NHL season|1959]], when it went to his teammate [[Tom Johnson (ice hockey)|Tom Johnson]].<ref name=\"100 Greatest\">{{harvnb|Coffey|2017}}</ref>\n\nPrior to the [[1960–61 NHL season|1960–61 season]], the Canadiens players voted for Harvey to be their captain; he succeeded [[Maurice Richard]], who had served in that role for his last four years as a player. This was not welcomed by team management, who were not happy with Harvey's actions on and off the ice.<ref name=\"Leonetti 55\"/>\n\nHarvey was an outspoken critic of the hockey establishment who controlled players' careers via the [[reserve clause]], which restricted player rights. In Harvey's day, players were not highly paid, with Harvey earning less than $30,000 a season at the peak of his career.\n\n===New York Rangers===\n[[File:1963 Topps Doug Harvey.jpg|thumb|right|Harvey on a [[Topps]] card from 1963]]\nAfter the Canadiens lost in the 1961 playoffs, Canadiens' general manager [[Frank J. Selke]] singled out Harvey for the team's poor performance and began to look at ways to get rid of him. Though he was still considered one of the best players in the NHL, Selke and the Canadiens had tired of his antics and soon were in discussions with the [[New York Rangers]] about a possible trade. [[Muzz Patrick]], the coach and general manager of the Rangers, had tired of the dual role, and agreed to take on Harvey if he could be convinced to be a [[player-coach]]. While Harvey was reluctant to move to New York he agreed to talk to Patrick, who offered a two-year contract worth $25,000 per year, a fairly high salary. After initially refusing, he agreed after a third year was added to the contract.<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|pp=192–195}}</ref>\n\nHarvey again won the Norris Trophy in [[1961–62 NHL season|1961–62]], the first Ranger to do so. As coach, he tried to have the team play a similar style to what he had seen in Montreal, which helped the Rangers make the playoffs for the first time since 1958.<ref name=\"Kreiser 152\">{{harvnb|Kreiser|Friedman|1996|p=152}}</ref> Desiring to be closer to the players, which he felt was not possible as their coach, Harvey resigned as coach for the [[1962–63 NHL season|1962–63 season]], and was only convinced to remain with the Rangers when Patrick offered him a $30,000-per-year salary, reportedly the highest in NHL history to that point.<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|p=217}}</ref> Harvey's play remained at a high level: he led all NHL defencemen in scoring with 39 points, but was criticized for the team's lack of success.<ref name=\"Kreiser 152\"/> Harvey missed the Rangers' training camp prior to the start of the [[1963–64 NHL season|1963–64 season]], owing to issues with his restaurant, and when he returned was sent to the team's minor league affiliate, the [[St. Paul Rangers]] of the [[Central Professional Hockey League]], where he played five games before rejoining New York.<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|pp=219–220}}</ref> After recording two assists in 14 games during the [[1963–64 NHL season|1963–64 season]], Harvey continued to attract negative attention; rather than return to the minor leagues, he asked to be released from his contract.<ref name=\"Kreiser 152\"/>\n\n===Minor leagues===\nAfter leaving the Rangers, Harvey spent two years with the [[Quebec Aces]] of the AHL. He followed that with one and a half seasons with the [[Baltimore Clippers]] and a further half season with the [[Pittsburgh Hornets]].\n\nIn 1964 Harvey, [[Gump Worsley]], and [[Red Berenson]] played for the [[Montreal Jr. Canadiens]] in a game against the [[Soviet national ice hockey team|Soviet national team]]. Harvey played almost 50 minutes during the 3–2 loss.<ref>{{harvnb|Scott|1964|p=34}}</ref>\n\n===Detroit Red Wings and St. Louis Blues===\nIn January 1967, Harvey was called up to play for the [[Detroit Red Wings]] in a back-to-back series against the [[Chicago Black Hawks]]. However he disappointed Red Wings management by showing up roughly {{convert|20|lbs|kg}} overweight, and was largely ineffective in the two games, so was sent back to Pittsburgh for the remainder of the season.<ref name=\"Brown 230\">{{harvnb|Brown|2002|p=230}}</ref> With the Hornets he won the [[Calder Cup]], the AHL championship, though the team disbanded after the season as the [[Pittsburgh Penguins]] were due to start playing in the NHL for [[1967–68 NHL season|1967–68]].<ref name=\"Brown 230\"/> He finished his NHL career in [[1968–69 NHL season|1969]] with the [[St. Louis Blues]]. In addition, he was hired as coach and manager of the [[Kansas City Blues (ice hockey)|Kansas City Blues]], which was the St. Louis Blues' minor league affiliate in 1967–68.<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|p=231}}</ref> Harvey served as player-coach during his first season in New York, but was never entirely comfortable with this dual role.<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|p=213}}</ref>\n\n==Post-playing career==\nAfter retiring from playing, Harvey became head coach of the [[Laval Saints]] of the newly formed [[Quebec Major Junior Hockey League]]. However, he only coached 16 games before leaving the team, finishing with a record of four wins and 12 losses.{{sfn |Doug Harvey Page|2020}} Offered a role as an assistant coach with the [[Los Angeles Kings]] of the NHL he went there, serving out the rest of the season with the team. He was offered a chance to play for the team but declined as he was 45 at that point and had not played in over a year.<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|pp=241–243}}</ref>\n\nIn 1973, Harvey was hired as an assistant coach and scout by the [[Houston Aeros (WHA)|Houston Aeros]] of the upstart [[World Hockey Association]]. With the Aeros he helped sign former NHL star [[Gordie Howe]] and his two sons, [[Mark Howe|Mark]] and [[Marty Howe|Marty]], which was considered a major coup for the new league.<ref>{{harvnb|Willes|2004|pp=72–75}}</ref> Though he had initially stayed sober with Houston, Harvey relapsed and the team let him go at the end of the [[1973–74 WHA season|1973–74 season]], which saw the Aeros win the [[1974 WHA playoffs|Avco World Trophy]].<ref>{{harvnb|Willes|2004|p=75}}</ref>\n\n==Personal life==\n===Family===\nHarvey married Ursula Hardie on May 21, 1949, in Montreal.<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|p=56}}</ref> It is not certain when they met, but they had been together since at least 1946.<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|p=55}}</ref> They had six children: Doug Jr., Darlene, Glen, Nancy, Diane, and Maria.<ref name=\"Brown 2002 166\">{{harvnb|Brown|2002|p=166}}</ref> The family lived in NDG throughout Harvey's playing career, though they moved to [[Long Island]] during his first season with the Rangers before returning to Montreal after a few months, living in a house he built with his brothers in 1950.<ref name=\"Brown 120\">{{harvnb|Brown|2002|p=120}}</ref> Doug and Ursula would separate in 1980.<ref name=\"Feige 98\">{{harvnb|Feige|2011|p=98}}</ref>\n\n===Off-ice business===\nOutside of hockey, Harvey had several business ventures. After building his own home, Harvey and his brothers began a housebuilding business in 1953, and they later established an aluminum window business as well. Harvey, who was well known for his hockey career at this point, would spend most of his time talking to clients, leaving Alf and Howard to do the physical work.<ref name=\"Brown 120\"/> In the early 1960s Harvey opened a restaurant in Montreal, Chez Doug Harvey, with an associate he had recently met.<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|pp=120–121}}</ref> The restaurant proved a massive financial failure, with his partner absconding with a large amount of money, and ultimately cost Harvey around $65,000, equal to nearly two years' pay for him.<ref>{{harvnb|Feige|2011|p=96}}</ref> It also took a serious toll on his family's finances, which were exacerbated when he played in the minor leagues, making far less than he had in the NHL; on several occasions friends would help cover the mortgage to prevent Harvey from defaulting.<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|p=167}}</ref>\n\nStarting in the mid-1960s Harvey started a summer hockey school for young boys. He would lead a two-week school instructing them on how to play better, and would often buy equipment and board players who were unable to cover the associated costs.<ref name=\"Brown 2002 166\"/> The school ran yearly until 1979.<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|p=257}}</ref> While in Ottawa in 1972 Harvey was arrested for having a concealed weapon without a permit, as he was trying to board a plane. He was given a six-month suspended sentence, and the gun was confiscated.<ref name=\"Feige 98\"/> In the early 1980s Harvey was offered a job at the [[Connaught Park Racetrack]] in [[Aylmer, Quebec]], living with and working for the family of NHL founder Tommy Gorman's son, Joe Gorman, as well as the opportunity to live in retired [[passenger car (rail)|railcar]] that had been used by [[Prime Minister of Canada|Canadian prime minister]] [[John Diefenbaker]] in the 1950s, and subsequently purchased by the Gorman family. Doug accepted the position and lived with the Gormans as a part of their family until his return to Montreal.<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|p=261}}</ref>\n\nFor years, Harvey battled [[alcoholism]] while suffering from [[bipolar disorder]]. In 1985 he was offered a job with the Montreal Canadiens as a scout. He died on December 26, 1989, due to [[cirrhosis]] of the liver, a week after his 65th birthday, and was interred in the [[Notre-Dame-des-Neiges Cemetery]] in Montreal.<ref>{{harvnb|Dryden|1997|pp=40–41}}</ref>\n\n==Playing style==\n[[File:Doug Harvey Rangers.jpg|thumb|Harvey with the [[New York Rangers]] in 1962]]\nPrior to the start of Harvey's career, it was normal for defencemen to pass the puck off to forwards or dump it into the [[ice hockey rink#zones|offensive zone]]; the goal was to move it out of the defensive zone quickly and limit chances for the opponent to set up plays. Harvey was not interested in this system, preferring to keep control of the puck as long as he could. In this way Harvey felt he could control the tempo of the play; he felt that quickly dumping the puck only turned over possession to the opponent.<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|p=35}}</ref> He would then pass the puck to a teammate who would quickly enter the offensive zone and set up scoring chances that way.<ref name=\"Leonetti 55\"/> This style of play was unusual at the time and the Canadiens' fans and coaches alike perceived Harvey as a lazy player.<ref name=\"Fayne 23\">{{harvnb|Frayne|1958|p=23}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Feige|2011|p=91}}</ref> That Harvey, who was roughly {{height|ft=5|in=11}} and {{convert|190|lb|kg}} during his playing career, had a stocky look did not help this perception.<ref>{{harvnb|Frayne|1958|p=47}}</ref> However once it became apparent what he was doing he earned recognition for his ability.<ref name=\"Fayne 23\"/>\n\nHarvey's ability to set up offence helped the Canadiens create one of the strongest offensive teams in NHL history. Though he did not score many goals during his career, Harvey helped others score, and recorded several seasons with high [[assist (ice hockey)|assist]] totals.<ref name=\"Leonetti 55\"/> With this Harvey led NHL defencemen in assists five times and scoring three times during his career.<ref>{{harvnb|Dryden|1997|p=40}}</ref> Indeed, the Canadiens of the late 1950s were so strong on the [[Power play (sporting term)#Ice hockey|power play]] that they repeatedly could score multiple goals on one power play.<ref name=\"100 Greatest\"/> Other teams began to resent this, and so at the end of the [[1955–56 NHL season|1955–56 season]] the NHL adopted a rule that ended a power play after one goal was scored.<ref>{{harvnb|Jenish|2008|p=154}}</ref>\n\n==Legacy==\nFrom early in his playing career, Harvey was recognized as one of the top defencemen in NHL history and one of the best players in general. With seven Norris Trophy wins he is tied with [[Nicklas Lidström]] for second most all-time, behind [[Bobby Orr]]'s eight.<ref>{{harvnb|Hedger|2012}}</ref> He was inducted into the [[Hockey Hall of Fame]] in 1973, though he had been eligible since 1972. It was said that the one-year delay was because of Harvey's lifestyle and that he was asked to clean himself up if he wanted to be elected.<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|pp=246–247}}</ref> Harvey apparently took this as a slight; he refused to attend his own induction ceremony in 1973, reportedly going fishing instead.<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|p=250}}</ref><ref name=\"One on One\"/>\n\nPrior to a home game against the [[Hartford Whalers]] on October 26, 1985, the Montreal Canadiens [[List of National Hockey League retired numbers|retired]] Harvey's number 2.<ref name=\"One on One\"/> In 1991, the Confederation Arena in NDG was renamed the ''Doug Harvey Arena''. Efforts had been made to rename the arena prior to Harvey's death, but Montreal rarely renamed arenas after still-living people.<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|2002|p=269}}</ref> ''[[The Hockey News]]'', the premier hockey magazine, released a list of the top 100 NHL players of all time in 1997; at sixth, Harvey was the highest-ranked deceased player on the list at the time it was compiled.<ref>{{harvnb|Dryden|1997|p=8}}</ref> He was also named one of the [[100 Greatest NHL Players]] in 2017.<ref name=\"100 Greatest\"/>\n\n==Career statistics==\n===Regular season and playoffs===\n{| border=\"0\" cellpadding=\"1\" cellspacing=\"0\" style=\"text-align:center; width:60em\"\n|- bgcolor=\"#e0e0e0\"\n! colspan=\"3\" bgcolor=\"#ffffff\"|\n! rowspan=\"100\" bgcolor=\"#ffffff\"|\n! colspan=\"5\"|[[Regular season]]\n! rowspan=\"100\" bgcolor=\"#ffffff\"|\n! colspan=\"5\"|[[Playoffs]]\n|- bgcolor=\"#e0e0e0\"\n! !! 8 !! 64 !! 72 !! 152\n|}\n*Source: ''Total Hockey''<ref>{{harvnb|Diamond|2002|p=1161}}</ref>\n\n==NHL coaching record==\nHarvey has the distinction of being the [[National Hockey League|NHL's]] last-ever full-time [[player-coach]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Fischler |first1=Stan |title=Harvey had remarkable season as last player-coach in NHL history |url=https://www.nhl.com/news/doug-harvey-remarkable-season-as-last-nhl-player-coach-for-rangers |website=nhl.com |publisher=National Hockey League |access-date=15 November 2024 |language=en |date=5 June 2024}}</ref> He held the dual roles with the [[New York Rangers]] during the [[1961–62 New York Rangers season|1961–62 season]]—a year in which he led the team to the [[1961–62 NHL season#Playoffs|semi-finals]] and was awarded his seventh [[James Norris Memorial Trophy|Norris Trophy]] for best [[defenceman]] in the league.{{sfn|Coffey|2017}} He again served as a [[player-coach]] for the [[Kansas City Blues (ice hockey)|Kansas City Blues]] of the [[Central Hockey League (1963–84)|Central Professional Hockey League]] in [[1967–68 CPHL season|1967]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Doug Quebec]]\n[[Category:20th-century Canadian sportsmen]]"}}}]},{"pageid":431975,"ns":0,"title":"Terry Sawchuk","revisions":[{"slots":{"main":{"contentmodel":"wikitext","contentformat":"text/x-wiki","content":"{{Short description|Canadian ice hockey player (1929–1970)}}\n{{Use mdy dates|date=March 2019}}\n{{Use Canadian English |date=July 2026}}\n{{Infobox ice hockey player\n| position = [[Goaltender]]\n| catches = Left\n| height_ft = 5\n| height_in = 11\n| weight_lb = 195\n| played_for = [[Detroit Red Wings]]<br>[[Boston Bruins]]<br>[[Toronto Maple Leafs]]<br>[[Los Angeles Kings]]<br>[[New York Rangers]]\n| birth_date = {{birth date|1929|12|28|mf=y}}\n| birth_place = [[Winnipeg]], Manitoba, Canada\n| death_date = {{death date and age|mf=yes|1970|5|31|1929|12|28}}\n| death_place = [[New York City]], New York, U.S.\n| career_start = 1949\n| career_end = 1970\n| image = Terry Sawchuk 1963.JPG\n| caption = Sawchuk with the [[Detroit Red Wings]] in 1963\n| hall_of_fame = 1971\n}}\n'''Terrance Gordon Sawchuk''' (December 28, 1929 – May 31, 1970) was a Canadian [[professional sports|professional]] [[ice hockey]] [[goaltender]] who played 21 seasons in the [[National Hockey League]] (NHL) for the [[Detroit Red Wings]], [[Boston Bruins]], [[Toronto Maple Leafs]], [[Los Angeles Kings]], and [[New York Rangers]] between 1950 and 1970. He won the [[Calder Trophy]], earned the [[Vezina Trophy]] four times, was a four-time [[Stanley Cup]] champion, and was elected to the [[Hockey Hall of Fame]] the year after his final season, one of 10 players for whom the three-year waiting period was waived.\n\nAt the time of his death, Sawchuk was the all-time leader among NHL goaltenders with [[List of NHL statistical leaders#Regular season: Wins|447 wins]] and with [[List of NHL statistical leaders#Regular season: Shutouts|103 shutouts]]. In the decades following his death, his NHL win record has been surpassed by eight goaltenders, and his NHL shutout record has been surpassed by one goaltender, though Sawchuk was the all-time leader in wins and shutouts by goaltenders who played in the [[Original Six]] era (1942–1967).<ref>{{cite web|work=Stathead|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/stathead/tiny/UzPxH|title=For combined seasons, from 1942-43 to 1966-67, playing goalie, in the regular season, sorted by descending Wins.|access-date=February 6, 2026}}</ref> In 2017, Sawchuk was named one of the \"[[100 Greatest NHL Players]]\".<ref name=\"100 Greatest NHL Players\">{{cite web |title=100 Greatest NHL Players |url=https://www.nhl.com/history/nhl-centennial/nhl-100-greatest-players |website=NHL.com |access-date=January 1, 2017 |date=January 1, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last=NHL |title=Terry Sawchuk was four-time Vezina-winning goalie |date=March 22, 2017 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rrgQ1gn0V_E&index=35&list=PL1NbHSfosBuHEp2Bphcgz16OKz0kjnCH6 |access-date=April 25, 2017}}</ref>\n\n==Early life and playing career==\n===Childhood and junior career===\nSawchuk was born in the [[North End, Winnipeg|North End of Winnipeg]]\nand raised there until his family moved to Bowman Avenue in East Kildonan, a working-class, formerly Ukrainian section of [[Winnipeg]], Manitoba, Canada. He was the third of four sons and one adopted daughter of Louis Sawchuk, a tinsmith who had immigrated to Canada as a boy from [[Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria|Galicia]], [[Austria-Hungary]] (now Ukraine), and his wife Anne (''nee'' Maslak), a homemaker. The second son died young from [[scarlet fever]] and the oldest, an aspiring hockey goaltender whom Terry idolized, died suddenly of a heart attack at age seventeen. At age twelve, Sawchuk injured his right elbow playing rugby and, not wanting to be punished by his parents, hid the injury, preventing the dislocation from properly healing. Thus, the injury left his right arm with limited mobility and was now also several inches shorter than the left, which bothered him for his entire athletic career. After inheriting his good friend's goalie equipment, Sawchuk began playing ice hockey in a local league and worked for a sheet-metal company installing vents over bakery ovens. His goaltending talent was so evident that at age fourteen a local scout for the [[Detroit Red Wings]] had him work out with the team, who later signed him to an amateur contract and sent him to play for their junior team in [[Galt, Ontario|Galt]], [[Ontario]], in 1946, where he also finished the eleventh grade but most likely did not graduate from high school.  He excelled in many sports.  He played baseball for a number of years for the Elmwood Giants first in the Manitoba Senior AA League starting in 1948, when he won the league's batting title, and then in Mandak League.  He played in both the infield and the outfield.\n\n===Detroit Red Wings===\nThe Red Wings signed Sawchuk to a professional contract in 1947, and he quickly progressed through their developmental system, winning honours as the [[Rookie of the Year (award)|Rookie of the Year]] in both the U.S. and American Hockey Leagues. Sawchuk also filled in for seven games when the Detroit goalie [[Harry Lumley (ice hockey)|Harry Lumley]] was injured in January 1950. Sawchuk showed such promise that the Red Wings traded Lumley to the [[Chicago Black Hawks]], though he had just led the team to the [[1950 Stanley Cup Final|1950 Stanley Cup]]. Nicknamed \"Ukey\" or \"The Uke\" by his teammates because of his [[Ukrainian Canadian|Ukrainian]] ancestry, Sawchuk led the Red Wings to three [[Stanley Cup]] wins in five years, winning the [[Calder Memorial Trophy]] as the top rookie and three [[Vezina Trophy|Vezina Trophies]] for the fewest goals allowed (he missed out the other two years by one goal). He was selected as an All-Star five times in his first five years in the NHL, had fifty-six shutouts, and his goals-against average (GAA) remained under 2.00. In the 1951–52 [[Stanley Cup playoffs|playoffs]], the Red Wings swept both the Toronto Maple Leafs and the [[Montreal Canadiens]], with Sawchuk surrendering five goals in eight games (for a 0.625 GAA), with four shutouts.<ref>John A. Drobnicki, \"Sawchuk, Terrance Gordon ('Terry'),\" in ''The Scribner Encyclopedia of American Lives, Thematic Series: Sports Figures'' (Scribner's, 2002), Vol. 2, pp. 335-336.</ref> During the last of these eight games, the [[Legend of the Octopus]] began as the first of the [[octopus|eight-limbed mollusc]]s was hurled onto the ice from the stands.\n\nSawchuk was ordered by Detroit general manager [[Jack Adams]] to lose weight before the [[1951–52 Detroit Red Wings season|1951–52]] season. After his weight loss, his personality seemed to change and he became sullen and withdrawn. He became increasingly surly with reporters and fans, preferring to do crossword puzzles than give interviews. He also struggled for years to regain the weight. Also contributing to his moodiness and self-doubt was the pressure of playing every day despite repeated injuries — there were no backup goaltenders. He frequently played through pain, and during his career he had three operations on his right elbow, an appendectomy, countless cuts and bruises, a broken foot, a collapsed lung, ruptured discs in his back, and severed tendons in his hand. A standup goaltender, he adopted a crouching stance to see through the legs of skaters.<ref>{{Citation|last=NHL|title=Terry Sawchuk was four-time Vezina-winning goalie|date=March 22, 2017|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rrgQ1gn0V_E&index=35&list=PL1NbHSfosBuHEp2Bphcgz16OKz0kjnCH6|access-date=April 24, 2017}}</ref> Years of crouching in the net caused Sawchuk to walk with a permanent stoop and resulted in [[lordosis]] (swayback), which prevented him from sleeping for more than two hours at a time. He also received approximately 400 stitches to his face (including three in his right eyeball) before finally adopting a protective facemask in 1962.<ref name=\"John A. Drobnicki 2002 p. 336\">John A. Drobnicki, \"Sawchuk, Terrance Gordon ('Terry'),\" in ''The Scribner Encyclopedia of American Lives, Thematic Series: Sports Figures'' (Scribner's, 2002), Vol. 2, p. 336.</ref> In 1966, [[Life Magazine]] had a make-up artist apply stitches and scars to Sawchuk's face to demonstrate all of the injuries his face sustained over the years.  The make-up artist did not have enough room for everything.<ref>\"Hockey's Reviled and Bludgeoned Fall-Guys: The Goalie is the Goat,\" ''Life'' (March 4, 1966), p. 33. See an image of the photo in the Life Photo Archive at: [https://web.archive.org/web/20131211064614/http://life.time.com/culture/terry-sawchuk-a-face-only-a-hockey-puck-could-love/#1]</ref>\n\n===Boston Bruins; return to Detroit; Toronto and Los Angeles===\nThe Red Wings traded Sawchuk to the [[Boston Bruins]] on June 3, 1955, because they had a capable younger goaltender in the minor leagues ([[Glenn Hall]]). This devastated Sawchuk. During his second season with Boston, Sawchuk was diagnosed with [[Infectious mononucleosis|mononucleosis]], but returned to the team after only two weeks. Physically weak, playing poorly, and on the verge of a nervous breakdown and exhaustion, he announced his retirement in early 1957 and was labeled a \"quitter\" by team executives and several newspapers. Detroit reacquired Sawchuk by trading young forward [[Johnny Bucyk]] to Boston on June 10, 1957. After seven seasons, when they had another promising young goalie ([[Roger Crozier]]) ready for promotion from the minor leagues, Detroit left Sawchuk unprotected in the [[1964 NHL Intra-League Draft]], and he was quickly claimed by the Maple Leafs on June 10, 1964.<ref>{{cite web|title=Historical Hockey Stats & Trivia - 1964 NHL Intra-League Draft|url=https://historicalhockey.blogspot.ca/2012/10/1964-nhl-intra-league-draft.html|website=historicalhockey.blogspot.ca|access-date=March 9, 2015|date=October 27, 2012}}</ref> With Sawchuk sharing goaltending duties with the forty-year-old [[Johnny Bower]], the veteran duo won the 1964–65 Vezina Trophy and led Toronto to the [[1967 Stanley Cup Final|1967 Stanley Cup]]. In Sawchuk's last game with the Maple Leafs, he stopped 40 of 41 shots in 3–1 victory over the Montreal Canadiens in the Cup-clinching game six. Left unprotected in the [[1967 NHL Expansion Draft|June 1967 expansion draft]], Sawchuk was the first player selected, taken by the [[Los Angeles Kings]] where he played one season before being traded back to Detroit.\n\n===New York Rangers===\nIn June 1969, the Red Wings traded Sawchuk and [[Sandy Snow]] to the [[New York Rangers]] for [[Larry Jeffrey]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/105985381/wings-trade-sawchuk-for-larry-jeffrey/ |title=Wings Trade Sawchuk For Larry Jeffrey |publisher=Newspapers.com |date=1969-06-20 |accessdate=2022-07-20}}</ref> Sawchuk played sparingly for the Rangers, starting only six games.<ref name=\"John A. Drobnicki 2002 p. 336\"/> On February 1, 1970, in only his fourth start of the season, he recorded the 103rd and final shutout of his career by blanking the [[Pittsburgh Penguins]] 6–0.<ref name=\"Sawchuk's final career shutout\">[https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=Fr8DH2VBP9sC&dat=19700202&printsec=frontpage The Montreal Gazette, Feb. 2, 1970], page 17. Retrieved March 16, 2015.</ref> This was also his last NHL win.<ref>{{cite web|title=Hockey Summary Project - Feb. 1, 1970, Pittsburgh Penguins 0 @ New York Rangers 6|url=http://www.flyershistory.com/cgi-bin/poboxscore.cgi?H19690283|website=Flyershistory.com|access-date=March 16, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402090009/http://www.flyershistory.com/cgi-bin/poboxscore.cgi?H19690283|archive-date=April 2, 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref> His last regular season start was on March 14, 1970, a 7–4 loss to the Chicago Black Hawks.<ref>{{cite web|title=Hockey Summary Project - Mar. 14, 1970, New York Rangers 4 @ Chicago Black Hawks 7|url=http://www.flyershistory.com/cgi-bin/poboxscore.cgi?H19690390|website=Flyershistory.com|access-date=March 16, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402090730/http://www.flyershistory.com/cgi-bin/poboxscore.cgi?H19690390|archive-date=April 2, 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref> Sawchuk's last playoff start was in a 5–3 playoff quarterfinals loss to the Bruins on April 9, 1970.<ref>{{cite web|title=Hockey Summary Project - April 9, 1970, New York Rangers 3 @ Boston Bruins 5|url=http://www.flyershistory.com/cgi-bin/poboxscore.cgi?O19700006|website=Flyershistory.com|access-date=March 16, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402133824/http://www.flyershistory.com/cgi-bin/poboxscore.cgi?O19700006|archive-date=April 2, 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref> Sawchuk appeared in his last NHL game on April 14 in the same [[1969–70 NHL season#Playoffs|playoff series]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Hockey Summary Project - April 14, 1970 New York Rangers 2 @ Boston Bruins 3|url=http://www.flyershistory.com/cgi-bin/poboxscore.cgi?O19700017|website=Flyershistory.com|access-date=March 16, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924052024/http://www.flyershistory.com/cgi-bin/poboxscore.cgi?O19700017|archive-date=September 24, 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref> In game five,<ref name=\"Sawchuk's final game\">[https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=Fr8DH2VBP9sC&dat=19700415&printsec=frontpage The Montreal Gazette, April 15, 1970], page 14. Retrieved March 16, 2015.</ref> after [[Phil Esposito]] had scored at 7:59 of the third period to put Boston in the lead, Rangers coach [[Emile Francis]], in an effort to slow down the game, replaced goalie [[Ed Giacomin]] with Sawchuk. He was in the net for less than a minute before Giacomin returned and the Rangers lost the game 3–2. Boston went on to win the [[1970 Stanley Cup playoffs|series]] four games to two.\n\n==Personal life==\n\nSawchuk married Patricia Ann Bowman Morey on August 6, 1953, after a brief courtship. They had seven children, and the family endured  many years of Sawchuk's increasing alcoholism, philandering (he impregnated a Toronto girlfriend in 1967), and verbal and physical abuse. Morey threatened to divorce him numerous times, and finally did so in 1969.<ref name=\"John A. Drobnicki 2002 p. 336\"/>\n\n==Death==\n[[File:Tombstone of Terry Sawchuk.jpg|thumb|Tombstone of Terry Sawchuk, at Mt. Hope Cemetery in [[Pontiac, Michigan|Pontiac]], [[Michigan]].]]\nSawchuk struggled with untreated [[clinical depression|depression]], a condition that often affected his conduct. On April 29, 1970, after the 1969–70 season ended, Sawchuk and Rangers teammate [[Ron Stewart]], both of whom had been drinking, physically fought over expenses for the house they rented together on [[Long Island]], New York.<ref>{{cite web | last=Eskenazi | first=Gerald | title=Sawchuk of Rangers Dies Here Following 'Horseplaying' Injury | website=The New York Times | date=1970-06-01 | url=https://www.nytimes.com/1970/06/01/archives/sawchuk-of-rangers-dies-here-following-horseplaying-injury-sawchuk.html | access-date=2025-05-09}}</ref> Sawchuk suffered severe internal injuries during the scuffle from falling on top of Stewart's bent knee. At Long Beach Memorial Hospital, Sawchuk's gallbladder was removed and he had a second operation on his damaged and bleeding liver. The press described the incident as \"horseplay\", and Sawchuk told the police that he accepted full responsibility for the events.\n\nAt New York Hospital [[Manhattan]], another operation was performed on Sawchuk's bleeding liver. He never recovered and died shortly thereafter from a [[pulmonary embolism]] on May 31, 1970, at the age of 40.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/105991074/great-goalie-terry-sawchuk-dies-police/ | title=Great goalie Terry Sawchuk dies; police investigation is launched | newspaper=North Bay Nugget | date=June 1970 | page=13 }}</ref> The last reporter to speak to him, a week before his death, was Shirley Fischler (wife of [[Stan Fischler]]), who went to see him in the hospital as a visitor, not identifying herself as a reporter. Sawchuk told her the incident with Stewart \"was just a fluke, a complete fluke accident.\" Fischler described him as \"so pale and thin that the scars had almost disappeared from his face.\"<ref>Shirley Fischler, \"Last Interview,\" ''Hockey Illustrated'' (Nov. 1970), pp. 21-23.</ref>  A Nassau County grand jury exonerated Stewart and ruled that Sawchuk's death was accidental. Sawchuk was buried in Mount Hope Cemetery in [[Pontiac, Michigan|Pontiac]], [[Michigan]].<ref name=\"John A. Drobnicki 2002 p. 336\"/>\n\n==Legacy==\n[[Image:Red Wings retired Banners.jpg|290px|left|thumb|Sawchuk's #1 banner hanging in Joe Louis Arena.]]\nDuring his career, Sawchuk won 501 games (447 regular season and 54 playoff), while recording 115 [[shutout]]s, (103 in the regular season and 12 in the playoffs).<ref>{{cite web|title=Hockey Hall of Fame - Legends Of Hockey, Terry Sawchuk|url=http://www.legendsofhockey.net/LegendsOfHockey/jsp/LegendsMember.jsp?mem=p197103&type=Player&page=statsawards&list=#photo|website=hhof.com|access-date=March 9, 2015}}</ref> Sawchuk set the standard for measuring goaltenders, and was publicly hailed as the \"best goalie ever\" by a rival general manager in 1952, during only his second season.<ref>John A. Drobnicki, \"Sawchuk, Terrance Gordon ('Terry'),\" in ''The Scribner Encyclopedia of American Lives, Thematic Series: Sports Figures'' (Scribner's, 2002), Vol. 2, p. 337.</ref> He was the first goaltender to 400 wins, doing so in the [[1964–65 NHL season]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/stathead/tiny/UzQZf|title=For combined seasons, up to 1964-65, playing goalie, in the regular season, sorted by descending Wins.|work=Stathead}}</ref> Sawchuk finished his hockey career with 447 wins, a record that stood for thirty years, and his career record of 103 shutouts remained unsurpassed among NHL goaltenders, until [[Martin Brodeur]] bested that mark on December 21, 2009.<ref>{{cite web|title=Martin Brodeur Sets NHL Shutout Record, Devils Win 4-0|work=NESN.com|date=December 21, 2009|url=https://nesn.com/2009/12/martin-brodeur-sets-nhl-shutout-record-devils-win-40/|access-date=February 7, 2026|archive-url=https://archive.today/20260207090856/https://nesn.com/2009/12/martin-brodeur-sets-nhl-shutout-record-devils-win-40/|archive-date=February 7, 2026}}</ref> In 1971, Sawchuk was posthumously elected to the [[Hockey Hall of Fame]] and awarded the [[Lester Patrick Trophy]] for his contribution to hockey in the United States. The Red Wings retired his number 1 on March 6, 1994, with Sawchuk's relatives being part of the hoisting of the jersey, the fourth retired by the Red Wings. Sawchuk's teammates in [[Gordie Howe]], [[Ted Lindsay]], and [[Alex Delvecchio]] (all of whom had their numbers retired by Detroit) attended the ceremony alongside defenceman [[Marcel Pronovost]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://newspaperarchive.com/medicine-hat-news-mar-08-1994-p-20/|title=Red Wings honor Sawchuk|work=Medicine Hat News|first=Frank|last=Orr|date=March 8, 1994}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://newspaperarchive.com/ironwood-daily-globe-mar-07-1994-p-9/|work=Ironwood Daily Globe|title=Sabre Hasek does fine imitation of Sawchuk|agency=Associated Press|date=March 7, 1994}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|first=Richard|last=Bak|title=The troubled genius of Terry Sawchuk|url=https://www.vintagedetroit.com/the-troubled-genius-of-terry-sawchuk/|website=Vintage Detroit|date=December 6, 2014|access-date=December 23, 2019|archive-date=August 17, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210817150733/https://www.vintagedetroit.com/the-troubled-genius-of-terry-sawchuk/|url-status=live}}</ref> In 1996, the book ''Shutout: The Legend of Terry Sawchuk'' by sports author Brian Kendall, was published. A second book ''Sawchuk: The troubles and triumphs of the World's Greatest Goalie'' was published in 1998 by David Dupuis, with the participation of the Sawchuk family. In 2001, he was honoured with his image on a [[List of people on stamps of Canada|Canadian postage stamp]], even though he had become a U.S. citizen in 1959.  In 2008, ''Night Work: The Sawchuk Poems,'' a book of poetry about Sawchuk by [[Randall Maggs]], was published. The Terry Sawchuk Arena in his hometown of [[Winnipeg]] is named in his honour. In 2019, a film about his life and times was released, titled ''[[Goalie (film)|Goalie]]''. Newfoundland singer-songwriter [[Ron Hynes]] recorded a ballad in 'Sawchuk', released October 12, 2010 for Borealis Records.\n\nWhen Sawchuk joined the Maple Leafs, he originally wore [[number (sports)|jersey number]] 24 but he switched to 30. In the decades since, NHL goaltenders have chosen numbers in the 30s inspired by his example and that of players like the Canadiens' [[Patrick Roy]], who would have used 30 (the jersey number [[Rogie Vachon]] had used), but he was forced to pick another since it was already taken by right winger [[Chris Nilan]] (he instead chose 33, which itself became popular as a choice).<ref name=goalie1>{{cite web|last=Pinchevsky|first=Tal|title=Why goalies are increasingly ditching traditional No. 1|publisher=[[ESPN]]|date=November 30, 2016|url=https://www.espn.com/nhl/story/_/id/18268822/nhl-goalies-increasingly-ditching-traditional-no-1-other-numbers-their-sweaters|access-date=August 28, 2017}}</ref>\n\n==Awards and name=CSHoF>{{cite web|title=Terry Sawchuk|url=http://www.sportshall.ca/stories.html?proID=231&catID=all|publisher=Canada Sports Hall of Fame|access-date=February 20, 2015}}</ref>\n* In January 2017, Sawchuk was part of the first group of players to be named '100 Greatest NHL Players' in history.<ref name=\"100 Greatest NHL Players\"/>\n\n==Records==\n*NHL record - Career ties leader - 172.<ref>{{cite web|last=Chaves|first=Kevin|title=The Best Non-Gretzky Records in NHL History|url=http://www.prohockey-fans.com/hockey-articles/best-non-gretzky-records_090108.html|work=nhl.com|access-date=June 4, 2012|archive-date=July 21, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120721234205/http://www.prohockey-fans.com/hockey-articles/best-non-gretzky-records_090108.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>\n*Sawchuk's NHL record for career shutouts (103) stood until broken by [[Martin Brodeur]] in 2009. Sawchuk held the record for shutouts for 46 years. He passed George Hainsworth with his 95th shutout on January 18, 1964, for the all-time shutout record.\n\n==Career statistics==\n===Regular season and playoffs===\n'''Bold''' indicates led league<br/>'''''Bold italics''''' indicate NHL record\n{| border=\"0\" cellpadding=\"1\" cellspacing=\"0\" style=\"width:75%; text-align:center;\"\n|- bgcolor=\"#e0e0e0\"\n! colspan=\"3\" bgcolor=\"#ffffff\" |  \n! rowspan=\"99\" bgcolor=\"#ffffff\" |  \n! colspan=\"9\" bgcolor=\"#e0e0e0\" | [[Regular season]]\n! rowspan=\"99\" bgcolor=\"#ffffff\" |  \n! colspan=\"8\" bgcolor=\"#e0e0e0\" | [[Playoffs]]\n|- bgcolor=\"#e0e0e0\"\n!
