goals and assists for 86 points in all 82 games as the Flames as a team improved compared to the previous year as they narrowly missed the [[2011 Stanley Cup playoffs|playoffs]], only missing by three points in the standings. His 43 goals was the most on the team and third in the league overall only behind the 45 goals from [[Steven Stamkos]] of the Tampa Bay Lightning and the 50 goals from [[Corey Perry]] of the Anaheim Ducks. His 86 points were also sixth in the league only behind the 91 points by the Lightning's Stamkos, 94 points by Vancouver Canucks centre and captain [[Henrik Sedin]], 98 points by the Ducks' Perry, 99 points by Tampa Bay Lightning winger [[Martin St. Louis]] and the league-leading 104 points by Vancouver Canucks' winger [[Daniel Sedin]], respectively.\n\nIginla scored his [[List of NHL players with 500 goals|500th goal]] on January 7, 2012, against [[Niklas Bäckström]] of the Minnesota Wild in a 3–1 victory. He was the 42nd player in league history to achieve the feat, and the 15th to do so with one organization.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://canucks.nhl.com/club/news.htm?id=611373|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120115025502/http://canucks.nhl.com/club/news.htm?id=611373|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 15, 2012|title=NHL Fills out All-Star game roster|publisher=National Hockey League|date=January 12, 2012 |access-date=January 12, 2012|author=Kimelman, Adam}}</ref> Midway through the [[2011–12 NHL season|2011–12 season]], Iginla was named an All-Star for the seventh time in his career (the sixth played), representing the Flames at the [[59th National Hockey League All-Star Game|2012 All-Star Game]].<ref>{{cite news |last=MacFarlane |first=Steve |title=Iggy rated an all-star |work=Calgary Sun |date=January 13, 2012 |page=S11}}</ref> Iginla scored his 30th goal of the 2011–12 season in a 3–2 win against goaltender [[Antti Niemi (ice hockey)|Antti Niemi]] of the [[San Jose Sharks]] on March 13, 2012. He is the seventh player in league history to score 30 goals in 11 consecutive seasons.<ref name=\"Iggy30\">{{cite news |url=http://espn.go.com/nhl/recap?gameId=400047545 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130111065048/http://espn.go.com/nhl/recap?gameId=400047545 |url-status=dead |archive-date=January 11, 2013 |title=Flames top Sharks in OT as Jarome Iginla reaches 30 goals for 11th straight season |publisher=ESPN |date=March 13, 2012 |access-date=March 14, 2012}}</ref>\n\n====Pittsburgh Penguins====\n[[File: Jarome Iginla - Boston Bruins.jpg|thumb|right|Iginla in March 2014 with the [[Boston Bruins]]|alt=Iginla states intently into the distance as he skates near a net.]] Playing the final year of his contract in [[2012–13 NHL season|2012–13]] and with the team languishing near the bottom of the NHL standings, speculation about Iginla's future in Calgary was again raised as April 3, 2013, trade deadline neared.<ref>{{cite news |last=Francis |first=Eric |title=Iggy, Flames not talking |work=Calgary Sun |date=March 10, 2013 |page=S2}}</ref> National media outlets reported that Iginla, who had a clause in his contract preventing the Flames from moving him to another team without his permission, had given the organization a list of four teams he would be willing to accept a trade with: the [[Chicago Blackhawks]], [[Los Angeles Kings]], [[Boston Bruins]], or [[Pittsburgh Penguins]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Destination unknown |work=Calgary Sun |date=March 25, 2013 |page=S3}}</ref> Those four teams had won the last four championships and all four would go on to make the conference finals that season. The Bruins were considered the leading contender to acquire Iginla's services, and after he was held out of the line-up of Calgary's March 27, 2013, game against the [[Colorado Avalanche]], it was reported that a trade between the two teams had been completed.<ref>{{cite news |last=Johnson |first=George |title=Iginla trade imminent |work=Calgary Herald |date=March 28, 2013 |page=F1}}</ref> Instead, Iginla's 16-year career in Calgary ended when he was sent to the Penguins in exchange for Pittsburgh's first round selection at the [[2013 NHL entry draft]] and college prospects [[Kenny Agostino]] and [[Ben Hanowski]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.cbc.ca/sports/hockey/nhl/jarome-iginla-traded-to-penguins-1.1345284 |title=Jarome Iginla traded to Penguins |publisher=[[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation]] |date=March 28, 2013 |access-date=March 28, 2013}}</ref> Iginla stated that playing with [[Sidney Crosby]] and [[Evgeni Malkin]] played a factor in his decision to move to the Penguins.<ref>{{cite news |last=Perry |first=Rob |title=Sidney Crosby Helped Lure Jarome Iginla to Pittsburg |url=https://www.cbc.ca/sports/hockey/nhl/sidney-crosby-helped-lure-jarome-iginla-to-pittsburgh-1.1381671 |publisher=[[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation]] |date=March 30, 2013 |access-date=April 1, 2013}}</ref> The Bruins and Penguins met in the 2013 Eastern Conference Finals. Despite having the top-scoring offence in the league, the Penguins lost the series without winning a game. Iginla, along with Crosby, Malkin, [[James Neal (ice hockey)|James Neal]] and [[Kris Letang]], registered a combined 0 points in the series. Iginla was moved to the third line after a 6–1 game&nbsp;2 loss. Bruins forward [[Milan Lucic]] said after the series that Iginla's spurning of Boston ignited the series sweep: \"When a guy chooses another team over your team, it does light a little bit of a fire underneath you.\"<ref>{{cite news|title=Milan Lucic Says Jarome Iginla Did 'Light a Fire' Underneath Bruins by Choosing to Join Penguins |url=http://nesn.com/2013/06/milan-lucic-says-jarome-iginla-did-light-a-fire-underneath-bruins-by-choosing-to-join-penguins-video/|publisher=NESN|access-date=June 8, 2013}}</ref>\n\n====Boston Bruins====\nAs a [[free agent]] following the season, Iginla chose to go to Boston and signed a one-year, $6&nbsp;million contract with the Bruins.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.tsn.ca/nhl/story/?id=427068 |title=Iginla chooses to continue his career with Bruins |publisher=The Sports Network |date=July 5, 2013 |access-date=July 5, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140227064756/http://www.tsn.ca/nhl/story/?id=427068 |archive-date=February 27, 2014 |url-status=dead }}</ref> He recorded nine games before scoring his first goal as a Bruin, as part of a 2–1 win over the [[San Jose Sharks]],<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.espn.com/nhl/recap?gameId=400484382 |title=Bruins solve Sharks behind David Krejci goal with less than second left |publisher=ESPN |date=October 24, 2013 |access-date=December 11, 2013}}</ref> but later settled in on Boston's first line with Milan Lucic and [[David Krejčí]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Johnson |first=George |url=https://calgaryherald.com/sports/hockey/calgary-flames/Jarome+Iginla+return+bigger+pandemonium/9266617/story.html |title=Iginla's return a bigger pandemonium than some teammates expected |work=Calgary Herald |date=December 9, 2013 |access-date=December 11, 2013}}</ref> He made his first return to Calgary on December 10, 2013, where the fans greeted him with a long standing ovation prior to the game as the Flames played a video tribute. Following the contest, a 2–1 Bruins victory, Iginla was named the game's third star and took two laps around the rink to more cheers from the crowd.<ref>{{cite news |last=Johnson |first=George |url=https://calgaryherald.com/sports/hockey/calgary-flames/Johnson+Unforgettable+National+Hockey/9271455/story.html |title=Unforgettable night as fans pay emotional tribute to Iginla |work=Calgary Herald |date=December 11, 2013 |access-date=December 11, 2013 |archive-date=December 15, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131215201613/http://www.calgaryherald.com/sports/hockey/calgary-flames/Johnson+Unforgettable+National+Hockey/9271455/story.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> He recorded his 600th career assist on a Milan Lucic goal in a 3–1 victory over the [[Vancouver Canucks]] on February 4, 2014.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.espn.com/nhl/recap?gameId=400485087 |title=Jarome Iginla, Milan Lucic lead Bruins over struggling Canucks |publisher=ESPN |date=February 4, 2014 |access-date=February 5, 2014}}</ref>\n\n====Colorado Avalanche====\n[[File:Jarome Iginla - Colorado Avalanche.jpg|thumb|left|Iginla in November 2014. He played three seasons with the Avalanche.|alt=Iginla stares to his right as he stands on the ice surface during a pre-game warm-up.]]\n[[NHL salary cap|Salary cap]] constraints prevented the Bruins from re-signing Iginla. Consequently, he left the team as a free agent and signed a three-year, $16 million contract with the Colorado Avalanche.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.tsn.ca/nhl/story/?id=456199 | title = Avalanche sign Iginla to three-years, $16 million deal | publisher = The Sports Network | date = July 1, 2014 | access-date = July 1, 2014 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140820171122/http://www.tsn.ca/nhl/story/?id=456199 | archive-date = August 20, 2014 | url-status = dead }}</ref> The Avalanche disappointed in [[2014–15 NHL season|2014–15]]; by mid-February, they stood in last place in the [[Central Division (NHL)|Central Division]], though Iginla himself was among the team's leading scorers.<ref>{{cite news |last=Sadowski |first=Rick |url=http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=753785 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150218184925/http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=753785 |url-status=dead |archive-date=February 18, 2015 |title=Iginla believes Avalanche heading in right direction |publisher=National Hockey League |date=February 18, 2015 |access-date=June 29, 2015}}</ref> He led the team with 29 goals, however, the Avalanche failed to qualify for the playoffs.<ref>{{cite news |last=Chambers |first=Mike |url=http://www.denverpost.com/chambers/ci_27943658/chambers-jarome-iginla-an-asset-colorado-avalanche-not-an-issue |title=Jarome Iginla an asset for Colorado Avalanche, not an issue |work=The Denver Post |date=April 19, 2015 |access-date=June 29, 2015}}</ref> On January 4, 2016, Iginla became the 19th player in NHL history to score 600 career goals. His milestone marker came in a 4–1 victory over the Los Angeles Kings.<ref>{{cite news |last=Frei |first=Terry |title=Milestone by Iginla highlights rout of L.A. |work=The Denver Post |date=January 5, 2016 |page=1B}}</ref> On December 10, 2016, Iginla played in his 1,500th NHL game, a 10–1 loss to the Montreal Canadiens. He is the 16th player to reach this milestone.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nhl.com/news/colorado-avalanche-montreal-canadiens-game-recap-284592154 |title=Canadiens score 10 in win against Avalanche |last=Farrell |first=Sean |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161211062210/https://www.nhl.com/news/colorado-avalanche-montreal-canadiens-game-recap/c-284592154 |publisher=National Hockey League |date=December 10, 2016 |archive-date=December 11, 2016 |access-date=December 11, 2016 |url-status=live }}</ref>\n\n====Los Angeles Kings====\nOn March 1, 2017, Iginla was traded to the [[Los Angeles Kings]] for a [[2018 NHL Entry Draft|2018]] conditional fourth-round pick.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.sportsnet.ca/hockey/nhl/jarome-iginla-traded-los-angeles-kings/ |date=March 1, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170305072220/http://www.sportsnet.ca/hockey/nhl/jarome-iginla-traded-los-angeles-kings/ |archive-date=March 5, 2017 |url-status=live |title=Avalanche trade veteran forward Jarome Iginla to L.A. Kings |work=Sportsnet.ca |access-date=March 1, 2017  }}</ref> He chose to wear the number 88, as number 12 was already taken by [[Marián Gáborík]].<ref name=Dillman>{{cite web|url=https://www.nhl.com/news/jarome-iginla-will-honor-wayne-gretzky-by-wearing-number-88-287285444 |title=Jarome Iginla to wear No. 88 with Kings |date=March 1, 2017 |publisher=National Hockey League |last=Dillman |first=Lisa |access-date=March 7, 2017 }}</ref> As a 10-year-old, Iginla had purchased a Kings jersey and placed his name and the number 88 on the back after [[Wayne Gretzky]] was traded to the team.<ref name=Dillman/> Kings general manager [[Dean Lombardi]] hoped a fresh start for Iginla would ignite him after playing for a struggling team in Colorado.<ref name=Dillman/>\n\nIginla was not re-signed by the Kings for the [[2017–18 NHL season|2017–18 season]].<ref>{{cite web | last=Price | first=Shepard | title=Los Angeles Kings Should Re-Sign Jarome Iginla | website=Puck Prose|publisher=FanSided | date=2017-12-21 | url=https://puckprose.com/2017/12/21/los-angeles-kings-should-re-sign-jarome-iginla/ | access-date=2025-08-06}}</ref> It was reported that he had hip surgery in the autumn of 2017, but that he hoped to make a return to the NHL when interviewed during a practice that he took part in with the [[Providence Bruins]] in February 2018.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://fullpresscoverage.com/2018/02/21/jarome-iginla-eyes-nhl-return/ |date=February 21, 2018 |title=Jarome Iginla eyes NHL Return |access-date=April 23, 2018  }}</ref>\n\nOn July 30, 2018, Iginla announced his retirement.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Vickers |first1=Aaron |title=Iginla retires after 20 NHL seasons |url=https://www.nhl.com/news/jarome-iginla-retires-after-20-nhl-seasons-299629660 |publisher=National Hockey League |access-date=August 22, 2018 |date=July 30, 2018}}</ref>\n\nOn June 24, 2020, Iginla was selected for the Hockey Hall of Fame, in his first year of eligibility.<ref name=\"Press\"/>\n\n==International play==\n{{MedalTableTop|JaromeIginla2010WinterOlympicsfaceoff.jpg|220px|Iginla won gold medals at the Olympics in [[Ice hockey at the 2002 Winter Olympics|2002]] and [[Ice hockey at the 2010 Winter Olympics|2010]].|name=no}}\n{{MedalCountry | {{flagicon|Canada}} [[Canada]] }}\n{{MedalSport | Men's [[ice hockey]]}}\n{{MedalCompetition|[[Olympic Games]]}}\n{{MedalGold | [[Ice hockey at the 2002 Championship]]}}\n{{MedalGold | [[1997 Men's World Ice Hockey Championships|1997 Finland]] | }}\n{{MedalCompetition|[[World Cup of Hockey|World Cup]]}}\n{{MedalGold | [[2004 World Cup of Hockey]] | }}\n{{MedalCompetition|[[World Junior Ice Hockey Championship|World Junior Championship]]}}\n{{MedalGold | [[1996 World Junior Ice Hockey Championships|1996 USA]] |}}\n{{MedalBottom}}\n\nIginla first represented Canada at the 1994 [[Ivan Hlinka Memorial Tournament|Nations Cup]], an unsanctioned tournament for players under the age of 18. He led Canada in scoring with five goals and nine points as it won the gold medal.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.hockeycanada.ca/4/2/2/0/index1.shtml |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060514092829/http://www.hockeycanada.ca/4/2/2/0/index1.shtml |title=La Copa Mexico 1994 |publisher=Hockey Canada |archive-date=May 14, 2006 |access-date=December 9, 2008}}</ref> Two years later, he joined the [[Canada men's national junior ice hockey team|national junior team]] at the [[1996 World Junior Ice Hockey Championships]]. He led the tournament in scoring with five goals and 12&nbsp; points as Canada won its fourth consecutive gold medal. He was named an all-star and the tournament's top forward.<ref name=\"Blaze1129\" /><ref name=\"TSN-WJHC\" /> One year later, Iginla played in his first tournament with the [[Canada men's national ice hockey team|senior team]], competing at the [[1997 Men's World Ice Hockey Championships|1997 World Championships]] as a 19-year-old, the youngest player on the team.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.hockeycanada.ca/index.php/ci_id/4722/la_id/1.htm |title=1997 IIHF World Championship |publisher=Hockey Canada |access-date=December 9, 2008}}</ref> He recorded two goals and three assists in 11&nbsp;games as Canada won the gold medal.<ref name=\"LOH\" />\n\nA late invitation to join Team Canada's summer camp in preparation for the [[Ice hockey at the 2002 Winter Olympics|2002 Winter Olympics]] helped Iginla emerge as a star player. He was so surprised by the invitation he initially thought one of his [[Calgary Flames]] teammates were playing a prank on him.<ref>{{cite web|last=Johnson |first=George |url=http://www.pressreader.com/Canada/national-post-latest-edition/20090820 |title=Iginla for the captain, and that's no joke |work=National Post |date=August 20, 2009 |access-date=August 21, 2009}}{{subscription required}}</ref> He scored two goals in the gold medal game, a 5–2 victory over the [[United States men's national ice hockey team|United States]], as Canada won its first Olympic gold medal in 50&nbsp; years.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/olympics/2002/ice_hockey/news/2002/02/24/usa_canada_ap/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020224224658/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/olympics/2002/ice_hockey/news/2002/02/24/usa_canada_ap/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=February 24, 2002 |title=Stand on guard for thee |publisher=CNN Sports Illustrated |date=February 24, 2002 |access-date=December 9, 2008}}</ref> With this win, Iginla became the first Black man to win a gold medal at the Winter Olympics.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2002/02/25/sports/olympics-the-pioneer-a-humble-iginla-raises-his-profile.html |title=OLYMPICS: THE PIONEER; A Humble Iginla Raises His Profile |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=February 25, 2002 |access-date=January 21, 2013 |first=Kate |last=Zernike}}</ref> Iginla also represented Canada at the [[2004 World Cup of Hockey]] as an alternate captain, playing on a line with [[Joe Sakic]] and [[Mario Lemieux]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.espn.com/espn/print?id=1877692 |title=Brodeur nabs first shutout of World Cup |publisher=ESPN |date=September 8, 2008 |access-date=January 2, 2009}}</ref> Canada won the gold medal.<ref>{{cite news |last=Lapointe |first=Joe |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2004/09/15/sports/hockey/15hockey.html?pagewanted=print&position= |title=Canada's Cup Victory May End Up Half Empty |work=The New York Times |date=September 15, 2004 |access-date=January 2, 2009}}</ref>\n\nIginla participated in his second Olympics and was an alternate captain at the [[2006 Winter Olympics|2006 Turin]] games, recording three points in six games.<ref name=\"LOH\"/> The Canadians were unable to defend their 2002 gold medal, losing to Russia in the quarter-finals.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.espn.com/olympics/winter06/hockey/news/story?id=2341523 |title=Gretzky questions future role with Hockey Canada |publisher=ESPN |date=February 23, 2006 |access-date=January 2, 2009}}</ref> Named an alternate captain once again for the [[Ice hockey at the 2010 Winter Olympics|2010 team]] in Vancouver,<ref>{{cite news |last=Wyman |first=Ted |url=http://www.torontosun.com/sports/hockey/2008/12/21/7817956-sun.html |title=Cream of the crop |newspaper=Toronto Sun |date=December 21, 2008 |access-date=January 2, 2009}}</ref> he opened the tournament with a hat trick against Norway.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://vancouversun.com/sports/2010wintergames/Olympic+hockey+Jarome+Iginla+trick+propels+Canada/2573220/story.html |title=Jarome Iginla's hat trick propels Canada to 8–0 win |work=The Vancouver Sun |date=February 17, 2010 |access-date=February 28, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100221061827/http://www.vancouversun.com/sports/2010wintergames/Olympic%2Bhockey%2BJarome%2BIginla%2Btrick%2Bpropels%2BCanada/2573220/story.html |archive-date=February 21, 2010 }}</ref> He finished as the tournament leader with five goals,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ctvolympics.ca/hockey/statistics/gender=m/fullGoals.html |title=Goal scoring leaders – Men |publisher=CTV |access-date=February 28, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100303142827/http://www.ctvolympics.ca/hockey/statistics/gender%3Dm/fullGoals.html |archive-date=March 3, 2010 }}</ref> and assisted on [[Sidney Crosby]]'s overtime winning goal in the gold medal final against the United States.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.cbc.ca/sports/2.722/canada-outlasts-u-s-for-hockey-gold-1.867197 |title=Canada outlasts U.S. for hockey gold |publisher=[[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation]] |date=February 28, 2010 |access-date=February 28, 2010|author=Wharnsin, Tim}}</ref><ref name=\"SIFarber2010\"/>\n\n==Playing style==\nIn his prime, Iginla was considered to be one of the NHL's most prominent [[Power forward (ice hockey)|power forwards]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Nichols |first=Chris |url=http://www.sportsnet.ca/hockey/2008/09/18/nichols_power_forwards/ |title=NHL Power Brokers |publisher=Rogers Sportsnet |date=September 18, 2008 |access-date=January 4, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080922053037/http://www.sportsnet.ca/hockey/2008/09/18/nichols_power_forwards/ |archive-date=September 22, 2008 }}</ref> Upon entering the league, he tried to emulate players like [[Brendan Shanahan]] and [[Keith Tkachuk]], hoping to match their combination of finesse and physicality.<ref name=\"Impact\" /> He was one of the most consistent scorers in the league; between 1998 and 2008, only [[Jaromír Jágr]] scored more NHL goals than Iginla.<ref name=\"Consistency\">{{cite web|last=Cruikshank |first=Scott |url=http://www2.canada.com/saskatoonstarphoenix/news/sports/story.html?id=7f057796-13e3-4995-b54c-5a5028b0d108 |title=Iginla's scoring consistency amazes most |work=Saskatoon Star-Phoenix |date=January 4, 2008 |access-date=May 28, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120609141440/http://www2.canada.com/saskatoonstarphoenix/news/sports/story.html?id=7f057796-13e3-4995-b54c-5a5028b0d108 |archive-date=June 9, 2012 }}</ref> Even so, scouting reports have argued that Iginla's lack of speed makes it easier for opponents to isolate him and restrict his ability to move if his teammates rely on him too much to lead the offence.<ref name=\"TSN2004Bio\">{{cite news |last=Yorio |first=Kara |title=Scouting Report: Jarome Iginla, RW, Calgary Flames |work=The Sporting News |date=March 15, 2004 |volume=228 |issue=11 |page=61}}</ref>\n[[File:Att snvända materialet i ishockeyklubban som är gjord av Carbon är viktigt för att öka hastigheten i skottet.jpg|thumb|left|Iginla taking a shot.]]\nThe abuse he faced at the hands of opponents early in his NHL career prompted Iginla's coaches to work at developing his physical play. While he was not enthusiastic about fighting, Iginla accepted then head coach [[Brian Sutter]]'s arguments that he needed to adopt a more aggressive style to improve as a player. Iginla was most effective when he had room to manoeuvre, and to create that space, he had to intimidate his opponents.<ref>{{cite news |last=Maki |first=Allan |title=Sutter tries to light a flame under Iginla |work=The Globe and Mail |date=October 16, 1998 |page=S5}}</ref> \"You've got a power forward who does it all,\" said [[Craig Conroy]]. \"I mean, he'll fight, and hit, and score goals. Maybe it's not the end-to-end rushes, but he does all those little things that win games and get things done.\"<ref name=\"Avery\">{{cite web|last=Hall |first=Vicki |url=http://www.canada.com/calgaryherald/news/sports/story.html?id=717c5c54-855e-42cd-9d43-d02fba8080bc |title=Avery takes jab at Iginla |work=Calgary Herald |date=October 9, 2008 |access-date=January 4, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101124231531/http://www.canada.com/calgaryherald/news/sports/story.html?id=717c5c54-855e-42cd-9d43-d02fba8080bc |archive-date=November 24, 2010 }}</ref> His opponents also respect his play. [[Rob Blake]] said that while Iginla is not known for fancy play, \"he'll run you over. Or he'll fight somebody. And then he'll score a goal. He does pretty much everything you'd want a guy to do.\"<ref name=\"Consistency\" />\n\nIginla recorded several [[Gordie Howe hat trick]]s – a fight, a goal and an assist in the same game – and as it is not an official statistic, ''[[The Hockey News]]'' estimated that as of 2012, he was the active leader with nine.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Howe to Hat Trick |journal=The Hockey News |date=March 16, 2012 |volume=65 |number=20 |issn=0018-3016 |page=14}}</ref> His fights, including one with [[Tampa Bay Lightning]] star [[Vincent Lecavalier]] in the [[2004 Stanley Cup Finals]], have had a motivating effect on his play and that of his teammates.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.espn.com/nhl/playoffs2004/news/story?id=1812373 |title=Calgary wins with intensity, goaltending |publisher=ESPN |date=May 30, 2004 |access-date=May 28, 2009}}</ref> Iginla suffered injuries as a result of his fighting, including a broken hand from a 2003 fight with [[Bill Guerin]] of the [[Dallas Stars]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Maki |first=Allan |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/sports/article734282.ece |title=Iginla says fight not to blame for injured knee |work=The Globe and Mail |access-date=May 28, 2009 |location=Toronto |date=January 5, 2007 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120112132834/http://www.theglobeandmail.com/sports/article734282.ece |archive-date=January 12, 2012 }}</ref> Iginla's truculent style of play gained approval from hockey commentator Don Cherry. In 2008 during a ceremonial handshake initiated by Iginla to Trevor Linden in his last game, Linden told Iginla he was the best player in the game at that time.\n\nHe commands the respect of his peers and has been known to stand up to the coaching staff to defend a fellow player. Former teammate [[Andrew Ference]] — a former Bruins player himself, before Iginla's arrival on the Boston team's roster — once described following Iginla as like \"following a friend.\"<ref name=\"Consistency\" /> Preferring to lead by example, Iginla is not regarded as a vocal captain. He likes to speak with players individually and tries to ensure that all of his teammates are comfortable.<ref name=\"Captain\" /> He was named the recipient of the [[Mark Messier Leadership Award]] in 2009.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.tsn.ca/nhl/story/?id=282273 |title=Ovechkin captures Hart and Pearson Awards in Las Vegas |publisher=The Sports Network |date=June 18, 2009 |access-date=June 19, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140429075945/http://www.tsn.ca/nhl/story/?id=282273 |archive-date=April 29, 2014 |url-status=dead }}</ref>\n\n==Personal life==\nIginla married his high school sweetheart Kara. The couple have three children: daughter [[Jade Iginla|Jade]] and sons [[Tij Iginla|Tij]] and Joe. They had been dating since they were in grade eight.<ref name=\"Blaze1129\" /> Jade attended and played hockey for [[Shattuck-Saint Mary's]] and [[Kelowna]]'s RINK Hockey Academy, before attending [[Brown University]] and playing for the [[Brown Bears women's ice hockey|Brown Bears]] in the [[NCAA]].<ref name=Athletic220426>{{cite web |last1=Clark |first1=Ryan S. |title=You know Jarome Iginla. Now meet the next generation of Iginlas making their mark|url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/3240269/2022/04/26/jarome-iginla-kids/ |website=[[The Athletic]] |date=April 26, 2022 |access-date=May 31, 2022}}</ref> Internationally, she has represented [[Canada women's national under-18 ice hockey team|Canada]] at the under-18 level.<ref>{{cite web |title=Daughter of Flames great Jarome Iginla to play for Canada at women's U18 worlds|url=https://www.cbc.ca/sports/hockey/canada-women-under-18-world-hockey-championship-1.6471343 |website=[[CBC Sports]] |date=May 30, 2022 |access-date=May 31, 2022}}</ref> Tij currently plays for the [[Kelowna Rockets]] and was the first-ever draft selection for the [[Utah Mammoth]], after he was drafted sixth overall in the [[2024 NHL entry draft|2024 NHL entry draft]].<ref name=Athletic220426/><ref>{{cite web |title='I kind of blacked out': Like Jarome, Tij Iginla makes Utah history |url=https://www.sportsnet.ca/nhl/article/utah-hockey-club-selects-tij-iginla-with-first-draft-pick-in-franchise-history/ |last=Fox |first=Luke |website=[[Sportsnet]] |date=June 28, 2024 |access-date=June 29, 2024}}</ref> Joe played for [[Kelowna]]’s RINK Hockey Academy, with Jarome as his head coach, played for the [[Edmonton Oil Kings]] having been taken by them in the first round of the 2023, [[WHL Bantam Draft]], and now plays for the Vancouver Giants.<ref>{{cite web |title=Joe Iginla, 15, showing early flashes of father's scoring ability, ruggedness |url=https://www.sportsnet.ca/nhl/article/joe-iginla-15-showing-early-flashes-of-fathers-scoring-ability-ruggedness/ |last=Francis |first=Eric |website=[[Sportsnet]] |date=December 28, 2023 |access-date=June 29, 2024}}</ref>\n\nIginla has four paternal half-siblings; two brothers, Jason and Stephen, and two sisters, Theresa and Elizabeth.<ref>{{cite book |last=Elicksen |first=Debbie |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xiekI_Yuph8C&q=Jarome+Iginla+NHL+diversity&pg=PA49 |title=Positive Sports |publisher=Freelance Communications |year=2003 |page=90 |isbn=0-9730237-3-2}}</ref> Theresa played for the [[University of Saskatchewan Huskies]] women's hockey team for three seasons from 2004 to 2007. Jarome is an avid [[golf]]er and a regular participant in the Calgary Flames Celebrity Charity Golf Classic.<ref name=\"Blaze1129\" />\n\nIginla is a [[Christianity|Christian]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.calgarychristian.com/articles/2004/406-jarome_iginla.htm |last=Gulbranson |first=Davin |title=Jarome Iginla—The Smile Says It All |work=City Light News |access-date=February 27, 2009 |quote=His mom is a Buddhist; his dad, a Christian. \"I was playing in Kamloops as a junior when I accepted Christ as my Savior.\" |archive-date=July 21, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110721012409/http://www.calgarychristian.com/articles/2004/406-jarome_iginla.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref> The most notable quote regarding his faith was “I believe He died for us, and I believe He’s there for us and we can lean on Him. And I do.”<ref>{{cite web |last1=Ackerman |first1=Jon |title=Jarome Iginla inducted into Hockey Hall of Fame after 20-year NHL career leaning on God |url=https://sportsspectrum.com/sport/hockey/2020/06/25/jarome-iginla-hockey-hall-of-fame-god/ |website=Sports Spectrum |date=June 25, 2020 |access-date=July 10, 2020}}</ref>\n\nIginla is well known for his kind-hearted nature. Former Flames General manager [[Craig Button]] described Iginla as being grounded: \"He doesn't carry himself with any attitude or arrogance. He's confident in his abilities. He's self-assured. He's genuine. He's a better person than he is a player, and we all know what kind of player he is.\"<ref>{{cite news |last=Ross |first=Sherry |url=http://www.nydailynews.com/archives/sports/fanning-flames-jarome-iginla-hottest-ticket-canada-article-1.510138?pgno=2 |title=Jarome Iginla becoming the hottest ticket in Canada |work=Daily News|location=New York |date=October 6, 2002 |access-date=January 2, 2009}}</ref> In 2002, while in [[Salt Lake City]] for the [[2002 Winter Olympics|Winter Olympic Games]], Iginla struck up a conversation with four Calgarians sitting next to his table and found out they were sleeping in their car outside of the hotel. He excused himself from the conversation, and booked them accommodations at his own expense at the hotel his family was staying in.<ref>{{cite web |last=Francis |first=Eric |url=http://slam.canoe.com/Slam/Columnists/Francis/2007/11/30/4697730-sun.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150505175521/http://slam.canoe.com/Slam/Columnists/Francis/2007/11/30/4697730-sun.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=May 5, 2015 |title=Iggy's Salt of the Earth |work=Calgary Sun |date=November 3, 2007 |access-date=January 2, 2009}}</ref>\n\nSince 2002,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.canoe.com/WHLNews0102/0726.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20021118174528/http://www.canoe.com/WHLNews0102/0726.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=November 18, 2002 |title=Willie O'Ree to appear at Jarome Iginla Hockey School |publisher=Canoe.ca |date=July 26, 2002 |access-date=December 16, 2008 }}</ref> he has operated the Jarome Iginla Hockey School in Calgary as a non-profit organization, donating proceeds to the Diabetes Research Association.<ref name=\"Blaze1129\" /> In 2004, he was awarded the [[NHL Foundation Player Award]] for his community service and the [[King Clancy Memorial Trophy]] in recognition of his humanitarian contributions.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.legendsofhockey.net/LegendsOfHockey/jsp/SilverwareTrophyWinner.jsp?tro=KCT&year=2003-04 |title=2003–04 King Clancy Memorial Trophy winner – Jarome Iginla |publisher=Hockey Hall of Fame |access-date=December 16, 2008}}</ref> Iginla supports many charities. In 2000, he began donating $1,000 per goal he scored to KidSport, a figure he doubled to $2,000 in 2005. Between 2000 and 2013, he donated more than $700,000 from this initiative.<ref>{{cite news |last=Zickefoose |first=Sherri |title=Superstar's touch will continue to benefit charities: Iginla has been an ambassador for non-profit body|url=https://calgaryherald.com/entertainment/Superstar+touch+will+continue+benefit+charities/8168079/story.html |date=March 28, 2013 |access-date=March 6, 2014 |work=Calgary Herald}}</ref>\n\nIginla is a part owner of the [[Kamloops Blazers]] of the [[Western Hockey League]], for whom he played during his junior hockey days.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.blazerhockey.com/content/team/owners.php |title=Meet the Kamloops Blazers owners |publisher=Kamloops Blazers Hockey Club |access-date=January 2, 2009| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080302110819/http://www.blazerhockey.com/content/team/owners.php| archive-date = March 2, 2008}}</ref> He purchased a minority share in the franchise, along with fellow NHL players [[Shane Doan]], [[Mark Recchi]] and [[Darryl Sydor]], in October 2007.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.whl.ca/article/whl-board-of-governors-approve-sale-of-the-kamloops-blazers/75463 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130115154725/http://www.whl.ca/article/whl-board-of-governors-approve-sale-of-the-kamloops-blazers/75463 |url-status=dead |archive-date=January 15, 2013 |title=WHL Board of Governors Approve Sale of the Kamloops Blazers |publisher=Western Hockey League |date=October 10, 2007 |access-date=January 7, 2009 }}</ref> He is also an ambassador with the NHL Diversity program, which supports youth hockey organizations that offer economically disadvantaged children the opportunity to play.<ref>{{cite book |last=Elicksen |first=Debbie |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xiekI_Yuph8C&q=Jarome+Iginla+NHL+diversity&pg=PA49 |title=Positive Sports |publisher=Freelance Communications |year=2003 |page=49 |isbn=0-9730237-3-2}}</ref> Since 2008, he has been a hockey spokesperson for [[Scotiabank]], appearing in commercials and at events supporting its grassroots hockey programs,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cnw.ca/fr/releases/archive/October2008/02/c2694.html |title=Calgary Flames Captain Jarome Iginla Laces Up to Join Scotiabank's 2008–2009 NHL Lineup as Special Advisor on Hockey |publisher=Bank of Nova Scotia |date=October 2, 2008 |access-date=April 16, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110606072955/http://www.cnw.ca/fr/releases/archive/October2008/02/c2694.html |archive-date=June 6, 2011 }}</ref> as well as for [[Samsung Canada]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Dickie |first=Mary |url=http://www.strategymag.com/articles/magazine/20090101/biz.html |title=Samsung's human touch |work=Strategy Magazine |date=January 2009 |publisher=Brunico Communications |page=10 }}{{Dead link|date=August 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>\n\nHe was the cover athlete and spokesperson for the [[EA Sports]] video game [[NHL 2003]].<ref name=oldcovers>{{cite web|last=Bonanno |first=Rocky |publisher=[[National Hockey League]] |title=Kane lands on EA SPORTS NHL 10 cover |url=http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=426224 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110628180841/http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=426224 |archive-date=June 28, 2011 |date=June 22, 2009 |access-date=June 28, 2010 |url-status=dead }}</ref>\n\nSince retiring, Iginla has resided in [[Chestnut Hill, Massachusetts]]<ref>{{cite news |last=Shinzawa |first=Fluto |url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/445595/2018/07/26/jarome-iginla-retiring-as-a-calgary-flame-but-impact-in-boston-went-beyond-his-ice-time/ |title=Jarome Iginla retiring as a Calgary Flame, but the impact in Boston went beyond his ice time |work=The Athletic |date=July 26, 2018 |access-date=September 14, 2018}}</ref> and [[Lake Country]], [[British Columbia]].\n\n==Career He wears a green jersey with a logo of a stylized orca in the shape of a \"C\".\n| caption = Luongo practicing with the [[Vancouver Canucks]] in April 2009\n| birth_date = {{birth date and age|1979|4|4}}\n| birth_place = [[Montreal]], Quebec, Canada\n| height_ft = 6\n| height_in = 3\n| weight_lb = 215\n| position = [[Goaltender]]\n| catches = Left\n| played_for = [[New York Islanders]]<br>[[Florida Panthers]]<br>[[Vancouver Canucks]]\n| ntl_team = CAN\n| draft = 4th overall\n| draft_year = 1997\n| draft_team = [[New York Islanders]]\n| career_start = 1999\n| career_end = 2019\n}}\n'''Roberto Luongo'''{{#tag:ref|{{IPAc-en|l|u|ˈ|ɒ|ŋ|ɡ|oʊ}}, {{IPA|it|ˈlwɔŋɡo|lang}}, {{IPA|nap|ˈlwoŋɡə|lang}}|group=note}} (born April 4, 1979) is a Canadian former professional [[ice hockey]] player. He played 19 seasons in the [[National Hockey League]] (NHL) as a [[goaltender]] for the [[New York Islanders]], [[Florida Panthers]], and [[Vancouver Canucks]]. In 2022, Luongo was inducted into the Hockey Hall of Fame. Luongo is a two-time [[NHL All-Star team|NHL All-Star]] ([[2003–04 NHL season|2004]] and [[2006–07 NHL season|2007]]) and winner of the [[William M. Jennings Trophy]] for backstopping his team to the lowest [[goals against average]] in the league ([[2010–11 NHL season|2011]], with backup [[Cory Schneider]]). He was a finalist for several awards, including the [[Vezina Trophy]] as the league's best goaltender (2004, 2007, and 2011), the [[Lester B. Pearson Award]] as the top player voted by his peers (2004 and 2007), and the [[Hart Memorial Trophy]] as the league's most valuable player (2007).<ref name=\"2004 Awards\">{{cite news |title=St. Louis, Tortorella, Richards win awards |url=https://www.espn.com/nhl/news/story?id=1819644 |date=June 11, 2004 |work=[[ESPN]] |access-date=February 2, 2010 |archive-date=November 6, 2012 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121106192519/http://sports.espn.go.com/nhl/news/story?id=1819644 }}</ref><ref name=\"2007 Awards\"/> Luongo is third all-time in games played as an NHL goaltender (1,044) and [[List of NHL goaltenders with 300 wins|fourth all-time in wins]] (489). He employed the [[butterfly style]] of goaltending.<ref name=groin/>\n\nBorn in [[Montreal]], Quebec, he played in the [[Quebec Major Junior Hockey League]] (QMJHL) for the [[Val-d'Or Foreurs]] and the [[Acadie-Bathurst Titan]], winning back-to-back [[President's Cup (QMJHL)|President's Cups]] and establishing the league's all-time playoff records for games played and wins.<ref name=qmjhlalltime/> Following his second QMJHL season, Luongo was selected fourth overall by the Islanders in the [[1997 NHL entry draft]]. After splitting his professional rookie season between the Islanders and their [[American Hockey League]] (AHL) affiliate, the [[Lowell Lock Monsters]] in [[1999–2000 NHL season|1999–2000]], he was traded to the Panthers. In five seasons with Florida, Luongo established team records for games played, wins, and [[Shutout#Ice hockey|shutouts]]; despite several strong seasons, however, the Panthers remained a weak team and were unable to qualify for the [[Stanley Cup playoffs]] during Luongo's initial stint with the team. During the 2006 offseason, he was traded to the Canucks after failed contract negotiations with the Panthers.\n\nIn his first season in Vancouver, Luongo won 47 games, and was runner-up for both the [[Hart Memorial Trophy]] (league MVP) and [[Vezina Trophy]] (best goaltender). Following his second year with the Canucks, he became the first NHL goaltender to serve as a [[captain (ice hockey)|team captain]] since [[Bill Durnan]] in the [[1947–48 NHL season|1947–48 season]].<ref name=captain/> Luongo served in that capacity for two seasons before resigning from the position in September 2010.<ref name=\"step down\">{{cite news|title=Luongo steps down as captain |url=https://www.cbc.ca/sports/hockey/luongo-steps-down-as-captain-1.900547 |access-date=September 13, 2010 |work=[[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation]] |date=September 13, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100916040957/http://www.cbc.ca/sports/hockey/story/2010/09/13/sp-canucks-captain.html |archive-date=September 16, 2010 |url-status=live}}</ref> In the subsequent 2010–11 season, he helped the Canucks to Game 7 of the [[2011 Stanley Cup Final|Stanley Cup Final]] but lost to the [[Boston Bruins]]. During his eight-year tenure with Vancouver, Luongo became the team's all-time leader in wins and shutouts. He returned to the Panthers during the [[2013–14 NHL season|2013–14 season]], where he spent the remainder of his career, qualifying for the playoffs with the Panthers only once during that time. He was the last active goaltender to have played in the NHL in the 1990s. Following his playing career, Luongo joined the Panthers' front office as an executive, ultimately winning back-to-back [[Stanley Cup]] championships in [[2024 Stanley Cup Final|2024]] and [[2025 Stanley Cup Final|2025]].\n\nInternationally, Luongo has competed for [[Canada national men's ice hockey team|Team Canada]] in numerous tournaments. As a junior, he won a silver medal at the [[1999 World Junior Ice Hockey Championships|1999 World Junior Championships]], while being named [[List of IIHF World Under 20 Championship Directorate award winners|Best Goaltender]] in his second tournament appearance. Luongo won two gold medals at the [[2003 Men's World Ice Hockey Championships|2003]] and [[2004 Men's World Ice Hockey Championships|2004 World Championships]] and a silver in the [[2005 Men's World Ice Hockey Championships|2005 World Championships]]. He also won the [[2004 World Cup of Hockey|2004 World Cup]] championship and appeared in the [[Ice hockey at the 2006 Winter Olympics|2006 Winter Olympics]] in [[Turin]] as a backup to [[Martin Brodeur]] in both instances. He succeeded Brodeur as Canada's starting goaltender during the [[Ice hockey at the 2010 Winter Olympics|2010 Winter Olympics]] in [[Vancouver]], winning a gold medal. On January 7, 2014, he was named to the [[Canada men's national ice hockey team#Players|2014 Canadian Olympic hockey team]], where he won his second Olympic gold medal in a largely backup role to [[Carey Price]].\n\n==Early life==\nLuongo was born to Pasqualina and Antonio Luongo in [[Montreal]], Quebec.<ref name=fuhr/> His father is an Italian immigrant, born in [[Santa Paolina]], Avellino.<ref name=stampa>{{cite news|title=Stasera la finale di hockey, Luongo: \"Battero gli Usa sentendomi Buffon |url=http://www.lastampa.it/sport/cmsSezioni/vancouver2010/201002articoli/25533girata.asp |date=February 28, 2010 |work=La Stampa |author=Brusorio, Paolo |language=Italian |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100303215546/http://www.lastampa.it/sport/cmsSezioni/vancouver2010/201002articoli/25533girata.asp |archive-date=March 3, 2010 |url-status=dead}}</ref> He worked in the construction and delivery of furniture,<ref name=fuhr/> while Luongo's mother, an Irish-Canadian,<!--DO NOT CHANGE! There are two references, one of which is an interview with Luongo himself, stating that his mother is of Irish descent. See talk page for more details.--><ref name=alive>{{cite journal|title=Roberto Luongo Setting a gold standard |url=http://www.aliveonline.ca/7544a20a2.php |access-date=March 2, 2010 |date=February 2010 |author=Niemer, Ellen |journal=[[Alive Magazine]] |issue=328 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110221202918/http://www.aliveonline.ca/7544a20a2.php |archive-date=February 21, 2011 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=NYTimes/><ref name=espresso/> worked in [[marketing]] with [[Air Canada]].<ref name=fuhr/> Antonio and Pasqualina married in Montreal after Antonio immigrated there in 1976.<ref name=stampa/>\n\nLuongo has two younger brothers, Leo and Fabio, who also aspired to be goaltenders.<ref name=fuhr/> Fabio progressed the further of the two, playing Junior A in the [[British Columbia Hockey League]] (BCHL) with the [[Williams Lake Timberwolves]] in 2004–05 before injuries ended his career.<ref name=curse/> He has since become a Junior AAA coach, while Leo is a goaltending coach with [[HC Lugano]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hclugano.ch/index.cfm?u=staff_en&lan=en|title=Hockey Club Lugano|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://archive.today/20140812002300/http://www.hclugano.ch/index.cfm?u=staff_en&lan=en|archive-date=August 12, 2014}}</ref> Luongo and his family lived in [[Saint-Leonard, Quebec]], a [[borough]] north of Montreal with a strong Italian community,<ref name=fuhr/><ref name=NYTimes/> just four blocks away from [[Martin Brodeur]],<ref name=\"Early life\">{{cite web |url=http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=406018 |title=Return to Montreal as All-Star special to \"Bobby Lu\" |publisher=[[National Hockey League]] |date=January 23, 2009 |author=Dan Rosen |access-date=January 24, 2009 |archive-date=February 3, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090203122633/http://nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=406018 }}</ref> who became the goaltender for the [[New Jersey Devils]] six years before Luongo entered the NHL. Luongo is fluent in English, French and Italian.<ref name=fuhr/><ref name=NYTimes/> His father spoke Italian and his mother spoke English with a little French at home.<ref name=curse/>\n\nLuongo graduated from Montreal [[Francophone]] [[high school]] Antoine de St-Exupéry in 1996.<ref name=curse>{{cite news |title=Luongo looks to lift the curse |url=https://www.straight.com/article/luongo-looks-to-lift-the-curse |date=September 28, 2006 |work=[[Georgia Straight]] |access-date=September 10, 2017 |archive-date=October 29, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181029065802/https://www.straight.com/article/luongo-looks-to-lift-the-curse }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Association des anciens de l'école secondaire Antoine-de-St-Exupéry |url=http://www.anciens-de-st-ex.org/?page=membres/anciens_honneur.html |date=February 2, 2010 |publisher=Antoine de St-Exupéry |language=French |access-date=March 1, 2010 |archive-date=April 8, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100408035242/http://www.anciens-de-st-ex.org/?page=membres/anciens_honneur.html }}</ref> He began playing organized hockey at the age of eight as a [[forward (ice hockey)|forward]].<ref name=NYTimes/> His father taught all his sons [[soccer]] and Luongo played until he was 14, at which point he decided to concentrate on hockey.<ref name=fuhr/> Although he initially had the desire to play in net, his parents wanted him to develop his skating first.<ref name=NYTimes/> Several years later, after Luongo was cut from a peewee team, he made the switch to goaltender.<ref name=NYTimes/> At 11 years old, his team's usual goaltender did not show up and after begging his mother, still hesitant about Luongo playing the position, he went in net and posted a [[shutout]].<ref name=arena>{{cite web |title=Roberto Luongo joins Martin Brodeur after arena named in his honour |url=http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=480116 |date=August 22, 2009 |publisher=[[National Hockey League]] |access-date=September 9, 2009 |archive-date=June 4, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110604115944/http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=480116 }}</ref> In August 2009, the arena in which Luongo played his minor hockey in St. Leonard was named after him as the Roberto Luongo Arena. It is the second arena in the community to be named after an NHL goaltender after the Martin Brodeur Arena was renamed as such in 2000.<ref name=arena/>\n\nBy 15, Luongo was playing midget with Montreal-Bourassa, the same team that produced NHL Quebecer goaltenders Brodeur and [[Félix Potvin]].<ref name=NYTimes/> Luongo has credited [[Hockey Hall of Fame|Hall of Fame]] goaltender [[Grant Fuhr]] as his inspiration growing up, citing an admiration for his \"spectacular glove saves\".<ref name=NYTimes/> He had the opportunity to first meet Fuhr before a game against the [[Calgary Flames]] during his rookie season with the Islanders.<ref name=fuhr>{{cite news|url=http://www.nydailynews.com/archives/sports/1999/12/26/1999-12-26_luongo_has_reached_goal_fuhr.html |title=Luongo has reached goal: Fuhr inspired Isles' rookie to pursue career in the net |access-date=August 24, 2008 |date=December 26, 1999 |work=[[New York Daily News]] |archive-url=https://archive.today/20110109003549/http://www.nydailynews.com/archives/sports/1999/12/26/1999-12-26_luongo_has_reached_goal_fuhr.html |archive-date=January 9, 2011 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=NYTimes/>\n\n==Playing career==\n\n===Junior career (1995–1999)===\nThe [[Val-d'Or Foreurs]] made Luongo the highest-drafted goaltender in [[Quebec Major Junior Hockey League]] (QMJHL) history, at second overall, in 1995.<ref name=sportsill/> He began his [[junior ice hockey|junior]] career in the [[1995–96 QMJHL season|1995–96 season]] with Val-d'Or and posted six wins in 23 games played. As the team's starting goaltender the following season in [[1996–97 QMJHL season|1996–97]], he improved to a team-record 32 wins,<ref name=32wins>{{cite news |title=Pickard proud of New Brunswick roots |url=http://telegraphjournal.canadaeast.com/sports/article/528643 |date=January 3, 2009 |work=[[Telegraph-Journal]] |access-date=February 6, 2010 |archive-date=March 27, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120327111952/http://telegraphjournal.canadaeast.com/sports/article/528643 }}</ref> and was awarded the [[Mike Bossy Trophy]] as the league's best professional prospect.<ref name=bossy>{{cite web |title=Les honneurs individuels / Individual Awards |url=http://www.lhjmq.qc.ca/navcache/getcontents.php?currentpath=/root/Honneurs/GUIDE_SECT4_HonneursIND_de1969a2007.pdf |access-date=August 24, 2008 |publisher=[[Quebec Major Junior Hockey League]] |url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081031111511/http://www.lhjmq.qc.ca/navcache/getcontents.php?currentpath=%2Froot%2FHonneurs%2FGUIDE_SECT4_HonneursIND_de1969a2007.pdf |archive-date=October 31, 2008}}</ref> After his performance at the 1997 [[CHL Top Prospects Game]], opposing coach [[Don Cherry]] likened Luongo to [[Montreal Canadiens]]' [[Hockey Hall of Fame]]r [[Ken Dryden]], while [[NHL Central Scouting Bureau]] director Frank Bonello heralded him as a \"franchise goaltender\".<ref name=sportsill/>\n\nAt the [[1997 NHL entry draft]], Luongo was selected in the first round, fourth overall, by the [[New York Islanders]]. The pick originally belonged to the [[Toronto Maple Leafs]] but was traded to the Islanders in exchange for [[Wendel Clark]], [[Mathieu Schneider]] and [[D. J. Smith (ice hockey)|D. J. Smith]].<ref name=\"Ross\">{{cite news |title=Isles create trade deficit |work=[[New York Daily News]] |date=January 14, 1999 |author=Sherry Ross }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Oilers' recent success adds more intrigue to Draftgate |url=https://www.espn.com/nhl/columns/story?columnist=cox_damien&id=3302375 |author=Damien Cox |work=[[ESPN]] |date=March 20, 2008 |access-date=August 23, 2008 |archive-date=September 22, 2008 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080922185810/http://sports.espn.go.com/nhl/columns/story?columnist=cox_damien&id=3302375 }}</ref> At the time of the draft, Luongo was the highest-picked goaltender in NHL history,<ref>{{cite magazine|title=The First to Go Fourth|url=https://www.si.com/vault/1997/06/30/228923/the-first-to-go-fourth-roberto-luongo-was-drafted-earlier-than-any-other-netminder-in-nhl-history-does-that-mean-the-league-is-finally-changing-the-way-it-sizes-up-goalies|date=June surpassing [[Tom Barrasso]], [[John Davidson (ice hockey)|John Davidson]], and [[Ray Martynuik]]'s fifth overall selections in [[1983 NHL Entry Draft|1983]], [[1973 NHL Amateur Draft|1973]], and [[1970 NHL Amateur Draft|1970]] (Luongo's selection was later surpassed by [[Rick DiPietro]]'s first overall selection by the Islanders in [[2000 NHL Entry Draft|2000]]).<ref>{{cite news|title=Lining Up For a Shot at Luongo|url=http://www.courant.com/news/connecticut/hc-xpm-1997-06-20-9706200392-story.html|date=June 20, 1997|work=[[Hartford Courant]]|author=Mark Pukalo|access-date=December 18, 2019|archive-date=December 18, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191218031949/https://www.courant.com/news/connecticut/hc-xpm-1997-06-20-9706200392-story.html}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=DiPietro first goalie to go first overall|url=https://www.espn.com/nhl/draft00/s/2000/0624/601853.html|date=June 24, 2000|work=[[ESPN]]|agency=[[Associated Press]]|access-date=December 18, 2019|archive-date=April 3, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190403174639/http://www.espn.com/nhl/draft00/s/2000/0624/601853.html}}</ref><ref name=\"sportsillustrated.cnn.com\">{{cite
