Republic]]|}}\n{{MedalBronze | [[1994 Men's World Ice Hockey Championships|1994]] [[Italy]]|}}\n| show_medals = yes\n}}\n'''Erik Nicklas Lidström''' ({{IPA|sv|ˈnɪ̌kːlas ˈlîːdstrœm|pron}}; born 28 April 1970) is a Swedish former professional [[ice hockey]] [[defenceman]] and current vice president of hockey operations for the [[Detroit Red Wings]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kujawa |first=Kyle |date=11 January 2022 |title=Nicklas Lidstrom hired as Red Wings vice president of hockey operations |url=https://www.nhl.com/redwings/news/nicklas-lidstrom-hired-as-red-wings-vice-president-of-hockey-operations/c-329670610 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220111170132/https://www.nhl.com/redwings/news/nicklas-lidstrom-hired-as-red-wings-vice-president-of-hockey-operations/c-329670610 |url-status=dead |archive-date=11 January 2022 |access-date=11 January 2022 |website=NHL.com |language=en-US}}</ref> He played 20 seasons in the [[National Hockey League]] (NHL) for the Detroit Red Wings from 1991 to 2012, where he played in six [[Stanley Cup Final]]s, winning four championships, and [[Captain (ice hockey)|captained]] the team for the final six seasons of his career.<ref>{{cite news|last=LeBrun|first=Pierre|title=Nicklas Lidstrom, 'The Perfect Human'|url=https://www.espn.com/nhl/columns/story?columnist=lebrun_pierre&id=5918807|work=ESPN|date=15 December 2010}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.yardbarker.com/nhl/articles/nicklas_lidstrom_honoring_a_legend/10911776|title=Nicklas Lidstrom: Honoring a Legend|website=www.yardbarker.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140115040308/http://www.yardbarker.com/nhl/articles/nicklas_lidstrom_honoring_a_legend/10911776|archive-date=15 January 2014}}</ref><ref>[http://www.freep.com/article/20120617/COL01/206170619/Nicklas-Lidstrom-unplugged-Mitch-Albom-s-exit-interview-with-the-legendary-Red-Wing?odyssey=tab|topnews|text|FRONTPAGE Mitch Albom: Exit interview with legendary Red Wing Nicklas Lidstrom]{{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120619191230/http://www.freep.com/article/20120617/COL01/206170619/Nicklas-Lidstrom-unplugged-Mitch-Albom-s-exit-interview-with-the-legendary-Red-Wing?odyssey=tab%7Ctopnews%7Ctext%7CFRONTPAGE |date=19 June 2012 }}</ref> He is widely regarded as one of the greatest defencemen in NHL history and nicknamed \"'''the Perfect Human'''\".\n\nOver his 20 NHL seasons, Lidström won four [[Stanley Cup]] championships, seven [[James Norris Memorial Trophy|James Norris Memorial Trophies]] (awarded to the NHL's top defenceman), named to twelve [[NHL All-Star team]]s (ten First Team and two Second Team selections), was voted into 12 [[National Hockey League All-Star Game|NHL All-Star Games]], and received one [[Conn Smythe Trophy]] (the first European to win the trophy) as the playoffs [[most valuable player]]. The Red Wings never missed the playoffs during his career, tied with Larry Robinson for the longest streak of playoff appearances for a player in league history. Lidström was the first European-born-and-trained captain of a Stanley Cup-winning team. Lidström is also the all-time leader in games played with a single NHL team by a European-born player.\n\nLidström was inducted into the [[IIHF Hall of Fame]] in 2014. He was inducted into the [[Hockey Hall of Fame]] on 9 November 2015.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://redwings.nhl.com/club/news.htm?id=772907 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150702093626/http://redwings.nhl.com/club/news.htm?id=772907 |url-status=dead |archive-date=2 July 2015 |title=Lidstrom, Fedorov head to Hall of Fame|website=NHL.com |first=Bill |last=Roose |date=29 June 2015 |access-date=29 June 2015}}</ref> In 2017, Lidström was named one of the \"[[100 Greatest NHL Players]]\" in history.<ref>{{cite web|title=100 Greatest NHL Players|url=https://www.nhl.com/history/nhl-centennial/nhl-100-greatest-players| website = NHL.com|access-date=27 January 2017|date=27 January 2017}}</ref>\n\n== Playing career ==\nWidely considered one of the greatest defencemen of all time,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=633436|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120601225351/http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=633436|url-status=dead|archive-date=1 June 2012|title=Numbers help tell story of Lidstrom's brilliance|website=NHL.com}}</ref> Lidström was awarded the James Norris Memorial Trophy seven times, a feat matched by only one other player ([[Doug Harvey (ice hockey)|Doug Harvey]]) and exceeded only by [[Bobby Orr]] (who won the trophy eight times). Lidström was nominated for the Norris a total of 12 times in his last 14 seasons in the NHL, the first three times finishing as the runner-up (1998 to 2000), and won the award in seven of his last ten ([[2004–05 NHL season|2004–05]] had no winner due to the [[2004–05 NHL lockout|NHL lockout]]), including three consecutive awards from 2001 to 2003 to become the first defenceman since Orr to win three straight.<ref name=\"3rdNoris\">{{cite news|url=https://www.usatoday.com/sports/hockey/nhl/2003-06-12-nhl-awards_x.htm|title=Forsberg, Lidström, Brodeur among the feted|access-date=21 September 2006|work=USA Today|author=Alan Adams | date=13 June 2003}}</ref> In his final 16 seasons (beginning in [[1995–96 NHL season|1995–96]]), he finished no lower than sixth place in Norris Trophy voting.<ref name=\"hockey-ref\">{{cite web | title= Hockey Reference| url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/players/l/lidstni01.html | access-date=28 April 2020}}</ref> Lidström was also named to twelve NHL All-Star Teams, including ten First Team and two Second Team selections.\n\nLidström played his entire 20-year NHL career with the [[Detroit Red Wings]], finishing his career with the second-most [[Stanley Cup playoffs|Stanley Cup playoff]] games played in NHL history, with 263 appearances ([[Chris Chelios]] ranks first with 266).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nhl.com/ice/careerstats.htm?fetchKey=00003ALLSAHAll&sort=gamesPlayed&viewName=careerLeadersAllSeasons|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090417080330/http://www.nhl.com/ice/careerstats.htm?fetchKey=00003ALLSAHAll&sort=gamesPlayed&viewName=careerLeadersAllSeasons|url-status=dead|archive-date=17 April 2009|title=NHL.com – Stats|website=www.nhl.com}}</ref> He was a member of four Stanley Cup-winning teams, in [[1996–97 NHL season|1996–97]], [[1997–98 NHL season|1997–98]], [[2001–02 NHL season|2001–02]] and [[2007–08 NHL season|2007–08]]. Save for the cancelled 2004–05 season lockout year, Lidström played in the playoffs for an NHL record 20 consecutive seasons (an honour he shares with [[Larry Robinson]]).<ref name=consecutiverecord>{{cite web | title=Numbers help tell story of Lidstrom's brilliance| website=NHL.com| url=http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=633436 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120601225351/http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=633436 | url-status=dead | archive-date=1 June 2012 | date=31 May 2012 | access-date=1 February 2013}}</ref>\n\nKnown for his durability, Lidström consistently ranked amongst the top in the NHL in ice time per game. He averaged 28:07 minutes in the [[2005–06 Detroit Red Wings season|2005–06 season]], a career-high. In the [[2003–04 Detroit Red Wings season|2003–04 season]], he played in the 1,000th game of his career, having missed only 17 games in {{frac|12|1|2}} seasons (1994–95 was shortened to 48 games instead of the usual 82 by a labour dispute).<ref name=\"espn\">{{cite web | title=ESPN.com – NHL – Recap – Philadelphia Flyers at Detroit Red Wings | publisher=ESPN Internet Ventures | url=http://sports.espn.go.com/nhl/recap?gameId=240229005 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040602115736/http://sports.espn.go.com/nhl/recap?gameId=240229005 | url-status=dead | archive-date=2 June 2004 | access-date=23 August 2006}}</ref>\n\nAt the conclusion of the [[2001–02 NHL season#Stanley Cup playoffs|2002 Stanley Cup playoffs]], Lidström was named the winner of the Conn Smythe Trophy as most valuable player in the postseason, becoming the first European to ever be awarded the honor.<ref name=\"Smythe\">{{cite news|url=https://www.usatoday.com/sports/hockey/cup02/2002-06-14-usat-cupline.htm|title=Lidstrom makes history in winning Smythe|access-date=21 September 2006|work=USA Today|author=Kevin Allen | date=14 June 2002}}</ref>\n\n=== Early career ===\nLidström began his career in [[Avesta Municipality|Avesta]], Sweden, playing with Skogsbo SK, before moving on to play with [[Västerås IK|VIK Västerås HK]] of the Swedish [[Swedish Hockey League|Elitserien]]. In three seasons with the team, he played 103 games, scoring 12 goals and 30 assists.\n\n=== NHL career (1991–2012) ===\n[[File:NicklasLidstrom.jpg|thumb|right|upright|Lidström in November 2006, the [[2006–07 NHL season|2006–07 season]] was his first season as captain of the Red Wings]]\n\nDrafted by the Detroit Red Wings 53rd overall in the [[1989 NHL entry draft]], Lidström joined the team in the [[1991–92 NHL season|1991–92 season]], though he returned to play for Västerås IK for a brief period during the [[1994–95 NHL lockout]]. Lidström scored 60 points in his rookie season, finishing second to [[Pavel Bure]] in voting for that year's [[Calder Memorial Trophy|Calder Trophy]]. He was selected to the 1992 [[NHL All-Rookie Team]], along with fellow Red Wings defenceman [[Vladimir Konstantinov]].\n\nLidström was set to make $10 million during the [[2005–06 Detroit Red Wings season|2005–06 season]]. However, due to the new terms of the [[NHL Collective Bargaining Agreement]] that was implemented during the 2004–05 season, salaries on pre-existing contracts were reduced by 24%, which lowered his compensation to $7.6 million. That season, he posted a career-high 64 assists and 16 goals to for 80 points.\n\nOn 30 June 2006, it was announced that Lidström had signed a two-year, $15.2 million contract extension with the Red Wings. Instead of seeking more money elsewhere for a defenceman of his caliber, Lidström decided to remain with Detroit for the same annual salary as he earned during the 2005–06 season.<ref>{{cite web | title=Lidstrom remains a Wing | work=CBC News |publisher=Canadian Broadcasting Corporation | url=https://www.cbc.ca/sports/hockey/lidstrom-remains-a-wing-1.594500 | archive-url=https://archive.today/20130115093707/http://www.cbc.ca/news/story/2006/06/30/lidstrom-contract.html | url-status=live | archive-date=15 January 2013 |date=30 June 2006 | access-date=3 June 2012}}</ref>\n\nLidström had been an alternate [[Captain (ice hockey)|captain]] of the Red Wings since the 1997–98 season. Long-time Red Wings captain [[Steve Yzerman]] retired after Detroit was eliminated in the [[2006 Stanley Cup playoffs|first round]], despite winning the [[President's Trophy]] for the season, by the eventual Western Conference champion [[Edmonton Oilers]] in six games. To replace Yzerman, Lidström was named captain, an honor made more special by the fact that he became the first European captain in franchise history. In his first year of captaincy, Lidström led the Red Wings to the Western Conference Finals, but lost to eventual Stanley Cup champions, the [[Anaheim Ducks]], in six games. In the off-season, Lidström joined an elite group by capturing the Norris Trophy as the NHL's outstanding defenceman for the fifth time. Lidström became the fourth defenceman in NHL history with as many as five Norris Trophy wins, joining [[Hockey Hall of Fame]]rs Bobby Orr (eight), Doug Harvey (seven) and [[Ray Bourque]] (five).\n\nNear the beginning of the [[2007–08 NHL season|2007–08 season]], in an 8 October win against the [[Edmonton Oilers]], Lidström registered two assists to surpass [[Peter Forsberg]] as the second-highest scoring Swedish-born NHL player of all time. Accordingly, he trails only [[Mats Sundin]] (as of the end of the [[2011–12 NHL season|2011–12 season]], Lidström has 1,142 points to Sundin's 1,349).<ref>{{cite web|title=New lines find scoring touch in win|url=http://www.mlive.com/redwings/index.ssf/2007/10/red_wings_4_oilers_2.html|access-date=25 September 2008|date=8 October 2007|archive-date=12 December 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071212130352/http://www.mlive.com/redwings/index.ssf/2007/10/red_wings_4_oilers_2.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> Later in the season, on 26 December, Lidström signed a contract extension through the [[2009–10 NHL season|2009–10 season]].<ref>{{cite web | title=Wings re-sign Lidström through 2009–10 | publisher=TSN.ca | url=https://www.tsn.ca/ctvnews/sportsstory.asp?story_id=225876 | access-date=26 December 2007 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080209231848/http://www.tsn.ca/ctvnews/sportsstory.asp?story_id=225876 <!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archive-date = 9 February 2008}}</ref> Several months later, on 3 April 2008, he assisted on a goal by [[Johan Franzén]] to tie [[Luc Robitaille]] at 42nd in the all-time NHL assists, with 726.<ref name=\"espn\"/>\n\n[[File:Lidstrom stanleycup2.jpg|200px|thumb|left|Lidström with the Stanley Cup in July 2008. He won the Stanley Cup four times in his career.]]\n\nEntering the playoffs as the [[Presidents' Trophy]] winners for the highest team point total again during the regular season, the Red Wings met the [[Pittsburgh Penguins]] in the [[2008 Stanley Cup Final]]. Despite a game five, triple-overtime victory by the Penguins to stave off elimination and prevent a Stanley Cup win on home ice by tying the game with less than a minute left, Lidström and the Red Wings defeated Pittsburgh in game six to capture the Stanley Cup. Lidström and teammates [[Tomas Holmstrom]], [[Kris Draper]], [[Kirk Maltby]], and [[Darren McCarty]], were the only players to be part of all four Stanley Cup-winning Red Wings teams between 1997 to 2008. In doing so, also Lidström became the first European-born-and-trained captain to win the Stanley Cup. In [[1934 Stanley Cup Final|1934]], [[Charlie Gardiner (ice hockey)|Charlie Gardiner]], a goaltender born in [[Scotland]], had captained the [[Chicago Blackhawks|Chicago Black Hawks]] to win the Stanley Cup and in [[1938 Stanley Cup Final|1938]], [[Johnny Gottselig]], a left-winger born in [[Russia]], also captained Chicago to a championship, but both players were trained in [[Canada]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Lidstrom becomes first European captain to win Stanley Cup |url=https://www.espn.com/nhl/playoffs2008/news/story?id=3426718 |publisher=[[ESPN]] |date=5 June 2008 |access-date=10 June 2008}}</ref> Just over one week after winning his fourth Stanley Cup in 11 seasons, on 12 June, Lidström won the Norris Trophy for the third-straight season and the sixth time in seven seasons.<ref>{{cite news|title=Red Wings get hat trick at 'NHL Awards Show'|author=Ted Kulfan|newspaper=The Detroit News|url=http://www.detnews.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=/20080613/SPORTS0103/806130400/1128|access-date=13 June 2008}}</ref>\n\nAs the Red Wings opened the [[2008–09 NHL season|2008–09]] pre-season against the [[Montreal Canadiens]], Lidström suffered a [[Nasal fracture|broken nose]] as a shot from Canadiens forward [[Chris Higgins (ice hockey)|Chris Higgins]] ricocheted and hit him in the face.<ref>{{cite web|title=Lidstrom suffers broken nose|url=http://redwings.nhl.com/team/app/?service=page&page=NewsPage&articleid=383367|access-date=25 September 2008|date=25 September 2008|publisher=[[Detroit Red Wings]]|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080926093003/http://redwings.nhl.com/team/app/?service=page&page=NewsPage&articleid=383367|archive-date=26 September 2008}}</ref> From then on, he began wearing a visor. He returned in time for the regular season and was selected to the [[57th National Hockey League All-Star Game|2009 NHL All-Star Game]] in [[Montreal]]. However, in the midst of dealing with [[tendinitis]] that had been bothering him all season, Lidström chose to sit out All-Star weekend, along with teammate [[Pavel Datsyuk]]. Consequently, Lidström and Datsyuk were both suspended one game by the NHL due to League policy for missing the All-Star Game without significant injury.<ref>{{cite web|title=Nicklas Lidstrom, Pavel Datsyuk must sit out Detroit Red Wings' next game|url=https://www.espn.com/nhl/allstar2009/news/story?id=3855534|access-date=23 January 2009|date=23 January 2009|work=ESPN}}</ref> On 22 May, in game three of the third round of the [[2009 Stanley Cup playoffs|2009 playoffs]] against the Chicago Blackhawks, Lidström suffered a testicle injury as a result of getting speared in the groin area by Blackhawks' winger [[Patrick Sharp]], requiring surgery to remove the damaged testicle. He would miss the last two games of the series, which the Red Wings would win in five games for a second consecutive appearance, as the defending champions, in the [[2009 Stanley Cup Final|Stanley Cup Final]], which was a rematch of the previous year's final against the Penguins. Lidström was able to return in time for the series which was his second consecutive and second consecutive overall, and sixth appearance altogether, in a Cup Final. However, unlike the previous year, the Red Wings would lose the series in seven games, despite having a 3–2 series lead, which meant two chances to win, the first in Pittsburgh again like in the previous year's game six, and game seven in Detroit, which prevented him from a second consecutive Stanley Cup for the second time in his career and fifth Stanley Cup altogether. Lidström was unable to tie game seven and sent it into overtime despite having the puck with an open net with seconds left after Penguins goaltender [[Marc-Andre Fleury]] leapt just in time to block the shot.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/blogs/sports-now/story/2009-06-15/nicklas-lidstrom-loses-stanley-cup-gains-every-mans-respect |title=Nicklas Lidstrom loses Stanley Cup, gains every man's respect |website=[[Los Angeles Times]] |author=Adam Rose |date=15 June 2009 |access-date=26 January 2025}}</ref>\n[[File:Nicklas Lidstrom 2010-01-31.JPG|thumb|Lidström with the Red Wings in January 2010]]\nThe Red Wings opened the [[2009–10 NHL season|2009–10 season]] in [[Stockholm]], Sweden. During the team's trip in Sweden, Lidström was honored by his home county, [[Dalarna County|Dalarna]], as an Ambassador of Honor.<ref>{{cite news|title=Lidstrom receives Swedish honor|url=http://www.detnews.com/article/20090929/SPORTS0103/909290385/1128/Lidstrom-receives-Swedish-honor|access-date=16 October 2009|date=29 September 2009|newspaper=[[The Detroit News]]}}</ref> On 15 October 2009, in a game against the [[Los Angeles Kings]], Lidström became the first European-born defenceman to reach 1,000 points after recording two assists in the game. He is the fourth player to score 1,000 points as a Red Wing (after [[Gordie Howe]], [[Alex Delvecchio]] and Steve Yzerman), and the eighth defenceman to do so in the history of the NHL. On 5 March 2010, Lidström earned his 800th career assist. Also during the 2009–10 season, Lidström played in his 1,395th game (finishing the season with 1,412), setting an all-time record for NHL games played by a player born in Europe; earlier in the season, Lidström had passed [[Teppo Numminen]] for games played by a player trained in Europe. Lidström is also second all-time in games played in a Red Wing uniform, behind only Howe. Despite the team under performing due to key injuries to key players, especially at the beginning of the season, the team was still able to make the [[2010 Stanley Cup playoffs|Stanley Cup playoffs]]. On 23 April, Lidström played in his 237th career playoff game, moving past [[Mark Messier]] into sole possession of third place on the NHL's all-time list, behind goaltender; [[Patrick Roy]] with 247, and former teammate [[Chris Chelios]] in first with 266.<ref>{{cite web|title=Red Wings captain Nicklas Lidström admits taking pride in status as third-most-seasoned playoff vet|date=17 April 2010 |url=http://blog.mlive.com/snapshots/2010/04/red_wings_captain_nicklas_lids_32.html}}</ref> In the same game, he had an assist to tie [[Al MacInnis]] (121) for the third-most assists in the post-season by a defenceman (Ray Bourque 139; [[Paul Coffey]] 137).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://scores.espn.go.com/nhl/recap?gameId=300423024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100427040619/http://scores.espn.go.com/nhl/recap?gameId=300423024 |url-status=dead |archive-date=27 April 2010 |title=Detroit Red Wings vs. Phoenix Coyotes – Recap |date=23 April 2010 |work=ESPN |access-date=17 May 2010}}</ref> On 27 April, a day before his 40th birthday, Lidström had three points in a game seven win over the [[Arizona Coyotes|Phoenix Coyotes]] in the first round of the [[2010 Stanley Cup Playoffs|2010 playoffs]], pushing his active playoff points lead to 171 points, and tying him for 17th on the all-time playoff points list with fellow countryman [[Peter Forsberg]]. After defeating the Coyotes in game seven to take the series in seven games, the Red Wings would go on to lose in the second round in five games against the San Jose Sharks.\n\nAs of the end of the 2009–10 season, Lidström has missed only 28 of a possible 1,440 regular-season team games (one due to suspension).\n\nAfter contemplating retirement, Lidström agreed on a one-year contract with the Red Wings on 1 June 2010; the contract paid him slightly over $6 million.<ref>{{cite web|title=Lidstrom agrees to 1-year deal with Red Wings|url=https://www.tsn.ca/nhl/story/?id=323258|publisher=TSN|access-date=1 June 2010|author=TSN.ca|date=1 June 2010}}</ref> On 15 December 2010, Lidström recorded his first career hat-trick, at 40 years of age, against the [[St. Louis Blues]], sealing a 5–2 Detroit victory. After the game, he was asked how it feels to score his first hat-trick, responding, \"It feels great, I've never in my life been able to notch three goals in a game.\" The hat-trick made him the oldest player in NHL history to record his first hat-trick (previously held by [[Scott Mellanby]] at 36 years of age), and the oldest defenceman in NHL history to record a hat-trick (previously held by [[Mathieu Schneider]] at 37 years of age).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/nhl/team/_/name/det/detroit-red-wings|title=Detroit Red Wings Hockey Clubhouse|date=16 December 2010|work=ESPN|access-date=16 December 2010}}</ref> On 18 January 2011, Lidström was named a team captain in the [[58th National Hockey League All-Star Game|2011 NHL All-Star Game]] in [[Raleigh, North Carolina]]. His team won by a final score of 11–10 over Team Staal, captained by [[Eric Staal]] of the [[Carolina Hurricanes]]. Lidström finished +7 with one assist.\n\nOn 20 June 2011, after briefly contemplating retirement yet again, Lidström signed a one-year contract after being happy with his proformance during the previous season (he finished however with a minus -2 plus/minus rating, the first and only time he finished a season with a minus rating) given his age at the time, worth $6.2 million with Detroit, the same amount he had been paid the previous season. On 23 June 2011, he won his seventh Norris Trophy, tying with Doug Harvey and remaining one behind Bobby Orr for most Norris Trophies. This was only the third time in history that a player with a negative plus/minus rating managed to win a Norris Trophy.\n\nOn 22 October 2011, in a game against the [[Washington Capitals]], Lidström became the 14th player in the history of the NHL to play 1,500 games. He is the first player not being born in North America, and therefore the first Swedish and European player, as well as the first player to accomplish this in his 20th NHL season. Lidström played in his 1,550th game on 12 February 2012, against the [[Philadelphia Flyers]], surpassing Alex Delvecchio's previous Red Wing record of 1,549 games. This also makes him the NHL player who has played the most games while always playing for the same NHL team (Gordie Howe played more games, 1,687, with the Red Wings, but also played for the [[Hartford Whalers]] for one season). In this regard, Lidström joins former Red Wings Alex Delvecchio and former teammate and captain Steve Yzerman as the only three players with over 1,500 games having played exclusively for just one team throughout their careers.\n\n=== Retirement ===\n[[File:Retired numbers at Joe Louis Arena.jpg|thumb|right|250px|alt=The banners of seven retired numbers. The banners, from left to right, read \"Lidstrom 5\" \"Yzerman 19\" \"Sawchuk 1\" \"Delvecchio 10\" \"Lindsay 7\" \"Abel 12\" \"Howe 9\". The Yzerman banner has a small \"C\" at the top right corner.|Lidström's #5 banner hanging at Joe Louis Arena.]]\nOn 31 May 2012, Lidström announced his retirement from the NHL via a press conference with Red Wings Owner [[Mike Ilitch]] and General Manager [[Ken Holland]] present, after finishing the season with his lowest point total in a full season in his career. The night before, he told the Swedish tabloid ''[[Expressen]],'' \"I came to the decision last week and I informed our general manager, Ken Holland.\"<ref name=\"nhl\">{{cite web|url=http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=633292 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120601224326/http://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=633292 |url-status=dead |archive-date=1 June 2012 |title=Seven-time Norris Trophy winner Lidstrom retires – NHL.com – News |website=[[National Hockey League|NHL]] |date=31 May 2012 |access-date=31 May 2012}}</ref> Discussing Lidström's retirement, former teammate Steve Yzerman described Lidström as \"one of the all-time best defencemen to ever play.\"<ref name=\"Nhl-red-light.si.com\">{{cite web |url=http://nhl-red-light.si.com/2012/05/31/was-nick-lidstrom-mvp-of-his-era/ |title=Red Light \" Posts Was Lidstrom the MVP of his era? \" |publisher=Nhl-red-light.si.com |date=31 May 2012 |access-date=31 May 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120602075723/http://nhl-red-light.si.com/2012/05/31/was-nick-lidstrom-mvp-of-his-era/ |archive-date=2 June 2012 }}</ref> Former teammate and fellow Norris Trophy winning defenseman [[Paul Coffey]] said, \"He was an incredible player\"<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.timescolonist.com/sports/Lidstrom+there+with+Bourque/6705453/story.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120913012507/http://www.timescolonist.com/sports/Lidstrom+there+with+Bourque/6705453/story.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=13 September 2012 |title=Lidstrom up there with Orr, Bourque |publisher=Timescolonist.com |date=31 May 2012 |access-date=31 May 2012 }}</ref> while Chris Chelios said, \"There's been guys who are great players, but no one's better than Nick. As good? Yes. But this is as big as it gets. He's one of the best athletes ever and...if you're going to talk about someone who's perfect, Nick's pretty darn close to being perfect.\"<ref name=\"nhl\" /> Washington Capitals defenceman [[John Carlson (ice hockey)|John Carlson]] described Lidström as \"one of the game's all-time greats on and off the ice.\"<ref name=\"nhl\" /> Ken Holland stated his belief that Lidström was \"the [[Most Valuable Player|most valuable player]] of his era.\"<ref name=\"Nhl-red-light.si.com\"/>\n\nThe following weekend, on 3 June 2012, Lidström and his wife took out a full-page ad giving thanks to the city of [[Detroit]] for making his family feel at home for the past 21 years.<ref name=\"fullpagead\">{{cite web|url=http://detroit.sbnation.com/detroit-red-wings/2012/6/3/3061239/nicklas-lidstrom-retirement-thank-you-ad|title=Nicklas Lidstrom Thanks Detroit With Full-Page Ad|author=Yuille, Sean|publisher=[[SB Nation]]|date=3 June 2012|access-date=3 June 2012}}</ref> On 8 July 2012, Lidström was named a scout for the Red Wings.\n\nOn 28 February 2014, Lidström was inducted into the [[Michigan Sports Hall of Fame]].<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20140305215734/http://redwings.nhl.com/club/news.htm?id=707001 Lidstrom inducted into MSHOF] NHL.com, 28 February 2014</ref>\n\nDuring the [[2013–14 Detroit Red Wings season|2013–14 season]], Lidström had his number 5 jersey retired by the Red Wings. Initially, ceremonies were planned for the previous season, on 5 February 2013 — however, the [[2012–13 NHL lockout|lockout]] had made it hard to determine when Lidström would be able to attend the ceremony.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.mlive.com/redwings/index.ssf/2013/01/red_wings_will_wait_until_next.html|title=Red Wings will wait until next season to retire Nicklas Lidstrom's No. 5 jersey in ceremony|access-date=29 January 2013|publisher=Mlive.com|year=2013|author=Knan, Ansar}}</ref> The Red Wings officially retired his number on 6 March 2014, in a [[pre-game ceremony]] at [[Joe Louis Arena]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://redwings.nhl.com/club/news.htm?id=679395|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130916223654/http://redwings.nhl.com/club/news.htm?id=679395|url-status=dead|archive-date=16 September 2013|title=Red Wings to retire Lidstrom's No. 5|website=NHL.com}}</ref>\n\n== International play ==\n\nRepresenting [[Sweden men's national ice hockey team|Sweden]], Lidström won the [[Ice Hockey World Championship|World Championship]] in [[1991 Men's World Ice Hockey Championships|1991]]. At the [[Ice hockey at the 2006 Winter Olympics – Men's tournament|2006 Winter Olympics]], Lidström was a major factor in Sweden's win over [[Finland men's national ice hockey team|Finland]] in the finals, scoring the gold medal-clinching goal, thus earning him a spot on the Olympic All-Star team. He also became the 17th member of the [[Triple Gold Club]]. ''[[The Hockey News]]'' selected Lidström as the \"Best European-trained player ever in the NHL.\"<ref>{{cite magazine|title=Lidstrom – No. 1 Euro; No. 2 blueliner of all time|author=Brian Costello|magazine=The Hockey News|url=https://thehockeynews.com/news/news/thn-com-blog-lidstrom-no-1-euro-no-2-blueliner-of-all-time|access-date=10 December 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071203182330/http://www.thehockeynews.com/articles/11520-THNcom-Blog-Lidstrom-No-1-Euro-No-2-blueliner-of-all-time.html|archive-date=3 December 2007|url-status=live}}</ref> The ''[[Sporting News]]'' and ''[[Sports Illustrated]]'' selected Lidström as the \"NHL Player of the Decade.\"<ref>{{cite magazine|title=Sporting News' NHL Player of the Decade: Nicklas Lidstrom, D, Red Wings|magazine=Sporting News|url=http://www.sportingnews.com/nhl/article/2009-09-24/sporting-news-nhl-player-decade-nicklas-lidstrom-d-red-wings|access-date=24 September 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090927091306/http://www.sportingnews.com/nhl/article/2009-09-24/sporting-news-nhl-player-decade-nicklas-lidstrom-d-red-wings|archive-date=27 September 2009|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=NHL: Highlights and lowlights|publisher =Sports Illustrated|url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/2009/magazine/specials/2000s/12/10/nhl.highlights.lowlights/index.html\n|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091217060821/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/2009/magazine/specials/2000s/12/10/nhl.highlights.lowlights/index.html\n|url-status=dead\n|archive-date=17 December 2009\n|access-date=28 April 2010 | date=14 December 2009}}</ref>\n\nPrior to his NHL career, Lidström competed in one [[IIHF European Junior Championships|European Junior Championships]] in [[1988 IIHF European U18 Championship|1988]], one [[IIHF World Junior Championship|World Junior Championship]] in [[1990 World Junior Ice Hockey Championships|1990]] and one [[Canada Cup]] in [[1991 Canada Cup|1991]] for Sweden.\n\nPrior to his rookie season with the Red Wings, he earned his first gold medal with [[Sweden men's national ice hockey team|Sweden]] at the [[1991 Men's World Ice Hockey Championships|1991 World Championships]]. Three years later, he competed in the [[1994 Men's World Ice Hockey Championships|1994 World Championships]] in Italy and won a bronze medal. Two years later, he participated in the inaugural [[1996 World Cup of Hockey]] (successor of the Canada Cup) and contributed three points in four games.  He made his [[Ice hockey at the Winter Olympics|Olympic]] debut with Sweden at the [[Ice hockey at the 1998 Winter Olympics|1998 Winter Olympics]] in [[Nagano, Nagano|Nagano]], [[Japan]].\n\nFour years later was his next international appearance, playing in his second Olympics at the [[Ice hockey at the 2002 Winter Olympics|2002 Winter Olympics]] in [[Salt Lake City]], where Sweden was upset by [[Belarus men's national ice hockey team|Belarus]] in the quarter-final after being heavy favourites in the round-robin.  Lidström made his third [[World Ice Hockey Championships|World Championships]] appearance in [[2004 Men's World Ice Hockey Championships|2004]], but only appeared in two games. That summer, he also competed in the [[2004 World Cup of Hockey]], where he scored one goal.\n\nIn the [[Ice hockey at the 2006 Winter Olympics – Men's tournament|2006 Winter Olympics]] in [[Turin]], [[Italy]], Lidström helped Sweden avenge their quarter-final upset to Belarus in Salt Lake City, scoring the [[game winning goal]] in the gold medal game against [[Finland men's national ice hockey team|Finland]]. In doing so, Lidström became a member of the [[Triple Gold Club]], adding an Olympic gold medal to go with his previous [[Stanley Cup]]s with Detroit and his World Championship gold medal in 1991.<ref>{{cite web | title=Sweden ranked No. 1 in men's; Canada No. 1 in women's, Niittymaki MVP | author=Andrew Podnieks | publisher=IIHF.com | url=http://www.iihf.com/news/OG06/torino1100.htm | access-date=23 August 2006 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20060426125945/http://www.iihf.com/news/OG06/torino1100.htm |archive-date = 26 April 2006}}</ref>  Lidström was also selected to the 2010 Olympic All-Star team.\n\nLidström also played for Sweden in the [[Ice hockey at the 2010 Winter Olympics – Men's tournament|2010 Winter Olympics]] in [[Vancouver]], serving as team captain in what would be his final Olympic appearance.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2010-feb-06-la-sp-olympics-sweden6-2010feb06-story.html |title=Sweden hopes for more hockey gold |newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=6 February 2010 |first=Helene |last=Elliott }}</ref> Lidström announced his retirement from Olympic competition following Sweden's loss to [[Slovakia men's national ice hockey team|Slovakia]].<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.freep.com/article/20100226/SPORTS17/2260357/1053/SPORTS/After-tough-loss-Lidstrom-39-says-hes-done-with-Olympics-competition |title=After tough loss, Lidstrom, 39, says he's done with Olympics competition |newspaper=[[Detroit Free Press]] |date=26 February 2010 |first=Shannon |last=Shelton }}.</ref>\n\n== Personal life ==\nGrowing up, Lidström idolized trailblazing defenceman [[Börje Salming]], whom he considers to be his hero.<ref name = \"Hero\">{{cite web |last1=Zeisberger |first1=Mike |title=Lidstrom 'true representation' of what Borje Salming Courage Award stands for |url=https://www.nhl.com/news/nicklas-lidstrom-presented-with-borje-salming-courage-award |work=National Hockey League |access-date=17 November 2023 |date=16 November 2023}}</ref> In November 2023, Lidström was the recipient of the inaugural Börje Salming Courage Award, which is given to the European NHL alumnus who has been a positive influence in their community and best embodies Salming's legacy.<ref name = \"Hero\"/>\n\nLidström is married to Annika,<ref>{{cite news| url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1011786/index.htm | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140503012059/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1011786/index.htm | url-status=dead | archive-date=3 May 2014 | work=CNN | title=Video | date=12 January 1998}}</ref> with whom he has four children. All four sons play high-level hockey: Kevin (born 1994), is currently a defenceman for [[Swedish Division 1 (ice hockey)|Swedish Division 1]] team [[SK Lejon]];<ref>{{cite web|title=Kevin Lidstrom|url=https://www.eliteprospects.com/player/73566/kevin-lidstrom|work=Elite Prospects|access-date=30 March 2019}}</ref> Adam (born 1996) also plays in Division 1 with [[Enköpings SK]];<ref>{{cite web|title=Adam Lidstrom|url=https://www.eliteprospects.com/player/57339/adam-lidstrom|work=Elite Prospects|access-date=30 March 2019}}</ref> Samuel (born in 2000) plays on Elitettan team Köping HC<ref>{{cite web|title=Samuel Lidstrom|url=https://www.eliteprospects.com/player/319569/samuel-lidstrom|work=Elite Prospects|access-date=30 March 2019}}</ref> and Lucas (born in 2003) also plays for VIK Västerås HK on its U16 team.<ref>{{cite web|title=Lucas Lidstrom|url=https://www.eliteprospects.com/player/587638/lucas-lidstrom|work=Elite Prospects|access-date=30 March 2019}}</ref>\n\nLidström was featured on an episode of NHL 36.\n\nIn October 2019, Lidström released his authorized biography in North America titled ''Nicklas Lidstrom: The Pursuit of Perfection''.\n\n== Career statistics ==\n\n===Regular season and playoffs===\n{| border=\"0\" cellpadding=\"1\" cellspacing=\"0\" style=\"text-align:center; width:60em\"\n|- bgcolor=\"#e0e0e0\"\n! colspan=\"3\" bgcolor=\"#ffffff\"|\n! rowspan=\"100\" bgcolor=\"#ffffff\"|\n! colspan=\"5\"|[[Regular season]]\n! rowspan=\"100\" bgcolor=\"#ffffff\"|\n! colspan=\"5\"|[[Playoffs]]\n|- bgcolor=\"#e0e0e0\"\n! 8th overall\n| draft_year = 1981\n| draft_team = [[Edmonton Oilers]]\n| career_start = 1981\n| career_end = 2000\n| medal_templates = {{MedalCountry | {{flag|Canada}} }}\n{{MedalSport | Men's [[ice Championships|World Championships]]}}\n{{MedalSilver | [[1989 World Ice Hockey Championships|1989 Sweden]] |}}\n}}\n'''Grant Scott Fuhr''' ({{respell|fyoo|er}}<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r0CZJXqF1IY&t=39s|website=YouTube|access-date=June 21, 2026|title=\nGrant Fuhr was first black player in Hall of Fame}}</ref>; born September 28, 1962) is a Canadian former professional [[ice hockey]] [[goaltender]]. He played 19 seasons as a goaltender in the [[National Hockey League]] (NHL), 10 of them for the [[Edmonton Oilers]], with whom he won five [[Stanley Cup]] championships in 14 postseason campaigns. He also won the [[Canada Cup]] two times with Canada, his first as the backup goaltender for the team in 1984, and his second as the starting goaltender in 1987 as well as finishing second in the [[IIHF World Championships|World Championships]] in 1989. Fuhr is widely regarded as one of the best goaltenders of his era. He was elected to the [[Hockey Hall of Fame]] in 2003. In 2017, he was named by the league as one of the \"[[100 Greatest NHL Players]]\".<ref>{{cite web|title=100 Greatest NHL Players|url=https://www.nhl.com/history/nhl-centennial/nhl-100-greatest-players|website=NHL.com|access-date=January 27, 2017|date=January 27, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|last=NHL|title=Grant Fuhr was first half-black player in Hall of Fame|date=March 22, 2017|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r0CZJXqF1IY&list=PL1NbHSfosBuHEp2Bphcgz16OKz0kjnCH6&index=56 |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211212/r0CZJXqF1IY| archive-date=December 12, 2021 |url-status=live|access-date=April 25, 2017}}{{cbignore}}</ref>\n\nFuhr holds select NHL and franchise records among goaltenders; he ranks as the leader in most games played by a goaltender in a single season (79) and most assists and points by a goaltender in regular season and playoffs combined (61). His rookie season saw him go on an undefeated streak of 23 straight games without a loss. In his first eight seasons as a goaltender, Fuhr won 211 games as the starting goaltender for four Stanley Cup championships while winning the Vezina Trophy in the {{NHL Year|1987}} season (which saw him play a then-record 75 games) and being selected to the NHL All-Star Game six times. Injuries limited Fuhr in the {{NHL Year|1989}} season to where he missed the entire playoff run that saw the Oilers win the Cup for the fifth time. Amidst personal issues, Fuhr was traded in 1991 to the [[Toronto Maple Leafs]], where he spent the following two seasons before being traded to the [[Buffalo Sabres]] midway through the {{NHL Year|1992}} season. He shared the [[William M. Jennings Trophy]] for allowing the fewest number of goals in the {{NHL Year|1993}} season. He spent the following six seasons with three further teams, most notably with the [[St. Louis Blues]], where he played a record 79 games as goaltender in the {{NHL Year|1995}} season. He concluded his career in the {{NHL Year|1999}} season with the [[Calgary Flames]], where he became the sixth goaltender to win 400 games. Fuhr had only three seasons where he posted more losses than wins.\n\nA trailblazing player for his generation with fearless athleticism, Fuhr was the first Black ice hockey player to win the Stanley Cup and the first inducted into the Hockey Hall of Fame.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.theblackiceproject.com/blackiceproject/index.cfm?fuseaction=home.newsDetail&NEWS_ID=819 |title=Soul on Ice: Blacks and Historic Firsts in Hockey |publisher=The Black Ice Project |access-date=March 8, 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140331112702/http://www.theblackiceproject.com/blackiceproject/index.cfm?fuseaction=home.newsDetail&NEWS_ID=819 |archive-date=March 31, 2014 }}</ref> After retiring, Fuhr served as a goaltending coach for the [[Calgary Flames]] from 2000 to 2002 and [[Arizona Coyotes]] from 2004 to 2010.\n\n==Early life==\nFuhr was born on September 28, 1962, in [[Spruce Grove, Alberta]], west of [[Edmonton]] to a [[Black Canadians|Black Canadian]] and a [[First Nations in Canada|First Nation-Canadian]] from the [[Enoch Cree Nation]]; he never knew his birth parents.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1989/02/06/sports/tarnished-season-for-an-all-star.html|website=The New York Times|title=Tarnished Season for an All-Star|first=Joe|last=Sexton|date= February 6, 1989|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171221053719/https://www.nytimes.com/1989/02/06/sports/tarnished-season-for-an-all-star.html|archive-date=December 21, 2017}}</ref> Less than three weeks after he was born, he was adopted by Betty Wheeler and Robert Fuhr and he grew up in Spruce Grove.<ref name=\"NYTimes\">{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/08/23/sports/sports-of-the-times-hockey-s-minority-players-moving-past-trailblazer-stage.html|title= Sports of The Times; Hockey's Minority Players Moving Past Trailblazer Stage|first=George|last=Vescey|website=The New York Times|date=August 23, 2001|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250530121820/https://www.nytimes.com/2001/08/23/sports/sports-of-the-times-hockey-s-minority-players-moving-past-trailblazer-stage.html|archive-date=May 30, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Laskaris |first1=Sam |title=Indigenous players have hoisted Stanley Cup in the past; unclear when others will join them with NHL season on pause |url=https://windspeaker.com/news/sports/indigenous-players-have-hoisted-stanley-cup-past-unclear-when-others-will-join-them-nhl |access-date=October 31, 2024 |work=Windspeaker.com |language=en}}</ref>\n\nIn the mid-1970s, Fuhr played for the [[Enoch Cree Nation|Enoch]] Tomahawks hockey team.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sportsnet.ca/hockey/nhl/hockey-pastime-enoch-cree-nation/|title=Why hockey is more than a pastime for Enoch Cree Nation|website=Sportsnet.ca|access-date=July 3, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nhl.com/oilers/news/alumni-minor-hockey-in-spruce-grove-shaped-fuhr-s-legendary-career-299550830|title = ALUMNI: Minor hockey in Spruce Grove helped shape Fuhr's legendary career|website=Nhl.com| date=July 22, 2018 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sprucegroveexaminer.com/2017/12/31/hometown-hockey-in-spruce-grove/wcm/094c864e-e8fb-dee2-7413-aa1e7ca82754|title = Hometown Hockey in Spruce Grove|website=Sprucegroveexaminer.com}}</ref> Fuhr's mother came from Enoch Cree Nation.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ammsa.com/publications/alberta-sweetgrass/grant-fuhr-coming-edmonton|title = Grant Fuhr coming to Edmonton|website=Ammsa.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://aptnnews.ca/2017/10/25/cree-man-collects-hockey-cards-with-a-twist/|title=Cree man collects hockey cards with a twist|newspaper=Aptn News |date=October 25, 2017|last1=Martens |first1=Kathleen }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ammsa.com/publications/windspeaker/cree-goalie-hopes-succeed-his-hero|title = Cree goalie hopes to succeed his hero|website=Ammsa.com}}</ref>\n\nIn 1979, at the age of 16, Fuhr joined the [[Victoria Cougars (WHL)|Victoria Cougars]] of the [[Western Hockey League]] (WHL). After two outstanding seasons in [[Victoria, British Columbia|Victoria]], which included the league championship and a trip to the [[Memorial Cup]] in [[1981 Memorial Cup|1981]], Fuhr was drafted eighth overall by the [[Edmonton Oilers]] in the [[1981 NHL entry draft]], on June 10, 1981.\n\n==Playing career==\n===Edmonton Oilers (1981–1991)===\n[[File:GrantFuhrEDM.png|thumb|Fuhr with the [[Edmonton Oilers]] {{c.|1984}}]]\nFuhr was selected as the eighth overall pick of the [[1981 NHL entry draft]] by the [[Edmonton Oilers]]. It was noted years later that although the Oilers had drafted [[Andy Moog]] at goaltender, the Oilers were attracted by Fuhr's .907 save percentage for the Victoria Cougars in a high-scoring era. Reportedly, the Oilers briefly considered drafting [[James Patrick (ice hockey)|James Patrick]], who was still on the board at No. 8 but went with Fuhr. In his first season with the Oilers, Fuhr lost his debut game on October 14 against the Winnipeg Jets before going on an unprecedented run that saw him win or tie in his next 23 games, which became a new record for a rookie goaltender. In 48 games (with one appearance in relief), Fuhr went 28–5–14.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/players/f/fuhrgr01/gamelog/1982|website=Hockey Reference|access-date=May 9, 2026|title=Grant Fuhr 1981-82 Game Log}}</ref> He was tabbed to start the first round of the [[1982 Stanley Cup playoffs]], which saw the Oilers upset by the [[Los Angeles Kings]] where he gave up 26 goals in five games (six coming in the \"[[Miracle on Manchester]]\" game where the Oilers gave up six unanswered goals).\n\nFuhr played ten seasons for the Oilers, where he teamed up first with [[Andy Moog]] from 1981 through 1987, then [[Bill Ranford]] from 1988 through 1991 to form one of the most formidable goaltending tandems in history, winning the [[Stanley Cup]] four times in five seasons (1983–84 through 1987–88); Fuhr was quoted in an interview as being appreciative of having Moog and Ranford as partners because it made him play better.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/592520/2018/10/17/qa-grant-fuhr-talks-about-his-journey-drug-use-and-the-state-of-goaltending/|website=The Athletic|date=October 17, 2018|access-date=May 9, 2026|title=Q&A: Grant Fuhr talks about his journey, drug use and the state of goaltending|first=Daniel|last=Nugent-Bowman}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://edmontonjournal.com/sports/hockey/nhl/cult-of-hockey/edmonton-oilers-top-10-all-time-best-draft-picks-5-grant-fuhr|title=Edmonton Oilers' top 10 all-time best draft picks: #5 Grant Fuhr|first=Bruce|last=McCurdy|website=Edmonton Journal|date=October 12, 2012}}</ref>\n\nMoog was given the starting job in the [[1983 Stanley Cup playoffs]] and helped lead the Oilers to their first [[1983 Stanley Cup Final|Stanley Cup Final]], though they were swept by the [[New York Islanders]], who captured their fourth straight Stanley Cup. The next year general manager and head coach [[Glen Sather]] chose to go with Fuhr in the [[1984 Stanley Cup playoffs|Stanley Cup playoffs]]. The Oilers advanced all the way to the [[1984 Stanley Cup Final|Stanley Cup Final]] to set up a rematch with the Islanders. In Game 3, Fuhr suffered an injury when he collided with [[Pat LaFontaine]]. Moog stepped in and played the next two games that the Oilers won to win the Final; Fuhr became the first Black player to have his name engraved on the Stanley Cup.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nhl.com/news/black-history-month-spotlight-grant-fuhr-304588320|title=Black History Month spotlight: Fuhr gets Hall call|date=February 11, 2019|website=Nhl.com|access-date=July 3, 2026}}</ref>  After that, Fuhr remained the number one goaltender.\n\nIn the [[1986 Stanley Cup playoffs]], the Oilers were engaged in a tight battle with the [[Calgary Flames]] in the second round. In Game 7, late in the third period, teammate [[Steve Smith (ice hockey, born April 30, 1963)|Steve Smith]] accidentally sent a pass that bounced off Fuhr's skate for an own goal that gave Calgary the lead that they would not relinquish as the Flames eliminated the Oilers to de-throne them as defending champions.\n\nIn February of [[1986–87 NHL season|1987]], Fuhr played in goal for the NHL All-Stars in both games of the [[Rendez-Vous '87]] series against the [[USSR national ice hockey team|Soviet National Team]]. In August 1987, Fuhr backstopped Canada at the [[1987 Canada Cup|Canada Cup]], which saw him play all nine games for the victorious squad. Fuhr became part of history with the {{NHL Year|1987}} season, as he played in 75 games and went 40–24–9 with a GAA of 3.43 to set a new record for most games played a goaltender in one season.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/stathead/tiny/DOxk9|website=Stathead|access-date=May 9, 2026|title=For single seasons, playing goalie, in the regular season, sorted by descending Games Played (Goalie).}}</ref> He won his only [[Vezina Trophy]] as the NHL's top goaltender and finished second in voting for the [[Hart Memorial Trophy]] as league MVP, behind [[Mario Lemieux]] and ahead of teammate [[Wayne Gretzky]]. In the playoffs, he went 16–2 as the Oilers won the Stanley Cup once again. As an Oiler he had played in six All-Star games, by playing in the [[National Hockey League All-Star Game]] in 1982, 1984, 1985, 1986, 1988, and 1989.\n\nFrom February 14 to March 25, 1986, Fuhr won ten straight games for the Oilers to set a new franchise record that would not be eclipsed until 2024.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nhl.com/news/grant-fuhr-on-stuart-skinner-winning-oilers-record-11-straight-games|title=Skinner winning Oilers record 11 straight as goalie 'awesome,' Fuhr says|first=Derek |last=Van Diest|website=NHL.com|date=January 24, 2024}}</ref> He also played for the NHL All-Star team in the two-game series against the [[Soviet Union national ice hockey team]] in [[Rendez-vous '87]] as the starting goaltender.  Fuhr's playoff success fed into his reputation as the supreme clutch goaltender of his era, and there was a period from 1987 through at least 1989 where Fuhr was often called \"the best goaltender in the world\".  On January 28, 1989, Fuhr attained his 200th career win with a 7–6 road win over the Los Angeles Kings at the [[Great Western Forum]]. In the 1989 offseason, Fuhr had reached an endorsement deal with [[Pepsi]] to wear the logo on his pads. The NHL soon enacted a new policy that would require all manufacturers to pay the league a select fee before any identifiable logos could be worn by players. Fuhr briefly retired from the Oilers on June 8, 1989, citing only that he had felt a \"lack of respect\" from teammates. Fuhr's agent Rich Winter stated that another factor was the refusal of the Oilers to sign papers allowing to continue his endorsement obligations. Two months later, on August 24, 1989, the two sides made up and Fuhr returned to the team.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1989-08-25-sp-1229-story.html|website=Los Angeles Times|date=August 25, 1989|title=Goalie Fuhr to End Retirement but Is Irked by Ad Ban on Pads}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1989/06/10/sports/sports-people-hockey-sather-is-sanguine-at-fuhr-s-retirement.html|website=The New York Times|date=June 10, 1989|access-date=May 9, 2026|title=SPORTS PEOPLE: HOCKEY; Sather Is Sanguine At Fuhr's Retirement}}</ref>\n\nIn the {{NHL Year|1989}} season, Fuhr played in just 21 games due to various injuries, which started in September 1989 when he felt pain in his abdomen that led to him having to undergo emergency appendectomy surgery that led to speculation he might be sidelined for two months.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1989-09-15-sp-249-story.html|title=Emergency Appendectomy May Sideline Oiler Goalie Fuhr for Up to Two Months|website=Los Angeles Times|date=September 15, 1989|access-date=May 10, 2026}}</ref> While [[Bill Ranford]] served as goaltender for the Oilers to start the season, Fuhr did return to action after over a month, which saw him play two games with the AHL [[Cape Breton Oilers]] team before returning to play for Edmonton on October 29, where he took the loss against Montreal after giving up five goals.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://edmontonjournal.com/sports/hockey/nhl/edmonton-oilers/edmonton-oilers-history-grant-fuhr-starts-in-goal-after-appendectomy-forces-him-to-miss-start-of-season-oct-29-1989|date=October 30, 1989|title=Habs spoil Fuhr's big-time return|first=Jim|last=Matheson|website=Edmonton Journal}}</ref> He played most of the games in November before suffering an injury in the December 16 game against the St. Louis Blues that saw his left shoulder require reconstructive surgery that knocked him out until March. He played in four games in March but re-injured his shoulder. While Fuhr was healthy enough to play by May, but the Oilers, as goaltended by Ranford, won the [[1990 Stanley Cup Final|Stanley Cup]] once again.<ref>{{cite web|title=Ranford plays, Fuhr watches|date=May 21, 1990|website=Tampa Bay Times|url=https://www.tampabay.com/archive/1990/05/21/ranford-plays-fuhr-watches/|access-date=May 10, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1989/12/27/Fuhr-undergoes-surgery/8487630738000/|date= December 27, 1989|title=Fuhr undergoes surgery|website=UPI|access-date=May 10, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/players/f/fuhrgr01/gamelog/1990|website=Hockey Reference|title=Grant Fuhr 1989-90 Game Log|access-date=May 10, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://edmontonjournal.com/sports/hockey/nhl/edmonton-oilers/edmonton-oilers-history-grant-fuhr-re-injures-shoulder-at-quebec-march-13-1990|website=Edmonton Journal|date=March 13, 2017|title=Edmonton Oilers history: Grant Fuhr re-injures shoulder at Quebec, March 13, 1990|access-date=May 10, 2026}}</ref>\n\nIn the 1990 offseason, Fuhr's problem with substance abuse came to the forefront of the team and soon the media. Sather confronted Fuhr several times about any potential problems but Fuhr had denied having a problem and had tested negative for cocaine three times. In the summer, he was treated for cocaine abuse at a counseling centre in [[St. Petersburg, Florida|St. Petersburg]], [[Florida]] for two weeks. On September 1, the Edmonton Journal reported that Fuhr admitted to lying to Sather, who confirmed Fuhr's treatment for cocaine abuse. Fuhr stated that he had abused a \"substance\" since 1983 on a period of every few weeks. Details of Fuhr's drug use were supplied by his ex-wife, Corrine, who told the press in Edmonton that she often found cocaine hidden in his clothing and that she fielded numerous threatening telephone calls from drug dealers who had not been paid. That same day saw the announcement by the NHL that they began an investigation on Fuhr after receiving the information and set a hearing for September 26.\n \nOn September 27, 1990, Fuhr was suspended by NHL President [[John Ziegler Jr.|John Ziegler]] for one year, calling Fuhr's conduct “dishonorable and against the welfare of the league.” He provided grounds for reinstatement as early as February 1991 provided that Fuhr met certain conduct requirements. The suspension was later reduced to the first 59 games of the [[1990–91 NHL season|1990–91 season]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1990-09-28-sp-1245-story.html |title=Fuhr Suspended One Year by NHL for Using Drugs |website=Los Angeles Times |date=September 28, 1990 |access-date=October 16, 2016}}</ref><ref name=\"one on one\">{{cite web|url=http://www.legendsofhockey.net/html/spot_oneononep200301.htm |title=Legends of Hockey - Spotlight - One on One with Grant Fuhr |access-date=April 22, 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080517163254/http://www.legendsofhockey.net/html/spot_oneononep200301.htm |archive-date=May 17, 2008 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.brainyhistory.com/events/1991/february_18_1991_164665.html |title=Edmonton Oiler goalie Grant Fuhr returns to... February 18 in History |website=Brainyhistory.com |date=February 18, 1991 |access-date=October 16, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9C0CE5DB1E38F932A3575AC0A966958260 |work=The New York Times |title=HOCKEY; Fuhr Used Cocaine, Paper Says |date=September 1, 1990}}</ref>  After missing 59 games and entering a two-week rehab program, the suspension was lifted by the league on February 18, 1991.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://thehockeywriters.com/nhl-drug-policy-fuhr-suspension/ |work=The Hockey Writers |title=Fuhr Suspension Helped Pave Way for NHL Drug Policy |date=January 18, 2019|access-date=September 15, 2019}}</ref>\n\nIn the second game Fuhr played in the [[American Hockey League]] prior to returning to the NHL, he heard chants from the [[New Haven Nighthawks]] crowd taunting with such phrases as “Grant does it up the nose, doo dah, doo dah\" while one fan held up a plastic bag with white powder behind him when he was on the bench. Returning to the Oilers in February, he recorded a shutout against the [[New Jersey Devils]]; he ultimately went 6–4–3 with one shutout.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/players/f/fuhrgr01/gamelog/1991|website=Hockey Reference|access-date=May 9, 2026|title=Grant Fuhr 1990-91 Game Log}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1991-02-20-sp-1697-story.html|website=Los Angeles Times|date=February 20, 1991|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260509101300/https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1991-02-20-sp-1697-story.html|archive-date=May 9, 2026|title=Fuhr Is a Target for Fans : Hockey: Before Oiler goalie's return to NHL, he gets plenty of abuse in a minor league game.|first=Steve|last=Springer}}</ref> Prior to Game 1 of the [[1991 Stanley Cup playoffs]], Fuhr was tabbed by Oilers head coach [[John Muckler]] to start against the [[Calgary Flames]] over Ranford and allowed just one goal in the 3–1 win; Fuhr ultimately started 16 of the 18 postseason games as the Oilers lost to the [[Minnesota North Stars]] in the Conference Finals.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1991-04-05-sp-1785-story.html|website=Los Angeles Times|date=April 5, 1991|title=NHL STANLEY CUP PLAYOFFS : Fuhr Lifts Oilers to Victory Over Flames|access-date=May 9, 2026}}</ref>\n\n===Post-Oilers career (1991–2000)===\nOn September 19, 1991, Fuhr was traded to the [[Toronto Maple Leafs]] in a seven-player deal.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1991-09-20-sp-2608-story.html|website=Los Angeles Times|date=September 20, 1991|title=Oilers Trade Fuhr, Anderson to Toronto|access-date=May 10, 2026}}</ref> The {{NHL Year|1991}} season saw him set a career and league high for losses with 33 in a 25–33–5 campaign that saw him leed the league in goals allowed with 230. After a season and a half in Toronto, with the emergence of [[Felix Potvin]], Grant was traded again, this time to the [[Buffalo Sabres]], on February 2, 1993.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/1993/02/03/maple-leafs-deal-fuhr-to-sabres/|website=Chicago Tribune|date=February 3, 1993|title=MAPLE LEAFS DEAL FUHR TO SABRES|access-date=May 10, 2026}}</ref>\n\nIn Buffalo, he played a role in the Sabres' dramatic first-round playoff victory over the [[Boston Bruins]], helped instill a winning attitude in the organization, and mentored a still relatively inexperienced [[Dominik Hašek]]. Focusing on conditioning, Fuhr then had a successful [[1993–94 NHL season|1993–94 season]] with the Sabres, initially sharing goaltending duties with Hašek. Fuhr and Hašek were awarded the [[William M. Jennings Trophy]] for the fewest goals allowed that year. Hasek was tabbed to start the [[1994 Stanley Cup playoffs|Stanley Cup playoffs]] by head coach [[John Muckler]], a move that did not please Fuhr, who later stated during the [[1994–95 NHL lockout]] that he wanted out of Buffalo.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://thehockeynews.com/hockey-history/history/for-two-years-in-early-nineties-sabres-employed-two-hall-of-fame-goalies-in-fuhr-and-hasek|website=The Hockey News|title=For Two Years In Early Nineties, Sabres Employed Two Hall-of-Fame Goalies In Fuhr And Hasek|first=Adam|last=Proteau|date=February 9, 2025}}</ref> Hašek became the Sabres' full-time starting goaltender after Fuhr suffered multiple injuries.\n\nIn May 1993, while a member of the Sabres, Fuhr was denied membership in the neighbouring Transit Valley Country Club. At the time, rumours floated that the denial was based on race, as several of Fuhr's white teammates had been granted membership.<ref name=kelley>Kelley, Jim. [https://www.espn.com/nhl/columns/story?columnist=kelley_jim&id=1653375 \"First black inductee pleased to be role model\"], ''[[ESPN|ESPN.com]]'', November 3, 2003. Retrieved on March 16, 2008</ref> Club officials denied they rejected Fuhr based on his race; rather, his application contained \"incorrect and incomplete\" information. Various acts of vandalism at the club occurred after news of Fuhr's rejection surfaced, including an incident where vandals burned a [[swastika]] onto one of the greens.<ref>{{cite web|agency=Associated Press|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1993/06/04/sports/club-is-vandalized-in-fuhr-incident.html|title=Club Is Vandalized In Fuhr Incident|website=The New York Times|access-date=May 10, 2026|date=June 4, 1993}}</ref> In light of the negative publicity, the club reversed its position and offered Fuhr not only membership but an apology as well. Fuhr rejected the membership and joined the nearby Lancaster Country Club. The club also temporarily suspended its membership committee and had an anti-bias policy written into its by-laws.\n\nFuhr played in just 17 games of the {{NHL Year|1994}} season. With Hašek now ensconced in the Sabres net, Fuhr was dealt to the [[Los Angeles Kings]] on February 14, 1995, reuniting him with Gretzky.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Dillman |first1=Lisa |title=Kings Pay Dearly for a Worn Fuhr : Hockey: They acquire veteran goalkeeper, 32, two young defensemen from Sabres in exchange for Zhitnik, Huddy, Stauber. |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1995-02-15-sp-32216-story.html |website=Los Angeles Times |access-date=November 22, 2023 |date=February 14, 1995}}</ref> His time in Los Angeles proved dismal, as he went 1–7–3 in his starts.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/players/f/fuhrgr01/gamelog/1995|website=Hockey Reference|title=Grant Fuhr 1994-95 Game Log|access-date=May 9, 2023}}</ref>\n\nDuring the summer Grant signed as an unrestricted [[free agent]] with the [[St. Louis Blues]] on July 14, 1995, just a few months before the [[1995–96 NHL season|1995–96 season]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://thehockeynews.com/nhl/st-louis-blues/community/players/this-date-in-blues-history-july-14-1995-the-acquisition-of-grant-fuhr-20-years-later-1|website=The Hockey News|title=THIS DATE IN BLUES HISTORY (July 14, 1995): The Acquisition Of Grant Fuhr, 20 years later|first=Lou|last=Korac|date=July 14, 2025}}</ref> Although he began the season out of shape and was considered to be past his prime, his career saw a resurgence as he played 79 games that season, including 76 consecutively, both NHL records.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/1996/04/04/knee-injury-ends-fuhrs-streak-at-76-games/|website=Chicago Tribune|date=April 4, 1996|title=KNEE INJURY ENDS FUHR'S STREAK AT 76 GAMES|access-date=May 10, 2026}}</ref> On November 30, 1995, Fuhr earned his 300th career win versus the Winnipeg Jets with a 4–1 road win at the [[Winnipeg Arena]] in [[Winnipeg]]; he became the 11th goaltender to achieve the mark, doing so in his 581st game as a starter.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.spokesman.com/stories/1995/dec/01/blues-fuhr-racks-up-300th-career-victory/|website=Spokesman.com|title=Blues' Fuhr Racks Up 300th Career Victory|access-date=May 10, 2026|date=December 1, 1995}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://apnews.com/article/sports-history-5b09b100ea2024af9933e425f1c39df3|website=AP News|date=November 28, 2022|access-date=May 10, 2026|title=Today in Sports History-Grant Fuhr wins his 300th game}}</ref> Fuhr and Gretzky became teammates for the third time when the Blues acquired Gretzky in a trade with the Kings on February 27, 1996. The 1996 playoff run for Fuhr ended prematurely in Game 2 of the first round as the result an injury that occurred when a cross-check of Maple Leafs forward [[Nick Kypreos]] by [[Chris Pronger]] saw Fuhr's leg twisted in the resulting collision that saw Fuhr tear his right ACL.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/1996/04/19/blues-lose-fuhr-out-for-playoffs/|website=Chicago Tribune|date=April 19, 1996|access-date=May 10, 2026|title=BLUES LOSE; FUHR OUT FOR PLAYOFFS}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.deseret.com/1996/4/19/19237476/blues-lose-game-fuhr-to-knee-injury/|website=Deserert News|agency=Associated Press|title=BLUES LOSE GAME, FUHR TO KNEE INJURY|date=April 19, 1996|access-date=May 10, 2026}}</ref> While the Blues (as goaltended by [[Jon Casey]]) won the first round matchup, they were eliminated by Detroit in the next round. Amidst fears that the injury would end his career, Fuhr returned to play 73 games in the {{NHL Year|1996}} season, going 33–27–11 with a 2.72 GAA. In February 1999, Fuhr had his second operation on his right knee in the span of a year to repair cartilage damage. He returned in March and started all but one of the subsequent playoff run that saw the Blues lose in the second round.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/blues-fuhr-out-4-6-weeks/|website=CBS News|date=February 7, 1999|title=Blues Fuhr Out 4-6 Weeks|access-date=May 10, 2026}}</ref> After the Blues made a deal to acquire [[Roman Turek]] as their new number-one goaltender on June 19, 1999, Fuhr was traded to the [[Calgary Flames]] on September 5, 1999. His 108 wins as a Blues goaltender were third most in team history (behind only [[Mike Liut]] and [[Curtis Joseph]]) at the time of the trade.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/stathead/tiny/VcBjR|website=Stathead|access-date=May 9, 2026|title=For combined seasons, up to 1999-00, playing goalie, playing for the St. Louis Blues, in the regular season, sorted by descending Wins.}}</ref>\n\nHe spent one season there being a mentor for Calgary's young goaltenders, including [[Fred Brathwaite]], and on October 22, 1999, he earned his 400th career win against the [[Florida Panthers]] with a 3–2 road win in overtime, becoming the sixth goaltender to achieve the mark (doing so on his 799th start).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/1999/10/23/fuhr-joins-select-400-win-club/|website=Chicago Tribune|date=October 23, 1999|title=FUHR JOINS SELECT 400-WIN CLUB}}</ref> Ailing knees led to him missing 25 games. On April 5, 2000, following a 6–5 loss to St. Louis, which statistically eliminated the Flames from playoff contention that postseason, Fuhr announced that he would retire after the [[1999–2000 NHL season|1999–2000 season]].<ref name=\"Retire\">{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/nhl/news/2000/0406/467073.html|title=Fuhr poised to end 18-year career|agency=[[Associated Press]] |publisher=[[ESPN]] |date=April 6, 2000|access-date=August 3, 2023}}</ref> He signed a deal for $200,000 in the offseason in a move meant to protect one of the team's goalies in the expansion draft. Fuhr attempted to make a comeback plan in August, but his plans proved to be short-lived. Fuhr would officially retire as a player from the National Hockey League on September 6, 2000, and he subsequently became an assistant coach with the Flames.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cbc.ca/sports/hockey/grant-fuhr-retires-expected-to-be-named-assistant-coach-1.233585|website=CBC.ca|title=Grant Fuhr retires, expected to be named assistant coach|access-date=May 9, 2026}}</ref>\n\n==International play==\nFuhr was named to the [[1984 Canada Cup]] team but saw limited action during the tournament due to an injury. Fuhr was again selected to represent Canada in the 1987 Canada Cup. It was here that he cemented his reputation as one of the best goaltenders in the game. Playing against a tough Soviet Union squad, Fuhr turned away shot after shot during the three-game final.<ref name=\"hockeygoalies\">[http://www.hockeygoalies.org/bio/fuhr.html Grant Fuhr Bio], Hockey Goalies.org</ref> After the Edmonton Oilers were eliminated by the Los Angeles Kings in the 1st round of the [[1989 Stanley Cup Playoffs]], Grant also played for Team Canada at the [[1989 World Ice Hockey Championships|1989 World Championships]] where he won a silver medal.\n\n==Post-playing career==\n[[File:Grant Fuhr - Farewell Rexall Place (26190344112) (cropped).jpg|thumb|upright=0.75|Grant Fuhr during the Farewell of Rexall Place (2016)]]\nFuhr was hired to be the [[Phoenix Coyotes]] goaltending coach on July 22, 2004. Fuhr held the position until the end of the 2008–09 season when he was replaced by [[Sean Burke]]. He held a similar post with the Calgary Flames in the 2000–2001 and 2001–2002 seasons.{{citation needed|date=August 2022}}\n\nIn 2015, Fuhr collaborated on his biography with [[Bruce Dowbiggin]], ''Grant Fuhr: The Story of a Hockey Legend''.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Whyno |first1=Stephen |title=Grant Fuhr shows comfort in life and decisions in new book |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/sports/hockey/grant-fuhr-shows-comfort-in-life-and-decisions-in-new-book/article21410632/ |access-date=March 8, 2019 |publisher=The Globe and Mail |date=October 31, 2014}}</ref>\n\nIn 2022, Fuhr began doing radio and television broadcasting for the [[Coachella Valley Firebirds]], the [[American Hockey League]] affiliate of the [[Seattle Kraken]],<ref>{{cite news |last1=Bohannan |first1=Larry |title=Firebirds hockey team making its pitch in golf-friendly Coachella Valley |url=https://www.desertsun.com/story/sports/golf/2022/11/17/in-golf-crazy-coachella-valley-hockeys-firebirds-will-fit-in-well/69658214007/ |access-date=June 17, 2023 |work=The Desert Sun |date=November 17, 2022}}</ref> and joined the [[3ICE]] 3-on-3 professional ice hockey summer league as a coach.\n\n==Personal life==\nFuhr married Lisa Cavanaugh in the [[Cayman Islands]] on September 14, 2014.  He has four children from previous marriages and a step-daughter.{{citation needed|date=June 2023}}\n\nFuhr was a regular competitor at the [[American Century Championship]], an annual competition to determine the best golfers among American sports and entertainment celebrities.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://tahoecelebritygolf.com/tournamentstats/topten.html |title=American Century Celebrity Golf Championship Tournament – American Century Celebrity Golf Championship Tournament at Edgewood, South Lake Tahoe, Nevada |website=Tahoecelebritygolf.com |date=June 23, 2015 |access-date=October 16, 2016}}</ref> The tournament is played at Edgewood Tahoe Golf Course along the edge of [[Lake Tahoe]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.edgewoodtahoe.com/ |title=Authentic. Relaxed. Inspiring |publisher=Edgewood Tahoe |access-date=October 16, 2016}}</ref>\n\n==Career statistics==\n===Regular season and playoffs===\n{| border=\"0\" cellpadding=\"1\" cellspacing=\"0\" style=\"text-align:center; width:75%\"\n|- bgcolor=\"#e0e0e0\"\n!  colspan=\"3\" bgcolor=\"#ffffff\" |  \n! rowspan=\"99\" bgcolor=\"#ffffff\" |  \n! colspan=\"9\" bgcolor=\"#e0e0e0\" | [[Regular season]]\n! rowspan=\"99\" bgcolor=\"#ffffff\" |  \n! colspan=\"8\" bgcolor=\"#e0e0e0\" | [[Playoffs]]\n|- bgcolor=\"#e0e0e0\"\n!
