Bourque}}\n{{Use Canadian English|date=October 2026}}\n{{Use mdy dates|date=November 2011}}\n{{Infobox ice hockey player\n| name = Ray Bourque\n| hall_of_fame = 2004\n| image = Ray Bourque 54118194017 (1).jpg\n| caption = Bourque at [[Fenway Park]] in 2024\n| birth_date = {{birth date and age|1960|12|28}}\n| birth_place = [[Saint-Laurent, Quebec]], Canada\n| height_ft = 5\n| height_in = 11\n| weight_lb = 219\n| position = [[Defenceman|Defence]]\n| shoots = Left\n| played_for = [[Boston Bruins]]<br>[[Colorado Avalanche]]\n| ntl_team = CAN\n| draft = 8th overall\n| draft_year = 1979\n| draft_team = [[Boston Bruins]]\n| career_start = 1979\n| career_end = 2001\n| medal_templates = {{MedalSport | Men's [[ice hockey]]}}\n{{MedalCountry | {{flagicon|Canada}} [[Canada]] }}\n{{MedalCompetition|[[Canada Cup]]}}\n{{MedalGold | [[1984 Canada Cup|1984 Canada]] | }}\n{{MedalGold| [[1987 Canada Cup|1987 Canada]] | }}\n}}\n\n'''Raymond Jean Bourque''' (born December 28, 1960) is a Canadian-American former professional [[ice hockey]] player. He holds records for most career goals, assists, and points by a [[defenceman]] in the [[National Hockey League]] (NHL). He won the [[James Norris Memorial Trophy]] as the NHL's best defenceman five times, while finishing second for that trophy a further six times. He also twice finished second in the voting for the [[Hart Memorial Trophy]], a rarity for a defenceman. He was named to the end-of-season [[NHL All-Star team|All-Star teams]] 19 times (second only to [[Gordie Howe]]'s 21 selections), with a record 13 on the first-team and six on the second-team.\n\nBourque became nearly synonymous with the [[Boston Bruins]] franchise, for which he played 21 seasons and became Boston's longest-serving [[captain (ice hockey)|captain]]. Bourque finished his career with the [[Colorado Avalanche]], with whom he won his only [[Stanley Cup]] championship in his final NHL game. He is often considered one of the best offensive defenseman in NHL history,<ref>{{Cite news |last=McIndoe |first=Sean |date=2023-01-26 |title=NHL99: Ray Bourque had to be in our top 10 — here are 77 reasons why |url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/4058435/2023/01/26/nhl99-ray-bourque/ |access-date=2026-01-02 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> and in 2017, he was named one of the [[100 Greatest NHL Players]]. Following his retirement his #77 was retired by both the Bruins and the Avalanche. Bourque also played with [[Canadian men's national ice hockey team|Canada]] for three Canada Cups and in the [[1998 Winter Olympics]], the latter being the first time that active NHL players were eligible to participate.\n\nSince his retirement Bourque has been involved in many philanthropic activities in the [[New England]] area and also owns an Italian restaurant in Boston.\n\n==Early life==\nBourque was born in [[Saint-Laurent, Quebec|Saint-Laurent]], Quebec, the son of Raymond Bourque Sr. and Anita Allain.<ref>[http://www.elhatton.com/English/Obituaries/43950/ Raymond J. Bourque - Obituary] Frenette Funeral Home</ref><ref name=\"Father dies\">[https://www.boston.com/sports/boston-bruins/2009/04/01/ray_bourques_fa/ Ray Bourque’s father, 79, dies] Boston.com - April 1, 2009</ref> Both of his parents were originally from [[New Brunswick]], and moved to Montreal in the 1950s.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.capebretonpost.com/sports/hockey/habs-bruins-alumni-to-face-off-at-sydneys-centre-200-17044/|title=Habs, Bruins alumni to face off at Sydney's Centre 200|date=December 9, 2015|work=[[Cape Breton Post]]|location=Sydney, Nova Scotia|access-date=March 9, 2019}}</ref> His mother died from cancer when he was 12 years old, while his father died in 2009.<ref name=\"Father dies\"/><ref>{{cite news |last=LaPointe|first=Joe|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/01/21/sports/hockey-bourque-at-33-is-still-mr-defense.html |title= HOCKEY; Bourque, at 33, Is Still Mr. Defense |work=[[The New York Times]] |location=New York City |access-date=October 24, 2017 | date=January 21, 1994}}</ref> Bourque was raised bilingual, speaking both English and French at home, though he went to a French school.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://extras.denverpost.com/hockey/focus1008.htm|title=Do you speak hockey?|last=Frei|first=Terry|date=October 8, 2000|work=[[Denver Post]]|location=Denver|access-date=March 10, 2019}}</ref> He began playing hockey at the age of 5, and dropped out of school at the age of 15 to devote all his time to his junior team, the Verdun Black Hawks.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sports illustrated vault Ray Bourque |url=https://vault.si.com/vault/1987/03/09/bulwark-of-the-bruins-bostons-ray-bourque-might-resemble-linus-at-home-but-on-the-ice-he-could-be-the-best-defenseman-in-the-nhl|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201027124500/https://vault.si.com/vault/1987/03/09/bulwark-of-the-bruins-bostons-ray-bourque-might-resemble-linus-at-home-but-on-the-ice-he-could-be-the-best-defenseman-in-the-nhl|url-status=dead|archive-date=October 27, 2020}}</ref>\n\n==Playing career==\n===Early career===\nBourque was the third-round pick of the [[Trois-Rivières Draveurs]] of the [[Quebec Major Junior Hockey League]] (QMJHL; now known as the Quebec Maritimes Junior Hockey League). Halfway through his rookie season, head coach and general manager (GM) [[Michel Bergeron (hockey coach)|Michel Bergeron]] traded Bourque to Sorel for high-scoring [[Benoit Gosselin|Benoît Gosselin]]. After a stellar junior career with Sorel and Verdun of the QMJHL, in which he was named the league's best defenceman in 1978 and 1979, Bourque was drafted eighth overall by the Bruins in the [[1979 NHL Entry Draft]], with a first-round draft choice obtained from the [[Los Angeles Kings]] in a [[1976–77 NHL season|1977]] trade for goaltender [[Ron Grahame]]. Boston GM [[Harry Sinden]] had intended to select defenceman [[Keith Brown (ice hockey)|Keith Brown]], but Brown was selected by the [[Chicago Blackhawks]] immediately prior to Boston's selection. Panicking, the Bruins settled on Bourque, allegedly against their better judgment.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20160310194213/http://slam.canoe.com/Slam/Hockey/NHL/Draft/2012/06/19/19897566.html Good and lucky at NHL draft]</ref>\n\n===Boston Bruins ===\n[[File:Defenseman Ray Bourque 1979.jpg|right|thumb|Bourque (wearing #7) being chased by [[Errol Rausse]] of the [[Washington Capitals]] during his rookie season (1979).]]\n\n==== Rise to prominence (1979–1985) ====\nBourque made an immediate impact in Boston during his rookie season of [[1979–80 NHL season|1979–80]], scoring a goal in his first game while facing the [[Winnipeg Jets (1972–96)|Winnipeg Jets]].<ref name=\"Timeline\">{{cite news |last=Harding |first=Thomas |title= Raymond Bourque timeline |work=[[The Gazette (Colorado Springs)|The Gazette]] |location=Colorado Springs | date=June 10, 2001}}</ref> Bourque played all 80 games his rookie year scoring 17 goals and 48 assists and quickly asserted himself from the start as one of the best defensemen in the league, winning both the [[Calder Memorial Trophy]] as Rookie of the Year and a First [[NHL All-Star team|Team All-Star selection]], the first time in NHL history a rookie non-goaltender had ever achieved the distinction. His 65 points that season was a record at the time for a rookie defenseman.<ref name=\"HHOF\">{{cite web |url=http://www.legendsofhockey.net/LegendsOfHockey/jsp/LegendsMember.jsp?mem=p200401&type=Player&page=bio&list=ByName#photo|title=Ray Bourque biography |publisher=[[Hockey Hall of Fame]] |access-date=July 22, 2008}}</ref> The following year in [[1980–81 NHL season|1980-81]] Bourque missed part of the season with broken jaw, he suffered during a Nov. 11, 1980, game at vs Detroit.<ref name=\"www.hockeydraftcentral.com\">{{Cite web |title=1979 NHL Entry Draft -- Ray Bourque |url=https://www.hockeydraftcentral.com/1979/79008.html |access-date=2025-12-15 |website=www.hockeydraftcentral.com}}</ref> He still played in 67 games scoring 27 goals and 29 assists as the Bruins lost in the first round of the playoffs. Despite the injury Bourque was named to the Second Team All-Star at the end of the season.\n\nFrom here, Bourque continued to shine for the Bruins, proving his rookie season was no fluke. During the offseason Bourque signed a multiyear contract extension with the Bruins on July 15, 1981.<ref name=\"www.hockeydraftcentral.com\" /> The following season quickly established himself as one of the league's top defensemen while also contributing outstanding offensive numbers. Once again in [[1981–82 NHL season|1981-82]] Bourque missed a portion of the season due to a shoulder injury he suffered in October.<ref name=\"www.hockeydraftcentral.com\" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=1981 NHL transactions |url=https://www.prosportstransactions.com/hockey/Search/SearchResults.php?Player=&Team=&BeginDate=&EndDate=&InjuriesChkBx=yes&submit=Search&start=250}}</ref> Following his return he helped lead the team back to the postseason scoring 17 goals and 49 assists while also being named an NHL first team All-Star for a second time. The Bruins beat Buffalo in the first round, however during a second round matchup vs [[Quebec Nordiques|Quebec]] he fractured his wrist while checking against [[André Dupont|Andre Dupont]] resulting in him missing the rest of the series.<ref name=\"UPI\">{{Cite web |title=Injury-plagued Boston Bruins All-Star defenseman Ray Bourque suffered a... - UPI Archives |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1982/07/15/Injury-plagued-Boston-Bruins-All-Star-defenseman-Ray-Bourque-suffered-a/9988395553600/ |access-date=2025-12-15 |website=UPI |language=en}}</ref>\n\nDuring the offseason Bourque suffered more injuries as he re-fractured his wrist while playing a [[softball]] game in Montreal however he was able to recover.<ref name=\"UPI\" /> He then suffered one more injury prior to the [[1982–83 NHL season|1982-83]] season during the team's final preseason game when he was struck by a puck while going to the bench. This resulted in him missing the first month of the season.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Injury-plagued defenseman Ray Bourque will be out for at... - UPI Archives |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1982/10/04/Injury-plagued-defenseman-Ray-Bourque-will-be-out-for-at/4018402552000/ |access-date=2025-12-15 |website=UPI |language=en}}</ref> Following his return the injury led to him wearing a face shield for the first time in his career.<ref name=\"www.hockeydraftcentral.com\" /> During a game vs. the Quebec Nordiques Bourque recorded his first and only hat trick of his career, scoring all 3 goals in the second period in a 11-5 Bruins victory.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Admin |date=2022-03-08 |title=This Day in Bruins History: \"Hats Off\" to Ray Bourque! |url=https://blackngoldhockey.com/2022/03/this-day-in-bruins-history-hats-off-to-ray-bourque/ |access-date=2026-01-09 |website=Black N' Gold Hockey |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Boston Bruins - Quebec Nordiques - Mar 8, 1983 {{!}} NHL.com |url=https://www.nhl.com/gamecenter/bos-vs-que/1983/03/08/1982020709 |access-date=2026-01-09 |website=www.nhl.com |language=en}}</ref> Despite all the injuries Bourque ended up having his best statistical season up to that point. Scoring 70+ points for the first time in his career with 22 goals and 51 assists. During the postseason Bourque led all defensemen 23 points helping lead the Bruins all way to the conference semifinals where they were defeated by the [[New York Islanders]].<ref name=\"www.hockeydraftcentral.com\" /> Bourque was once again named to a Second Team NHL All-Star.\n\nThe [[1983–84 NHL season|1983–84]] season became Bourque's best statistical season, as he scored a career-high 31 goals and 96 points. He led all defensemen in points that season, was named a First Team NHL All-Star and finished 5th in voting for the [[Hart Memorial Trophy]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ray Bourque Hockey Stats and Profile at hockeydb.com |url=https://www.hockeydb.com/ihdb/stats/pdisplay.php?pid=520 |access-date=2025-08-25 |website=www.hockeydb.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Legends of Hockey - Induction Showcase - Ray Bourque |url=https://www.hhof.com/induction_archives/ind04Bourque.shtml#:~:text=Raymond%20Bourque,%20a%20model%20of,Star%20in%20the%20same%20year. |access-date=2025-08-26 |website=www.hhof.com}}</ref> However the Bruins lost in the opening round of the playoffs. During the [[1984–85 NHL season|1984-85]] season Bourque went 17 consecutive games with a point the 5th longest streak by a defenseman in the history of the NHL.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Skater Records - Longest Point Streaks, Defenseman, Season {{!}} NHL Records |url=https://records.nhl.com/records/skater-records/scoring-streaks/longest-consecutive-point-streak-defenseman |access-date=2025-12-16 |website=records.nhl.com}}</ref> Bourque finished the year with 86 points 10 less than the previous year however he was named an NHL First Team All-Star for a second consecutive year. He also finished runner up to Paul Coffey for the [[James Norris Memorial Trophy|Norris Trophy]].<ref name=\"records.nhl.com\">{{Cite web |title=James Norris Memorial Trophy {{!}} NHL Records |url=https://records.nhl.com/awards/trophies/james-norris-memorial-trophy |access-date=2025-12-16 |website=records.nhl.com}}</ref> The Bruins were once again first round exits in the playoffs. During the offseason Bourque signed a 6-year contract extension with the Bruins worth 2-3 million making him the highest paid defenseman in the league.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The New York Times Archive Ray Bourque Rewarded |url=http://www.nytimes.com/1985/08/13/sports/sports-people-bourque-rewarded}}</ref>\n\n==== Captaincy, Stanley Cup appearances and Norris Trophy wins (1985–1996) ====\n[[File:Bourque 7.jpg|thumb|Bourque with the Bruins in 1981]]\nIn [[1985–86 NHL season|1985]], upon the retirement of Bruins' captain [[Terry O'Reilly]] to coach the club, Bourque and veteran [[Rick Middleton]] were named co-captains of the team, Middleton to wear the \"C\" during home games and Bourque for road games.<ref name=\"www.nhl.com-2021\">{{Cite web |date=2021-01-07 |title=The History of the Bruins Captaincy {{!}} Boston Bruins |url=https://www.nhl.com/bruins/news/the-history-of-the-bruins-captaincy-320038260 |access-date=2025-12-16 |website=www.nhl.com |language=en}}</ref> That season Bourque played 74 games scoring 19 goals and 58 assists he and Bruins once again were first round exits in the playoffs. He also earned his third Second Team NHL All Star Selection.\n\nDuring the [[1986–87 NHL season|1986-87]] Bourque came one point shy of tying his career best in points scoring 95 (23 goals 72 assists). He led all defensemen in scoring and won his first Norris Trophy as the leagues best defenseman.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ray Bourque of the Boston Bruins, named the NHL&#039;s... - UPI Archives |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1987/06/10/Ray-Bourque-of-the-Boston-Bruins-named-the-NHLs/7158550296000/ |access-date=2025-12-16 |website=UPI |language=en}}</ref> He also finished as runner up to [[Wayne Gretzky]] for the Hart Memorial Trophy.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Hart Memorial Trophy {{!}} NHL Records |url=https://records.nhl.com/awards/trophies/hart-memorial-trophy |access-date=2025-12-16 |website=records.nhl.com}}</ref> Despite Bourque's terrific season the Bruins lost to Montreal in the first round of the playoffs. He was then named a First NHL Team All-Star for a sixth time.\n\nThe following year in [[1987–88 NHL season|1987-88]] Bourque broke [[Bobby Orr]]'s record for most consecutive games with a point scored by a Bruins defenseman with 19. This is also the second most in NHL history behind Paul Coffey who scored in 28 straight games during the 1985–86 season.<ref name=\"www.nhl.com-2021\" /> Bourque played in 78 games and scoring 17 goals and 64 assists for 81 total points. This resulted in him repeating as the Norris Trophy winner.<ref name=\"records.nhl.com\" /> During the postseason Bourque led all defensive in points with 21 and helped the Bruins reach the [[1988 Stanley Cup Final]]s, in which they were ultimately defeated by the [[Edmonton Oilers]].\n\nUpon Rick Middleton's retirement in [[1987–88 NHL season|1988]], Bourque became the team's sole captain, and retained the position for the remainder of his Bruins' tenure. In so doing, he passed [[Dit Clapper]] as the longest-tenured Bruins' captain in history, as well as passing [[Alex Delvecchio]] of the [[Detroit Red Wings]] as the longest-serving team captain in NHL history, a mark since surpassed by [[Steve Yzerman]] of the Red Wings. That season Bourque missed 20 games with sprained ligaments in left knee, which he suffered when he collided with [[Michel Petit]] during a game on December 10, 1988, vs. the New York Rangers.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Hockey News Archive |url=https://archive.thehockeynews.com/issue/611886/57 |access-date=2025-12-16 |website=archive.thehockeynews.com}}</ref> Bourque was still selected as an NHL Second Team All-Star scoring 18 goals and 43 assists for 61 points. The Bruins were eliminated in the second round of the playoffs.\n\nDuring the [[1989–90 NHL season|1989-90]] season Bourque had a career performance during a game on February 18, 1990 vs. Vancouver when he scored 6 points (1 goal and 5 assists) in a Bruins 7-2 victory.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Skater Records - Most Points, Game {{!}} BOS Records |url=https://records.nhl.com/bos/records/skater-records/points/most-points-one-game |access-date=2026-01-09 |website=records.nhl.com}}</ref> played in 76 games scoring 84 points (19 goals and 65) assists. For his efforts he won his third Norris Trophy and finished second to [[Mark Messier]] in 1990 in the closest race ever for the [[Hart Memorial Trophy]] with Messier winning by two singular votes.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-06-12 |title=NHL Hart Memorial Trophy Winners {{!}} NHL.com |url=https://www.nhl.com/news/nhl-hart-memorial-trophy-winners-complete-list-287743272 |access-date=2025-12-16 |website=www.nhl.com |language=en}}</ref> Bourque earned another First Team All-Star nod, as he helped lead the Bruins to their first [[Presidents' Trophy]] with the leagues best record.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-04-17 |title=NHL Presidents' Trophy Winners {{!}} NHL.com |url=https://www.nhl.com/news/nhl-presidents-trophy-winners-complete-list-287820790 |access-date=2026-01-09 |website=www.nhl.com |language=en}}</ref> He scored 17 points during the playoffs to help the Bruins reach the [[1990 Stanley Cup Final]]s however just like two years prior they were defeated by Edmonton.\n\nDuring the offseason Bourque signed a four-year contract extension with the Bruins worth 1.1 million a year once again making him the highest paid defenseman in the league.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bruins sign Bourque to record contract - UPI Archives |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1990/08/31/Bruins-sign-Bourque-to-record-contract/9251652075200/ |access-date=2025-12-16 |website=UPI |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=The Hockey News Archive |url=https://archive.thehockeynews.com/issue/615914/50 |access-date=2025-12-16 |website=archive.thehockeynews.com}}</ref> In [[1990–91 NHL season|1990-91]] Bourque had his third 90+ point season scoring 21 goals and tallying a career high 73 assists. In addition he broke Bobby Orr's Bruins record for career points by a defenseman when he scored his 889th point on January 24, 1991.<ref name=\"www.hockeydraftcentral.com\" /> During a game on March 21, vs. the [[Quebec Nordiques]] Bourque had an NHL record 19 shots on goal, scoring one in a 3–3 tie.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Boston Bruins - Quebec Nordiques - Mar 21, 1991 {{!}} NHL.com |url=https://www.nhl.com/gamecenter/que-vs-bos/1991/03/21/1990020783 |access-date=2026-01-02 |website=www.nhl.com |language=en}}</ref> Borque also won back to back Norris Trophy's for the second time in his career marking his fourth total.<ref name=\"records.nhl.com\" /> During the postseason Bourque became Boston's all-time playoff points leader with an assist on April 21, 1991, vs. Montreal. Breaking [[Phil Esposito]]'s record of 102.<ref name=\"www.hockeydraftcentral.com\" /> However he and the Bruins lost in the conference finals to the eventual Cup champions [[Pittsburgh Penguins]].\n\nBourque continued to make even more history the following year in [[1991–92 NHL season|1991-92]], broke Bobby Orr's Bruins record for career goals by a defenseman when he scored his 271st goal&nbsp;on January 22, 1992.<ref name=\"www.hockeydraftcentral.com\" /> The following month he scored his 1,000th career point during Boston's February 29, game vs. the [[Washington Capitals]], becoming just the third defenseman in league history to achieve the milestone.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bourque Hits 1,000-Point Milestone {{!}} The Seattle Times |url=https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/19920301/1478697/bourque-hits-1000-point-milestone |access-date=2026-01-24 |website=archive.seattletimes.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Bourque Hits 1,000-Point Milestone {{!}} The Seattle Times |url=https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/19920301/1478697/bourque-hits-1000-point-milestone |access-date=2025-12-16 |website=archive.seattletimes.com}}</ref> He played in all 80 games that year scoring 81 points (21 goals and 61 assists). However he missed the end of the Bruins postseason run due to a broken finger, and the Bruins lost the conference finals to the Penguins who went on to defend their Cup.<ref>{{Cite news |date=1992-05-31 |title=NOTEBOOK |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/1992/05/31/notebook/6be24d09-2914-4bc0-9f34-5172ccef92e7/ |access-date=2025-12-16 |work=The Washington Post |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Lemieux out indefinitely |url=https://www.tampabay.com/archive/1992/05/07/lemieux-out-indefinitely/ |access-date=2025-12-16 |website=Tampa Bay Times |language=en}}</ref> He also finished runner up to [[Brian Leetch]] for the Norris Trophy.<ref name=\"records.nhl.com\" />\n\nIn [[1992–93 NHL season|1992-93]] Bourque yet again set another Bruins record when he broke [[Johnny Bucyk]]'s career assists record with his 795th assist on March 20, 1993.<ref name=\"www.hockeydraftcentral.com\" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Troiani |first=Gayle |date=2023-07-25 |title=37 Reasons Patrice Bergeron Is An All-Time Bruin |url=https://nesn.com/2023/07/patrice-bergeron-retires-37-reasons-no-37-is-all-time-bruin/ |access-date=2025-12-16 |website=NESN.com |language=en-US}}</ref> Following an 82-season (19 goals and 63 assists) Bourque was named a First Team All-Star for the 10th time and once again finished runner up to the Norris Trophy for a second consecutive year, losing to [[Chris Chelios]].<ref name=\"records.nhl.com\" /> He and the Bruins were swept in the first round of the playoffs to the [[Buffalo Sabres]]. In [[1993–94 NHL season|1993-94]] Bourque appeared in 72 games and had his fourth and final 90+ points season scoring 20 goals and 71 assists. He missed the last 11 games of the season due to a knee injury.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Hockey News Archive |url=https://archive.thehockeynews.com/issue/613548/43 |access-date=2025-12-16 |website=archive.thehockeynews.com}}</ref> At the end of the year Borque was named the Norris Trophy winner for the fifth and final time of his career.<ref name=\"records.nhl.com\" /> However the Bruins were eliminated in the second round of the playoffs.\n\nDuring the lock out shortened [[1994–95 NHL season|1994-95]] season he only played 46 games that year and was named a Second Team All-Star after scoring 12 goals and 31 assists. During the postseason he and the Bruins lost in the first round to New Jersey. Bourque the following year in [[1995–96 NHL season|1995-96]] he played in all 80 games and scored 20 goals and 62 assists. He was also named the [[1996 National Hockey League All-Star Game|1996 National Hockey League All-Star Game MVP]] after scoring the game-winning goal in front of a hometown crowd at the [[TD Garden|Fleet Center]].<ref>{{Cite web |author1=BOB DICESARE |author2= JIM KELLEY |date=1996-01-21 |title=BOURQUE GETS WINNER FOR EAST ALL-STARS |url=https://buffalonews.com/news/article_6fc400c0-0efd-5f46-8915-bb9239ed4b57.html |access-date=2025-12-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230817185035/https://buffalonews.com/news/article_6fc400c0-0efd-5f46-8915-bb9239ed4b57.html|archive-date=August 17, 2023 |website=Buffalo News |language=en}}</ref> That year Bourque finished runner up to Chris Chelios for the Norris once again and the Bruins lost in the first round of the playoffs.<ref name=\"records.nhl.com\" />\n\n==== Final years (1996–1999) ====\nThroughout the [[1996–97 NHL season|1996-97]] campaign Bourque missed 18 games due multiple injuries he sustained throughout the season.<ref name=\"www.hockeydraftcentral.com\" /> During a game on May 27, vs the New York Islanders, Bourque recorded his 1,000th career assist on a goal scored by [[Jean-Yves Roy (ice hockey)|Jean-Yves Roy]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=writer |first=Howard Ulman, Associated Press |title=Bourque gets 1,00th assist in Bruins loss |url=https://www.southcoasttoday.com/story/sports/1997/03/28/bourque-gets-1-00th-assist/50622707007/ |access-date=2026-01-24 |website=New Bedford Standard-Times |language=en-US}}</ref> Bourque’s injuries throughout the year resulted in his production declining as he only scored 50 points (19 goals and 31 assists). Despite this Bourque set another record when he scored his 1,340th career point on February 1, 1997 which was a goal vs. Tampa Bay setting the Bruins all-time record for points.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-01-20 |title=New Blood, New Beginnings {{!}} Top 10 Moments from 1986-2000 {{!}} Boston Bruins |url=https://www.nhl.com/bruins/news/new-blood-new-beginnings-top-10-moments-from-1986-2000 |access-date=2026-01-24 |website=www.nhl.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-01-20 |title=New Blood, New Beginnings {{!}} Top 10 Moments from 1986-2000 {{!}} Boston Bruins |url=https://www.nhl.com/bruins/news/new-blood-new-beginnings-top-10-moments-from-1986-2000 |access-date=2025-12-16 |website=www.nhl.com |language=en}}</ref> During Bourque's tenure with the Bruins, the team appeared a North American professional record twenty-nine consecutive seasons in the playoffs, however that streak ended this year as it was the only time Bourque missed the playoffs as Bruins finished with the NHL's worst record that season.<ref name=\"Hartscrewjob\">{{cite book |title=The National Hockey League Official Guide and Record Book, 1990–91 |publisher=Running Press |year=1990 |isbn=0-89471-870-3 |editor=Ralph Dinger |location=Philadelphia |page=151}}</ref> This also marked the first time in his career that he was not named either a first or second team All-Star.\n\nDuring Bourque's final years with the club his scoring decreased however he still served as a valuable member of the team. As after missing multiple games the previous year Bourque played all 82 games in [[1997–98 NHL season|1997-98]] scoring 13 goals and 35 assists however the Bruins lost in the first round of the playoffs. Borque's final full season with the Bruins came in [[1998–99 NHL season|1998-99]] where he played in 81 games scoring 10 goals and 47 assists. He also broke Johnny Bucyk's record for career games played when he played his 1,437th game on March 13, 1999, at Buffalo.<ref name=\"www.hockeydraftcentral.com\" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Skater Records - Most Games Played, Career {{!}} BOS Records |url=https://records.nhl.com/bos/records/skater-records/seasons-and-games/most-games-played |access-date=2025-12-16 |website=records.nhl.com}}</ref>\n\nDespite a nucleus of young talent and high expectations for [[1999–2000 NHL season|1999–2000]], injuries caused the Bruins to plummet to the bottom of their division, and they went on track to miss the playoffs. This was further exacerbated by negative attention over teammate [[Marty McSorley]]'s hit on [[Donald Brashear]].<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.cbc.ca/sports/bruins-marty-mcsorley-charged-with-assault-1.200872 | publisher=[[CBC News]] | title=Bruins' Marty McSorley charged with assault | date=March 8, 2000 |access-date=June 4, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/nhl-brass-promises-to-re-evaluate-mcsorley-s-career-1.241930 | publisher=[[CBC News]] | title=NHL brass promises to 're-evaluate' McSorley's career | date=November 11, 2000 |access-date=June 4, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Bruins Hit Bottom\\ Carter, Dafoe Hurt; McSorley Head-Hunts |last1= Marrapese-Burrell |first1=Nancy |newspaper=[[The Boston Globe]] |date= February 22, 2000 |url=http://nl.newsbank.com/nl-search/we/Archives?p_product=BG&p_theme=bg&p_action=search&p_topdoc=1&p_text_direct-0=0EADDE32A40C5D10&p_field_direct-0=document_id&p_sort=YMD_date:D }}</ref> With his career nearing an end and the team going in the wrong direction, Bourque requested a trade from the fading Bruins so he would have a chance to win the Stanley Cup. Bourque initially preferred a team on the East Coast like the [[Philadelphia Flyers]] which would be closer to his home in Boston, but general manager [[Harry Sinden]] had secretly been working out a deal with the Colorado Avalanche and convinced Bourque that this was the best destination to finish his career.<ref name=\"HHOF\"/> Bourque and fellow veteran [[Dave Andreychuk]] were sent to Colorado in exchange for [[Brian Rolston]], [[Martin Grenier]], [[Samuel Påhlsson]] and a first-round draft pick (2000 draft, 27th overall, [[Martin Samuelsson]]).\n\nBourque played for Boston for 21 seasons (1979–2000), known for combining offensive prowess with defensive ability. He was a perennial shot accuracy champion at [[National Hockey League All-Star Game|All-Star Games]].<ref name=\"Plus-Minus\">{{cite web |url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/leaders/plus_minus_career.html |title=NHL & WHA Career Leaders and Records for Plus/Minus |publisher=Hockey-Reference.com |access-date=July 21, 2008}}</ref> The Bruins' reliance on Bourque's on-ice mastery was so total that—while Bourque was very durable throughout much of his career with his toughness, consistency, and skill, when he was not on the ice, the team was seen by many to flounder whenever he was out of the lineup.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-12-28 |title=Bruins Alumni: Happy Birthday, Ray Bourque |url=https://blackngoldhockey.com/2021/12/bruins-alumni-happy-birthday-ray-bourque/ |access-date=2025-08-25 |website=Black N' Gold Hockey |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=\"Almanac\">{{cite book|editor=Paul Kelly |title= Hockey Almanac: 1993–94 |location=Lincolnwood, IL |publisher=Publications International Ltd |page=42 |oclc=29917276}}</ref> Many consider Bourque to be one of the most notable defensemen in hockey history.\n\nBourque was also popular among Bruins fans because of his willingness to re-sign with Boston without any acrimonious or lengthy negotiations. He passed over several opportunities to set the benchmark salary for defencemen; instead, he usually quietly and quickly agreed to terms with the Bruins, and this stance irritated the [[National Hockey League Players' Association]] (NHLPA), which had been pushing to drive up players' wages.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/hockey/nhl/news/2001/02/15/sayitaintso_bruins/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010501233824/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/hockey/nhl/news/2001/02/15/sayitaintso_bruins/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=May 1, 2001 |title=Say It Ain't So: Boston Bruins |date=May 9, 2001 |publisher=[[CNN]]/[[Sports Illustrated]] |access-date=April 25, 2011}}</ref>\n\nDuring his 21 seasons with the Bruins he set many records becoming the all-time career leader in games played (1,518), assists (1,111) and points (1,506).<ref name=\"BOSTON BRUINS ALUMNI\">{{Cite web |title=Ray Bourque |url=https://www.bostonbruinsalumni.com/ray-bourque.html |access-date=2025-08-25 |website=BOSTON BRUINS ALUMNI |language=en}}</ref>\n\n===Colorado Avalanche (2000–2001)===\n[[File:Bourque is back (25430904726).jpg|thumb|Bourque wore number 77 with Colorado in 2000 and 2001, and again for the Colorado Avalanche alumni in 2016]]\n\nBourque was traded from Boston Bruins to the Colorado Avalanche on March 6, 2000. Although Bourque played just one-and-a-half seasons with the Avalanche, he proved to be a force both on the ice and in the locker room. Bourque became teammates with goaltender [[Patrick Roy]], who as a previous member of the Montreal Canadiens had frequent playoff encounters with Bourque's Boston Bruins. In the remainder of the 1999-2000 season, Bourque helped the struggling Avalanche improve their form and capture their division. During the playoffs, they advanced to the conference finals, where they lost to the [[Dallas Stars]] in a hard-fought series. Bourque hit the post in the last minutes of Game 7, which would have tied the game after his team rallied from a 3–0 deficit in the third period to 3–2.\n\nBourque returned to the Avalanche for the 2000–01 season and was named as an alternate captain. He led all Colorado defencemen in scoring with 7 goals and 52 assists in 80 games, and formed a solid defensive pairing with [[Adam Foote]] and [[Rob Blake]], the latter of whom the Avs received from the Los Angeles Kings in a trade. Bourque was named to the post-season First All-Star team, finishing as runner-up to the Detroit Red Wings' [[Nicklas Lidström]] for the Norris Trophy.\n\nThe Avalanche advanced all the way to the [[Stanley Cup Final]], against the defending Cup holders, the [[New Jersey Devils]]. Bourque scored the game-winning goal in game three. After the Avalanche lost game five at home which led them trailing the series 3-2, Bourque flew in his relatives for game six in New Jersey, which the Avalanche won 4-0 to even the series. The Avalanche then won game seven at home with a score of 3-1 to capture their second Stanley Cup in franchise history. During the post-game presentation that followed the Avalanche's victory in the decisive seventh game, team captain [[Joe Sakic]] broke with tradition and gave the Cup to Bourque so he could skate with it first. Colorado goaltender Patrick Roy, whose fourth championship had come the same day as Bourque's first, said of the Stanley Cup and his teammate, \"A name was missing from that [Cup], and today it is back to normal.\"<ref name=\"2000-2001 Stanley Cup Final\">{{cite book |editor1-last=Falla |editor1-first=Jack |title=Quest for the Cup: A History of the Stanley Cup Finals, 1893–2001 |publisher=Key Porter Books |location=Toronto |year=2001 |page=266 |isbn=978-1-55263-343-4}}</ref> Bourque had waited longer to win his first Cup than any other Cup-winning player had in the 108-year history of the Stanley Cup, having played 1,612 regular season and 214 playoff games before winning the ultimate prize.\n\nOn June 12, 2001, three days after the Cup victory, Bourque brought the Cup back to Boston for an emotional rally attended by some 20,000 fans at Boston's City Hall Plaza.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Buckley |first=Steve |date=2021-05-26 |title='He was handing the Cup to all of us': The day Boston celebrated Ray Bourque's Stanley Cup title |url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/2581117/2021/05/26/he-was-handing-the-cup-to-all-of-us-the-day-boston-celebrated-ray-bourques-stanley-cup-title/ |access-date=2025-12-24 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Throughout the Stanley Cup Final, local Massachusetts newspapers covered the series as though the Avalanche were the hometown team, and TV ratings for game seven were higher in Massachusetts everywhere besides Denver.<ref name=\"Justin Pope\">{{Cite web |author=Justin Pope|agency= Associated Press |title=Bourque finally brings Cup to Boston |url=https://www.southcoasttoday.com/story/sports/2001/06/14/bourque-finally-brings-cup-to/50427892007/ |access-date=2025-12-24 |website=New Bedford Standard-Times |language=en-US}}</ref> During the event Bourque told the crowd \"This [Boston] is home for me and my family. I had some great years with the Bruins, but I'd never come really close to Stanley, my friend,\" \"But to touch this, we felt there was a move that had to be made.\"<ref name=\"Justin Pope\" />\n\nBourque retired shortly thereafter, having set defensive regular-season records in goals (410) and assists (1169) for 1579 points. During the 2000–01 season, which would be the last for both players, Bourque surpassed [[Paul Coffey]] (who had signed as a free agent with the Bruins and was waived in December 2000) to become the all-time leader in goals, assists and points for a defenceman at any senior professional level.\n\n==International play==\nBourque made his international debut for Team Canada at the 1981 [[Canada Cup]], He scored one goal and four assists in sevem games as Team Canada lost in the final to the Soviet Union.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Team Canada - Canada Cup 1981 - Player Stats |url=https://www.quanthockey.com/world-cup/en/teams/team-canada-players-1981-world-cup-stats.html |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=QuantHockey |language=en}}</ref> Bourque was then selected for the team once again in 1984 where he recorded four assists in eight games as he and team Canada won the gold medal 6–5 over Sweden.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Team Canada - Canada Cup 1984 - Player Stats |url=https://www.quanthockey.com/world-cup/en/teams/team-canada-players-1984-world-cup-stats.html |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=QuantHockey |language=en}}</ref> Bourque also participated in the 1987 Canada Cup, where he scored 2 goals and 6 assists as he helped Team Canada win another gold medal.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Team Canada - Canada Cup 1987 - Player Stats |url=https://www.quanthockey.com/world-cup/en/teams/team-canada-players-1987-world-cup-stats.html |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=QuantHockey |language=en}}</ref> Bourque did not play in the 1991 edition, despite attempts by [[Wayne Gretzky]] and Mark Messier to persuade him to take part.\n\nBourque also played for the NHL All-Stars in [[Rendez-vous '87]] against the Soviet Union.\n\nBourque played for the Team Canada in the [[1998 Winter Olympics]], the first edition in which active NHL players were eligible to participate. Controversially, the team captaincy went to [[Eric Lindros]], passing over longer-tenured NHL captains like Bourque, [[Wayne Gretzky]], and [[Steve Yzerman]].<ref>{{cite Sports-Reference}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Lapointe |first=Joe |url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9506E2D6153AF932A35751C0A96E958260 |title=Nagano '98; Wearing C, for Canada |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=February 1, 1998 |access-date=April 17, 2008}}</ref> Bourque led all defencemen in scoring with one goal and two assists in six games.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.quanthockey.com/olympics/en/teams/team-canada-players-1998-olympics-stats.html |access-date=March 12, 2014|title=Team Canada – Olympics – Nagano 1998 – Player Stats}}</ref> Canada reached the semi-finals where they were eliminated by the [[Czech national men's ice hockey team|Czech Republic]] after a 1-1 tie, as Bourque and four of his teammates could not beat Czech goaltender [[Dominik Hašek]] in the shootout.<ref>{{cite news |last=Alexander |first=Rachel |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/sports/longterm/olympics1998/sport/hockey/articles/olyhock21.htm |title=Hasek Stares Down Canada in Shootout, 2–1 |newspaper=The Washington Post |date=February 21, 1998 |access-date=April 17, 2008 |archive-date=April 29, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140429163516/http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/sports/longterm/olympics1998/sport/hockey/articles/olyhock21.htm |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Molinaro |first=John |url=http://www.cbc.ca/sports/columns/newsmakers/crawford_marc.html |title=Crawford leaves an uneven legacy |publisher=Canadian Broadcasting Corporation |date=April 26, 2006 |access-date=April 17, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080215182725/http://www.cbc.ca/sports/columns/newsmakers/crawford_marc.html |archive-date=February 15, 2008 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Beacon |first=Bill |title=Nagano still nags at Gretzky |publisher=Canadian Broadcasting Corporation |date=November 8, 2000 |url=http://www.cbc.ca/sports/hockey/nagano-still-nags-at-gretzky-1.253478 |access-date=December 19, 2015 |archive-date=December 22, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151222205955/http://www.cbc.ca/sports/hockey/nagano-still-nags-at-gretzky-1.253478 |url-status=live }}</ref> Fans and sportscasters have alternatively praised and criticized the decision to have Bourque in the shootout instead of Gretzky; Gretzky was the all-time leading scorer in the NHL but was mediocre on breakaways, while Bourque was a perennial shot accuracy champion at the NHL All-Star skills competition. General manager [[Bobby Clarke]] said “As great a player as he was, defencemen don’t get breakaways, so to put him in that position was probably unfair. It was a poor decision in my opinion not to use Gretzky and to put Raymond in that position.” A demoralized Team Canada then lost the bronze medal match to Finland 3-2 and went home empty-handed.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Brophy |first1=Mike |title=‘98 problems: How it all went wrong for Canada’s Olympic hockey team in Nagano |url=https://www.cbc.ca/sportslongform/entry/1998-olympic-hockey |publisher=CBC Sports |access-date=27 March 2026}}</ref>\n\n== Playing style/legacy ==\nThroughout his career Bourque was a prominent player, recognized for his defensive instincts. Specializing in reading plays, using positioning rather than physical play, and his balance enabled him to keep possession under physical pressure. Bourque's skating ability was characterized by speed, agility and lateral movement. This allowed him to transition between defense to leading a counterattack.<ref name=\"Smith-2023\">{{Cite web |last=Smith |first=Ryan |date=2023-10-10 |title=Ray Bourque: A Hockey Journey from Humble Beginnings to Hall of Fame Glory |url=https://hockeyprime.com/ray-bourque-a-hockey-journey-from-humble-beginnings-to-hall-of-fame-glory/ |access-date=August 26, 2025|website=HockeyPrime |language=en-US}}</ref>\n\nBourque was also known for his offensive prowess as a puck-moving defenseman. He initiated offense with smooth breakout passes and often joined the attack, almost acting as a 4th forward. His vision and passing were both key components of his playmaking prowess.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-03-15 |title=Prime time: Ray Bourque's career may have topped Orr's |url=https://www.si.com/nhl/2016/03/15/bobby-orr-1970-71-boston-bruins-ray-bourque |access-date=2025-08-26 |website=SI |language=en-US}}</ref> Besides his play making he is also known as one of the best scoring defensemen in NHL history, scoring 20 or more goals 9 times throughout his career. In total he scored 10 or more goals in every season until his final year. Bourque also excelled on the power play, scoring 173 career goals on the unit, as well as setting a record for defensemen with 60 game-winning goals. In 2000, he became the all-time scoring leader among NHL defensemen, when he reached 1,520 points. He ended his NHL career with 1,579 points in 1,612 regular-season games and 180 points in 214 playoff games. He has the most points for a player with under 500 goals in NHL history. This has resulted in him being widely regarded as one of the greatest offensive defensemen in NHL history.<ref>{{Cite web |title=For combined seasons, playing defenseman, in the regular season, sorted by descending Goals.|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/stathead/tiny/wlVTQn |access-date=April 17, 2026|website=Stathead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=For combined seasons, playing skater, in the regular season, requiring Goals <= 500, sorted by descending Points.|website=Stathead|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/stathead/tiny/1GCaK|access-date=April 17, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=July 6, 2025 |title=The Best NHL Defensemen Ever - The Hockey Writers Hockey History Latest News, Analysis & More |url=https://thehockeywriters.com/best-nhl-defensemen-ever/ |access-date=August 26, 2025 |website=The Hockey Writers |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Ray Bourque {{!}} EBSCO Research Starters |url=https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/sports-and-leisure/ray-bourque |access-date=August 26, 2025|website=www.ebsco.com |language=en}}</ref>\n\nBourque also possessed a powerful yet accurate wrist shot, which has been described one of the best among all players.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lillhannus |first=Andreas |date=November 7, 2023 |title=When Ray Bourque scored a goal from his own end and delivered a hilarious roast to shut down a cocky opponent |url=https://www.thehockeybeast.com/nhl/ray-bourques-hilarious-words-after-scoring-from-his-own-end/ |access-date=August 26, 2025 |website=The Hockey Beast |language=en-US}}</ref> He showed how good his shooting ability was during NHL All Star shooting competition winning the event 8 times throughout his career.<ref name=\"AllStarShooting\" />\n\nHe was one of the most consistent players of his era, being voted one of the top defenseman throughout his entire career.<ref name=\"Smith-2023\" /> Even as he entered the twilight of his career he adapted his style to continue his effectiveness, his former teammate Patrick Roy once commented on Bourque stating “ He’s like a bear out there,” in comparison to Bourque's pride and work ethic.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ESPN.com: NHL - Bourque's game changes, gets better with age |url=https://www.espn.com/nhl/columns/frei_terry/986140.html |date=December 31, 2000|access-date=March 11, 2026|website=ESPN}}</ref>\n\nBourque was also known for his leadership abilities as well as his sportsmanship. Once being described as “a symbol of class, hard work, determination, and above all, a leader” who \"never put himself ahead of the team.\"<ref>{{Cite web |title=ESPN.com: NHL - Users: No regrets for champion Bourque |url=https://www.espn.com/nhl/s/2001/0626/1218915.html |access-date=March 11, 2026|website=www.espn.com}}</ref>\n\nDuring his 21 seasons with the Boston Bruins Bourque became one of the best player in team history and set many records becoming their all-time career leader in games played (1,518), assists (1,111) and points (1,506).<ref name=\"BOSTON BRUINS ALUMNI\" />  His 13 First NHL All Star Team selections are the most in NHL history and six Second Team All-Star squads, second in total in league history only behind [[Gordie Howe]] and most amongst defencemen.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ray Bourque |url=https://www.bostonbruinsalumni.com/ray-bourque.html |access-date=2025-12-24 |website=BOSTON BRUINS ALUMNI |language=en}}</ref>\n\nEven with Bourque's career overlapping other great defensemen, such as [[Paul Coffey]], [[Chris Chelios]], [[Denis Potvin]], [[Al MacInnis]], [[Brian Leetch]], and [[Scott Stevens]] he still remained the gold standard of his era. Bourque's former coach [[Brian Sutter]] once stated \"Al, Pronger, Potvin, those other guys … all great players,\" \"And I mean great players. But Raymond was a notch above them, above everybody. In my opinion, he was the greatest defenseman since the greatest-ever defenseman, [[Bobby Orr]].”<ref name=\"www.nhl.com-2017\">{{Cite web |date=2017-01-01 |title=Ray Bourque: 100 Greatest NHL Players {{!}} NHL.com |url=https://www.nhl.com/news/ray-bourque-100-greatest-nhl-hockey-players-285594564 |access-date=2025-08-25 |website=www.nhl.com |language=en}}</ref>\n\nHe is often regarded as not just one of the best defensemen in NHL history, but as one of the all-around greatest players.<ref name=\"www.nhl.com-2017\" /><ref>{{Cite news |date=2025-07-30 |title=NHL99: A project ranking the greatest players in modern NHL history |url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/3550299/2023/02/08/nhl99-ranking-the-greatest-players-in-modern-nhl-history/ |access-date=2025-08-26 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> in 1998 he was voted the 14th greatest hockey player of all time in [[The Hockey News]]' list of [[List of 100 greatest NHL players by The Hockey News|100 greatest NHL players]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kay |first=Jason |date=2015-04-02 |title=The Top 100 NHL players of all-time, throwback style |url=https://thehockeynews.com/news/news/the-top-100-nhl-players-of-all-time-throwback-style |access-date=2025-12-24 |website=The Hockey News |language=en}}</ref> In 2023 he was named the 10th greatest hockey player of all time by ''[[The Athletic]]''.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2025-12-23 |title=NHL99: A project ranking the greatest players in modern NHL history |url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/3550299/2023/02/08/nhl99-ranking-the-greatest-players-in-modern-nhl-history/ |access-date=2026-01-02 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>\n\n==Jersey number==\nFor a majority of his NHL career, Bourque wore jersey number 77. After he retired following the 2000–01 season, both the Bruins and the Avalanche honored him by retiring number 77.\n\nWhen he was initially called up to the Bruins, Bourque was assigned the number 7, which had been worn by former Bruins star forward [[Phil Esposito]] from the time he was acquired by the team in 1967 until he departed in 1976 via trade. Bourque was the third player to be issued the number following Esposito's departure, following [[Sean Shanahan]] and [[Bill Bennett (ice hockey)|Bill Bennett]].<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/teams/BOS/numbers.html |title = Boston Bruins Sweater Numbers}}</ref>\n\nIn 1987, six years after Esposito's retirement, and three years after he was elected to the Hockey Hall of Fame, the Bruins decided to retire number 7 in his honor. Bourque, thus, would be the last Bruin to wear number 7 and was permitted to do so as long as he desired to even after Esposito's retirement ceremony, which was scheduled for December 3 of that year. Bourque, however, came up with his own way to honor the veteran Bruin and did so at the ceremony.\n\nAs the Bruins were dressing for that night's game, Bourque put on two jerseys with his normal number 7 as the top layer. When the team came out for the retirement ceremony, Bourque skated over to Esposito just before he was about to speak to the Boston crowd. He removed his number 7 jersey and handed it to Esposito, a move that was seen as \"surrendering\" the number to him. In doing this, Bourque also revealed his new number to the crowd, as the jersey he had been wearing underneath his number 7 bore the number 77 he would wear for the remainder of his career.<ref name=\"Timeline\"/>\n\n==Personal life and retirement==\nBourque married his high school sweetheart Christiane in 1982, the couple live in Massachusetts,<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-06-12 |title=Bourque pulling for Avalanche in Final 21 years after he hoisted Cup {{!}} NHL.com |url=https://www.nhl.com/news/ray-bourque-rooting-for-colorado-in-2022-stanley-cup-final-334556936 |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=www.nhl.com |language=en}}</ref> and have two sons, [[Chris Bourque|Christopher]] and [[Ryan Bourque|Ryan]] and a daughter, Melissa.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Ray Bourque's daughter Melissa weds |url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/arts/2012/01/10/ray-bourque-daughter-melissa-weds/b6rIyBZOBlonFriR2owaQM/story.html |website=The Boston Globe |access-date=2025-11-28|language=en-US}}</ref> Christopher and Ryan both became professional hockey players. Bourque's younger brother Richard was also a hockey player and was drafted by the Bruins in the [[1981 NHL Entry Draft]] in the tenth round, but never played professional hockey.\n\nBourque was named a Bruins team consultant on November 3, 2005.\n\nWhile Bourque's children were attending [[Cushing Academy]] he served as an assistant coach for the hockey team from 2002 to 2007.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Raymond Bourque - Assistant Coach, Cushing Academy (USHS-Prep) - Elite Prospects |url=https://www.eliteprospects.com/staff/39565/raymond-bourque |website=www.eliteprospects.com|access-date=2025-11-28}}</ref>\n\nBourque is the co-owner of an Italian restaurant called Tresca located in Boston's [[North End, Boston, Massachusetts|North End]]. The restaurant was opened in 2005; he owns it alongside executive chef Rich Ansara.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Functions|url=https://trescanorthend.com/functions/|website=Tresca North End Boston|access-date=2025-11-28 |language=en-US}}</ref> In 2016 lower portion of the restaurant was converted into a bar arena and was renamed Cafe 77 in reference to Bourque's jersey number.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Tresca Is Evolving with a New Co-Owner and Chef |url=https://boston.eater.com/2016/7/27/12284904/tresca-north-end-new-chef |website=Eater Boston|date=2016-07-27|access-date=2025-11-28|language=en-US|first=Dana|last=Hatic}}</ref> Bourque wanted to open the restaurant due to his love for the North End because of the Italian food, culture and heritage that he developed during his playing days in Boston.<ref name=\"Scene Magazine-2020\">{{Cite web|title=Ray Bourque, off the Ice now owns Tresca. |url=https://scenenorthend.com/2020/10/22/ray-bourque-on-and-off-ice/|date=2020-10-22 |magazine=Scene Magazine |access-date=2025-11-28|language=en-US}}</ref>\n\nBourque was involved with charitable events throughout most of his career and helped create contributions totaling more than $20 million to over 1,000 different charities. In 2017 he and his wife decided then decided to start their own charity called the Bourque Family Foundation.<ref>{{Cite web|title=About |url=https://bourquefamilyfoundation.org/about/ |publisher=Bourque Family Foundation |date=2024-04-26|access-date=2025-11-28|language=en-US}}</ref> The foundation supports charitable events around the Boston and [[New England]] area from establishing after school programs to famine relief efforts.<ref>{{Cite web|title=About Ray Bourque |url=https://bourquefamilyfoundation.org/about-ray/ |publisher=Bourque Family Foundation |date=2018-04-01|access-date=2025-11-28|language=en-US}}</ref> The charity is a family oriented Bourque stated \"With the Bourque Family Foundation, my wife and I wanted to create something where we could get the kids — and grandkids — involved.\"<ref>{{Cite web|title='O Captain! The foundation holds multiple annual events including the 7.7K road race in the spring, Bourques celebrity Golf tournament in summer and the Captain's Ball in honor of [[Pete Frates]] which takes place in September and the proceeds of the event go directly to [[ALS]] research.<ref name=\"Scene Magazine-2020\" /> Since its inception the charity has donated over $1.5 million to over 50 different charities.<ref>{{Cite web|title=CURE ALZHEIMER'S FUND RECEIVES DONATION FROM BOURQUE FAMILY FOUNDATION GOLF multiple organizations.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Men’s Hockey: Raffle Raises $2700 for Make-A-Wish Bourque lifts Bruins alumni to shootout victory |url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/sports/2015/12/31/ray-bourque-lifts-bruins-alumni-shootout-victory/zD2QmjXQvYMnwCLHtm0XmN/story.html|website=The Boston Globe|access-date=2025-11-28|language=en-US}}</ref>\n\nHe is also an avid golfer and is a member of the [[Salem, Massachusetts|Salem]] Country Club, in 2017 Bourque served as the Honorary Chairman of U.S. Senior Open Golf Championship in [[Peabody, Massachusetts|Peabody Massachusetts]].<ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RmssrrdIh54|title=Ray Bourque Honored To Be Chairman Of returned as the coach for the 2025 season but missed the playoffs going 1–3.<ref>{{Cite web|title=2025 Standings|url=https://www.3ice.com/2025-standings|website=www.3ice.com|access-date=2025-11-28}}</ref>\n\nIn 2025 he launched Bourque's Brew, a [[lager]] developed in partnership with Jack's Abby Craft Lagers and [[Legal Sea Foods]], with a portion of every can sold benefiting Bourque's charity.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Bourque's Brew {{!}} Bourque Family 1.JPG|thumb|The Aréna Raymond-Bourque in [[Saint-Laurent, Quebec|Saint-Laurent, QC]]]]\nDuring his time with the Boston Bruins Bourque received the [[King Clancy Memorial Trophy]], for his Involvement with numerous charities; most notably he served as the chairman for Boston's Floating Hospital for Infants and Children.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Fame |first=Hockey Hall of |title=HHOF {{!}} Silverware Trophy Tour |url=https://www.hhof.com/thecollection/silverwaretrophytour.html |access-date=2025-08-26 |website=Hockey Hall of Fame}}</ref>\n\nOn October 4, 2001, the Bruins held Ray Bourque night, where they retired his number 77 jersey, receiving a standing ovation from the sold out crowd. Then on November 24, 2001, the Avalanche also retired his number 77 jersey.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ESPN.com - NHL - Avs -- and Bruins -- to retire Bourque's No. 77 |url=https://www.espn.com/nhl/news/2001/0625/1218618.html |access-date=2025-08-26 |website=www.espn.com}}</ref>\n\nIn 2003 Bourque was awarded the [[Lester Patrick Trophy]] for his outstanding service to hockey in the United States.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Lester Patrick Trophy {{!}} NHL Records |url=https://records.nhl.com/awards/trophies/lester-patrick-trophy |access-date=2025-08-26 |website=records.nhl.com}}</ref>\n\nBourque was inducted into the [[Hockey Hall of Fame]] in 2004, his first season of eligibility. His uniform number 77 has been retired by both the Bruins and the Avalanche; he is one of only nine players whose jersey has been [[List of National Hockey League retired numbers|retired]] by more than one club. His birthplace of [[Saint-Laurent, Quebec|Saint-Laurent]] named the \"Aréna Raymond-Bourque\" in his honour.<ref name=\"Arena\">{{cite web |title=L'Agenda Spring-Summer 2008 |url=http://saintlaurent.ville.montreal.qc.ca/en/intro/publication/agenda/agendaen20080227.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110706201646/http://saintlaurent.ville.montreal.qc.ca/en/intro/publication/agenda/agendaen20080227.pdf |archive-date=July 6, 2011 |access-date=July 22, 2008 |df=mdy-all}}</ref> He was also inducted into the [[Quebec]] Sports Hall of Fame in 2004.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Québec Sports Hall of Fame (Le Panthéon des sports du Québec) |url=https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/quebec-sports-hall-of-fame-le-pantheon-des-sports-du-quebec |access-date=2025-08-26 |website=thecanadianencyclopedia.ca |language=en}}</ref>\n\nIn 2011 he was inducted into the [[List of members of Canada's Sports Hall of Fame|Canada Sports Hall of Fame]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Hall of Famers {{!}} Canada's Sports Hall of Fame {{!}} Home: Mobile |url=https://halloffamers.sportshall.ca/mobile.html#ray_bourque |access-date=2025-08-26 |website=halloffamers.sportshall.ca}}</ref>\n\nOn July 29, 2014 [[Endicott College|Endicott college]] held a groundbreaking ceremony unveiling their new hockey rink [[Raymond J. Bourque Arena]]. While Bourque did not have any formal connection to the school at the time, he is a 30-year resident of the [[North Shore (Massachusetts)|North Shore]] and has contributed to the local community inspiring them to name the arena after him.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dedication of Raymond J. Bourque Arena |url=https://www.endicott.edu/news-events/news/news-articles/2015/10/10-5bourque |access-date=2025-08-26 |website=Endicott College |language=en}}</ref> On May 16, 2015, Bourque served as the commencement speaker for the college and was also a recipient of an Honorary Doctor of Humane Letters.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hatch |first=Erin |date=2015-05-14 |title=Ray Bourque to Speak Endicott College Commencement |url=https://patch.com/massachusetts/beverly/endicott-college-commencement-may-16-0 |access-date=2025-12-26 |website=Beverly, MA Patch |language=en}}</ref>\n\nIn January 2017, he was part of the first group of players to be named one of the '[[100 Greatest NHL Players]]' in history by the National Hockey League.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-11-18 |title=NHL 100 Greatest Players {{!}} NHL.com |url=https://www.nhl.com/history/nhl-centennial/nhl-100-greatest-players |access-date=2025-08-26 |website=www.nhl.com |language=en}}</ref>\n\nIn 2019, Bourque received the NHL Alumni's Keith Magnuson Man of the Year Award in recognition of his charitable efforts, having raised over 20 million dollars in support of more than 1,000 different charities.<ref>{{Cite web  |date=2020-10-23 |title=2019 NHL Alumni Awards Gala Recap - NHL Alumni Association |url=https://nhlalumni.com/2020/10/23/2019-nhl-alumni-awards-gala-recap/ |access-date=2025-08-26 |language=en-US}}</ref>\n\nIn 2024 he was honored during the Bruins centennial celebrations being [[List of Boston Bruins award winners|Named to the Boston Bruins All-Centennial Team]].<ref name=\"www.nhl.com-2023\" />\n\n==Awards and achievements==\nBourque's exceptional talent as a player has led him to become one of the most honored players in hockey history. During his career, he was selected to thirteen NHL First Team (the most in history) and six Second Team All-Star squads, second in total in league history only to [[Gordie Howe]] and most amongst defencemen. He won the [[James Norris Memorial Trophy|Norris Trophy]] as the top defenceman in the league five times, fourth all-time after [[Bobby Orr]], [[Doug Harvey (ice hockey)|Doug Harvey]] and [[Nicklas Lidström]]. Among his numerous other records and honors are the following:\n\n===Career===\n* 11th all-time (4th among defencemen) in career games played with 1,612.\n* 4th all-time in career assists with 1,169; a record for defencemen.\n* 11th all-time in career points scored (1,579).\n* 1st in career points scored by a defenceman (1,579).\n* 1st in career goals scored by a defenceman (410).\n* Career leader in shots on goal by a defenceman (6,206).<ref>{{cite web|title= Alex Ovechkin passes Ray Bourque for most shots in NHL history|date=22 December 2022|url=https://russianmachineneverbreaks.com/2022/12/22/alex-ovechkin-passes-ray-bourque-for-most-shots-in-nhl-history/|access-date=22 December 2022}}</ref>\n* Is third in career  plus-minus with 528, behind [[Larry Robinson]] and Orr.<ref name=\"Plus-Minus\"/>\n* Bruins' all-time career leader in games played (1,518), assists (1,111) and points (1,506), also ranking fourth in goals and first in assists with a single team (any position).\n* 3rd all-time in playoff assists and 10th all-time in playoff points.\n* In 1998, three years before the end of his career, he was ranked number 14 on ''[[The Hockey News]]''' [[List of 100 greatest hockey players by The Hockey News|list of the one hundred greatest hockey players of all time]]. He was the highest-ranking player who had not yet won a Stanley Cup, the next highest being No. 38-ranked [[Marcel Dionne]].<ref name=\"The100\">{{cite book|last=Dryden|first=Steve|title=The Top 100 NHL Players of All-Time|publisher=McClelland & Stewart|year=1999|isbn=978-0-7710-4175-4}}</ref>\n*In 2017, he was named one of the [[100 Greatest NHL Players]].\n*[[List of Boston Bruins award winners|Named One of the Top 100 Best Bruins Players of all Time]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-09-12 |title=Bruins Announce \"Historic 100\" Ahead of All-Centennial Team Reveal {{!}} Boston Bruins winners|Named to the Boston Bruins All-Centennial Team]].<ref name=\"www.nhl.com-2023\">{{Cite web |date=2023-10-13 |title=Bruins Announce All-Centennial Team {{!}} Boston Bruins 2022}}\n{{Use Canadian English|date=June 2017}}\n{{Infobox ice hockey player\n| image = Mike Bossy 1978.JPG\n| caption = Bossy with the [[New York Islanders]] in 1978\n| position = [[Winger (ice hockey)|Right wing]]\n| shoots = Right\n| height_ft = 6\n| height_in = 0\n| weight_lb = 185\n| ntl_team = Canada\n| played_for = [[New York Islanders]]\n| birth_date = {{birth date|1957|1|22}}\n| birth_place = [[Montreal]], Quebec, Canada\n| death_date = {{death date and age|2022|4|15|1957|1|22}}\n| death_place = [[Rosemère]], Quebec, Canada\n| career_start = 1977\n| career_end = 1987\n| draft = 15th overall\n| draft_year = 1977\n| draft_team = [[New York Islanders]]\n| wha_draft = 44th overall\n| wha_draft_year = 1977\n| wha_draft_team = [[Indianapolis Racers]]\n| hall_of_fame = 1991\n}}\n\n'''Michael Dean Bossy''' (January 22, 1957{{Spnd}}April 15, 2022) was a Canadian professional [[ice hockey]] player with the [[New York Islanders]] of the [[National Hockey League]] (NHL). He spent his entire NHL career, which lasted from 1977 to 1987, with the Islanders, and was a crucial part of their four consecutive [[Stanley Cup]] championships in the early 1980s.\n\nBossy won the [[Calder Memorial Trophy]] in 1978 as NHL rookie of the year when he set the then-record for most goals by a rookie with 53. He won the [[Conn Smythe Trophy]] in the [[1982 Stanley Cup playoffs]] as the most valuable player and the [[Lady Byng Trophy]] for combining high quality play with sportsmanship three times. He led the NHL in goals twice and was second three other times. Bossy was voted to the league's first all-star team as right wing five times, with three further selections to the second all-star team. He is one of two players ([[Jack Darragh]] being the other) to score consecutive Stanley Cup-winning goals ([[1982 Stanley Cup Final|1982]] and [[1983 Stanley Cup Final|1983]]) and the only player to record four game-winning goals in one playoff series ([[1983 Stanley Cup playoffs|1983 Conference Final]]).\n\nBossy is the NHL's all-time leader in average goals scored per regular season game, holds the NHL's fourth-highest all-time average points scored per regular season game, and is the second of five players to score [[50 goals in 50 games]], being the first to accomplish this feat 36 years after [[Maurice Richard]]. He jointly holds the record for most 50-goal seasons with [[Wayne Gretzky]] and [[Alexander Ovechkin]] with nine, being the only player of the three whose 50-goal seasons ran consecutively.\n\nBossy was elected to the [[Hockey Hall of Fame]] in 1991, was named one of the [[100 Greatest NHL Players]] in history, and is considered one of the greatest goal scorers in NHL history.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Silverman |first=Steve |title=The NHL's 25 Best Pure Goal Scorers of All Time |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/1325852-the-nhls-25-best-pure-goal-scorers-of-all-time |access-date=2025-05-12 |website=bleacherreport.com |language=en}}</ref>\n\n==Early life==\nBossy was the fifth son among ten children,<ref name=\"phantom\" /> and grew up in a family of [[Detroit Red Wings]] fans in the parish of Saint-Alphonse,<ref name=\"Vecsey\">{{cite news |last1=Vecsey |first1=George |title=An Islander From Montreal |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1984/04/29/sports/sports-of-the-times-155800.html |website=The New York Times |access-date=April 28, 2020 |date=April 29, 1984}}</ref> in the [[Ahuntsic-Cartierville]] area of [[Montreal]].<ref name=\"cohen\">{{cite web |last1=Cohen |first1=Mike |title=Laval hockey icon Mike Bossy on the Islanders and TVA Sports |url=http://www.thesuburban.com/columnists/mike_cohen_cohen_chatter/laval-hockey-icon-mike-bossy-on-the-islanders-and-tva-sports/article_2bf892a1-2bad-59e7-a9f0-7cba49dad4f3.html |website=The Suburban Newspaper |access-date=April 29, 2020 |language=en |date=January 20, 2016}}</ref> Bossy attended St. Pius X Comprehensive High School and then [[Laurier Senior High School|Laval Catholic High School]].<ref name=\"cohen\" /> His mother Dorothy was English and French-Canadian, and his father Borden,<ref name=\"phantom\" /> who maintained a backyard ice rink at their apartment building, was Ukrainian.<ref name=\"Vecsey\" /> When he was 12 years old, Bossy broke a kneecap while competing in [[long jump]] at school, later developing chronic knee problems during his hockey career.<ref name=\"Goldaper\">{{cite news |last1=Goldaper |first1=Sam |title=SCOUTING; Bossy's Back To Business |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1984/08/30/sports/scouting-bossy-s-back-to-business.html |website=The New York Times |access-date=May 4, 2020 |date=August 30, 1984}}</ref>\n\nAs a youth, Bossy played in the 1969 [[Quebec International Pee-Wee Hockey Tournament]] with a [[minor ice hockey]] team from Montreal.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Dubé |first1=Kevin |title=Tournoi international pee-wee: Mike Bossy attire encore les foules |url=https://www.journaldequebec.com/2020/02/16/bossy-attire-encore-les-foules |website=Le Journal de Québec |access-date=April 28, 2020 |language=fr |date=February 16, 2020}}</ref> He started his junior career with the [[Laval Titan|Laval National]] of the [[Quebec Major Junior Hockey League]] at the age of 15. Despite scoring 309 goals in five seasons, he was considered \"not rugged enough\" and defensively weak by NHL scouts.<ref name=\"Valuable\">{{cite news |last1=Vecsey |first1=George |title=Valuable To Hockey |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1982/05/17/sports/valuable-to-hockey.html |website=The New York Times |access-date=April 28, 2020 |date=May 17, 1982}}</ref><ref name=\"himself\">{{cite web |title=This Man Is An Islander Unto Himself |url=https://vault.si.com/vault/1979/01/22/this-man-is-an-islander-unto-himself-the-fastest-draw-in-hockey-belongs-to-new-yorks-mike-bossy-who-already-has-35-goals |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211028084555/https://vault.si.com/vault/1979/01/22/this-man-is-an-islander-unto-himself-the-fastest-draw-in-hockey-belongs-to-new-yorks-mike-bossy-who-already-has-35-goals |url-status=dead |archive-date=October 28, 2021 |website=Sports Illustrated Vault {{!}} SI.com |publisher=Sports Illustrated |access-date=April 29, 2020 |language=en-us |date=January 22, 1979}}</ref> His total of 532 points remains a QMJHL record, and his 309 goals is the record for all of major junior.<ref>{{cite web |title=QMJHL Top 50 {{!}} #6 – Mike Bossy – LHJMQ |url=https://theqmjhl.ca/video/qmjhl-top-50-6-mike-bossy |website=theqmjhl.ca |publisher=QMJHL |access-date=April 28, 2020 |language=en-CA |date=April 3, 2013}}</ref> Bossy's #17 is retired by the [[Acadie–Bathurst Titan]], the current incarnation of the former Laval franchise.<ref>{{cite web |title=Retired Numbers |url=https://en.letitan.com/retired-numbers/ |website=en.letitan.com |publisher=Acadie-Bathurst Titan |access-date=April 29, 2020 |language=en-CA}}</ref>\n\n==Playing career==\n===Early stardom===\nBossy, who had averaged 77 goals per season in junior with Laval, was passed over by twelve teams in the [[1977 NHL amateur draft]], including the [[New York Rangers]] and [[Toronto Maple Leafs]], who each passed over him twice.<ref name=\"sabres\">{{cite web |last1=Harrington |first1=Mike |title=Buffalo sports' greatest what-ifs: What if Sabres had drafted Mike Bossy instead of Ric Seiling? |url=https://buffalonews.com/2020/04/04/buffalo-sabres-nhl-new-york-islanders-mike-bossy-ric-seiling/ |website=The Buffalo News |access-date=April 28, 2020 |language=en-us |date=April 4, 2020}}</ref> Toronto expected him to hold out for more than they wanted to pay, according to Bossy, while the Rangers opted for highly-ranked [[Lucien DeBlois]] and [[Ron Duguay]].<ref name=\"maven\">{{cite web |last1=Fischler |first1=Stan |title=Maven's Memories: How Mike Bossy Fell To The Islanders |url=https://www.nhl.com/islanders/news/mavens-memories-how-mike-bossy-fell-to-the-islanders/c-302932924 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190330154340/https://www.nhl.com/islanders/news/mavens-memories-how-mike-bossy-fell-to-the-islanders/c-302932924 |url-status=dead |archive-date=March 30, 2019 |website=NHL.com |access-date=April 28, 2020 |date=December 14, 2018}}</ref> Other teams passed for various reasons: the [[Buffalo Sabres]] took [[Ric Seiling]], preferring his checking ability,<ref name=\"sabres\" /> while the [[Cleveland Barons (NHL)|Cleveland Barons]], who had the fifth overall pick, passed when Bossy's agent [[Pierre Lacroix (ice hockey, born 1948)|Pierre Lacroix]] gave the Barons inflated salary requirements, prompting them to select [[Mike Crombeen]] instead.<ref name=\"maven\" /> [[Scotty Bowman]], coach of the [[Montreal Canadiens]], later regretted that Montreal had passed on Bossy;<ref name=\"himself\" /> Bowman and his assistant [[Claude Ruel]] had each been impressed with Bossy's play – and scoring – in person, but team scouts questioned his toughness and the Canadiens took [[Mark Napier (ice hockey)|Mark Napier]] with their first pick instead.<ref name=\"phantom\" /><ref name=\"dryden\">{{cite book |last1=Dryden |first1=Ken |title=Scotty: A Hockey Life Like No Other |date=2019 |publisher=McClelland & Stewart |isbn=978-0-7710-2751-2 |pages=222–225 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=R5qdDwAAQBAJ&q=bossy+world+hockey+association&pg=PA224 |access-date=April 28, 2020 |language=en}}</ref>\n\nThe New York Islanders picked Bossy with the 15th overall selection. General manager [[Bill Torrey]] was torn at first between taking Bossy and [[Dwight Foster (ice hockey)|Dwight Foster]]. Bossy was known as a scorer who could not check, while Foster, who had led the [[Ontario Hockey Association]] with 143 points, had a defensive aspect to his game.<ref name=\"maven\" /> Various stories exist explaining who persuaded Torrey to select Bossy. One common story credits coach [[Al Arbour]], who figured it would be easier to teach a scorer how to check.<ref name=\"Champions\">{{cite book |title=Champions: The Illustrated History of Hockey's Greatest Dynasties |last=Hunter |first=Douglas |year=1997 |publisher=Triumph Books |location=[[Chicago]] |isbn=1-57243-213-6}}</ref> Another credits Islanders scout Harry Saraceno,<ref name=\"McFarlane\">{{cite book |last1=McFarlane |first1=Brian |title=Real Stories from the Rink |date=2002 |publisher=Tundra Books |isbn=978-0-88776-604-6 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/realstoriesfromr0000mcfa/page/n77 66]-67 |url=https://archive.org/details/realstoriesfromr0000mcfa |url-access=registration |access-date=April 28, 2020 |language=en}}</ref> while another credits both Arbour and Saraceno.<ref name=\"maven\" />\n\n[[File:Mike Bossy 1978 (2).JPG|thumb|Bossy in 1978]]\nBossy replaced [[Billy Harris (ice hockey, born 1952)|Billy Harris]] on the Islanders' top line with [[Bryan Trottier]] and [[Clark Gillies]], creating a new combination that came to be known as [[The Trio Grande]].<ref name=\"unto\">{{cite web |last1=Kirshenbaum |first1=Jerry |title=Three Islanders Unto Themselves |url=https://vault.si.com/vault/1977/12/12/three-islanders-unto-themselves |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211014185739/https://vault.si.com/vault/1977/12/12/three-islanders-unto-themselves |url-status=dead |archive-date=October 14, 2021 |website=Sports Illustrated Vault {{!}} SI.com |publisher=Sports Illustrated |access-date=April 28, 2020 |language=en-us |date=December 12, 1977}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Keese |first=Parton |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1977/12/06/archives/islanders-hot-trio-grande-islanders-trio-grande-gillies-trottier.html |title=Islanders' Hot Trio Grande |work=New York Times |date=December 6, 1977 |access-date=October 30, 2011 |page=63}}</ref> He scored against [[Don Edwards (ice hockey)|Don Edwards]] of the [[Buffalo Sabres]] in his first career game, a 3–2 loss to Buffalo on October 13, 1977,<ref name=\"brophy\">{{cite book |last1=Brophy |first1=Mike |title=My First Goal: 50 players and the goal that marked the beginning of their NHL career |date=2011 |publisher=McClelland & Stewart |isbn=978-0-7710-1683-7 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/myfirstgoal50pla0000brop/page/n257 242]-246 |url=https://archive.org/details/myfirstgoal50pla0000brop |url-access=registration |access-date=May 1, 2020 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Islanders Bow To Sabres, 3-2, In Opener |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1977/10/14/archives/islanders-bow-to-sabres-32-in-opener.html |website=The New York Times |access-date=May 1, 2020 |date=October 14, 1977}}</ref> and by mid-November already had 11 goals.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Keese |first1=Parton |title=Bossy Gets 2 In Islander 6-0 Victory |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1977/11/14/archives/bossy-gets-2-in-islander-60-victory.html |website=The New York Times |access-date=May 1, 2020 |date=November 14, 1977}}</ref> On February 4, 1978, Bossy collected his first career [[hat trick]] in a 6–1 win against the [[Washington Capitals]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Keese |first1=Parton |title=Capitals Defeated – Trottier Excels |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1978/02/05/archives/capitals-defeated-trottier-excels-islander-lead-to-4-points.html |website=The New York Times |access-date=May 2, 2020 |date=February 5, 1978}}</ref> On February 25, Bossy scored his 45th goal of the season, to pass the previous rookie record of 44 held by [[Rick Martin]].<ref name=\"45th\">{{cite news |last1=Herman |first1=Robin |title=Islanders Win |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1978/02/26/archives/islanders-win-bossy-no-45-black-hawk-power-plays-fail-bossy-sets.html |website=The New York Times |access-date=May 1, 2020 |date=February 26, 1978}}</ref> Bossy had boldly told Bill Torrey before the season he would score 50 goals, and wound up with a total of 53,<ref name=\"McFarlane\" /> setting a rookie record which stood until broken by [[Teemu Selanne]] in 1993.<ref>{{cite web |title=People: Rookie with a record |url=https://archive.macleans.ca/article/1993/4/5/people |website=Maclean's |access-date=May 1, 2020 |page=46 |date=April 5, 1993 |volume=106 |issue=14 |archive-date=April 17, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220417192649/https://archive.macleans.ca/article/1993/4/5/people |url-status=dead }}</ref> Bossy additionally led the league with 25 powerplay goals.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Kirshenbaum |first1=Jerry |title=SHADOWERS, SNIPERS AND SUPERPESTS |url=https://vault.si.com/vault/1978/04/17/shadowers-snipers-and-superpests
