|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/star-phoenix-lady-bing-trophy/170122310/ |access-date=April 20, 2025 |publisher=Saskatoon Star-Phoenix |date=June 12, 1974|via=newspapers.com}}</ref>\n\nIn his final season with the Red Wings, Dionne scored 47 goals and 74 assists through 80 games. He received the 1975 Lady Byng Memorial Trophy after only accumulating 14 penalty minutes all season.<ref>{{cite news |title=Dionne Gets Byng Cup Over Bucyk |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-bay-city-times-dionne-gets-byng-cup/174937376/ |access-date=June 20, 2025 |publisher=The Bay City Times |date=June 18, 1975|via=newspapers.com}}</ref>\n\n====Los Angeles Kings (1975–1987)====\n[[File:Marcel Dionne Panini 1979.jpg|thumb|upright|Marcel Dionne with [[Canada men's national ice hockey team|Team Canada]] in 1979]]\nAs a free agent, Dionne and Eagleson fielded offers from the [[Edmonton Oilers]] of the WHA, [[Chicago Blackhawks]], [[Toronto Maple Leafs]], [[Los Angeles Kings]], Montreal Canadiens, [[St. Louis Blues]], Buffalo Sabres, and [[New York Islanders]]. However, his agent felt that the Red Wings were deterring offers as they wanted \"a couple of regulars and a super-star for Marcel.\"<ref>{{cite news |title=Dionne, Oilers still talk |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-daily-herald-tribune-dionne-oilers/170746600/ |access-date=April 20, 2025 |publisher=Grande Prairie Daily Herald-Tribune |date=May 27, 1975|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> Despite being offered a six-figure contract from the Oilers to join the WHA,<ref>{{cite news |title=Oilers Withdraw on Dionne |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-moncton-transcript-oilers-withdraw-o/170660923/ |access-date=April 19, 2025 |publisher=The Moncton Transcript |date=June 18, 1975|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> he agreed to a $1.5 million contract with the Kings.<ref>{{cite news |title=Kings' new superstar receives super salary |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/ventura-county-star-kings-new-superstar/170660995/ |access-date=April 19, 2025 |publisher=Ventura County Star |date=June 24, 1975|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> In an effort to avoid arbitration, the Kings offered the Red Wings [[Terry Harper]], [[Dan Maloney]], cash, and draft picks in exchange for Dionne.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Dulmage |first1=Jack |title=No suit this time |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-windsor-star-no-suit-this-time/170661086/ |access-date=April 20, 2025 |publisher=The Windsor Star |date=June 24, 1975|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> However, after Harper failed to appear at the Red Wings' training camp, an injunction was requested to prohibit Dionne from joining the Kings. A judge ultimately rejected the injunction, and Dionne was able to continue participating in the Kings' training camp.<ref>{{cite news |title=Wings may get player from Kings |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-saginaw-news-wings-may-get-player-fr/170700930/ |access-date=April 20, 2025 |publisher=The Saginaw News |date=October 8, 1975|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> Upon arriving in Los Angeles, head coach [[Bob Pulford]] assigned Dionne to a weight loss regimen which included skating extra laps with plastic sheets around his stomach.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Greenberg |first1=Alan |title=You Can Call Him Lou, You Can Call Him Fat Cat, You Can Call Him Tattoo |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-los-angeles-times-you-can-call-him-l/170148896/ |access-date=April 19, 2025 |publisher=The Los Angeles Times |date=April 4, 1980|via=newspapers.com}}</ref>\n\nWhile the Kings started the  [[1975–76 NHL season|1975–76 season]] with back-to-back losses, Dionne helped them win their next four consecutive games.<ref name=\"two\">{{cite news |last1=Larson |first1=Al |title=Dionne scores two, paces 5-3 Kings win |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/press-telegram-dionne-scores-two-paces/171108801/ |access-date=April 25, 2025 |publisher=Press-Telegram |date=October 19, 1974|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> He quickly accumulated five goals and six assists through six games<ref name=\"two\"/> while centering a line with [[Gene Carr (ice hockey)|Gene Carr]] and [[Mike Murphy (ice hockey, born 1950)|Mike Murphy]].<ref name=\"happy\">{{cite news |title=Dionne happy to be with Kings |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-times-transcript-dionne-happy-to-be/171109308/ |access-date=April 25, 2025 By the end of October, he had maintained an eight-game goal streak for 10 goals overall and 14 assists.<ref name=\"subdues\">{{cite news |title=Los Angeles Subdues Penguins 4-0 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/pittsburgh-post-gazette-los-angeles-subd/170762098/ |access-date=April 20, 2025 |publisher=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette |date=October 31, set a Kings franchise record with 11 shots on net in one game.<ref name=\"subdues\"/> While he found success offensively, he also received criticism from coaching staff and hockey pundits for his lack of defensive mindedness.<ref name=\"happy\"/><ref>{{cite news |last1=Hanley |first1=Bob |title=Kings now 14th in NHL defence 2025|via=newspapers.com}}</ref>\n\nDuring the offseason, Dionne was chosen to represent Team Canada in the inaugural [[1976 Canada Cup]]. Due to an overabundance of centremen, Canada's head coach [[Scotty Bowman]] chose to convert Dionne into a [[Winger (ice hockey)|right winger]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Morrissey |first1=Bob |title=Team man Dionne, unselfish Lafleur meet tonight as Canadiens play L.A. |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-gazette-team-man-dionne-unselfish-l/171154951/ |access-date=April 26, 2025 |publisher=Montreal Gazette |date=February 5, 1977|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> After witnessing Dionne's success in this position, Kings head coach Bob Pulford chose to keep him as a winger for the [[1976–77 NHL season|1976–77 season]]. In this new role, Dionne and his linemates [[Tom Williams (ice hockey, born 1940)|Tom Williams]] and [[Butch Goring]] became one of the highest-scoring lines that season.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Henderson |first1=Tom |title=Dionne a Right Wingers Now...Still Leads Kings in Goals |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/detroit-free-press-dionne-a-right-winger/171152329/ |access-date=April 26, 2025 |publisher=The Daily Breeze |date=January 19, 1977|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> Following the All-Star Game, Dionne recorded his second hat-trick of the season to reach 40 goals and tie the Kings' franchise record for most goals in a single season, which he had set the previous year.<ref>{{cite news |title=Dionne's trick paces Kings in 5-1 runaway at Buffalo |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/rutland-daily-herald-marcel-dionne-aims/171155299/ |access-date=April 26, 2025 |publisher=Independent |date=February 28, 1977|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> In March, Dionne broke the Kings' franchise goal record and reached 100 points for the second time in his career.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Davis |first1=Mike |title=Los Angeles tie Penguins, 3-3, with 7 seconds to spare |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-san-bernardino-county-sun-los-angele/171155779/ |access-date=April 26, 2025 |publisher=The San Bernardino County Sun |date=March 6, 1977|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> He finished the 1976–77 regular season with a career-high 53 goals and 69 assists for 122 points,<ref name=\"EP\"/> while playing mostly as a right winger.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Fisher |first1=Red |title=Marcel Dionne shift will muddle year-end voting |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-times-transcript-marcel-dionne-shift/171156058/ |access-date=April 26, 2025 |publisher=The Times-Transcript |date=March 28, 1977|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> In recognition of his efforts, Dionne became the first Los Angeles Kings player to be named to the [[1976–77 NHL season#All-Star teams|NHL All-Star team]] at the end of the season.<ref>{{cite news |title=Five Habs make the all-stars |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-moncton-transcript-five-habs-make-th/170744784/ |access-date=April 25, 2025 |publisher=The Moncton Transcript |date=June 7, 1977|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> He also received the 1977 Seven Crowns of Sports award as the NHL's most consistent player<ref>{{cite news |title=Marcel Dionne wins NHL award |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-lima-news-marcel-dionne-wins-nhl-awa/169652933/ |access-date=April 26, 2025 |publisher=The Lima News |date=April 27, 1977|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> and his second Lady Byng Memorial Trophy.<ref>{{cite news |title=Canadiens rake in trophies |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-morning-call-canadiens-rake-in-troph/169652464/ |access-date=April 26, 2025 |publisher=[[The Morning Call]] |date=June 9, 1977|via=newspapers.com}}</ref>\n\nDionne experienced a significant dip in his production level during the [[1977–78 NHL season|1977–78 season]]. King's general manager [[George Maguire (ice hockey)|George Maguire]] later stated that the team's experimenting with different linemates was to blame for Marcel's lack of scoring.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Merry |first1=Don |title=The Marcel Dionne Puzzle: Something Is Missing |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-los-angeles-times-the-marcel-dionne/169593934/ |access-date=June 20, 2025 |publisher=The Los Angeles Times |date=March 8, 1978|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> Due to an injury to captain [[Mike Murphy (ice hockey, born 1950)|Mike Murphy]] early in the season, Dionne was named the Kings' acting captain.<ref>{{cite news |title=Kings Notes |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/independent-kings-notes/174930008/ |access-date=June 20, 2025 |publisher=Independent |date=October 13, 1977|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> After the Kings acquired [[Syl Apps]] in a trade, coach Stewart moved Dionne to right wing and placed him on a line with Apps and [[Glenn Goldup]].<ref>{{cite news |title=It's a steal of a deal, says Dionne |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-morning-union-its-a-steal-of-a-deal/174905166/ |access-date=June 20, 2025 |publisher=The Morning Union |date=November 13, 1977|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> However, they did not spend an extended period of time together as Dionne suffered a shoulder injury on November 23.<ref>{{cite news |title=Kings 8, Black Hawks 3 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/goldsboro-news-argus-kings-8-black-hawk/171168044/ |access-date=June 19, 2025 |publisher=Goldsboro News-Argus |date=November 24, 1977|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> Over his two-week absence, Dionne continued to skate daily and practiced shooting the puck.<ref>{{cite news |title=Sports in Brief |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-millville-daily-sports-in-brief/174879555/ |access-date=June 19, 2025 |publisher=The Millville Daily |date=December 17, 1977|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> Despite describing his shoulder as sore,<ref>{{cite news |last1=Larson |first1=Al |title=Kings welcome Dionne's return |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/press-telegram-kings-welcome-dionnes-re/174879310/ |access-date=June 19, 2025 |publisher=Press-Telegram |date=December 15, 1977|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> he returned to the Kings' lineup on December 15 and recorded an assist that night against the Sabres.<ref>{{cite news |title=Dionne Returns |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-daily-herald-tribune-dionne-returns/174879775/ |access-date=June 19, 2025 |publisher=The Daily Herald-Tribune |date=December 16, 1977|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> Dionne also continued to ice his shoulder between periods and after each game.<ref>{{cite news |title=The other Marcel |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-standard-the-other-marcel/174931643/ |access-date=January 20, 2025 |publisher=St. Catharines Standard |date=January 13, 1978|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> Upon his return, the Kings moved Dionne between centerman and right wing alongside various linemates. He would occasionally center a line between [[Dave Taylor (ice hockey)|Dave Taylor]] and [[Danny Grant (ice hockey)|Danny Grant]], or serve as a winger to Apps.<ref>{{cite news |title=Marcel Dionne: a Falling Star? |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-los-angeles-times-marcel-dionne-a-f/171157591/ |access-date=June 20, 2025 |publisher=The Los Angeles Times |date=March 8, 1978|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> Despite his lack of consistency in the lineup, Dionne continued to lead the team in scoring.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Fink |first1=David |title=Pens Take Dead Aim on LA, Second |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/pittsburgh-post-gazette-pens-take-dead-a/171168425/ |access-date=June 20, 2025 |publisher=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette |date=February 18, 1978|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> He finished the regular season with 36 goals and helped the Kings qualify for the first round of the [[1978 Stanley Cup playoffs]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Here's how teams match up in playoffs |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/detroit-free-press-heres-how-teams-matc/174932877/ |access-date=June 20, 2025 |publisher=Detroit Free Press |date=April 11, 1978|via=newspapers.com}}</ref>\n\nDionne was named to Team Canada for the [[1978 Ice Hockey World Championships]] and was elected team captain the night before the tournament began. After losing their opening game to Team Finland, Dionne and Team Canada won their next three consecutive contests.<ref name=\"Coleman\">{{cite news |last1=Coleman |first1=Jim |title=Dionne a bit chubby but he is the leader |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-gazette-dionne-a-bit-chubby-but-he-i/171157524/ |access-date=June 20, 2025 |publisher=Montreal Gazette |date=May 2, 1978|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> Dionne finished the tournament with three goals and 12 points through nine games as Team Canada clinched third place.<ref>{{cite news |title=Bronze to Canada, gold to USSR |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-standard-bronze-to-canada-gold-to-u/174930657/ |access-date=June 20, 2025 |publisher=St. Catharines Standard |date=May 15, 1978|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> Despite placing fifth in total scoring and receiving 42 votes, Dionne was not named to the Tournament's All-Star Team.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Proudfoot|first1=Jim|title=No Canadians make tourney all-stars |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-toronto-star-no-canadians-make-tourn/174933388/ |access-date=June 20, 2025 |publisher=Toronto Star |date=May 15, 1978|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> \n\nDionne started the [[1978–79 NHL season|1978–79 season]] playing alongside Taylor and newly acquired winger [[Murray Wilson]].<ref name=\"Crown\">{{cite web |last1=Stephens |first1=Eric |title=Triple Crown Line still resonates with Kings fans |url=https://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=490696 |publisher=National Hockey League |access-date=June 20, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090901124508/https://www.nhl.com/ice/news.htm?id=490696 |archive-date=September 1, 2009 |date=August 30, 2009}}</ref> He accumulated five goals and 16 points through his first 10 games of the season, the best start of his career.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Pastin |first1=Bob |title=Kings' hopes center on Dionne |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-san-bernardino-county-sun-kings-hop/171157629/ |access-date=June 21, 2025 |publisher=The San Bernardino County Sun |date=November 7, 1978|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> Dionne continued to improve as the season progressed and set two new franchise recoreds by December. He became the first player in franchise history to record one goal in seven consecutive games and became the fastest Kings player to score 20 goals in a season.<ref>{{cite news |title=Dionne first player to hit 20-goal mark |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-standard-dionne-first-player-to-hit/174980374/ |access-date=June 21, 2025 |publisher=St. Catharines Standard |date=December 5, 1978|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> On January 13, 1979, coach [[Bob Berry (ice hockey)|Bob Berry]] put Dionne on a line with [[Charlie Simmer]] and Dave Taylor after the team scored one goal over three consecutive losses. The trio would soon be known as the \"[[Triple Crown Line]]\" due to their accomplishments.<ref name=\"Crown\"/> The trio remained a unit for six season until Simmer was traded to the Boston Bruins in 1984.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Strong |first1=Gregory |title=NHL 100: Legion of Doom highlights hockey's all-time iconic lines |url=https://www.cbc.ca/sports/hockey/nhl/nhl-100-iconic-lines-nhl-history-1.3992137 |publisher=Canadian Broadcasting Corporation |access-date=April 19, 2025 |date=February 21, 2017}}</ref> In their first game together on January 13 against the Detroit Red Wings,<ref name=\"Crown\"/> Dionne scored four goals for the fifth time in his career. His second goal of the game was also his 300th career NHL goal.<ref>{{cite news |title=Dionne nets four as L.A. Kings trim Detroit Red Wings |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-toronto-star-dionne-nets-four-as-la/174979656/ |access-date=June 21, 2025 |publisher=The Toronto Star |date=January 14, 1979|via=newspapers.com}}</ref>\n\nDionne signed a six-year, $3.6 million contract with the Kings before the start of the [[1980–81 NHL season|1980–81 season]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Dionne signs hefty contract |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-desert-sun-dionne-signs-hefty-contra/170692719/ |access-date=April 19, 2025 |publisher=The Desert Sun |date=August 21, 1980|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> On January 7, 1981, Dionne recorded two goals and an assist against the [[Hartford Whalers]] to become the fastest NHL player to reach 1,000 points. He accomplished this feat in 740 games, 83 games faster than the previous record holder [[Phil Esposito]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Marcel Dionne scores 1,000th point in NHL |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-york-dispatch-marcel-dionne-scores-1/169651565/ |access-date=April 26, 2025 |publisher=[[The York Dispatch]] |date=January 8, 1981|via=newspapers.com}}</ref>\n\nOn December 7, 1985, Dionne scored his 500th goal with the Kings organization to help the team beat the Winnipeg Jets.<ref>{{cite news |title=Dionne scores 500th as Kings win |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/camarillo-star-dionne-scores-500th-as-ki/169652039/ |access-date=April 19, 2025 |publisher=Camarillo Star |date=December 8, 1985|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> \n\nDionne was traded to the New York Rangers upon his request on March 10, 1987. The Kings sent Dionne, Jeff Crossman, and a third-round pick to the Rangers in exchange for [[Bobby Carpenter (ice hockey)|Bobby Carpenter]] and [[Tom Laidlaw]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Cart |first1=Julie |title=Dionne Asks for a Trade, Goes to Rangers |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-los-angeles-times-dionne-asks-for-a/170660546/ |access-date=April 19, 2025 |publisher=The Los Angeles Times |date=March 11, 1987|via=newspapers.com}}</ref>\n\n====New York Rangers (1987–1989)====\n[[File:Marcel Dionne 1987 (2).JPG|thumb|upright|Dionne with the [[New York Rangers]] in 1987]]\nDionne played his remaining two and a half seasons with the Rangers. \n\nOn November 7, 1987, playing against the Kings, he recorded his 1,000th career assist, becoming the third player to reach the mark in NHL history.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1987-11-08-sp-21367-story.html|website=The Los Angeles Times|date=November 8, 1987|title=Marcel Dionne Attains Milestone, but Kings Win It Before 16,005|first=Jerry|last=Crowe}}</ref> During his short tenure, the Rangers lost in the first round of the playoffs twice and missed the playoffs once.<ref>{{cite news| url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/hockey/nhl/news/2001/02/22/sayitaintso_kings/ | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010526183923/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/hockey/nhl/news/2001/02/22/sayitaintso_kings/ | url-status=dead | archive-date=May 26, 2001 | publisher=CNN Sports Illustrated| title=Say It Ain't So: Los Angeles Kings}}</ref>\n\nIn February 1989, Dionne and his agent asked [[Phil Esposito]] and coach [[Michel Bergeron]] to assign him to their minor league affiliate so he could get back into proper condition. They reluctantly agreed to the request when Dionne insisted that the move would not be degrading.<ref>{{cite news |title=Name in the news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-standard-name-in-the-news/170693239/ |access-date=June 21, 2025 |publisher=St. Catharines Standard |date=February 7, 1989|via=newspapers.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Dionne excited about playing in the minors |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-toronto-star-dionne-excited-about-pl/170678082/ |access-date=June 21, 2025 |publisher=The Toronto Star |date=February 11, 1989|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> Dionne was cut from the Rangers training camp roster ahead of the [[1989-1990 NHL season|1989–90 season]]. Rangers general manager [[Neil Smith (ice hockey)|Neil Smith]] said that the cut was a mutually agreed upon descison and they would explore the possibility of sending him to another team.<ref>{{cite news |title=Rangers cut Dionne |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-jersey-journal-rangers-cut-dionne/170677847/ |access-date=June 21, 2025 |publisher=The Jersey Journal |date=October 4, 1989|via=newspapers.com}}</ref>\n\n==Retirement and legacy==\nWhen Dionne retired, he was second all-time in goals and third all-time in assists and points. He was the first player to record seven 100-point seasons in NHL history, recording his seventh in the {{nhly|1982}} season. His eight 100-point seasons has only been surpassed by three other players in league history.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/stathead/tiny/Olazd|website=Stathead|title=Number of seasons player meets criteria, up to 1983-84, playing skater, in the regular season, requiring Points >= 100, sorted by descending instances.|access-date=June 2, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/stathead/tiny/QX5Xx|website=Stathead|access-date=June 2, 2026|title=Number of seasons player meets criteria, playing skater, in the regular season, requiring Points >= 100, sorted by descending instances.}}</ref> Success, alongside roster consistency, eluded Dionne in the playoffs, as he played for sixteen different coaches in his eighteen seasons in the NHL and he played in just 49 playoff games.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nhl.com/news/savour-every-moment-marcel-dionne-always-played-bigger-than-his-size-333630456|title='Savour Every Moment': Dionne always played bigger than his size|first=Dave|last=Stubbs|date=May 1, 2022|website=NHL.com|access-date=June 17, 2026}}</ref>\n\nDionne has maintained a large business and investment portfolio since his playing days, owning the Blue Line Diner in Niagara Falls, operating a sports memorabilia store in [[Buffalo, New York|Buffalo]] and buying and selling real estate.<ref name=\"edge\"/> On November 8, 1990, his number 16 jersey was retired by the Kings, the second player to be honored by the team.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1990-11-08-sp-5858-story.html|website=The Los Angeles Times|title=Kings Ready to Honor Dionne, Their Sweet 16|first=Bernie|last=Wilson|date=November 8, 1990}}</ref> He was the franchise leader in goals (550) and assists (757) until he was passed by [[Luc Robitaille]] and [[Anže Kopitar]], respectively.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/stathead/tiny/ly4oZ|access-date=June 2, 2026|website=Stathead|title=For combined seasons, playing skater, playing for the Los Angeles Kings, in the regular season, sorted by descending Goals.}}</ref>\n\nDionne was inducted into the [[Hockey Hall of Fame]] in 1992.<ref>{{cite news |title=Hockey |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-tribune-hockey/170037284/ |access-date=April 10, 2025 |publisher=Chicago Tribune |date=September 22, 1992|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> Prior to the start of the 1993–94 season, Dionne helped to create local interest in the [[ECHL]]'s newest franchise, the [[South Carolina Stingrays]]. With the help of some young players, Dionne gave an on-ice demonstration of the rules of hockey to the southern audience.<ref>{{cite book|first=Jon C.|last=Scott|title=Hockey Night in Dixie: Minor Pro Hockey in the American South|year=2006|publisher=Heritage House Publishing Company Ltd.|page=70|isbn=1-894974-21-2|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/hockeynightindix0000stot}}</ref> In 1998, he was ranked number 38 on ''[[The Hockey News]]''' list of the 100 Greatest Hockey Players, the highest-ranking player to have not won a Stanley Cup since 2001 when No. 14-ranked [[Ray Bourque]] won with the [[Colorado Avalanche]]. The Centre Civique arena in Drummondville was renamed [[Centre Marcel-Dionne]] in his honour in 1980.<ref>{{cite web |title=Modernisation du centre Marcel-Dionne |url=https://www.drummondville.ca/projets-majeurs/modernisation-centre-marcel-dionne/ |website=drummondville.ca |access-date=April 19, 2025}}</ref> In January 2004, Dionne was featured on a Canadian postage stamp. As part of the NHL All-Stars Collection, Dionne was immortalized along with five other All-Stars.<ref>Canada's Stamp Details, January to March 2004, Volume XIII, No. 1</ref>\n\n==Personal life==\nDionne married St. Catharines native Carol Gaudet in [[Troy, Michigan]] in April 1974.<ref>{{cite news |title=Wings' Marcel Dionne Marries |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/detroit-free-press-wings-marcel-dionne/170121886/ |access-date=April 11, 2025 |publisher=Detroit Free Press |date=April 6, 1974|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> They have three children together, two sons and one daughter.<ref name=\"Brown\">{{cite news |last1=Brown |first1=Ben |title=Marcel Dionne: Kings star tutors heirs to throne |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/usa-today-marcel-dionne-kings-star-tuto/170743951/ |access-date=April 20, 2025 |publisher=USA Today |date=February 21, 1987|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> After he retired, the Dionne's settled in Buffalo and his sons, Drew and Garrett, played Junior B hockey for the [[Niagara Falls Canucks]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Dakin |first1=Dan |title=Hockey in their blood |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/niagara-falls-review-hockey-in-their-blo/170747543/ |access-date=April 20, 2025 |publisher=Niagara Falls Review |date=November 10, 1999|via=newspapers.com}}</ref>\n\n==Career statistics==\n\n===Regular season and playoffs===\n<small>'''Bold''' indicates led league</small>\n{| border=\"0\" cellpadding=\"1\" cellspacing=\"0\" style=\"text-align:center; width:60em;\"\n|- bgcolor=\"#e0e0e0\"\n! colspan=\"3\" bgcolor=\"#ffffff\"|\n! rowspan=\"100\" bgcolor=\"#ffffff\"|\n! colspan=\"5\"|[[Regular season]]\n! rowspan=\"100\" bgcolor=\"#ffffff\"|\n! colspan=\"5\"|[[Playoffs]]\n|- bgcolor=\"#e0e0e0\"\n! Pearson Award winners]]\n[[Category:Lester Patrick Trophy recipients]]\n[[Category:Los Angeles Kings players]]\n[[Category:National Hockey League All-Stars]]\n[[Category:NHL first-round draft picks]]\n[[Category:National Hockey League players with retired numbers]]\n[[Category:New York Rangers players]]\n[[Category:St. Catharines Black Hawks players]]\n[[Category:20th-century Canadian sportsmen]]"}}}]},{"pageid":586750,"ns":0,"title":"Paul Coffey","revisions":[{"slots":{"main":{"contentmodel":"wikitext","contentformat":"text/x-wiki","content":"{{Short description|Canadian ice hockey player (born 1961)}}\n{{other uses}}\n{{Use Canadian English|date=August 2017}}\n{{Use mdy dates|date=March 2023}}\n{{Infobox ice hockey player\n| hall_of_fame = 2004\n| image = Paul Coffey in 2007.jpg\n| caption = Coffey in 2007\n| birth_date = {{birth date and age|1961|6|1}}\n| birth_place = [[Weston, Toronto|Weston, Ontario]], Canada\n| height_ft = 6\n| height_in = 0\n| weight_lb = 205\n| position = [[Defenceman|Defence]]\n| shoots = Left\n| played_for = [[Edmonton Oilers]]<br />[[Pittsburgh Penguins]]<br />[[Los Angeles Kings]]<br />[[Detroit Red Wings]]<br />[[Hartford Whalers]]<br />[[Philadelphia Flyers]]<br />[[Chicago Blackhawks]]<br />[[Carolina Hurricanes]]<br />[[Boston Bruins]]\n| ntl_team = CAN\n| draft = 6th overall\n| draft_year = 1980\n| draft_team = [[Edmonton Oilers]]\n| career_start = 1980\n| career_end = 2001\n| website = {{URL|https://paulcoffey.ca/}}\n}}\n'''Paul Patrick Coffey''' (born June 1, 1961) is a Canadian former professional [[ice hockey]] [[defenceman]] who played for nine teams over 21 seasons in the [[National Hockey League]] (NHL) from 1980 to 2000. Coffey ranks second all-time among NHL defencemen in [[Goal (ice hockey)|goals]], [[Assist (ice hockey)|assist]]s, and [[Point (ice hockey)|point]]s, behind only [[Ray Bourque]]. He won the [[James Norris Memorial Trophy]] as the NHL's best defenceman three times and was voted to eight end-of-season All-Star teams (four first-team and four second-team). He holds the record for the most goals by a defenceman in one season, 48 in 1985–86, and is the only defenceman to have scored 40 goals more than once, also doing it in 1983–84. He is also one of two defencemen to score 100 points in a season more than once, as he did it five times; [[Bobby Orr]] did it six times. Coffey holds or shares 33 NHL records in the regular season and playoffs.\n\nDuring his NHL career, he played for the [[Edmonton Oilers]], [[Pittsburgh Penguins]], [[Los Angeles Kings]], [[Detroit Red Wings]], [[Hartford Whalers]], [[Philadelphia Flyers]], [[Carolina Hurricanes]], [[Chicago Blackhawks]], and [[Boston Bruins]]. He is a four-time [[Stanley Cup]] champion, winning three times with Edmonton and a fourth with Pittsburgh.\n\nCoffey was born in [[Weston, Toronto|Weston]], [[Ontario]], and grew up in [[Malton, Ontario]]. The city of [[Mississauga]] renamed Malton Arena to Paul Coffey Arena and Wildwood Park to Paul Coffey Park in a ceremony on September 23, 2016.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Colpitts|first1=Iann|title=NHL great Coffey humbled by arena renaming ceremony|url=http://www.mississauga.com/news-story/6879018-nhl-great-coffey-humbled-by-arena-renaming-ceremony/|publisher=The Mississauga News|date=September 26, 2016}}</ref> In 2017, Coffey was named one of the [[100 Greatest NHL Players]] in history.<ref>{{cite web|title=100 Greatest NHL Players|url=https://www.nhl.com/history/nhl-centennial/nhl-100-greatest-players|publisher=National Hockey League|access-date=January 27, 2017|date=January 27, 2017}}</ref>\n\n==Playing career==\n===Minor league hockey===\nIn his youth, Coffey played in the 1974 [[Quebec International Pee-Wee Hockey Tournament]] with a [[minor ice hockey]] team from [[Mississauga]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.publicationsports.com/ressources/files/439/Joueurs_Pro.pdf|title=Pee-Wee players who have reached NHL or WHA|year=2018|website=Quebec International Pee-Wee Hockey Tournament|access-date=January 11, 2019|archive-date=March 6, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190306085544/https://www.publicationsports.com/ressources/files/439/Joueurs_Pro.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>\n\n===Edmonton Oilers===\n[[File:PaulCoffey.png|thumb|left|Coffey with the [[Edmonton Oilers]] {{c.|1984}}]]\nCoffey was drafted sixth overall by the [[Edmonton Oilers]] in the [[1980 NHL entry draft]]. In the [[1981–82 NHL season|1981–82 season]] he scored 89 points and was named a second-team [[NHL All-Star team|NHL All-Star]]. In the Oilers' first [[Stanley Cup]]-[[1983–84 NHL season|winning season]], 1983–84, he became only the second defenceman in NHL history to score 40 goals in a season, and added 86 assists to finish second in point scoring. He won his first [[James Norris Memorial Trophy]] in [[1984–85 NHL season|1984–85]] while posting 37 goals and 121 points. On December 26, 1984, in a game against the [[Calgary Flames]], Coffey became the last defenceman in the 20th century to score four goals in one game.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.flyershistory.com/cgi-bin/poboxscore.cgi?H19840358 |title=Flyers History - Philadelphia Flyer Game Summary |access-date=October 31, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150504100413/http://www.flyershistory.com/cgi-bin/poboxscore.cgi?H19840358 |archive-date=May 4, 2015 }}</ref> Coffey went on to post a historic post-season in the 1985 playoffs, setting records for most goals (12), assists (25), and points (37) in one playoff year by a defenceman on the way to another Stanley Cup. In the [[1985–86 NHL season|1985–86]] season, where he was awarded his second Norris Trophy, Coffey scored 48 goals, which broke [[Bobby Orr]]'s record for regular season goals by a defenceman (46 goals in [[1974–75 NHL season|1974–75]]), and Coffey's 138 regular season points was second only to Orr (139 points in [[1970–71 NHL season|1970–71]]) among defencemen.<ref>[http://www.legendsofhockey.net/LegendsOfHockey/jsp/LegendsMember.jsp?mem=p200402&type=Player&page=bio&list=ByName#photo Legends of Hockey - The Legends - Honoured Player - Coffey, Paul - Biography<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref>\n\nCoffey helped Edmonton to a third Cup in [[1986–87 NHL season|1986–87]], but the deciding game seven of that year's [[1987 Stanley Cup Final|Stanley Cup Final]] against the [[Philadelphia Flyers]] would be his last in an Oiler uniform. Coffey had two years remaining on a contract that paid him a reported $320,000 a year, but [[holdout (sports)|held out]] at the beginning of the [[1987–88 NHL season|1987–88 season]], wanting the contract renegotiated to pay him $800,000 a year. Team owner [[Peter Pocklington]] refused to do so, and offended Coffey by suggesting he lacked courage when playing; Coffey vowed never to put on an Edmonton uniform again and demanded a trade.<ref>{{cite web|last=Crowe|first=Jerry|title=Coffey Wants Trade After Oilers Owner Questions Courage|work=[[Los Angeles Times]]|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/405077580/?fcfToken=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJmcmVlLXZpZXctaWQiOjQwNTA3NzU4MCwiaWF0IjoxNzA2NTc2OTI0LCJleHAiOjE3MDY2NjMzMjR9.N5IFN-91OLVrF7e6kwywO0VFV3BdFCIA7QM9Do1TMp0|date=1987-10-28|accessdate=2024-01-29}}</ref> On November 24, 1987, the Oilers traded Coffey, along with [[Dave Hunter]] and [[Wayne Van Dorp]], to the [[Pittsburgh Penguins]] for [[Craig Simpson]], [[Dave Hannan]], [[Moe Mantha, Jr.|Moe Mantha]], and [[Chris Joseph (ice hockey)|Chris Joseph]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Oilers trade Coffey to Penguins|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/1987/11/25/oilers-trade-coffey-to-penguins/6acd6fc9-e3f4-415f-bf29-0dc60860c92f/|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=1987-11-24|accessdate=2024-01-29}}</ref>\n\n===Pittsburgh Penguins===\n[[File:PaulCoffey1989.png|thumb|Coffey with the Penguins in 1989|282x282px]]\nAs the Penguins' [[Rod Buskas]] was already wearing uniform number 7, Coffey agreed to change his uniform number from 7 to 77. Coffey would wear 77 for most of the rest of his career until his final season in Boston, where he wore 74. Coffey played four and a half seasons with Pittsburgh. On December 22, 1990, Coffey became the second defenceman after [[Denis Potvin]] to record 1,000 points, doing so in a record-breaking 770 games. In [[1990–91 NHL season|1990–91]], Coffey helped Pittsburgh to win their [[1991 Stanley Cup Final|first Stanley Cup]], which was also his fourth Cup, defeating the [[Minnesota North Stars]] in six games. During the 1991-92 season, the Penguins were coached by [[Scotty Bowman]], who had stepped in after head coach [[Bob Johnson (ice hockey, born 1931)|Bob Johnson]] took a leave of absence for cancer treatment. Coffey passed [[Denis Potvin]] to become the career leader in goals, assists, and points by a defenceman, with Coffey leading these categories until the final season of his career. After 54 games, with Pittsburgh struggling despite being the defending Cup champions, Coffey's large salary made him expendable so he was traded to the [[Los Angeles Kings]]. In Los Angeles, he was reunited with former Oilers teammates [[Wayne Gretzky]] and [[Jari Kurri]] for parts of two seasons.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hockeydb.com/ihdb/stats/pdisplay.php?pid=1042|title=Paul Coffey Hockey Stats and Profile at hockeydb.com|website=www.hockeydb.com}}</ref>\n\n===Detroit Red Wings===\nHaving played just 10 games with the Kings in the 1992-93 season, he was traded to the [[Detroit Red Wings]], where he played for three and a half seasons. Coffey was reunited with Scotty Bowman, who became the head coach of the Red Wings for 1993-94. In the lock-out shortened [[1994–95 NHL season]], Coffey led his team in scoring for the only time in his entire career and was awarded the Norris Trophy for the third time, as the Red Wings won the [[Presidents' Trophy]] for their first-place regular season finish. In the 1995 playoffs, he led all defencemen in scoring while helping Detroit to the Stanley Cup Finals. The Red Wings, however, were swept by the [[New Jersey Devils]] in four games. Coffey would then help the Red Wings to 62 regular season wins the following year as they clinched their second consecutive Presidents' Trophy, but they were upset by the [[Colorado Avalanche]] in the Western Conference Finals. During Game 1 of that series, Coffey scored two goals but also accidentally scored on his own net after Colorado's [[Stephane Yelle]] attempted to pass the puck into the slot, but it instead ended up on Coffey's stick.\n\n===Hartford Whalers and Philadelphia Flyers===\nAfter a falling-out with Red Wings head coach [[Scotty Bowman]], Coffey was traded to the [[Hartford Whalers]] at the start of the [[1996–97 NHL season|1996–97 season]] as part of a package to acquire [[Brendan Shanahan]] – a move that Coffey was unhappy with since the Whalers were a non-contending team.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.vintagedetroit.com/blog/2013/02/09/the-trade-that-changed-the-wings-but-almost-didnt-happen/|title=The trade that changed the Wings – but almost didn't happen|website=www.vintagedetroit.com |date=February 9, 2013 }}</ref> Coffey only played 20 games for the Whalers before engineering a trade to the Philadelphia Flyers. He played for the Flyers for a season and a half. In the 1997 Stanley Cup playoffs, Coffey's experience helped the Flyers get past the Pittsburgh Penguins (playing against old teammate [[Mario Lemieux]]) and [[New York Rangers]] (featuring former Oilers teammates [[Wayne Gretzky]] and [[Mark Messier]]) to reach [[1997 Stanley Cup Final]], which was also Coffey's seventh appearance in the Finals. In the Finals series against his former team, Detroit, Coffey was on the ice for six of Detroit's goals and was in the penalty box for a seventh when the Flyers conceded a power-play goal, having no points and being minus-2 and minus-3 in the first two games. Bowman had directed Detroit's players to specifically go after Coffey as a pressure point in the Flyers roster; a hit from [[Darren McCarty]] in game two left Coffey sidelined for the rest of the series with a concussion.<ref>[http://www.nydailynews.com/archives/sports/1997/06/04/1997-06-04_flyers_can_t_stomach_weak_an.html]{{dead link|date=December 2017|bot=InternetArchiveBot|fix-attempted=yes}}</ref>\n\n===Chicago Blackhawks, Carolina Hurricanes and Boston Bruins===\n[[File:Paul Coffey.jpg|thumb|left|upright|Coffey in 2009.]]\nAfter 10 games with the [[Chicago Blackhawks]], where he only picked up 4 assists and had a -6 rating, Coffey was traded to the [[Carolina Hurricanes]] (the relocated Hartford Whalers, whom Coffey had briefly played for in the 1996–97) for the rest of the 1998-99 season, where he played one and a half seasons. He had a slow start in the 1999-2000 season but finished strong with one of his best seasons in years.<ref name=\"The Coffey wasn't fresh\">{{cite web |last1=Colageo |first1=Mick |title=The Coffey wasn't fresh |url=https://www.southcoasttoday.com/story/sports/2000/12/06/the-coffey-wasn-t-fresh/50468553007/ |publisher=South Coast Today |access-date=7 March 2026}}</ref>\n\nAs a free agent in the off-season of 2000, Coffey signed a two-year $4 million contract with the [[Boston Bruins]], intending to fill the void left by [[Ray Bourque]], who had been traded away to the [[Colorado Avalanche]] in spring 2000. This was also the last free agent acquisition by [[Harry Sinden]], who relinquished his title as Bruins general manager early in the 2000-01 season. While Coffey wore number 77 since leaving the Edmonton Oilers, he wore 74 since Bourque had long worn 77 with the Bruins. Coffey missed 9 games due to injury and only appeared in 18 games, where he was unable to make defensive stops without being penalized, while also only getting four assists and failed to improve the Bruins' powerplay. After playing what would be his final NHL game at the [[Atlanta Thrashers]] on December 4, 2000, Coffey was waived by the Bruins. After his stint with the Bruins was finished, Coffey reported turned down two offers to return to the NHL.<ref>{{cite web |title=Coffey calls it quits |url=https://www.cbc.ca/sports/hockey/coffey-calls-it-quits-1.293559 |publisher=CBC Sports |access-date=27 March 2026}}</ref> That season, Bourque passed his career goal, assist, and point records, and Bourque and Coffey both retired after the 2000–01 season.<ref>{{cite web |title=Coffey waived by Bruins |url=https://www.cbc.ca/sports/hockey/coffey-waived-by-bruins-1.217017 |publisher=CBC |access-date=7 March 2026}}</ref><ref name=\"The Coffey wasn't fresh\"/>\n\nCoffey finished his NHL career with 396 goals, 1135 assists, and 1531 points, and remains second only to Bourque in all-time career scoring by a defenceman. Coffey, however, averaged more points per game than did Bourque, having played 203 fewer games but lagging by only 48 points.\n\nCoffey was traded seven times during his NHL career, with four of the teams that traded Coffey away ending up reaching the Stanley Cup Finals in that season or the subsequent season (Edmonton in 1988, Pittsburgh in 1992, Los Angeles in 1993, Detroit in 1997). Philadelphia did reach the 1997 Stanley Cup Finals in the same season that they acquired Coffey in a trade. Coffey was voted into the [[Hockey Hall of Fame]] in 2004, his first year of eligibility, and the Edmonton Oilers retired his uniform number 7 in 2005.\n\n==Post-playing career==\n[[File:Mario Lemieux and Paul Coffey 2010 Alumni Game 2010-12-31.JPG|thumb|Coffey skated with former [[Pittsburgh Penguins]] teammate [[Mario Lemieux]] in the [[2011 NHL Winter Classic|NHL Legends Game]], December 31, 2010.]]\nWhile coaching a game for the Toronto Marlboros midget 'AAA' team in February 2014, Coffey was assessed a gross misconduct penalty for a \"discriminatory slur\".<ref name=\":0\" /> The [[Greater Toronto Hockey League]] investigated the misconduct penalty and Coffey was handed a three-game suspension.<ref name=\":0\">{{cite web|last1=Campbell|first1=Ken|title=Hall of Famer Paul Coffey in hot water after 'discriminatory slur'|url=https://thehockeynews.com/news/news/hall-of-famer-coffey-in-hot-water-after-discriminatory-slur|publisher=thehockeynews.com|access-date=February 20, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150220202322/http://www.thehockeynews.com/blog/hall-of-famer-coffey-in-hot-water-after-discriminatory-slur/|archive-date=February 20, 2015|url-status=live}}</ref> Coffey is a co-owner of the [[Ontario Junior Hockey League|OJHL]]'s [[Pickering Panthers]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://pickeringpanthers.pointstreaksites.com/view/pickeringpanthers|title=Pickering Panthers Jr.A - OJHL Pickering Panthers|website=pickeringpanthers.pointstreaksites.com}}</ref>\n\nOn November 12, 2023, Coffey returned to the Edmonton Oilers as the assistant coach. For the next two seasons, the Oilers would make the [[Stanley Cup Final]], losing both times to the [[Florida Panthers]]. Prior to the beginning of the [[2025–26 NHL season|2025–26 season]], the Oilers announced that Coffey would be stepping back from coaching to resume his duties as an [[adviser]] for the team. Coffey returned to his coaching job in February 2026 during the [[Olympic Games|Olympic]] break, following continued struggles by the team.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sportsnet.ca/nhl/article/paul-coffey-returning-to-oilers-as-assistant-coach/|title=Paul Coffey returning to Oilers' bench as assistant coach|website=sportsnet.ca}}</ref>\n\n==Personal life==\nCoffey was the owner of a car dealership in [[Bolton, Ontario]]. Coffey and his wife have three children.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Wheeler |first=Scott |date=2023-01-17 |title=NHL99: Paul Coffey, after building a life away from the game, has returned to it |url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/3953183/2023/01/17/nhl99-paul-coffey/ |access-date=2026-02-18 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>\n\n==Awards==\n* Named to the of the 2016 inductees into [[Legends Row: Mississauga Walk of Fame]].\n\n==NHL records==\n* Most goals by a defenceman regular season and playoffs combined – 455\n\n===Regular season===\n* Most goals in one season by a defenceman – 48 in 1985–86\n* Most shorthanded goals in one season by a defenceman – 9 in 1985–86\n* Most assists in one game by a defenceman – 6 on March 14, 1986\n* Most points in one game by a defenceman – 8 on March 14, 1986 (2 goals, 6 assists; shared with [[Tom Bladon]] 4 goals, 4 assists)\n* Most seasons leading the league in scoring by a defenceman – 8\n* Fastest Marie Greyhounds players]]\n[[Category:Stanley Cup champions]]"}}}]},{"pageid":587844,"ns":0,"title":"Bryan Trottier","revisions":[{"slots":{"main":{"contentmodel":"wikitext","contentformat":"text/x-wiki","content":"{{Short description|Canadian-American ice hockey player and coach (born 1956)}}\n{{Use Canadian English|date=January 2024}}\n{{Use mdy dates|date=June 2022}}\n{{Infobox ice hockey biography\n| name = Bryan Trottier\n| hall_of_fame = 1997\n| image = BryanTrottier.jpg\n| image_size = \n| caption = Trottier with the [[New York Islanders]] in 1985\n| birth_date = {{birth date and age|1956|7|17}}\n| birth_place = [[Val Marie]], Saskatchewan, Canada\n| height_ft = 5\n| height_in = 11\n| weight_lb = 195\n| position = [[Centre (ice hockey)|Centre]]\n| shoots = Left\n| played_for = [[New York Islanders]]<br />[[Pittsburgh Penguins]]\n| ntl_team = CAN\n| ntl_team_2 = USA\n| draft = 22nd overall\n| draft_year = 1974\n| draft_team = [[New York Islanders]]\n| wha_draft = 18th overall\n| wha_draft_year = 1974\n| wha_draft_team = [[Cincinnati Stingers]]\n| career_start = 1975\n| career_end = 1992<br />1993–1994\n}}\n'''Bryan John Trottier''' (born July 17, 1956)<ref>{{cite web| title =Legends of Hockey – The Legends – Honoured Player – Trottier, Bryan| work=Hockey Hall of Fame and Museum | publisher=The Learning Edge Corporation | date = 2001–2007 | url = http://www.legendsofhockey.net/LegendsOfHockey/jsp/LegendsMember.jsp?type=Player&mem=P199702&list=ByName#photo| access-date = 2007-11-15}}</ref> is a Canadian and American former professional [[ice hockey]] [[centre (ice hockey)|centre]] who played 18 seasons in the [[National Hockey League]] (NHL) for the [[New York Islanders]] and [[Pittsburgh Penguins]]. \n\nTrottier was drafted with the 22nd pick in 1974 by the Islanders and made the opening lineup in 1975, which saw him set a rookie record for points (95) and win the [[Calder Memorial Trophy]] for his play. In the {{nhly|1978}} season, he had a career-high 134 points; on December 23, he became the first Islander to [[List of players with five or more goals in an NHL game#Players who scored five or more goals in multiple games|score five goals in a game]] and set an NHL record that same night when he recorded the most [[Point (ice hockey)|points]] in a single period with six (four goals and two assists); the record has been matched but never broken.<ref>{{Cite web |title=NHL Records |url=https://records.nhl.com/records/skater-records/points/most-points-one-period |access-date=2024-01-24 |website=records.nhl.com}}</ref> In that season, he won the [[Art Ross Trophy]] as the leading-point scorer and also won the [[Hart Memorial Trophy]] for his valuable play; he was the first (and so far only) Islander to win both awards in franchise history. He won the [[Conn Smythe Trophy]] for his play in the [[1980 Stanley Cup playoffs]] with 29 points in 21 games as the Islanders won the first of four consecutive [[Stanley Cup]] championships. In a game on February 13 of the {{nhly|1981}} season, he recorded a five-goal game to become the [[List of players with five or more goals in an NHL game#Players who scored five or more goals in multiple games|seventh NHL player with multiple five-goal games]]. \n\nHe recorded his 500th goal in 1990, becoming the 15th player to reach the mark in NHL history. He was bought out of his contract by the Islanders after the season and subsequently signed as a free agent with Pittsburgh, where he provided veteran leadership as the Penguins won the Stanley Cup in [[1991 Stanley Cup Final|1991]] and [[1992 Stanley Cup Final|1992]]. He initially retired in 1992 but returned for one more season with Pittsburgh before finally retiring in 1994. One of the best Islanders in franchise history, Trottier recorded 524 goals and 901 assists for 1,425 points in over 1,200 games; in the playoffs, he recorded 182 points in 221 games played. He was inducted into the [[Hockey Hall of Fame]] in 1997 and his jersey was retired by the Islanders in 2001. In 2017, Trottier was named one of the \"[[100 Greatest NHL Players]]\" in history.<ref>{{cite web|title=100 Greatest NHL Players|url=https://www.nhl.com/history/nhl-centennial/nhl-100-greatest-players|website=NHL.com|access-date=January 27, 2017|date=January 27, 2017}}</ref>\n\nTrottier served as an assistant coach with the Penguins from 1993 to 1997. He became a coach with the [[Colorado Avalanche]] in 1998, where he was on the staff when the Avalanche won the Cup in [[2001 Stanley Cup Final|2001]] to give Trottier a seventh championship. He served as coach of the [[New York Rangers]] in 2002, where he coached for 54 games before being fired. He worked in the front office for the Islanders beginning in 2006 before being hired as an assistant coach with the [[Buffalo Sabres]] in 2014, where he coached the {{nhly|2014}} season.<ref name=\"Buffalo asst\">{{cite web|title=SABRES ADD FOUR TO NOLAN'S COACHING STAFF|url=http://sabres.nhl.com/club/news.htm?id=727804&navid=DL|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140810043700/http://sabres.nhl.com/club/news.htm?id=727804&navid=DL|url-status=dead|archive-date=August 10, 2014|publisher=Buffalo Sabres|access-date=August 4, 2014|date=August 4, 2014}}</ref> \n\n==Early life==\nTrottier grew up in the town of [[Val Marie, Saskatchewan]], Canada, located between [[Swift Current, Saskatchewan|Swift Current]] and the [[Montana]] border with his parents and four siblings.<ref name=\"Hall of Fame Article\">{{cite web|url=https://www.hhof.com/htmlstcjournal/exSCJ05_11.shtml|title=Bryan Trottier's journal|website=Hockey Hall of Fame|publisher=Kevin Shea|last1=Shea|first1=Kevin|access-date=March 23, 2017}}</ref> His father was of [[Cree]] [[Métis]] descent, and his mother is of [[Irish Canadians|Irish]] origin.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nhl.com/news/bryan-trottier-discusses-indigenous-upbringing-312326514|title=Trottier shares thoughts on indigenous upbringing with NHL.com|website=NHL.com|language=en-US|access-date=2019-12-10}}</ref> He experienced [[racism]] as a child, but his parents encouraged him to be proud of his native heritage.<ref name=\":0\">{{Cite web |last=Barnsley |first=Paul |title=Hockey all-time great is proud of his Aboriginal heritage |url=http://www.ammsa.com/sites/default/files/html-pages/old-site/achieve/AA98-B.Trottier.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170324084409/http://www.ammsa.com/sites/default/files/html-pages/old-site/achieve/AA98-B.Trottier.html |archive-date=March 24, 2017 |website=Wind Speaker}}</ref> Trottier has one older sister, Carol, and three younger siblings, Kathy, Monty and [[Rocky Trottier|Rocky]]. Monty played professional minor league hockey, and Rocky played in 38 games for the [[New Jersey Devils]].<ref name=\"Hall of Fame Article\" />\n\nGrowing up in the 1960s, Trottier wanted to be like his idol [[Jean Béliveau]]. When he was learning to skate, his father would clear out the dam on the creek across their home with a machete, to create a surface to practice on.<ref name=\"Letter to My Younger Self\">{{cite web|url=https://www.theplayerstribune.com/articles/bryan-trottier-nhl-letter-to-my-younger-self|title=Letter to My Younger Self|website=The Player's Tribune|publisher=Player's Tribune|last1=Trottier|first1=Bryan|date=November 23, 2015 |access-date=March 31, 2021}}</ref>\n\nAs a child, Trottier played for the Climax Hockey Team in [[Climax, Saskatchewan]]. He joined the [[Swift Current Broncos]] in 1972. It was with the Broncos that he met [[Tiger Williams]], who he credited with teaching key lessons (such as fighting) to Trottier. In one instance, a homesick Trottier was debating on quitting hockey, even planning to go back to school after having arrived back home for Christmas. Williams arrived at his house and insisted on him coming back with to the Broncos, which worked out for Trottier, who credited him as making hockey become fun again.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.slapshotdiaries.com/jiggs-macdonald-the-rookies.html|website=Slap Shot Diaries|access-date=May 30, 2026|title=HOW TIGER SAVED BRYAN, AND OTHER STORIES}}</ref><ref name=\"AQTrottier\">{{cite web|url=https://athletesquarterly.com/athletes/bryan-trottier/|website=athletesquarterly.com|first=Michael|last=Dolan|access-date=May 9, 2026|title=Bryan Trottier {{!}} The Hall of Fame center on leaving home to play hockey, rooming with Jaromir Jagr, and how Tiger Williams saved his career.}}</ref><ref name=\"Letter to My Younger Self\" /> In that season, Trottier recorded 157 total points in 135 games. Playing with the [[Lethbridge Broncos]] in the [[1974–75 WCHL season]]. he had 46 goals and 98 assists in 67 games and was named league MVP.<ref>{{cite web|author=Cory Toth - Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan |url=https://esask.uregina.ca/entry/trottier_bryan_1956-.jsp |title=The Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan &#124; Details |publisher=Esask.uregina.ca |access-date=2021-03-31}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://chl.ca/whl-broncos/bryan-trottier/|website=CHL.ca|title=Bryan Trottier|access-date=May 9, 2026}}</ref>\n\n==Playing career==\n{{BLP sources section|date=April 2021}}\nTrottier was drafted in both of the [[1974 WHA amateur draft]] and the [[1974 NHL entry draft]]. The WHA [[Cincinnati Stingers]] reportedly offered him $50,000 a year for the next ten years, but Trottier elected to go with the Islanders (who selected him in the second round as the 22nd overall pick), although he played in the WCHL one further season before going to training camp in 1975 in preparation of the {{nhly|1975}} season.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://calgaryherald.com/sports/hockey/nhl/scott-cruickshank-hockey-legend-bryan-trottier-remembers-well-his-draft-days|title=Scott Cruickshank: Hockey legend Bryan Trottier remembers well his draft day(s)|first=Scott|last=Cruickshank|website=Calgary Herald|date=June 23, 2016}}</ref> That year, he set an NHL rookie record of 95 points and won the [[Calder Memorial Trophy]] as the NHL's rookie of the year (his record was later broken by [[Peter Šťastný]] of the [[Quebec Nordiques]] in the [[1980–81 NHL season|1980–81]] season).\n\nTrottier's best offensive season was [[1978–79 NHL season|1978–79]] when he scored 134 points, earning him the [[Art Ross Trophy]] as the league's top scorer, as well as the [[Hart Memorial Trophy]] as the most valuable player. In winning the Art Ross, he became the first player from a post-[[Original Six]] expansion team to win the award. In that same season, he led the NHL in assists with 87, which he had also done the year before with 77.\n\nTrottier was one of the core players on the Islanders' [[Dynasty (sports)|dynasty]] teams from the 1980s. He won four Stanley Cups during his time with the Islanders from [[1979–80 NHL season|1980]] to [[1982–83 NHL season|1983]]. During New York's first Stanley Cup in 1980, he won the [[Conn Smythe Trophy]] as playoff MVP. In [[1981–82 NHL season|1981–82]], Trottier scored 50 goals, the highest single-season total of his career.\n\nDuring the early 1980s, when [[Wayne Gretzky]] set numerous scoring marks, Islanders broadcaster [[Stan Fischler]] and head coach [[Al Arbour]] nonetheless maintained that Trottier was the league's best player over Gretzky. Trottier was described as a forward possessing an all-around game including ruggedness and defensive responsibility, and there were comparisons to [[Milt Schmidt]] and [[Gordie Howe]]. Arbour stated, \"Gretzky is an offensive genius for sure. But at this stage Trots gives you more things. Defensively, he's outstanding. And he's physically tough. He comes up with his 100 points a year, automatically, along with everything else!\"<ref name=\"blogspot2006\">[https://nyislanderslegends.blogspot.com/2006/09/bryan-trottier.html nyislanderslegends]</ref>\n\nTrottier was often referred to as the \"glue\" on the Islanders team, leading his fellow stars [[Clark Gillies]] and [[Mike Bossy]] on a line known as \"[[The Trio Grande]].\" While the 1977–78 season was Bossy's rookie year, the Trio Grande at one point led the NHL in scoring above the top lines of the [[Montreal Canadiens]] and the [[Colorado Rockies (NHL)|Colorado Rockies]].<ref>{{cite news| url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1093175/1/index.htm | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121104161143/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1093175/1/index.htm | url-status=dead | archive-date=November 4, 2012 | work=CNN | title=Three Islanders Unto Themselves | date=December 12, 1977}}</ref> Other linemates that played with Trottier included [[John Tonelli]], [[Bob Bourne]] and [[Bob Nystrom]]. Trottier, however, was most known for his dynamic on-ice partnership with Mike Bossy during his prime years with the Islanders until Bossy's early retirement at the end of the 1987 season.\n\nIn the leadup to the [[1984 Canada Cup]], Trottier decided to play for the [[United States men's national ice hockey team|United States]] in the tournament, having previously represented [[Canada men's national ice hockey team|Canada]] in 1981, a decision that earned him boos in exhibition games held in Canada. Trottier stated, \"Nothing against Canada, but I'd like to play for the U.S. and do something for the country that has been good to me.\"<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1984/07/12/New-York-Islanders-center-Bryan-Trottier-appreciates-playing-hockey/6559458452800/|website=UPI|access-date=May 9, 2026|title=New York Islanders' center Bryan Trottier appreciates playing hockey...|date=July 12, 1984|first=Mike|last=Barnes}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://archive.thehockeynews.com/issue/607732/43|website=The Hockey News|title=Trottier’s A Marked Man In The Canada Cup|date=September 14, 1984|access-date=May 9, 2026}}</ref> He was able to obtain the necessary U.S. citizenship in July 1984 because he had [[Métis people (Canada)|Métis]] ancestry on his father's side ([[Cree]]/[[Chippewa]]).<ref name=\"Rogers Media\">{{cite web |last1=Fox |first1=Luke |title=Bryan Trottier is your daddy's Jonathan Toews |url=https://www.sportsnet.ca/hockey/nhl/bryan-trottier-seven-stanley-cup-canada-sports-hall-of-fame-new-york-islanders-pittsburgh-penguins-mike-liut/ |website=sportsnet.ca |publisher=Rogers Media |access-date=June 1, 2022}}</ref> His North American Indian Card (for which he qualified because his grandmother was a Chippewa) entitled him to citizenship in both the U.S. and Canada, as well as a U.S. passport, which was all he needed for tournament eligibility.<ref name=\"Rogers Media\"/>\n\nIn the {{nhly|1988}} season, Trottier had his first season with a negative plus-minus, doing so with a season that saw him drop to 17 goals and 28 assists in 73 games for a -7 rating. He was awarded the [[King Clancy Memorial Trophy]] for his leadership on and off the ice.  In the {{nhly|1989}} season, he played in just 59 games and recorded 13 goals with 11 assists. Trottier scored his [[List of NHL players with 500 goals|500th career goal]], doing so on February 13, 1990 against the [[Calgary Flames]] in his 1,104th game as a player; he was the 15th player to reach 500 goals and the second Islander to do so after Bossy. It was his last goal as an Islander. When the Islanders were eliminated in the [[1990 Stanley Cup playoffs|Stanley Cup playoffs]], Trottier was benched for the final game.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nhl.com/islanders/news/this-day-in-isles-history-feb-13-319831574|website=NHL.com|access-date=May 9, 2026|title=This Day in Isles History: Feb. 13|date=February 12, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://records.nhl.com/records/milestones/500-goal-career|website=NHL Records|title=500th Goals - Milestones {{!}} NHL Records|access-date=May 9, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/players/t/trottbr01/gamelog/1990|website=Hockey Reference|title=Bryan Trottier 1989-90 Game Log|access-date=May 9, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Brian Trottier Stats and News |url=https://www.nhl.com/player/bryan-trottier-8451965 |website=NHL |publisher=National Hockey League |access-date=June 1, 2022}}</ref> After that low output, on July 3, Islanders management bought out the last two years of Trottier's contract, which he remarked was a \"painful\" moment.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1990-10-14-sp-3651-story.html|website=The Los Angeles Times|date=October 14, 1990|title=Bryan Trottier Is Warming to Pittsburgh|first=Pat|last=Calabria}}</ref><ref name=\"NYP\">{{cite web|url=https://nypost.com/2015/01/17/why-trottier-decided-to-bury-the-hatchet-with-the-islanders/|website=New York Post|date=January 17, 2015|title=Why Trottier decided to bury the hatchet with the Islanders|first=Brett|last=Cyrgalis}}</ref> He ranks second in Islanders history in goals, and first in assists and points. It could be noted, however, that even as Trottier's scoring declined, he remained a strong defensive player and team leader.<ref name=\"blogspot2006\"/>\n\nThe [[Pittsburgh Penguins]] signed Trottier as a free agent on July 20, 1990, to provide experience and leadership to a young team, most notably with [[Jaromír Jágr]], who had recently emigrated from [[Czech Republic|Czechoslovakia]]; [[Randy Gilhen]], who wore the number 19 jersey in Pittsburgh the previous season, gifted Trottier the number in training camp.<ref name=\"AQTrottier\"/> Playing in 52 games, he logged nine goals with 19 assists. In the [[1991 Stanley Cup playoffs]] run, he had three goals (two of which proving to be the game-winner) and four assists as the Penguins won the [[1991 Stanley Cup Final|Stanley Cup]] that year for Trottier's fifth Cup as a player.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/players/t/trottbr01/gamelog/1991|title=Bryan Trottier 1990-91 Game Log|website=Hockey Reference|access-date=May 9, 2026}}</ref> He played in 63 games of the following {{nhly|1991}} season and earned a trip to the All-Star Game while scoring 11 goals with 18 assists. In the playoffs, he had four goals with three assists as Pittsburgh repeated in winning the [[1992 Stanley Cup Final|Stanley Cup]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/players/t/trottbr01/gamelog/1992|title=Bryan Trottier 1991-92 Game Log|website=Hockey Reference|access-date=May 9, 2026}}</ref> Trottier took the [[1992–93 NHL season|1992–93]] season off, returning to the Isles in a front-office capacity, but financial troubles, stemming from poor investments, forced Trottier to re-sign as a free agent with the Penguins on June 22, 1993, and return to the ice with the Penguins for the [[1993–94 NHL season|1993–94 season]].<ref name=\"NYP\"/> On the ice, he had just four goals in 41 games before closing out his career with two appearances in the playoffs. He retired after the season, doing so with a point total of 1,425 points that ranked sixth all-time in NHL history.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/stathead/tiny/XrCNv|website=Stathead|access-date=May 9, 2026|title=For combined seasons, up to 1993-94, playing skater, in the regular season, sorted by descending Points.}}</ref>\n\n==Coaching and executive career==\n[[File:Bryan Trottier.jpg|thumb|Trottier in 2008]]\nTrottier served as an assistant coach with the Pittsburgh Penguins from 1993 to 1997. He served as head coach of the [[Portland Pirates]] of the [[American Hockey League]] for the [[1997–98 AHL season|1997–98 season]]; the team went 33–33–12–2 in his only season with the Pirates.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.buffalohockeybeat.com/report-sabres-hire-hall-of-famer-bryan-trottier-as-assistant-coach/|website=Buffalo Hockey Beat|title=Report: Sabres hire Hall of Famer Bryan Trottier as assistant coach|first=Bill|last=Hoppe|date=July 29, 2014}}</ref> In 1998, he was hired by the [[Colorado Avalanche]] to serve on the coaching staff, where he won his seventh career Stanley Cup in [[2001 Stanley Cup Final|2001]]. \n\nPrior to the end of the [[2002 Stanley Cup playoffs]], Trottier stated his desire to leave the Avalanche for a coaching position and had the endorsement of GM [[Pierre Lacroix (ice hockey, born 1948)|Pierre Lacroix]]. Reportedly, when approached by the [[New York Rangers]] (as managed by GM [[Glen Sather]]) with a lengthy questionnaire to potential coaching candidates, Trottier's submission of eighty handwritten pages impressed Sather. On June 6, he was hired by the Rangers to be head coach on a three-year contract.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://nypost.com/2002/06/05/trottier-to-coach-rangers/|title=TROTTIER TO COACH RANGERS|first=Larry|last=Brooks|date=June 5, 2002}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nydailynews.com/2002/06/07/rangers-sure-that-trottier-is-answer/|title=RANGERS SURE THAT TROTTIER IS ANSWER|date=June 7, 2002|first=John|last=Dellapina|website=New York Daily News}}</ref> Trottier ultimately did not fare well as a coach for the Rangers, which went 21–26–6–1 (for a .454 winning percentage) in 54 games that saw criticism for his matchups alongside an inability to get along with star players [[Eric Lindros]] and [[Pavel Bure]]. On the cusp of a three-game losing streak that saw the Rangers outscored by a combined score of 16–5, Trottier was fired on January 29, 2003 by Sather, who served as interim coach for the rest of the season.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://nypost.com/2003/01/30/failure-reached-all-levels/|title=FAILURE REACHED ALL LEVELS|first=Larry|last=Brooks|website=New York Post|date=January 30, 2003}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/coaches/trottbr01c.html |title=Bryan Trottier NHL & WHA Hockey Coaching Record |publisher=Hockey-Reference.com |date=July 17, 1956 |access-date=2014-08-04}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com.au/nhl/news/2003/0129/1500929.html|website=ESPN.com|title=Slumping Rangers fire Trottier after 54 games|agency=Associated Press|date=January 29, 2003|access-date=May 9, 2026}}</ref>\n\nOn June 1, 2006, Trottier returned to the Islanders as the team's executive director of player development.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Grossman |first1=Evan |title=ISLES TURN TO TROTTIER |url=https://nypost.com/2006/06/01/isles-turn-to-trottier/ |access-date=June 3, 2024 |work=[[New York Post]] |date=June 1, 2006}}</ref>\n\nOn July 29, 2014, Trottier was hired as an assistant coach for the [[Buffalo Sabres]]. At the conclusion of the {{nhly|2014}} season, his contract was not renewed by the team.<ref>{{cite web|title=Report: Buffalo Sabres Sign Bryan Trottier as Assistant Coach|url=http://www.sportsmedia101.com/buffalosabres/2014/07/29/report-buffalo-sabres-sign-bryan-trottier-as-assistant-coach/|access-date=July 30, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140808061141/http://www.sportsmedia101.com/buffalosabres/2014/07/29/report-buffalo-sabres-sign-bryan-trottier-as-assistant-coach/|archive-date=August 8, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|date=April 12, 2015|website=SI.com|title=Sabres fire head coach Ted Nolan, three assistants|access-date=May 9, 2026|url=https://www.si.com/nhl/2015/04/12/buffalo-sabres-ted-nolan-fired-assistants}}</ref>\n\n==Legacy==\n[[Steve Yzerman]] considered Trottier his favourite player and wore number 19 in his honour. Trottier himself had chosen the number partly in reference to [[Paul Henderson]], who famously wore 19 during the [[1972 Summit Series]].\n<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.detroitnews.com/story/sports/nhl/red-wings/2023/03/18/yzermans-boyhood-hero-trottier-writes-book-on-leadership-winning-hockey/70018966007/?gnt-cfr=1&gca-cat=p&gca-uir=true&gca-epti=z114846e1147xxv114846d--53--b--53--&gca-ft=218&gca-ds=sophi|website=The Detroit News|access-date=May 9, 2026|title=Yzerman's boyhood hero Trottier writes book on leadership, winning hockey|first=Mark|last=Falkner|date=March 18, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cbc.ca/sports/hockey/nhl/2.7212/bryan-trottier-canadas-sports-hall-of-fame-1.3553613|website=CBC.ca|title=Bryan Trottier joins admirer Steve Yzerman in Canada's Sports Hall of Fame|first=Tim|last=Wharnsby|date=April 26, 2016}}</ref>\n\nTrottier was inducted into the [[Hockey Hall of Fame]] in his first year of eligibility in 1997.<ref>{{cite web |date=2001–2007 |title=Legends of Hockey – Induction Showcase – Mario Lemieux |url=http://www.legendsofhockey.net/html/ind97ees.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080224061224/http://www.legendsofhockey.net/html/ind97ees.htm |archive-date=February 24, 2008 |access-date=2007-11-15 |work=Bryan John Trottier, Player Category, Hockey Hall of Fame and Museum |publisher=The Learning Edge Corporation |df=mdy-all}}</ref> During his induction speech, Trottier spoke about his mother's encouragement of his pride in his Aboriginal identity.<ref name=\":0\" />\n\nLingering bitterness over how his Islanders tenure ended precluded Trottier's number from being honored by the Islanders organization for a few years; it was speculated that Trottier was looking to be compensated to attend a pre-game ceremony, although Trottier denied that claim. A March 2001 meeting with team owner [[Charles Wang]] led to a subsequent announcement in August that Trottier's jersey would be retired.<ref>{{cite web|title=TROTTIER’S 19 TO BE RETIRED|first=Marc|last=Berman|website=New York Post|date=August 7, 2001|url=https://nypost.com/2001/08/07/trottiers-19-to-be-retired/}}</ref> The retirement ceremony was held on October 20, 2001 prior to the game against the [[San Jose Sharks]]; Trottier was the sixth Islander to have his jersey retired.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nhl.com/islanders/news/this-day-in-isles-history-oct-20-319388720|website=NHL.com|access-date=May 9, 2026|date=October 19, 2024|title=This Day in Isles History: Oct. 20}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cbc.ca/sports/hockey/trottier-s-no-19-retired-unceremoniously-1.274182|title=Trottier's No. 19 retired unceremoniously|website=CBC.ca|date=January 17, 2001|access-date=May 9, 2026}}</ref>\n\nAs of 2025, Trottier sits 13th all-time with 182 playoff points (71 goals and 111 assists) in 221 games played.<ref>[https://records.nhl.com/records/playoff-skater-records/points/most-points-career-playoff NHL Playoff Skater Records: Most Points, Playoff Career] – NHL.com</ref> Trottier is currently ranked 19th all-time in NHL regular-season points. He is the Islanders' all-time career leader in assists and points, for the regular season and playoffs. In 2023, the ''[[New York Post]]'' named Trottier as the third best player in team history behind [[Mike Bossy]] and [[Denis Potvin]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://nypost.com/2023/04/12/ranking-best-players-in-islanders-50-year-history-nos-1-20/|website=New York Post|access-date=May 9, 2026|title=Ranking best players in Islanders’ 50-year history: Nos. 1-20|first=Larry|last=Brooks|date=April 12, 2023}}</ref> In 2023, ''[[The Athletic]]'' named him the 23rd greatest player in modern NHL history.<ref name=\"NHL99\">{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/4002696/2023/01/05/nhl99-bryan-trottier/|title=NHL99: Bryan Trottier’s lifelong passion for music is a window into his success|first=Corey|last=Masisak|date=January 5, 2023|website=The Athletic}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/3550299/2023/02/08/nhl99-ranking-the-greatest-players-in-modern-nhl-history/|title=NHL99: A project ranking the greatest players in modern NHL history|access-date=May 9, 2026|date=February 8, 2023|website=The Athletic}}</ref>\n\n[[Canada Post]] unveiled a [[postage stamp]] featuring Trottier on June 17, 2026 as part of a series honoring Canadian [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Indigenous]] leaders and advocates in sports.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-06-17 |title=Trottier cherishes ‘highest honor’ of receiving own Canadian stamp {{!}} NHL.com |url=https://www.nhl.com/news/bryan-trottier-cherishes-highest-honor-of-canadian-stamp |access-date=2026-06-17 |website=www.nhl.com |language=en}}</ref>\n\n==Personal life==\nTrottier has four children from two marriages. One of his sons, Dr. Bryan Trottier Jr, became a hematology/oncologist specialist in [[Minnesota]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nhl.com/news/bryan-trottier-cherishes-memories-after-losing-islanders-teammates-to--337408326|website=NHL.com|first=Jon|last=Lane|date=November 11, 2022|title=Trottier cherishes memories after losing Islanders teammates to cancer}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=About - Bryan Trottier |url=https://www.bryantrottier.com/about |website=bryantrottier.com |publisher=Bryan Trottier |access-date=June 1, 2022}}</ref> In September of 1994, feeling lethargic, Trottier went to the doctor and was diagnosed with clinical depression. He went on a ten-day stay at a facility to deal with issues of self-esteem.<ref name=\"TSN\">{{cite web|url=https://www.tsn.ca/nhl/hockey-hall-of-famer-bryan-trottier-reminisces-on-his-illustrious-life-in-new-memoir-1.1868699|website=TSN.ca|title=Hall of Famer Trottier reminisces on his illustrious life in new memoir|first=Brianne|last=Spiker|date= October 27, 2022}}</ref> Following his retirement from playing, Trottier played for the [[Pittsburgh Phantoms (RHI)|Pittsburgh Phantoms]] of the [[Roller Hockey International]] league in its 1994 season.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.post-gazette.com/sports/penguins/2019/08/20/pittsburgh-phantoms-25-years-later-bryan-trottier-civic-arena-penguins-howard-baldwin/stories/201908190028|website=Pittsburgh Post Gazette|title=25 years later, remembering the summer of the Pittsburgh Phantoms|date=August 20, 2019|first=Matt|last=Vensel}}</ref> After his playing career ended, Trottier returned to his old hobby in music (having played for the family band as a child), which has seen him play the guitar for various NHLPA alumni games alongside festivities for [[Hockey Day in Canada]] and even at the [[Hockey Hall of Fame]].<ref name=\"NHL99\"/> In 2022, Trottier's memoir, ''All Roads Home: A Life On and Off the Ice'' was published.<ref name=\"TSN\"/>\n\nOne of Bryan's grandsons, Parker Trottier, captained the [[United States at the 2024 Winter Youth Olympics|United States]] to the gold medal in the [[Ice hockey at the 2024 Winter Youth Olympics – Men's tournament|men's tournament]] at the [[2024 Winter Youth Olympics]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://olympics.com/en/news/gangwon-2024-usa-reclaim-youth-olympic-games-ice-hockey-gold-czechia-shutout|title=Gangwon 2024: USA reclaim Youth Olympics men's ice hockey gold with 4-0 shutout win over Czechia|last=Goh|first=ZK|website=Olympics|date=January 31, 2024|access-date=January 31, 2024}}</ref>\n\n==Playing statistics==\n\n===Regular season and
